Use parallel/parallel-decisions-fast as the model name. No separate Parallel account is required. These examples ask the same web-grounded question through the AI SDK, TypeSafe-compatible API, and OpenAI-compatible Decisions API.

Citations include source URLs, optional titles, and evidence excerpts. They apply to the whole request, rather than mapping individual sources to each answer. Your application can use answer probabilities to act automatically above a threshold and send uncertain results for review.

AI Gateway tracks these requests in logs and spend budgets alongside other model requests. Read the decision model documentation for question types, or browse the model catalog.

title: Build cache size limit on Vercel increased to 5 GB
description:
The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times.

Build machines are the compute environments that install dependencies and build your project before deployment. Previously, caches were discarded if they exceeded 1.5 GB on Basic and Standard, 3 GB on Enhanced, or 4.75 GB on Turbo, leaving the next build without a cache.

The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required.

Learn more in the build cache documentation.

title: Vercel Sandbox starts up to 4x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (iad1) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in iad1 on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
description:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Product

What a failed attempt costs the user

Metric to lead with

Order my morning coffee

Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust

Pass^k

Pass@k

Draft an email the user reviews

A quick edit before hitting send

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
description:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

Call the model using its private/<slug> ID:

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

title: Introducing Vercel Board
description:
Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects.

A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents.

We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects:

  • Our security agents: We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we track of their work via Board.

  • v0's software factory: After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs.

Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more.

Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows.

We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness.

How it works

Board is a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments. Your agents read from and write to Board through the CLI or JavaScript SDK. Install the Board skill to give your agent instructions for using it:

Each board is organized into channels and threads. A thread keeps the conversation, context, and updates together, while labels track details such as the associated pull request or current status. Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result. For example, a coding agent can use the CLI to find an open bug, claim it, and share a pull request for review:

The thread keeps the original report, findings, and pull request so another agent or person can review the work. Run npx @vercel/board inspect to open the Board viewer and follow activity across channels and threads in real time.

Wake agents and schedule follow-ups

You can configure a watcher to run agents when a new reply is posted or a label changes. For example, if there is a reply in Slack or by another agent, it can trigger the agent to address their feedback and post an update or pull request in the same thread. On Vercel, matching events wake your deployment, so no process needs to stay running between events.

Agents can also schedule follow-ups with vercel board schedule. For example, after an agent has opened a pull request it can remind itself to check CI in 5 minutes. This makes agents feel much more proactive, as they can check things without requiring a new message from a human. For a pull request tracked in Board thread 812, the agent would run:

Note that agents can keep internal notes and check-ins on Board with --no-sync, while sharing progress updates through connected tools.

Sync with existing tools

A task can be pushed directly to Board or synced from a connected tool like Slack or GitHub. The Board SDK handles two-way sync, mirroring replies, reactions, edits, and deletions between Board and your connected tools:

Share structured data

Messages in Board can also include structured data based on a schema you define. Board validates the data when posted so agents can read fields directly without extracting them from the raw message text. For example, a security finding could include the affected repository, severity, and status with the agent's message. Here is an example schema, security-finding@1 (where @1 is the version):

Control access to your board

A core part of why we built vercel board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability. Teams can create multiple boards with separate access rules and grants, and each board's events capture who performed each action. This is how you can use the CLI to set it up:

When working with Vercel Sandbox, use the SDK to give it board access with no credential inside the sandbox, limited to the channels and permissions you choose:

Use cases

We use Board to connect agents with our teams' existing workflows and coordinate across multiple agents. Here are the patterns we've implemented.

Coordinate work between people and agents

Your team may already be working in Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc. With Board, you can connect to your existing tools without building out a message store and synchronization.

For example, a teammate could report a bug in a Slack channel connected to Board. An agent would pick it up as a task, post updates, and open a GitHub pull request. Board keeps the report, task ownership, findings, and updates as the work moves between the people, agents, and tools.

We use this pattern for our internal software factory. Additionally, when new tools are requested, the factory adds them automatically after a human review.

Explore the Factory template →

Help agents work together

You can give agents running on different machines or in different harnesses a shared backlog, for example a set of security tickets or bugs to investigate. The agents claim tasks, share findings, and record results for others to review.

Board also supports dependencies between tasks. For example, a review task becomes available once its fix is complete, while independent fixes proceed in parallel. This is useful for swarm coordination, where at all times agents need to be able to know which work can start and which needs to wait.

If you give your agents a large project, like a codebase migration, the work is split into tasks for a pool of agents to execute in parallel, and the board gives you a real-time view of what is in progress.

title: Run Mobilerun with local and cheap models Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenRouter
description:
Every step a phone agent takes is a model call. Read the screen, pick one action, tap, repeat. A simple task can be 10 of those. A test suite can be thousands.

So the first question people ask after getting Mobilerun working is always the same: can I run this on something cheaper? Or on my own machine, with no API key at all?

Yes. The open-source Mobilerun framework doesn't care where the model lives. This post shows what runs where, the exact local setup with Ollama and Qwen, the hosted setup for DeepSeek and OpenRouter, and what actually changes your results.

The problem with "which model is best?"

You'll find plenty of opinions about which model is best for phone agents. You won't find a published Mobilerun benchmark broken out by Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen and OpenRouter. We haven't published one yet either.

That matters, because the answer depends on things only you know: your tasks, your device, your hardware, and whether you run with vision. So instead of a ranking, we'll give you the setup for each option and a simple way to measure them on your own work.

What runs where

The Mobilerun framework runs on your machine. It controls an Android device through Portal and ADB. The LLM provider is a separate choice you make in config or on the command line.

Here's how the options split:

  • Ollama runs inference locally. No model API key.
  • DeepSeek is a hosted API. It uses DEEPSEEK_API_KEY.
  • OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to many models. It uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
  • Qwen is a model family, not a provider. You can run Qwen locally through Ollama, and Qwen models are also available through hosted providers like OpenRouter.

Install and run it locally with Ollama and Qwen

You need Python 3.11 to 3.13. Python 3.14 isn't supported yet, and the docs warn that installing on 3.14 silently falls back to an old version. You also need ADB and an Android device with USB debugging on.

Install the framework:

Install Ollama, connect your Android device, then set up Portal and check the connection.

mobilerun setupmobilerun pingCopy

If ping prints "Portal is installed and accessible. You're good to go!", you're ready. Pull the model and run a task:

ollama pull qwen3:8bmobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider Ollama --model qwen3:8b --base_url http://localhost:11434Copy

That's the whole loop running on your hardware. The framework talks to Ollama at localhost:11434, and no request leaves your machine for inference.

Pass --provider and --model together. The CLI guide is clear that passing only one makes the run fail before the agent starts.

To make Ollama the default instead of typing flags every time, add a profile to your config file. Mobilerun creates it at ~/.config/droidrun/config.yaml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/droidrun/config.yaml on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\droidrun\droidrun\config.yaml on Windows. Yes, the folder still says droidrun. You can also point MOBILERUN_CONFIG or --config at your own file.

One Ollama detail worth knowing: Mobilerun sets the context size itself. The default context_window is 32,768, which keeps most models on the GPU. Setting it to -1 asks for the model's full context, which preallocates the whole KV cache and can spill onto your CPU.

DeepSeek and OpenRouter: hosted, pay per call

For the hosted options, set the key and pick the provider and model with CLI flags.

DeepSeek:

export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider DeepSeek --model deepseek-flashCopy

OpenRouter, here with a hosted Qwen model:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider OpenRouter --model qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

Or save them as profiles so every run uses them:

llm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: DeepSeek    model: deepseek-flashllm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: OpenRouter    model: qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

A note on mobilerun configure. The wizard's provider list today is gemini, openai, anthropic, xai, ollama, openai_like, minimax and zai. DeepSeek and OpenRouter aren't in it as named options, so use the CLI flags or the YAML profile for those. Model IDs change often on both services, so check DeepSeek's and OpenRouter's model lists before you copy ours.

What affects your results

Swapping the model is one line. Whether the task finishes is a different story. These are the four things that change the outcome.

Accessibility tree by default. Out of the box, the agent reads Android's accessibility tree, a structured list of what's on screen with text and bounds. No screenshots. That works with text-only models, including qwen3:8b.

--vision adds screenshots. With vision on, the agent gets a screenshot alongside the tree on every step. That needs a vision-capable model. If you test vision on a local model, pull one that accepts images. For local vision models that downsize images in a way Mobilerun can't detect, the docs suggest capping the screenshot so tap coordinates stay accurate:

agent:  model_screenshot_max_side: 1280Copy

There's also --vision-only, which drops the tree and drives the device from screenshots alone.

Native tool calling vs the fallback protocol. Mobilerun uses native tool calling where the model supports it. For other models, it falls back to a text protocol where the model writes tool calls as XML and the framework parses them. In v0.7.4 the native path covers providers like DeepSeek, OpenAI and xAI. Ollama and OpenRouter go through the fallback. If a model writes broken tool-call markup three times in a row, the run stops, and smaller models hit this more often.

Your hardware. With Ollama, speed is your GPU, your RAM and the model size. The same model can feel quick on one laptop and painful on another.

Success and speed will vary with the model, the task, the device and the hardware. That's why the next section exists.

Some tips to keep the numbers honest:

  • Run mobilerun --version and record it. Results change between releases.
  • Keep --steps the same across runs. The default is 15, and complex tasks may need more.
  • Turn on --tracing to see tokens per step, or use --debug and --save-trajectory action to see where a run went wrong.
  • Count completed tasks, not tokens. A cheap model that fails half the time isn't cheap.

On cost: Ollama removes per-call model API fees, but local hardware still has a cost. The GPU, the power and the machine that's busy while it runs all count. Hosted APIs flip that. No hardware to own, but you pay for every call.

Honest limits

  • There are no published per-provider Mobilerun benchmarks yet. Anyone giving you a confident ranking is guessing.
  • Small local models are more likely to drift from the tool-call format, especially on busy screens.
  • qwen3:8b is a text model. Keep --vision off with it, or switch to a vision-capable model.
  • The framework is the open-source, bring-your-own-device path. You manage the phone, ADB, Portal and the model.

Don't want to manage a device?

If you'd rather skip the phone and the ADB setup, Mobilerun Cloud gives you hosted devices and a managed agent behind an API. You send a task, it runs on a phone in the cloud. If you want to keep your own model and your own device, the open-source framework will always let you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I run Mobilerun with no API key at all? Is Qwen a provider?

Which model is the cheapest per task? Can I use DeepSeek or OpenRouter from mobilerun configure? 

The takeaway

The model is your choice, and the right one is the one that finishes your tasks on your hardware. Measure it, don't guess it. If you'd rather not manage a device at all, start at cloud.mobilerun.ai.

Docs: Quickstart · CLI and providers · Ollama profiles · Vision mode

Also Read:

  • Running an AI Agent on Your Android Device
  • How to Turn Old Android Phones into AI Agents (Complete Guide)
  • How to connect your mobile device to Mobilerun cloud

title: One post, five networks: what actually changes
description:
When people hear "a native post for every network", they picture five completely different posts. We build a scheduler that writes those versions, and that's mostly not what happens.

Here's one real example from our demo workspace. Kolo is a made-up coffee roaster. The note said: a new coffee is in (Ethiopia Guji, natural process), bags are in the shop from Friday, and there's a cupping at the roastery on Saturday at 10.

What changed

  • Bluesky (212 of 300 characters): one idea, two hashtags.
  • Mastodon (233 of 500): nearly the same text, three hashtags.
  • Discord (212 of 2,000): no hashtags, split into two short paragraphs, and a little more conversational.
  • Telegram (195 of 4,096): no hashtags, one line per thought.
  • Pinterest (146 of 800): a different post. No date and no event, just what the coffee is and how to brew it.

Why it's mostly small stuff

The facts don't change between networks, so the words mostly shouldn't either. What changes is the packaging: length, hashtags, line breaks and tone.

Pinterest is the exception. A post on Bluesky is old by tomorrow, but a Pin keeps getting found in search for months, so "Saturday at 10" would be wrong most of the time someone sees it.

The part that's easy to forget

Nobody forgets the character limit. People forget the small rules: no hashtags on Discord, short lines on Telegram, no dates on a Pin. That's what makes a cross-post look pasted.

In Refract those live as rules for each network, and when you keep making the same edit, it suggests a new rule instead of making you fix it again. It never adds one without asking.

How do you handle it: do you write a version per network, or post the same text everywhere?

title: Anthropic Sets IPO Price at $83 as AI Market Faces Its First Public Test
description:
Quick take

  • Anthropic said the SEC declared its registration statement effective on Nov. 18.
  • The $83 offering price does not establish Anthropic’s total equity value, which depends on shares outstanding, shares offered and other securities.
  • SOC Investment Group criticized Anthropic’s IPO disclosures as opaque or potentially misleading, raising concerns about valuation, credit profile and risk disclosures.
  • Capital.com analyst Kyle Rodda called the IPO a barometer of investor bullishness toward AI companies and appetite for AI monetization.

Why it matters

For public investors, the listing changes Anthropic from a private AI developer into a company whose finances, growth, costs and governance can be examined through ongoing market reporting. The next signal is trading performance and investor demand, which will indicate whether markets accept its path from costly model development to durable commercial returns.

Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, setting up a Nasdaq debut that will test how public investors value a high-profile AI company facing substantial execution and disclosure scrutiny.

A public-market test for Anthropic

“However, successful IPO pricing does not guarantee that shares will rise once trading begins.”

- Dilin Wu, SWI swissinfo.ch

Anthropic said in its IPO announcement that it priced its Class A common stock offering at $83 per share and expects trading to begin on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT. The company also said the Securities and Exchange Commission declared its registration statement effective on Nov. 18.

The $83 figure is the offering price for shares sold in the IPO. It does not, by itself, establish Anthropic’s total equity value. That calculation depends on the number of shares outstanding, the number offered to investors and any other securities that could affect the company’s share count.

The market will provide a more meaningful valuation signal once trading begins. The opening price, the scale of investor demand and the stock’s performance after the first session will show whether buyers view Anthropic primarily as a fast-growing software company, an infrastructure-heavy AI laboratory or a strategically important but still unproven technology business.

That distinction matters. Anthropic’s listing will give public investors direct exposure to one of the companies developing advanced AI models, while also requiring the company to operate under the greater transparency of public markets. Investors will be able to assess its financial disclosures, commercial growth and ability to translate model development into durable returns.

The IPO therefore represents more than a financing event. It is a market test of whether an AI company can persuade investors that the costs of developing and deploying increasingly capable models can eventually support attractive margins and sustained competitive advantage.

The strategic question behind the price

Anthropic’s central challenge is to turn technical capability into a business that can withstand public scrutiny. A private company can often emphasize long-term model development, strategic partnerships and future opportunity. A listed company must also show how those investments support revenue, customer retention and operating leverage.

The registration materials outline the proposed Class A common-stock offering and Anthropic’s application to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under ANT, according to Anthropic’s Form S-1 filing with the SEC. The filing is the foundation for the company’s public-market reporting obligations and gives investors a formal framework for evaluating the offering.

The competitive issue is equally important. Anthropic is entering public markets while competing for customers, computing capacity, talent and capital against other major AI developers. Its long-term value will depend not only on the quality of its models, but on whether it can build a defensible position in enterprise software, application programming interfaces and other commercial channels.

A strong debut could improve Anthropic’s access to capital and strengthen its ability to invest in infrastructure and product development. It could also make the company’s equity more useful when recruiting employees or pursuing strategic transactions. A weak debut would not necessarily undermine the business, but it could raise the cost of future financing and increase pressure to demonstrate near-term commercial progress.

The $83 price should therefore be viewed as a starting point rather than a final judgment. Public investors will quickly begin testing whether the company’s growth prospects justify the risks associated with its business model.

Critics question the company’s disclosures

The most pointed challenge comes from outside the company. In a prospective investor letter, SOC Investment Group criticized Anthropic’s IPO disclosures, arguing that they are opaque or potentially misleading.

The group said Anthropic’s valuation, credit profile and risk disclosures should give investors pause. Its argument goes beyond questioning whether the $83 price is high or low. It challenges whether investors have enough clarity to judge the company’s financial condition and the risks attached to its strategy.

That criticism goes to the heart of the IPO. AI companies can present unusually difficult valuation questions because their prospects depend on rapidly changing technology, uncertain pricing models and large investments in computing resources. If disclosures do not make those risks sufficiently clear, investors may struggle to distinguish a company with a durable commercial advantage from one benefiting mainly from enthusiasm around AI.

SOC Investment Group’s position is an opinion from a critical investor group, not a finding by the SEC that Anthropic’s registration statement is defective. The SEC’s declaration that the statement is effective clears a regulatory step, but it does not guarantee the company’s future performance or validate every investment judgment implied by the offering price.

Still, the criticism gives public investors a framework for the questions they are likely to ask. They will want to understand how Anthropic measures demand, how much it must spend to support model usage, how dependent it is on external infrastructure and whether its commercial relationships can produce sufficient returns over time.

Investor appetite will be the immediate signal

Market participants are already treating the offering as a broader test of sentiment toward AI companies. Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said the IPO will serve as a barometer of investor bullishness toward AI companies and public-market appetite for AI monetization, according to Swissinfo’s report on market reaction to Anthropic’s IPO pricing.

That view places Anthropic’s debut in a wider competitive and investment cycle. Investors are not simply evaluating one company. They are also assessing whether the market can continue assigning substantial value to businesses that are building the infrastructure and applications behind generative AI.

A strong reception would give Anthropic an important strategic advantage. It could validate the company’s positioning, improve its financing flexibility and create a public share price that supports future hiring and expansion. It could also encourage other AI companies to pursue listings, giving public markets more ways to compare business models across the sector.

A cautious response would send a different message. Investors may be willing to fund AI growth, but only when companies provide clear evidence of monetization, cost control and governance. Anthropic’s debut will show whether its public-market story is strong enough to overcome those concerns.

The immediate headline is $83 a share. The more important outcome will be whether investors believe Anthropic can convert advanced AI development into a durable, transparent and economically attractive enterprise.
