title: Eval-Driven Development: How to Test AI Features Beyond Traditional Unit Tests
description:
Traditional software testing generally starts with an expected input and a known output.

For example, a function receives two numbers and returns their sum. A unit test can verify the result against an exact expected value.

But what happens when an application uses a large language model to generate a response, summarize a document, recommend an action, or operate an AI agent?

The output may vary even when the input remains the same.

This creates a new testing challenge for software developers: how do you determine whether an AI-powered feature is working correctly when its output is not always identical?

This is where eval-driven development becomes useful.

What Is Eval-Driven Development?

Eval-driven development is an approach in which AI application quality is measured against predefined evaluation criteria throughout development.

Instead of relying only on manual testing or checking whether an AI response looks reasonable, developers create repeatable evaluations for important behaviors.

These evaluations can measure:

Answer accuracy.

Relevance to the user request.

Consistency across repeated runs.

Compliance with application instructions.

Safety and policy adherence.

Correct tool usage.

Structured output validity.

Response latency and cost.

The objective is to make AI application quality measurable rather than relying entirely on subjective judgment.

Why Traditional Unit Tests Are Not Enough

Consider a customer-support application that uses an LLM to answer questions from a product knowledge base.

A traditional test can verify that:

The API endpoint responds successfully.

The request contains valid parameters.

The database connection works.

The response follows the expected JSON structure.

However, these checks cannot fully establish whether the AI provided the correct answer.

The application may return a successful HTTP response while generating incorrect information.

This means AI-powered applications need both traditional software tests and evaluations designed around model behavior.

Five Types of Evaluations Developers Should Consider

  1. Accuracy and Relevance Evaluation

The first step is determining whether the response actually answers the user's question.

For a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application, developers can evaluate whether the response is supported by the retrieved documents.

Useful checks include:

Does the answer address the original question?

Is the information supported by the available context?

Does the response introduce unsupported claims?

Does it omit important details?

A curated dataset of representative questions and expected behavior can provide a repeatable starting point.

  1. Structured Output Validation

Many applications expect AI systems to return structured data.

For example, an AI assistant might extract:

Customer name.

Task description.

Deadline.

Priority.

Assigned owner.

Developers should validate the output against a schema.

JSON parsing, required-field checks, type validation, and allowed-value checks can prevent malformed responses from entering downstream workflows.

  1. Tool-Calling Evaluation

AI agents often interact with external tools and APIs.

A task-management agent, for example, might create a task, update its priority, or retrieve project information.

Evaluation should verify whether the agent:

Selected the correct tool.

Passed the correct parameters.

Respected permission boundaries.

Avoided unnecessary actions.

Requested human approval when required.

Testing the final response alone is not enough. The actions taken by the agent also need to be evaluated.

  1. Safety and Security Evaluation

AI applications may process sensitive business information or interact with important systems.

Developers should test how applications handle:

Prompt injection attempts.

Unauthorized data requests.

Sensitive information exposure.

Unsafe tool calls.

Attempts to bypass system instructions.

Incorrect permission assumptions.

Security evaluations should be repeated as prompts, models, tools, and application workflows change.

  1. Performance and Cost Evaluation

An AI feature can be accurate but still unsuitable for production if it is too slow or expensive.

Teams should monitor:

Average and percentile response latency.

Token consumption.

Model and infrastructure costs.

Retry frequency.

Tool-call failures.

Rate-limit errors.

These measurements help teams understand the operational trade-offs of different models and architectures.

Building a Simple Evaluation Pipeline

A practical evaluation workflow can follow these steps:

Step 1: Define the expected behavior.

Write down what a successful AI response or action should accomplish.

Step 2: Create a test dataset.

Include normal requests, ambiguous inputs, edge cases, and potentially harmful requests.

Step 3: Run the AI application.

Execute the same evaluation dataset against the application and collect outputs, tool calls, and execution traces.

Step 4: Score the results.

Use deterministic checks where possible and model-assisted or human evaluation where subjective judgment is required.

Step 5: Compare versions.

Run evaluations whenever the prompt, model, retrieval strategy, tools, or application code changes.

Step 6: Monitor production behavior.

A test dataset cannot represent every real-world interaction. Production monitoring and user feedback should help identify new failure patterns.

Example: Evaluating an AI Task Management Agent

Imagine an AI assistant that converts project conversations into actionable tasks.

A user sends:

"Please assign the payment integration review to Alex by Friday and mark it as high priority."

A reliable evaluation should check whether the agent:

Identifies the task as a payment integration review.

Extracts Alex as the owner.

Recognizes Friday as the deadline using the correct date context.

Sets the priority to high.

Produces the expected structured output.

Requests approval before creating the task if the workflow requires it.

This example shows why agent evaluation needs to examine both language understanding and real actions.

A response that sounds correct is not necessarily an action that was executed correctly.

How AI Engineering Platforms Can Support This Approach

Building reliable AI products requires more than connecting a model to an application.

Teams need structured requirements, implementation workflows, verification processes, and clear controls over how AI-generated changes are accepted.

GeekyAnts explores this broader approach through its AI-powered product engineering practice, which focuses on integrating AI into the engineering and product development lifecycle.

Learn more: https://geekyants.com/en-us/ai-powered-product-engineering

For agentic development workflows, AntFlow AI also brings together structured specifications, AI-assisted implementation, and independent verification.

Explore: https://geekyants.com/antflow-ai

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Evaluating only a handful of ideal prompts.

Treating an LLM's self-assessment as definitive proof of correctness.

Ignoring tool calls and downstream actions.

Measuring accuracy without considering latency and cost.

Failing to rerun evaluations after model or prompt changes.

Relying only on offline tests without production monitoring.

Evaluation should be part of the development lifecycle, not a final checklist before release.

Final Thoughts

AI applications introduce a different kind of engineering challenge.

Traditional tests remain essential for APIs, databases, business logic, and application behavior. But they do not fully measure the quality of probabilistic model outputs or autonomous agent actions.

Eval-driven development fills this gap by making AI behavior measurable, repeatable, and easier to improve.

As AI agents become part of everyday software products, the teams that build strong evaluation systems will have a clearer understanding of what works, what fails, and what is safe to deploy.

In AI engineering, generating an answer is easy. Proving that the answer and the actions behind it are reliable is the real work.

title: How zkDatabase Works: From Data Sampling to Verifiable Query Results
description:
TL;DR: zkDatabase works by turning database operations into provable steps: data sampling, processing, storage commitments, lookup proofs, transformation proofs, and verifiable query results. The goal is to let an external verifier check that a data operation was correct without relying only on the database operator or exposing sensitive records.

Smart contracts and auditors increasingly rely on off-chain data for reserves, asset state, eligibility, and collateral; zkDatabase exists to make that reliance verifiable. It applies Zero-Knowledge Proofs so a data condition can be checked without exposing the raw data behind it.

Key Takeaways

  • zkDatabase works by proving database operations across a Verifiable Data Pipeline.
  • The core workflow includes data sampling, processing, immutable storage, lookup proving, and transformation proving.
  • Verifiable query results matter because institutions need to know whether a returned value came from a committed data state.
  • Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow verification without exposing the full dataset.
  • zkDatabase is best understood as a proof layer for institutional data workflows, not as a generic blockchain database.

How does zkDatabase work at a high level?

zkDatabase works by generating cryptographic proofs for database operations over committed data. A verifier checks the proof to confirm that the operation satisfied defined rules, rather than trusting a database export or operator statement.

The high-level pipeline is:

  1. Data is sampled from a source.
  2. Raw data is processed into a structured format.
  3. The data is committed into storage using cryptographic commitments.
  4. A lookup or query is executed against the committed state.
  5. A proof is generated for the query or transformation.
  6. A verifier checks the proof on-chain or in another verification environment.

This structure is why Orochi Network describes zkDatabase as part of Verifiable Data Infrastructure. The database is not only a place to store records. It is a system for producing evidence about records.

For a business-facing overview, see the companion article on zkDatabase as a provable database for institutions.

What is verifiable data sampling in zkDatabase?

Verifiable data sampling is the process of proving that data was collected from an approved source according to a defined method. It addresses the first trust point in the pipeline: where did the data come from, and was the sample authentic?

In institutional workflows, sampling can involve APIs, internal databases, custody systems, user inputs, application data, IoT devices, or third-party data sources. The key issue is not simply connecting to those sources. It is creating evidence that the sampled data is the data the workflow claims to use.

Without this step, a later proof can become misleading. A system may prove that a calculation was performed correctly over the wrong input. Verifiable sampling helps reduce that risk by tying the downstream proof to a more defensible input state.

This is important for stablecoin reserves, RWA collateral, fund NAV, and compliance-state checks. The verifier needs confidence not just in the final answer, but in the path from source data to answer.

What happens during verifiable processing and storage?

Verifiable processing turns sampled data into structured data while preserving proof continuity. Storage then commits that structured data into a tamper-evident state that future lookups and transformations can reference.

Processing matters because raw institutional data is often messy. Reserve records, custodian statements, asset metadata, eligibility fields, and chain events may have different formats. A proof system needs a defined structure before it can prove anything useful.

zkDatabase uses schemas and provable data types so records can be serialized, hashed, and included in cryptographic commitments. The storage layer can then anchor the state in a form that later operations can reference.

The result is a committed database state. A verifier does not need to inspect the whole database to verify every later query. The verifier can check whether a query result or state transition is linked to that committed state.

For more detail on proof architecture, see Orochi's Groth16 and zkDatabase architecture.

How do lookup proofs create verifiable query results?

Lookup proofs create verifiable query results by proving that a returned document exists in the committed database state and that the lookup operation was performed correctly. The verifier checks the proof instead of trusting a query response.

This is the heart of a provable database. That shift is why oracles, databases, and attestations aren't enough on their own for institutional data. In zkDatabase, a query result can be accompanied by proof that the result corresponds to a committed state.

For example, a stablecoin workflow might ask whether reserve data satisfies a threshold. A tokenized fund workflow might ask whether a NAV input was part of the approved dataset. A compliance workflow might ask whether an address belonged to an approved set at a timestamp.

In each case, the value of the lookup proof is the same: it connects the answer to the committed data state. The verifier can check the relationship without receiving the entire dataset.

What are transformation proofs in zkDatabase?

Transformation proofs verify that updates, inserts, deletes, or schema transformations follow approved rules. They help prove that the database state changed correctly, not just that a current record exists.

This matters because institutional data is not static. Reserves move. Collateral values update. Investors onboard and offboard. Compliance statuses change. Loans hit covenant checkpoints. A database that can prove only a static snapshot is less useful than one that can prove how the state changed over time.

Transformation proofs help create a chain of evidence across the data lifecycle. A verifier can reason about the state transition instead of relying only on a final report.

Operation What needs proof Institutional example
Insert New record was added correctly New custodian balance record
Update Existing record changed under approved rules Reserve composition update
Delete Record removal followed policy Expired eligibility credential
Transform Data format or schema changed correctly Raw custody file converted into reporting schema

This is where zkDatabase becomes more than a query tool. It can support a verifiable audit trail for data operations.

Why do verifiable query results matter for institutions?

Verifiable query results matter because institutional on-chain workflows often depend on private off-chain facts. If the query result is wrong, stale, or manipulated, the smart contract or reporting workflow can still execute as designed while relying on bad data.

The most important institutional use cases share a pattern:

  • Stablecoin issuers need reserve and redemption data to match token liabilities.
  • RWA platforms need ownership, collateral, and valuation state to match token claims.
  • Institutional DeFi protocols need collateral and eligibility data before execution.
  • Compliance teams need proof that a required condition was checked.

In all of these cases, the institution does not necessarily want to publish the full dataset. It wants to prove a specific condition about the dataset. Verifiable query results make that possible.

This is also why zkDatabase should be framed carefully. It proves properties of data operations. It does not guarantee that the institution's source data, legal structure, or governance model is sufficient. Those remain separate controls.

Where does zkDatabase fit after the query proof is generated?

After a query proof is generated, zkDatabase can make the result usable for smart contracts, auditors, counterparties, or internal risk systems. The verifier checks the proof and decides whether to rely on the result.

For an on-chain workflow, a supported verifier contract can check the proof before a transaction uses the data. For an audit workflow, the proof can become part of an evidence package. For a compliance workflow, the proof can show that a condition was checked without moving raw data into every downstream system.

This is the practical value of Verifiable Data. The proof turns a database answer into something that can be independently verified.

For an applied RWA view, see How zkDatabase can be applied to Real-World Assets.

What should technical teams take away from how zkDatabase works?

Conclusion: zkDatabase works by proving the data path from sampling to verifiable query results. It samples data, structures it, commits it, proves lookups, proves transformations, and lets verifiers check the resulting evidence.

For institutions, that means off-chain data can become a more reliable input to on-chain finance, reporting, and audit workflows. Orochi Network's role is to provide the Verifiable Data Infrastructure that helps turn sensitive database operations into proof-backed evidence.

View Technical Docs

Review how zkDatabase maps data sampling, storage commitments, lookup proofs, and transformation proofs into verifiable workflows.

FAQ: What should technical readers ask next?

How does zkDatabase work?

zkDatabase works by generating proofs for database operations over committed data states. It uses a Verifiable Data Pipeline that includes data sampling, processing, storage commitments, lookup proofs, and transformation proofs. A verifier can check whether a result is tied to the committed data state without seeing the entire dataset.

What are verifiable query results?

Verifiable query results are query outputs accompanied by cryptographic evidence that the result came from a committed database state and followed the expected lookup logic. They are useful when a smart contract, auditor, or counterparty needs to rely on a database answer without trusting only the database operator.

Does zkDatabase put all data on-chain?

zkDatabase does not require all raw data to be placed on-chain. The sensitive data can remain off-chain, while commitments and proofs allow verification of specific conditions or operations. This is important for institutions that need assurance without exposing customer data, reserve details, or proprietary records.

Why does zkDatabase use Zero-Knowledge Proofs?

zkDatabase uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs because institutions often need to prove statements about sensitive data without revealing the data itself. The proof can show that a condition was satisfied, such as membership, threshold coverage, or query correctness, while the underlying records remain private under the institution's access controls.

Originally published on the Orochi Network blog.

title: Go 1.28 will flag the error your rows.Next() loop forgets
description:
A for rows.Next() loop that stops early looks like a shorter result. Without rows.Err(), your service returns a truncated list with a 200. Go 1.28 adds a vet analyzer for that mistake. I ran it on a dozen of my Go services. It found nothing, and that is exactly the problem.

TL;DR: the Go 1.28 release notes, still a draft, announce two vet analyzers: scannererr for bufio.Scanner and sqlrowserr for database/sql. Both already exist in golang.org/x/tools. On a dozen of my Go services, sqlrowserr reported zero cases. Not because the code is clean: because it reads Postgres through pgx, and the analyzer only looks at database/sql. A manual grep found four rows.Next() without rows.Err(), one of them in production.

Source status: snapshot as of November 3, 2026. The Go 1.28 notes are a draft. The analyzers may change before the release expected in February 2027.

This article is for Go developers who read SQL results or streams line by line.

A loop that stops early looks like a shorter result

Here is the database/sql contract. rows.Next() returns true when a row is ready. It returns false when there are no more rows. It also returns false when an error happens during the read.

The documentation says it word for word: "Rows.Err should be consulted to distinguish between the two cases." Without that call, the two cases blur. A connection cut after row 40 of a 200-row result gives a list of 40 items. And err is nil.

Your HTTP handler then returns a 200 with 40 rows. The client sees nothing wrong. Neither do your tests, because they run against a local database that never drops. It is the same family of failure as the green test suite on a broken product: success and failure look alike. Go has others, such as January 31 plus one month giving March 3, with no error.

The damage depends on the loop. A truncated list in a web page is a quiet bug. A partial sum in a billing calculation is lost money. An incomplete security export is a hole in your audit. In my MFA article, the export handler calls rows.Err() for that reason.

bufio.Scanner has the same flaw. sc.Scan() returns false at the end of the file, and also on a read error. A line too long for the buffer stops the loop without a sound. Only sc.Err() tells the difference.

Go 1.28 adds two vet analyzers for this mistake

go vet is the static analyzer that ships with Go. The Go 1.28 release notes add two analyzers to it. I quote the draft as is:

The new scannererr analyzer checks for failure to handle scanner errors after a loop around bufio.Scanner.Scan, which may cause scanning or I/O errors to go unreported. The sqlrowserr analyzer performs a similar check for loops around sql.Rows.Next, so that iteration errors are correctly distinguished from a smaller result.

The page is labeled "DRAFT RELEASE NOTES". It states: "Go 1.28 is expected to be released in February 2027." Nothing is final. An analyzer can still change its name, its rule, or disappear.

I read the code of both analyzers in golang.org/x/tools. The sqlrowserr rule is simple. It looks for a call to Query or QueryContext on a sql.DB, sql.Conn, sql.Tx or sql.Stmt. The result must land in a local variable. That variable must be used in a loop that calls Next. If Err is never called on it, the analyzer reports.

It stays silent as soon as the variable leaves the function: passed as an argument, returned, stored in a field. The package documentation owns that choice: the goal is to catch the simple oversight, not to guarantee all error handling. To silence a deliberate case, _ = rows.Err() is enough.

scannererr follows the same logic for bufio.NewScanner. It ignores scanners built on a strings.Reader or a bytes.Buffer, because an in-memory read does not fail.

My lab: a dozen Go services, zero reports

One of my projects has a dozen Go services. They declare go 1.25.0 and all read Postgres through pgx, mostly through code generated by sqlc. I compiled the two analyzers into a small binary, then ran go vet -vettool on each module.

Result: zero reports, across the twelve modules, for both analyzers. One test package in one module did not compile, because a fake gRPC client was one method behind. The analyzer skipped it. Everything else was analyzed.

I would have liked to write that my code is clean. The real reason is elsewhere. None of these modules imports database/sql. The pgx.Rows type is a pgx interface, not the standard library's *sql.Rows. And the analyzer only looks at seven methods, all in database/sql.

To be sure, I wrote the same loop twice in a test module. One version with db.QueryContext from database/sql, one with pool.Query from pgx. Neither calls rows.Err(). The analyzer reports the first one:

std.go:10:15: sql.Rows "rows" is used in Next loop at line 16 without final check of rows.Err()

It says nothing about the second. So zero reports on my services means zero coverage, not zero bugs. The project's only bufio.NewScanner, in a test, does call scanner.Err(). There, the silence is deserved.

Zero reports means zero coverage, not zero bugs. The analyzer only looks at database/sql. My services read Postgres through pgx, and the grep finds four gaps there.

What the analyzer cannot see, I looked for by hand

I counted with grep. The twelve modules contain 118 calls to rows.Next() and 114 to rows.Err(). The code generated by sqlc always calls rows.Err() after the loop. The four gaps are in hand-written code.

Two are in integration tests, one of them reading a single row. A third is in a command that loads users to seed a database: a truncated list seeds fewer users, with no error at all. The fourth is in a production repository. Here is the code, identifiers renamed:

func (r *HistoryRepo) ListByCaseID(ctx context.Context, caseID string) ([]domain.Event, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx,
        `SELECT id, event_type, title, created_at
         FROM case_events WHERE case_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at ASC`, caseID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var events []domain.Event
    for rows.Next() {
        var e domain.Event
        if err := rows.Scan(&e.ID, &e.EventType, &e.Title, &e.CreatedAt); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("scan event: %w", err)
        }
        events = append(events, e)
    }
    if events == nil {
        events = []domain.Event{}
    }
    return events, nil // rows.Err() is never read
}

This function returns the history of a case. If the connection drops halfway, it returns the first events and nil. The calling service builds the case view with a shortened history. The user sees a normal page, just shorter. No log, no alert.

This code is in one of my repositories anyway. It is exactly the oversight an analyzer should catch. And the pgx documentation is as clear as the standard library's. It says: "Callers should check rows.Err() after rows.Next() returns false to detect whether result-set reading ended prematurely due to an error."

The fix is three lines

For database/sql, add the check right after the loop:

for rows.Next() {
    // ...
}
if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
return ids, nil

For pgx, the same three lines work. pgx also offers helpers that do the check for you. pgx.CollectRows and pgx.ForEachRow call rows.Err() at the end of the loop, I checked their source. With db tags on the struct, the function above becomes:

rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx, query, caseID)
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
}
events, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[domain.Event])
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
}
return events, nil

For bufio.Scanner, it is if err := sc.Err(); err != nil after the loop. If you know the read cannot fail, write _ = sc.Err() with a comment. The analyzer goes quiet, and the reviewer understands it is a choice.

A test that fails when the loop stops early

An analyzer catches the oversight in the code. A test proves the consequence. With database/sql, the go-sqlmock library can simulate an error in the middle of the result with RowError. Here is the table test I ran on my two versions of the function:

func TestListIDs_StopsEarly(t *testing.T) {
    tests := []struct {
        name    string
        fn      func(context.Context, *sql.DB) ([]int64, error)
        wantErr bool
    }{
        {"buggy", listIDsBuggy, true},
        {"fixed", listIDs, true},
    }
    for _, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            db, mock, err := sqlmock.New()
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
            }
            defer db.Close()
            rows := sqlmock.NewRows([]string{"id"}).
                AddRow(int64(1)).AddRow(int64(2)).AddRow(int64(3)).
                RowError(1, errors.New("connection reset"))
            mock.ExpectQuery("SELECT id FROM things").WillReturnRows(rows)

            ids, err := tc.fn(context.Background(), db)
            if tc.wantErr && err == nil {
                t.Fatalf("got %d ids and no error, want an error", len(ids))
            }
        })
    }
}

The version without rows.Err() fails with the message got 1 ids and no error, want an error. Three rows in the result, one returned, no error. The fixed version passes.

With pgx, there is no official mock. Write a fake pgx.Rows whose Next returns false after one row and whose Err returns an error. The test must demand an error, not a list. In this lab, I only tested the database/sql version.

Run the analyzers today, without waiting for Go 1.28

Both analyzers are already in golang.org/x/tools v0.52.0. They have no ready-made command: the package's main.go carries a //go:build ignore. So you need a three-file module:

mkdir vet128 && cd vet128
go mod init vet128
cat > main.go <<'EOF'
package main

import (
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/multichecker"
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/scannererr"
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/sqlrowserr"
)

func main() {
    multichecker.Main(scannererr.Analyzer, sqlrowserr.Analyzer)
}
EOF
go mod tidy
go build -o vet128 .

Then, in each module to check:

go vet -vettool=/path/to/vet128 ./...

The binary weighs about 9 MB. It needs Go 1.26 or newer, not Go 1.28. My local go vet, on Go 1.26.3, knows neither analyzer. gopls 0.22 already enables scannererr by default in the editor, but not sqlrowserr.

If you use pgx, add a grep until something better exists:

for f in $(grep -rl 'rows.Next()' --include='*.go' .); do
  n=$(grep -c 'rows.Next()' "$f"); e=$(grep -c 'rows.Err()' "$f")
  [ "$n" -gt "$e" ] && echo "$f next=$n err=$e"
done

It is crude. It compares files, not functions. It still found my four gaps in a few seconds.

The checklist

A rows.Next() loop without rows.Err() cannot tell the end of the result from a failure.

  • [ ] Call rows.Err() after every rows.Next() loop, with database/sql and with pgx alike
  • [ ] Call sc.Err() after every sc.Scan() loop over a file or a network stream
  • [ ] With pgx, prefer pgx.CollectRows or pgx.ForEachRow over hand-written loops
  • [ ] Compile scannererr and sqlrowserr into a multichecker and run it in CI
  • [ ] Know what your analyzer covers: sqlrowserr only sees database/sql
  • [ ] Compare your rows.Next() to your rows.Err() with a grep for non-standard drivers
  • [ ] Write a test where the read fails halfway and demand an error
  • [ ] Re-read the Go 1.28 notes at release time: the draft can change

The takeaway

An iteration error looks like a smaller result. That is the sentence from the Go 1.28 notes, and it is the whole point. The analyzer is coming, but it only covers database/sql. If you are on pgx, your tools are still code review and a grep.

Run the binary on your code this week. Then count your rows.Next() against your rows.Err(). The gap is your list of silent bugs.

Want a review of your database access code and your Go CI? See my Go backend takeover offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Go 1.28 release notes (draft) · sqlrowserr analyzer · scannererr analyzer · database/sql, Rows.Next and Rows.Err · bufio, Scanner.Err · pgx v5, Rows interface and CollectRows · multichecker package · go vet documentation · go-sqlmock, RowError

title: Optimizing Rust Lock-Free MPMC for Latency Reduction
description:
💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

In large-scale event-driven clusters processing millions of messages per second, relying on synchronization primitives like std::sync::Mutex or RwLock introduces fatal systemic bottlenecks. When thousands of threads contend for the same mutex, kernel-level context switching and cache line bouncing inflate p99 tail latency to hundreds of milliseconds. Modern distributed systems require lock-free concurrency engineering that leverages atomic CPU instructions directly to maintain memory state consistency without engaging OS thread schedulers.

To understand how this mitigation operates in a real-world topology, let's examine the event processing architecture flowing from NATS JetStream to Tokio worker pools through the following diagram:

flowchart TD
 A[NATS JetStream Server] -->|TCP / Zero-Copy Stream| B(Tokio Reactor Core)
 B --> C{Crossbeam MPMC Ring Buffer}
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| D[Worker Thread 1]
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| E[Worker Thread 2]
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| F[Worker Thread N]
 D --> G[(Database / Sink)]
 E --> G
 F --> G

Implementing MPMC Queue with Crossbeam & Atomic Operations in Rust

The most effective approach to eliminate mutex overhead is utilizing atomic-backed ring buffers (AtomicUsize) using the crossbeam-queue crate or custom implementations. Below is an asynchronous message processing module integrating NATS subscribers with zero-copy deserialization and a lock-free queue in Rust:

use crossbeam_queue::SegQueue;
use std::sync::Arc;
use tokio::task;
use bytes::Bytes;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct EventPayload {
 pub id: u64,
 pub data: Bytes,
}

pub struct EngineSupervisor {
 queue: Arc<SegQueue<EventPayload>>,
 worker_count: usize,
}

impl EngineSupervisor {
 pub fn new(worker_count: usize) -> Self {
 Self {
 queue: Arc::new(SegQueue::new()),
 worker_count,
 }
 }

 pub fn push_event(&self, payload: EventPayload) {
 self.queue.push(payload);
 }

 pub async fn spawn_workers(&self) {
 for worker_id in 0..self.worker_count {
 let q = Arc::clone(&self.queue);
 task::spawn(async move {
 loop {
 if let Some(event) = q.pop() {
 process_payload(worker_id, event).await;
 } else {
 tokio::task::yield_now().await;
 }
 }
 });
 }
 }
}

async fn process_payload(worker_id: usize, event: EventPayload) {
 println!("Worker {} processing event ID: {}", worker_id, event.id);
}

Performance Benchmark: Traditional Mutex vs Rust Lock-Free MPMC

To quantify the effectiveness of this architecture, heavy load testing was conducted in a private cluster environment. Metrics focus on throughput (RPS), average latency (p50), and extreme tail latency (p99) under a load of 500,000 concurrent requests. As a foundation for high-performance infrastructure, similar architectures are frequently paired with networking optimizations such as those found in Traefik v3 API gateway architecture setups to maintain efficient communication pipelines.

Evaluation Metric Traditional Arc<Mutex<VecDeque>> Rust Lock-Free MPMC Queue Improvement / Reduction
Throughput (RPS) 142,500 req/sec 689,200 req/sec +383.6%
p50 Latency 4.2 ms 0.35 ms -91.6%
p99 Tail Latency 128.4 ms 2.1 ms -98.3%
CPU Context Switches 45,200 /sec 1,150 /sec -97.4%

Architectural Conclusion and Infrastructure Recommendations

Eliminating tail latency in enterprise event stream systems cannot be achieved solely by scaling physical CPU capacity. It requires low-level synchronization pattern overhauls toward lock-free data structures that minimize cache misses and preserve data pipeline integrity via NATS JetStream and Rust asynchronous runtime integration. To run such compute-intensive workloads optimally, ensure you utilize infrastructure supporting strict resource isolation like High-Performance VPS solutions from infrastruktur Hostinger KVM VPS.

title: Database Performance: Finding the Query That Is Killing You
description:
Database performance work usually begins with someone proposing a bigger instance, and it usually ends with the discovery that one query was doing a sequential scan over four million rows on every page load. The hardware was never the constraint. The plan was.

That pattern is consistent enough to be worth stating as a default assumption. When an application is slow and the database is busy, the cause is almost always a small number of specific queries, not a general shortage of capacity, and scaling up hides the problem for exactly as long as it takes the table to grow again.

Before changing anything, measure. Optimising a query you guessed at is how teams spend a week adding indexes that make writes slower and reads no faster. Every database can tell you which statements consume the most total time. Start there, fix the top one, measure again. Two or three iterations of that usually ends the incident.

Database Performance Starts With Finding the Query

Total time matters more than worst case. A query taking two seconds and running twice a day is irrelevant. A query taking forty milliseconds and running eight thousand times a minute is your problem, and it will never appear in a slow query log with a one-second threshold.

In Postgres, the pg_stat_statements extension aggregates exactly this: calls, total time and mean time per normalised statement. Sort by total time and the offender is usually in the top three. MySQL offers similar aggregation through the performance schema.

Two things worth checking before you conclude the query itself is at fault. Is it slow every time, or only at certain hours, which points at contention rather than the plan? And is it slow in isolation, or only under concurrency, which points at locking or connection limits?

Read the Plan Instead of Guessing

Once you have the statement, ask the database how it intends to run it. Postgres exposes this through EXPLAIN, and the important variant is EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually executes the query and reports real timings rather than estimates.

Three things in that output carry most of the signal.

Sequential scan on a large table. The database is reading every row. On a small table that is correct and fast. On a large one it means there is no usable index for the condition you wrote, or the planner decided the index was not worth using.

A large gap between estimated and actual row counts. The planner chooses its strategy from statistics, so when its estimate is off by orders of magnitude it is choosing badly for reasons that have nothing to do with your query. Stale statistics are a common and easily fixed cause.

Time concentrated in one node. Plans are trees, and the fix belongs at whichever node consumed the time. Optimising anything else changes nothing.

The instinct to add an index the moment you see a sequential scan is often right and worth resisting for thirty seconds, because the reason the index is not being used sometimes matters more than its absence.

Why Indexes Fail to Help

An index that exists is not an index that gets used.

The condition is not sargable. Wrapping a column in a function, or applying arithmetic to it, generally prevents the index on that column from being used, because the index stores the column values and not the transformed ones. Rewriting the condition to leave the column bare usually restores it.

Column order in a composite index is wrong. A composite index supports queries that use its leading columns. An index on one column then another does not help a query that filters only on the second, and this catches people constantly.

The planner thinks a scan is cheaper. If a query returns a large fraction of the table, reading it sequentially genuinely is faster than jumping through an index. This is correct behaviour, and the fix is to return less.

Statistics are stale. After a bulk load or a large deletion, the planner's picture of the data can be badly wrong until statistics are refreshed.

And every index costs something. Writes have to maintain it, and it consumes memory that would otherwise cache data. A table with fifteen indexes usually has several nobody needs, each making every insert slower.

The N+1 Problem Is Still the Biggest Single Cause

More application slowness comes from this than from any plan problem, and it never shows up as a slow query because each individual query is fast.

The shape is familiar. Fetch a list of a hundred records, then loop over them and fetch related data for each. The result is a hundred and one round trips where one or two would do. Every query returns in three milliseconds and the page still takes half a second, because the cost is the round trips and not the work.

Object-relational mappers make this easy to write by accident, since the related lookup looks like a property access rather than a database call. The fix is to load the related data in one query alongside the parent set, which every mature ORM supports and which most default to not doing.

Detecting it is straightforward: count queries per request. If a page issues a number of queries proportional to the number of items shown, you have found it. This is also the single highest-value thing to check when an application is slow at the edge, as our Cloudflare Hyperdrive guide covers, because round trips cost far more when the distance is greater.

Connections and Contention

Two problems that look like slowness but are not.

Connection exhaustion. Every database has a ceiling on concurrent connections, and each one costs memory. When an application opens more than the pool allows, requests queue waiting for a connection and the application appears slow while the database sits idle. The symptom is high application latency with low database CPU, and the fix is pooling rather than a larger machine.

Lock contention. A long transaction holding a lock blocks everything behind it. The usual cause is a transaction left open across work that does not need the database, such as an HTTP call to another service. Keep transactions short and confined to the database work itself.

Both cases are worth ruling out early, because both are easy to misread as a query problem and neither is fixed by an index.

What to Do in Order

Find the statements consuming the most total time. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the worst one and read where the time actually goes. Check the query count per request to rule out N+1 before optimising anything. Refresh statistics before adding an index, because sometimes that is the whole fix. Then add the narrowest index that serves the condition, and measure again.

Mecanik does this as part of our software development work, and the outcome is nearly always the same: two or three queries were responsible, the fix was small, and the larger instance nobody had bought was never needed.

Related reading

  • API Versioning: When to Break and How Not To
  • How to Build a Web App in 2026 - The UK Developer's Guide
  • Password Storage: What to Use in 2026
  • Custom Software Development UK - The Complete Buyer's Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find which query is slowing my application?
Sort by total time rather than worst case. A forty-millisecond query running eight thousand times a minute costs far more than a two-second query running twice a day, and it will never appear in a slow query log with a one-second threshold. In Postgres, pg_stat_statements aggregates calls and total time per statement; MySQL offers the same through the performance schema.

What should I look for in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output?
Three things carry most of the signal: a sequential scan on a large table, meaning no usable index; a large gap between estimated and actual row counts, meaning the planner is working from bad statistics; and time concentrated in one node of the plan tree, which is where the fix belongs. Optimising any other node changes nothing.

Why is my index not being used?
Usually one of four reasons. The condition wraps the column in a function or arithmetic, so the index no longer matches. The composite index has its columns in an order that does not support the query. The query returns a large enough fraction of the table that a scan genuinely is cheaper. Or statistics are stale after a bulk load or deletion.

What is an N+1 query problem?
Fetching a list of records, then issuing a separate query for related data on each one, producing a hundred and one round trips where one or two would do. It never appears in a slow query log because each query is fast; the cost is the round trips. Detect it by counting queries per request and looking for a count proportional to items shown.

Will a bigger database server fix slow queries?
Rarely, and only temporarily. When an application is slow and the database is busy, the cause is almost always a small number of specific queries rather than a shortage of capacity, so scaling up hides the problem until the table grows again. High application latency with low database CPU usually indicates connection pool exhaustion instead, which more hardware does not address.

title: The Transaction Only Covers Your Database. The Provider Key Is What Saves You
description:
Two readers asked me the same question from opposite sides last week, and I have been running it ever since. itsvicmoreno asked it on my piece about claiming a delivery once: the processed-keys table stops the second copy, but what if the receiver crashes between writing the key and charging the card? sunnatulla_dev asked the matching half on the other piece: he had already tried it in his own head, one crash, two attempts, zero charges: the key written, the retry refused as a duplicate, and nothing ever charged.

Both of them were right to worry. A key and a charge are two separate writes, and a crash can land between them. Which order breaks first, and what actually saves you? I crashed the receiver on purpose, in both orders, against four different shapes, with the same $29 payment for the same order, and counted the charges from the receiver's own tables. The results are clear, and one of them made me change my mind about a fix I used to recommend without thinking.

Problem 1: key first, and the payment quietly never happens

The first crash is the one sunnatulla_dev described. The receiver writes the key, then dies before the charge. The sender sees the connection drop and tries again. The retry finds the key already in the table and gets a polite 200 duplicate. Nothing charges. Ever.

My run: 2 attempts, 0 charges. Exactly his shape, down to the numbers. The customer is never charged, the order sits unpaid, and nobody gets an error. The system looks healthy from every angle except the one that matters: no money moved. A duplicate refusal is only correct if the first attempt actually did the work, and here it did not. The key is a promise that the charge happened, and the crash broke the promise.

This is the quiet failure, and I think it is the one people underestimate. A double charge shows up in a bank statement and somebody shouts. A lost charge shows up weeks later, in a report, as revenue that never arrived, and by then nobody remembers the crash.

Problem 2: charge first, and the customer pays twice

Now flip the order. The receiver charges first, then dies before writing the key. The retry finds no key, so it charges again. Same $29, same order, second charge.

My run: 2 attempts, 2 charges. $58 for a $29 order. This is the order that breaks first, and itsvicmoreno's question bet exactly that: the charge lands and the key never does. The retry has nothing to check, because the only record of the first charge lives at the provider, and this receiver never asks the provider anything.

So both orders are broken, in opposite directions. Key first loses the payment. Charge first doubles it. If you have to pick a failure, pick the lost one — at least nobody's card was charged twice. But picking a failure is not a design. The fix has to cover both orders, not one.

Problem 3: the transaction saves your database, not your money

The first fix people reach for is the obvious one: put the key and the charge in one transaction, so they commit together or roll back together. I ran it. Crash before the commit, the whole thing rolls back, the retry charges exactly once. 2 attempts, 1 charge. It works.

But it works only inside your own database. The transaction covers the key and your local record of the charge. The charge itself happens at the provider, outside your database, outside your transaction, outside everything you can roll back. If the crash lands between the provider's charge and your mark-done, the transaction has nothing to say about it. The provider took the money. Your database says processing. The retry has to decide, and the transaction cannot decide for it.

I used to describe the single transaction as the answer to this problem. It is not the answer. It is a good answer to a smaller problem: keeping your own records consistent. The money lives somewhere else, and the fix has to reach there.

Problem 4: the lease has to be measured, and 30 seconds was a guess

The second fix is a status column with a lease. The key goes in as processing, with a time limit. A retry while the lease is alive gets a 409 and waits. After the lease expires, the row can be reclaimed and the charge retried. A crashed holder stops holding the row, eventually.

sunnatulla_dev ran this shape in his own test with a 30 second lease: the copy in flight got a 409, the crashed one got a 409, then it was reclaimed at 60 seconds, one charge each. My job was to check that number, and to set the lease from something real instead of 30 seconds picked out of the air.

So I measured first. One hundred real charge calls through the receiver, and I took the p99, the time almost every healthy call finishes inside. Run 1: p99 1.89 seconds, so the lease was 2.39 seconds. Run 2: p99 0.96 seconds, lease 1.46 seconds. The p99 moved between runs because handler time on this small machine includes scheduling stalls; run 1 even caught a 5.48 second stall. That is the point of measuring: the lease has to beat the longest a healthy handler can actually run on the machine it runs on, stalls included, plus slack. A lease picked from a round number cannot know that.

Then I crashed the lease arm and retried every half second. Run 1: three 409s, reclaimed 3.21 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Run 2: two 409s, reclaimed 2.12 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Not 60 seconds. The reclaim lands one retry after the lease expires, so the honest number is the lease plus your retry gap. His 60 seconds came from his 30 second lease plus his retry rhythm, not from the mechanism. With a lease set from p99, the crashed row is reclaimable roughly one lease after the crash, about two to three seconds here.

One more detail that matters: while the charge runs, the handler renews the lease, every third of a lease. Without that, a slow-but-alive charge gets reclaimed mid-flight and charges twice, which is the exact failure the lease was supposed to prevent. A lease without renewal is a timer that punishes the slow and rewards the dead.

Problem 5: the provider key is the only shape that survives both orders

The third fix is the one itsvicmoreno pointed at. Insert the key as processing, pass that same key to the provider as its idempotency key, then mark it done. A retry that finds processing does not charge again. It asks the provider: did this key already charge? If yes, mark it done and stop.

I crashed this shape after the provider charge, before the mark-done. 2 attempts, 1 provider charge, 1 local charge. The retry asked, the provider said already charged, nothing charged twice. Then I ran it in the charge-first order too: provider charge first, local key still pending, crash, retry, and the retry asked the provider first, before touching the local key table. Same result: 1 provider charge. It is the only shape in the test that stays at exactly one charge in both orders, including the window the transaction cannot see.

That is my claim, and I expect people to argue with it: the single transaction is the wrong place to put your trust, because the money does not live in your database. The status column with a measured lease is good and honest, and I would keep it as the backstop. But the thing that actually saves you from a crash between the key and the charge is the provider's own idempotency key, the same key on both sides, with the retry asking instead of charging. Everything else is bookkeeping about a charge that already happened somewhere else.

Have you ever been charged twice for one order, or had a payment quietly never go through after a crash? Which side did it break on, and what did the retry do: ask first, or charge first? I would like to hear what it was, because the retry is where the money is decided, and most of us never look at it until it has already decided wrong.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Your coding agent may have installed an archived MCP server. Find it in 60 lines
description:
Earlier this month, Glow Security published research on something they call MCPhantom. The short version: when you ask a coding agent to "set up the GitHub MCP server", it often installs the one it remembers from training data. That is frequently an archived reference server from @modelcontextprotocol, not the maintained server the service now ships.

A few numbers from the write-up:

  • In 98% of the sessions they studied where a deprecated server was installed or suggested, the agent picked the package name itself. The user didn't ask for it.
  • The deprecated packages have been downloaded from npm more than 17.3 million times since July 2025.
  • They found four high-severity bugs in the archived servers, including a remote code execution path in the Puppeteer server through prompt injection. The archive won't be patched.
  • It happened across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others, with models from several vendors. This isn't one tool's bug.

The part that should worry a team lead is how invisible this is.

An MCP server started with npx -y some-package never appears in package.json or a lockfile. Your dependency scanner doesn't see it. There's no CVE for your security tooling to match. The only record that it exists is a JSON config file in someone's home directory.

So that's where we look.

Ask npm directly

npm already knows. When a package is deprecated, the registry returns a deprecated message on the version manifest. You can see it with one request:

curl -s https://registry.npmjs.org/@modelcontextprotocol%2fserver-github/latest | jq .deprecated
# "Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived"

The script below reads the MCP configs that common tools use, finds every server launched with npx or bunx, and asks the registry about each one. It has no dependencies and runs on Node 18 or later.

// mcp-audit.mjs: list the MCP servers your coding tools will start,
// and flag npm packages that are deprecated or archived.
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

const home = homedir();
const cwd = process.cwd();
const CONFIGS = [
  ["Claude Code (user)", join(home, ".claude.json")],
  ["Claude Code (project)", join(cwd, ".mcp.json")],
  ["Claude Desktop (macOS)", join(home, "Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json")],
  ["Claude Desktop (Windows)", join(process.env.APPDATA ?? "", "Claude/claude_desktop_config.json")],
  ["Cursor (user)", join(home, ".cursor/mcp.json")],
  ["Cursor (project)", join(cwd, ".cursor/mcp.json")],
  ["VS Code (project)", join(cwd, ".vscode/mcp.json")],
  ["Windsurf", join(home, ".codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json")],
];

// Pull every server block out of a config, wherever the tool keeps it.
function serversIn(json) {
  const blocks = [json.mcpServers, json.servers];
  for (const p of Object.values(json.projects ?? {})) blocks.push(p.mcpServers);
  return blocks.flatMap((b) => Object.entries(b ?? {}));
}

// "npx -y @scope/pkg@1.2.3 --flag" -> { name: "@scope/pkg", version: "1.2.3" }
function npmPackage(server) {
  if (!/^(npx|bunx)$/.test(server.command ?? "")) return null;
  const spec = (server.args ?? []).find((a) => !a.startsWith("-"));
  if (!spec) return null;
  const at = spec.lastIndexOf("@");
  return at > 0
    ? { name: spec.slice(0, at), version: spec.slice(at + 1) }
    : { name: spec, version: "latest" };
}

async function npmStatus({ name, version }) {
  const url = `https://registry.npmjs.org/${name.replace("/", "%2f")}/${version}`;
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) return `not on npm (${res.status})`;
  const meta = await res.json();
  return meta.deprecated ? `DEPRECATED: ${meta.deprecated}` : `ok (${meta.version})`;
}

let flagged = 0;
for (const [tool, path] of CONFIGS) {
  let json;
  try { json = JSON.parse(await readFile(path, "utf8")); } catch { continue; }
  for (const [id, server] of serversIn(json)) {
    const pkg = npmPackage(server);
    let status;
    if (server.url) status = `remote: ${server.url}`;
    else if (pkg) status = await npmStatus(pkg);
    else status = `local command: ${server.command}`;
    if (status.startsWith("DEPRECATED") || status.startsWith("not on npm")) flagged++;
    console.log(`${tool.padEnd(24)} ${id.padEnd(14)} ${pkg?.name ?? ""}\n  -> ${status}`);
  }
}
console.log(`\n${flagged} server(s) need attention.`);
process.exitCode = flagged ? 1 : 0;

Run it from a project folder so it picks up project-level configs too:

node mcp-audit.mjs

Here is what it printed against a test setup with five servers, two of which are the archived reference servers an agent typically reaches for:

Claude Code (user)       github         @modelcontextprotocol/server-github
  -> DEPRECATED: Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived
Claude Code (user)       browser        @modelcontextprotocol/server-puppeteer
  -> DEPRECATED: Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived
Cursor (user)            files          @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem
  -> ok (2.4.0)
Cursor (user)            gh-remote
  -> remote: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/
VS Code (project)        db
  -> local command: node
VS Code (project)        typo           mcp-server-that-does-not-exist-xyz
  -> not on npm (404)

3 server(s) need attention.

It exits with code 1 when anything is flagged, so you can drop it into a pre-commit hook or a CI job that checks a project's .mcp.json.

A few things worth knowing

Not everything under @modelcontextprotocol is archived. The filesystem server above is still maintained and came back clean. That's why the script asks the registry instead of matching a name pattern.

Claude Code keeps per-project servers inside ~/.claude.json, under projects. If you only check .mcp.json in the repo, you'll miss the servers an agent added "for this project" from inside a session. The script walks both.

"Not on npm" matters too. A name that 404s today is a name someone else can register tomorrow. If an agent invented or misspelled a package, you want to know before somebody publishes it.

The replacement is usually the service owner's server. For GitHub, that's github/github-mcp-server, available as a remote server at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, so there's nothing to install. Check the vendor's docs for the others.

What it doesn't cover

It only knows about npm. Python servers launched with uvx, Docker images, and local scripts show up as "local command" and need a human look. The config paths are the defaults. If your team keeps configs somewhere else, add a line to the list. And it audits what is already installed. It won't stop an agent from installing the next one. For that you want a check that runs before the agent's tool call, which is a separate post.

Make it a habit

Agents will keep suggesting packages from memory. Models are trained on the internet as it was, and the MCP ecosystem has moved quickly. You can't fix that from your side, but you can make sure every config on your team gets read by something that checks it.

A simple rule goes a long way: one approved server per service, written down, and nothing launched by npx that hasn't passed a check like this one.

I'm Mayursinh, founder of Redlio Labs. We build custom software and add AI features and agents to it for mid-size companies, and we use coding agents in our own work every day. The script was tested on Node 22 against the live npm registry.

title: Microservices Architecture: Real-World Examples
description:
Modern applications need to handle millions of users, large amounts of data, and multiple business operations. To manage these requirements, many organizations use microservices architecture to develop scalable and flexible software applications.

But what exactly is microservices architecture, how does it work, and where is it used? Let's explore its concepts, benefits, technologies, and practical examples.

What Is Microservices Architecture?

Microservices architecture is a software design approach that divides a large application into smaller, independent services. Each service performs a specific business function and communicates with other services through APIs or messaging systems.

Unlike monolithic architecture, where application components are combined into one system, microservices allow individual services to be developed, tested, deployed, and scaled independently.

Example: An online shopping application can contain separate services for user accounts, product catalogs, payments, order management, and delivery tracking.

How Does Microservices Architecture Work?

Microservices architecture works by allowing independent services to communicate and exchange information to complete business operations.

Consider an e-commerce application. When a customer places an order, the following services may work together:

  • API Gateway: Receives requests and directs them to the appropriate service.
  • User Service: Manages customer registration and authentication.
  • Product Service: Displays product details and availability.
  • Order Service: Creates and manages customer orders.
  • Payment Service: Handles payment processing.
  • Notification Service: Sends order confirmations and transaction updates. These services communicate through REST APIs, gRPC, or messaging platforms such as Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ.

Each service can maintain its own database, helping teams manage business functions independently.

What Are Some Real-World Examples of Microservices Architecture?

Several large digital platforms use distributed service-based approaches to manage complex operations.

1. Amazon – E-Commerce Platform

Amazon is a useful example of large-scale service-oriented software architecture.

When customers purchase products, several business functions work together, including product discovery, inventory management, order processing, payment handling, and delivery coordination.

Separating these responsibilities allows different application components to handle their workloads efficiently.

2. Netflix – Video Streaming Platform

Netflix operates a large digital streaming ecosystem supported by distributed services.

For example, when users access the platform, different functions support account authentication, content discovery, personalized recommendations, subscription management, and streaming delivery.

Independent services help different parts of the platform scale according to user demand.

3. Online Banking Applications

Modern banking applications can use microservices to organize different financial operations.

For example, when a customer transfers money:

  • The authentication service verifies the customer.
  • The account service retrieves account information.
  • The transaction service processes the transfer.
  • The notification service sends transa ction updates.

Financial applications also require strong security, transaction validation, and data consistency.

What Are the Advantages of Microservices Architecture?

Microservices offer several advantages for modern software development:

  • Scalability: Individual services can scale according to their workloads.
  • Flexibility: Teams can select suitable technologies for different services.
  • Independent Deployment: Developers can update individual services without redeploying the entire application.
  • Fault Isolation: Properly designed services can prevent certain failures from affecting the whole application.
  • Faster Development: Multiple teams can work on separate services simultaneously.
  • Maintainability: Smaller, focused services can be easier to understand and maintain.

What Are the Challenges of Microservices?

Despite their advantages, microservices introduce technical challenges that organizations must consider.

  • Communication Complexity: Managing communication between multiple services requires careful planning.
  • Data Consistency: Maintaining consistent information across distributed databases can be difficult.
  • Monitoring: Teams need centralized logging, monitoring, and tracing.
  • Security: Every service communication point must be properly secured.
  • Deployment Management: Managing multiple services requires automation and orchestration.

Tools such as Docker, Kubernetes, and Prometheus help teams manage these challenges.

Frequently Asked Questions
1. What is the main purpose of microservices architecture?

Its main purpose is to divide complex applications into smaller, independent services that can be developed, deployed, and scaled separately.

2. Is microservices architecture better than monolithic architecture?

Not always. Microservices are useful for complex applications requiring independent scaling and deployment. Monolithic architecture can be simpler and more cost-effective for smaller applications.

3. Is Docker required for microservices?

No. Docker is not mandatory, but it helps package and deploy services consistently across different environments.

4. Which programming language is best for microservices?

Java, Python, Node.js, and C# are popular choices. The best language depends on application requirements and team expertise.

Conclusion

Microservices architecture provides a flexible approach to developing and managing complex software applications. By dividing applications into independent services, organizations can improve scalability, deployment flexibility, and maintainability.

From e-commerce and video streaming to online banking, microservices support many modern digital operations.

For aspiring developers, learning Java, Spring Boot, REST APIs, Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud technologies can provide a strong foundation for building microservices-based applications.

title: I’m building an open-source Git GUI for Windows in Java Swing – here’s why
description:
For years I’ve used SmartGit at work. I like its multi-pane workflow: repositories, files, history graph and diff, all on one screen. But it’s free only for non-commercial use, and I wanted something I could use anywhere, change when I needed, and share with others.

So I started WinGit, an open-source Git client for Windows.

What it does today

  • Repository status, staging and committing
  • Push / pull / fetch
  • Commit history
  • Setting custom author/committer dates for a commit (I needed this myself – e.g. for fixing wrong clocks or time zones)

It covers my everyday needs, but it’s still early: expect rough edges.

Why Java and Swing in 2026?

I’m a Java developer, and modern Swing with FlatLaf looks surprisingly good – IntelliJ IDEA is proof of that. A few technical decisions:

  • JGit for reads, native git CLI for writes. Starting a process on Windows costs tens of milliseconds, so frequent reads go through JGit, while commits, push/pull and hooks go through the real git. That keeps it fast and fully compatible.
  • No Git work on the UI thread. Everything runs in the background and results are published back to Swing.
  • jpackage builds a Windows installer with an embedded runtime, so you don’t need Java installed.

Built with AI assistance

I develop WinGit with Claude Code as a coding assistant. It speeds things up a lot, but architecture, review and testing are on me. I’ll probably write a separate post about that experience.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A customer's bank rejects the transfer, and your code needs to know why. The National Automated Clearing House Association (NACHA) defines 85 standardized return codes—each with a specific reason, timing window, and recovery path.

Understanding these codes isn't just academic. It's the difference between a retry that works and one that wastes time and money. Let's walk through the most common returns and how to handle them programmatically.

The Big Three: R01, R03, R10

R01 — Insufficient Funds

The customer's account doesn't have enough money. This is the most common return, accounting for roughly 30–40% of all ACH returns in production systems.

  • When it fires: 1–2 business days after the debit entry is sent
  • Reversibility: The debit is reversed; funds are returned to your account
  • Developer action: Flag the payout as failed. Retry logic here is risky—if the account still lacks funds tomorrow, you'll just get another R01. Instead, notify the customer and ask them to add funds before you retry. 
{
  "return_code": "R01",
  "reason": "Insufficient Funds",
  "action": "notify_customer_and_hold",
  "retry_eligible": false,
  "settlement_days": 1
}

R03 — No Account / Invalid Account

The account number doesn't exist, or the routing number is invalid.

  • When it fires: 1–2 business days
  • Reversibility: Full reversal
  • Developer action: This is permanent. Don't retry. Update your customer database to flag the account as invalid and route future payouts to an alternate method (card, wire, RTP).

R10 — Customer Advises Not Authorized

The customer disputes the transaction—they claim they didn't authorize it. This is a fraud signal.

  • When it fires: Up to 60 days after the transaction
  • Reversibility: Full reversal
  • Developer action: This requires manual review. Flag the account, contact the customer, and pause automated payouts until resolved.

Mid-Tier Returns: R04, R05, R07

R04 — Invalid Routing Number

The routing number format is wrong or doesn't belong to an active bank.

  • Developer action: Validate routing numbers against the Federal Reserve's routing directory before attempting a payout. This is preventable.

R05 — Improper Debit Entry

The debit entry itself is malformed—wrong amount format, invalid transaction code, or missing required fields.

  • Developer action: This indicates a bug in your ACH file generation. Check your NACHA file formatting (record length, field alignment, checksums). Fix the code and retry.

R07 — Authorization Revoked

The customer revoked their authorization via their bank.

  • Developer action: Treat like R10—manual review required. The customer has formally objected.

Building Retry Logic

Here's a practical pattern for handling returns:

function handleACHReturn(returnCode, payout) {
  const returnRules = {
    R01: { retry: false, action: 'notify', days: 0 },
    R03: { retry: false, action: 'invalidate_account', days: 0 },
    R04: { retry: true, action: 'validate_routing', days: 1 },
    R05: { retry: true, action: 'fix_format', days: 1 },
    R10: { retry: false, action: 'manual_review', days: 0 },
  };

  const rule = returnRules[returnCode] || { retry: false, action: 'escalate' };

  if (rule.retry) {
    scheduleRetry(payout, rule.days);
  } else if (rule.action === 'notify') {
    notifyCustomer(payout, returnCode);
  } else if (rule.action === 'invalidate_account') {
    markAccountInvalid(payout.account_id);
    routeToAlternateRail(payout); // Try card or RTP instead
  }

  logReturn(payout.id, returnCode, rule.action);
}

Settlement Timing

ACH returns typically settle 1–2 business days after the original debit entry. Same-day ACH returns settle the same day. Plan your reconciliation window accordingly—don't assume a payout succeeded until 2 business days have passed.

Key Takeaway

Not all ACH returns are created equal. R01 needs customer intervention. R03 needs account replacement. R05 needs code fixes. Build your retry logic around the reason, not just the fact of failure. That's what separates a robust payout system from one that wastes time ch

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.
