title: How 5 Companies Use AI Coding Agents and Assistants Across the SDLC
description:
An agent-generated pull request has a green build and a full set of tests. A reviewer compares it with the ticket and discovers that the agent guessed how duplicate requests should behave. Every generated test uses the same guess.

The team can still fix the change during review. An earlier opportunity was to catch the missing rule when the agent proposed its implementation plan.

Start with an invoice request that can be retried

Consider a hypothetical invoice API. The ticket says the endpoint should handle duplicate submissions. That leaves several decisions open. Should a retry return the existing invoice? What happens if the caller reuses the same idempotency key with a different amount? What happens when two requests arrive together?

The approved plan could spell out three outcomes. A request with the same key and payload returns the existing invoice ID. A request with the same key and a different payload gets a conflict response. Two simultaneous requests with the same key and payload create one invoice record.

Those decisions give the agent something concrete to implement and the reviewer a way to judge the result.

Stage What the agent can prepare What the engineer can verify
Requirements A draft specification and a list of open questions The duplicate-request rules and acceptance criteria
Implementation An API change, a database migration, and a branch The database constraint, transaction boundaries, and existing behaviour
Testing API, integration, and concurrency tests Whether tests cover changed payloads and simultaneous requests
Merge A pull request with a summary of check results Which checks passed, how the change can be deployed, and who will own it

Two sequential requests can pass even when simultaneous requests create two records. A concurrency test gives the reviewer evidence about that third acceptance criterion. The reviewer can also check whether the test exercises the same database constraint the application uses in production.

Treat a failed test as a decision point

Suppose a generated integration test fails because it expects a conflict when the same key is reused with a different amount. The implementation currently returns the original invoice regardless of the payload.

The failure could indicate a bad implementation, a faulty test fixture, or a requirement that changed after the test was written. An engineer can trace it back to the approved rule and decide what needs to change. Here, the policy already says that a different payload should produce a conflict, so the implementation needs correction.

That review matters when the same agent wrote the code and the tests. A reviewer can add an independent scenario from the approved ticket and confirm that it fails against the incorrect implementation before the fix goes in.

Five company approaches developers can compare

GeekyAnts describes agents drafting requirements and plans, implementing changes, and running tests. Engineers approve the plan before coding, decide how to handle failures, and review and merge changes from a separate branch. The engineer who merges the change owns it in production. Requirements-to-release video

Thoughtworks documents how AI/works turns requirements and existing system context into a specification, then generates implementation stories, code, and tests from it. The specification gives reviewers a place to check that a change preserves existing invoice rules.

Globant describes a Test AI Agent that drafts and executes test plans. Teams evaluating AI-assisted QA can ask how generated plans cover concurrency, unexpected input, and behaviour across service boundaries.

EPAM describes using CodeMie in its own delivery process to keep requirements and architecture connected to implementation, QA, and release. The workflow illustrates how an approved rule can stay visible as work moves from a ticket to a pull request.

Accenture collaborated with GitHub on a randomized Copilot trial with enterprise developers and also studied adoption. The research gives teams a reference for evaluating how a coding assistant fits into an existing engineering workflow.

Put the evidence in the pull request

A pull request template can make this workflow easier to repeat. Three fields are enough for the invoice example. Link to the approved acceptance criterion, show the evidence for the riskiest behaviour, and name the person who owns the change after merge.

For the concurrency rule, that could mean linking to the ticket and attaching an integration test result showing that simultaneous retries produced one invoice. A reviewer can then start with the behaviour that matters and inspect the code that protects it.

Where does an AI coding agent need to pause in your team’s workflow?

title: Fix: “Next.js encountered the unstable value new Date()” in Next.js 16
description:
I upgraded a landing page to Next.js 16 and the production build failed on the most innocent line in the whole project, the copyright year in the footer:

<p>© {new Date().getFullYear()} Driftly</p>

next build stopped with this:

Error: Route "/": Next.js encountered the unstable value `new Date()` while prerendering.

This value can change between renders, so it must be either prerendered or computed later.

Ways to fix this:
  - [dynamic] Render at request time by adding a dynamic data access (e.g. `await connection()`) before this call
  - [cache] Prerender and cache the value with `"use cache"`
  - [client] Render the value on the client with `"use client"`
  - [measure] If the value is for telemetry, use a timing API such as `performance.now()`

Here's why it happens and how to pick the right fix.

Why Next.js 16 complains

The error only shows up when Cache Components is turned on. Check your next.config.ts:

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
};

My project was created with create-next-app, and it already had this option enabled.

With Cache Components, Next.js prerenders as much of each page as it can into static HTML at build time. A value like new Date() is different every time it runs, so Next.js can't tell whether you meant "the time when the site was built" or "the time when the visitor opened the page". Instead of guessing, it stops the build and asks you to decide.

The same rule applies to:

  • new Date() and Date.now()
  • Math.random()
  • crypto.randomUUID()

performance.now() is the exception. Next.js treats it as a timing tool for telemetry and doesn't guard it.

Fix 1: Cache the value with "use cache"

Use this when the value only needs to be fresh enough, not computed for every visitor. A copyright year is the perfect example.

Move the value into an async function marked with "use cache":

// components/year.tsx
async function getYear() {
  "use cache";
  return new Date().getFullYear();
}

export async function Year() {
  return <>{await getYear()}</>;
}

// components/footer.tsx
import { Year } from "./year";

export function Footer() {
  return <p>© <Year /> Driftly</p>;
}

The year is computed during prerendering and cached, so the page stays fully static. The cached value is refreshed when the cache revalidates or when you redeploy.

Fix 2: Compute it on every request with connection()

Use this when every visitor really needs a new value, like a request ID or a "rendered at" timestamp.

Call connection() before reading the value. This tells Next.js to wait for a real request. Wrap the component in <Suspense> so the rest of the page can still be prerendered:

import { connection } from "next/server";
import { Suspense } from "react";

async function RenderedAt() {
  await connection();
  return <p>Rendered at {new Date().toISOString()}</p>;
}

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}>
      <RenderedAt />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

The trade-off: this part of the page is now rendered on the server for every request. In the next build output, the route changes from ○ (Static) to ◐ (Partial Prerender): static HTML with the dynamic part streamed in.

Fix 3: Move it to the client (and watch for the second error)

My first instinct was to make the footer year a Client Component:

"use client";

export function Year() {
  return <>{new Date().getFullYear()}</>;
}

That produced a different error:

Error: Route "/": Next.js encountered the unstable value `new Date()` in a Client Component.

This value would be evaluated during the prerender, instead of recomputed on each visit.

With Cache Components, Client Components are prerendered too. "use client" alone doesn't move the work to the browser. The error message suggests two ways out:

Read the value in an effect, so it only runs in the browser:

"use client";

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function LocalTime() {
  const [time, setTime] = useState<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
  }, []);

  return <span>{time ?? "…"}</span>;
}

Or wrap the Client Component in <Suspense> so Next.js can stream it in instead of baking it into the static HTML.

Use this fix for values that depend on the visitor's browser, such as their local time zone.

Fix 4: For telemetry, use performance.now()

If you only need a duration for logging, performance.now() is allowed:

const start = performance.now();
await doWork();
console.log(`doWork took ${performance.now() - start}ms`);

Don't render this value in the UI. It's meant for measurements.

Which fix should you use?

What you need Fix
A value that's fine to compute once (copyright year, build date) "use cache"
A fresh value for every request (request ID, server timestamp) await connection() + <Suspense>
A value from the visitor's browser (local time, time zone) useEffect in a Client Component
A duration for logs or metrics performance.now()

One more gotcha: static export

If you deploy with output: "export" (a fully static site with no server), you can't render anything per request, so Fix 2 is not an option. For the static demo of my landing page, the simplest working setup was turning cacheComponents off for that build. Note that partialPrefetching requires cacheComponents, so it has to go too.

Wrapping up

The error looks scary, but it's Next.js asking a fair question: should this value be computed once, per request, or in the browser? Answer that, and the fix is a few lines.

The official docs go deeper: blocking-prerender-current-time and the Client Component version.

I ran into this while building Liftoff, a Next.js 16 + Tailwind CSS 4 landing page kit, which uses the "use cache" footer year from Fix 1.

  • Liftoff Lite is free (MIT): navbar, hero, features, footer and dark mode. Get Liftoff Lite
  • Liftoff is the full kit with pricing, FAQ, testimonials, email capture and a 22-page launch guide. Live demo · Get Liftoff

Have you hit this error with something other than dates? Let me know in the comments.

title: 16 Free CSS and UI Tools for Freelance Designers on Upwork and Fiverr
description:
By Muhammad Wasim, developer of ToolSphare

If you take design or front-end jobs on Upwork or Fiverr from Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, Lagos or Abuja, a lot of the work is small and visual: a client wants a card that looks like frosted glass, a grid that does not collapse on a phone, a rounded button, or a React component instead of the HTML you already wrote. Opening a full design tool for each of those tweaks slows you down, especially on a shared laptop or a tight revision round.

I built ToolSphare as a free, no-sign-up toolbox in the browser. The sixteen tools below are the ones I would keep in a freelancer bookmark folder for CSS and UI delivery.

Layouts you can see before you paste the code

CSS Flexbox Layout Generator

Flexbox is still how most nav bars, card rows and footers get built. The CSS flexbox generator lets you try direction, alignment, spacing and wrapping on a live container, then export the CSS. Useful when a client says "centre it" and you want to show two options in the same call.

CSS Grid Layout Generator

For galleries, dashboards and landing-page sections, the CSS grid generator builds column and row tracks, gaps and a live preview, then gives you the code. Check the layout at a mobile width before you send the revision; a pretty desktop grid can still break on a small phone.

HTML Table Generator

Admin pages, price lists and invoice previews still need tables. The HTML table generator helps you build and style a table you can paste into a theme or a client's CMS, instead of hand-writing every tag.

Visual details clients notice

CSS Border Radius Generator

The CSS border radius generator lets you shape each corner visually and copy the snippet. It is faster than guessing four values when a logo mark or a button needs an uneven radius.

CSS Box Shadow Generator

A light shadow can lift a card; a heavy one makes a page look dated. The CSS box shadow generator adjusts offset, blur and related values with a live preview so you can send a screenshot of two strengths and let the client pick.

Gradient Generator and CSS Gradient Text Generator

Backgrounds and headlines often share a brand gradient. The gradient generator builds linear and radial CSS gradients, and the CSS gradient text generator applies a gradient to text with angle and stop controls. Keep contrast high enough to read; a stylish heading that fails on a bright phone screen will come back as a revision.

CSS Glassmorphism Generator

Frosted-glass cards are a common request on modern landing pages. The CSS glassmorphism generator sets backdrop blur, opacity and border highlights, then exports the CSS. Test it over a busy photograph, not only over a plain colour.

CSS Clip Path Generator and CSS Triangle Generator

Badges, chevrons, hexagons and pointers are painful to draw by hand. The CSS clip-path generator and the CSS triangle generator give you shapes and a snippet you can paste. Use them for decorative UI, not as a substitute for accessible icons with text labels.

Pattern Generator

A subtle background often looks more finished than a flat fill. The pattern generator creates seamless SVG or CSS patterns you can copy. Keep the pattern quiet if the page already has a lot of content.

CSS Cursor Tester

Custom cursors are easy to overdo, but a client sometimes wants a pointer that matches the brand. The CSS cursor tester previews cursor values and can generate a rule with a fallback, which matters when an image cursor fails to load.

Clean code for handover

CSS Formatter and JavaScript Formatter

Clients and future you will thank you for readable code. The CSS formatter beautifies or minifies CSS in the browser, and the JavaScript formatter does the same for JS. Format before you paste into a repo; minify only a copy you are sending to production.

SVG Optimizer

Logos and icons often arrive as messy SVG exports. The SVG optimizer cleans and minifies the markup so the file is smaller and easier to hand over. Open the result and check that nothing visible disappeared.

HTML to JSX Converter

If the brief is React or Next.js and your first pass was HTML, the HTML to JSX converter turns the markup into JSX you can drop into a component. Review class names, self-closing tags and any inline styles before you commit.

A clean revision workflow

  1. Build the layout in the flexbox or grid generator and screenshot it for approval.
  2. Tune radius, shadow, gradient or glass effects only after the structure is agreed.
  3. Format the CSS and JS, then optimise any SVG.
  4. Convert to JSX if the stack needs it, and paste a tidy file, not a dump from a chat window.

Clear, reusable snippets are easier to defend in a revision than a one-off design that nobody can edit.

About ToolSphare

I am Muhammad Wasim, a software engineer at MindSphare IT in Pakistan. Freelancers in Pakistan, Nigeria and elsewhere should not need a paid design suite for every CSS tweak. ToolSphare is free, with no sign-up. If a UI tool would help your workflow, email contact@toolsphare.com.

See all the free developer and design tools at ToolSphare.

title: How to Create an Effective API Test Plan: A Practical Guide for QA Engineers and Developers
description:
APIs are the backbone of modern applications. Whether you're building a microservices architecture, integrating third-party services, or developing a mobile application, APIs play a critical role in ensuring that different systems communicate correctly.

But here's a common problem: many development teams start API testing without having a clearly defined testing plan.

They write a few test cases, validate successful responses, check status codes, and move on. Unfortunately, this approach often misses important scenarios such as invalid inputs, authorization issues, integration failures, performance bottlenecks, and backward compatibility problems.

This is where an API Test Plan becomes essential.

In this article, we'll explore what an API test plan is, why it matters, what it should include, and how you can create one for your next API project.

What Is an API Test Plan?

An API test plan is a structured document that defines how an API will be tested throughout a development cycle or release.

It outlines:

  • What APIs and endpoints need testing.
  • Which testing approaches will be used.
  • What environments are required.
  • Which test data and tools will be used.
  • What risks need attention.
  • What conditions must be satisfied before releasing an API.

Think of it as a roadmap for your API testing activities.

Without a proper plan, testing can become inconsistent, resulting in missed scenarios and unexpected production issues.

Why Do You Need an API Test Plan?

A well-defined API test plan provides several benefits.

  1. Better Test Coverage

An API can have multiple endpoints, request parameters, authentication mechanisms, and response structures.

A testing plan helps ensure that important scenarios aren't overlooked.

  1. Early Detection of Defects

Testing shouldn't happen only after development is complete.

By defining testing activities early, teams can identify contract violations, validation issues, and integration problems before they reach production.

  1. Improved Team Collaboration

Developers, QA engineers, product managers, and DevOps teams can work with a shared understanding of testing responsibilities and release expectations.

  1. Reduced Production Risks

Identifying security vulnerabilities, performance issues, and backward compatibility problems before deployment helps reduce the chances of production failures.

10 Essential Components of an Effective API Test Plan

Let's look at the important sections every API test plan should cover.

  1. Testing Objectives and Scope

Start by defining what you want to achieve through API testing.

Identify:

  • APIs and endpoints included in testing.
  • API versions being tested.
  • Features covered in the release.
  • Integrations with external services.
  • Functional and non-functional testing requirements.

For example, if you're testing an e-commerce application, your scope might include product, customer, payment, and order management APIs.

Clearly document what is excluded from testing as well.

  1. Testing Approach and Methodology

Define the different types of API testing that will be performed.

Some important testing types include:

  • Functional Testing: Validates business logic and expected API behavior.
  • Negative Testing: Checks how APIs handle invalid inputs and unexpected requests.
  • Contract Testing: Ensures API requests and responses follow the defined specification.
  • Integration Testing: Validates communication between connected services.
  • Regression Testing: Ensures existing functionality continues working after changes.
  • Performance Testing: Measures response times, throughput, and stability under load.
  • Security Testing: Identifies authentication, authorization, and other security vulnerabilities.

Your testing approach should be based on the API's complexity, business requirements, and potential risks.

  1. Test Environment Configuration

A consistent test environment is essential for reliable results.

Document the environments where testing will happen, such as:

  • Local development.
  • Continuous Integration (CI).
  • QA or testing.
  • Staging.
  • Production smoke testing.

Also specify API base URLs, authentication configurations, database dependencies, external service mocks, and environment access permissions.

Keep sensitive credentials secure and avoid exposing production data in lower environments.

  1. Test Data Management

API testing requires different types of test data.

For example, when testing a user registration API, you should consider:

  • Valid user information.
  • Missing mandatory fields.
  • Invalid email addresses.
  • Duplicate usernames.
  • Boundary values.
  • Unauthorized requests.

Use synthetic or appropriately masked data wherever possible.

A good test data strategy makes test execution more repeatable and reliable.

  1. Entry and Exit Criteria

One of the most important parts of an API test plan is defining when testing can begin and when it can be considered complete.

Example entry criteria:

  • API specification is reviewed and approved.
  • Test environment is available.
  • Required test data is prepared.
  • Build deployment is successful.
  • Authentication credentials are configured.

Example exit criteria:

  • All critical test cases have been executed.
  • No unresolved critical or high-severity defects remain.
  • Positive and negative scenarios are covered.
  • Contract validation tests pass.
  • Performance requirements are satisfied.
  • Security checks meet agreed acceptance criteria.

Avoid vague statements such as "testing is completed successfully." Use measurable conditions instead.

  1. Risk Assessment

Not every API endpoint carries the same level of risk.

For example, a payment processing API requires more attention than a simple health-check endpoint.

Identify potential risks such as:

  • Unauthorized access to customer information.
  • Incorrect financial calculations.
  • Breaking changes in API responses.
  • Unexpected failures during high traffic.
  • Third-party integration failures.

Prioritize testing based on the likelihood and business impact of each risk.

This helps QA teams focus their efforts where they matter most.

  1. Test Coverage and Traceability

Define how you will measure API test coverage.

Useful coverage metrics include:

  • Percentage of API operations tested.
  • Positive and negative scenario coverage.
  • Request and response schema validation.
  • HTTP status code coverage.
  • Boundary value coverage.
  • Requirement-to-test traceability.

For example, every documented API operation should have appropriate positive and negative test scenarios.

Connecting requirements, API specifications, and test cases also makes it easier to identify gaps when an API changes.

  1. Tools and Technologies

Choose tools based on your testing requirements.

Some commonly used tools include:

  • Postman for API requests and functional validation.
  • REST Assured for Java-based API automation.
  • Pytest for Python-based testing.
  • Apache JMeter and k6 for performance testing.
  • OWASP ZAP for security testing.
  • Swagger and OpenAPI for API documentation and contract validation.

Your tool selection should support repeatable execution and integration with your development workflow.

  1. CI/CD Integration and Quality Gates

API testing becomes more effective when integrated into CI/CD pipelines.

Instead of waiting until the release stage, automate important checks throughout development.

A typical pipeline could look like this:

Pull Request

  • API specification validation.
  • Contract testing.
  • Functional smoke tests.

Merge to Main

  • Full functional testing.
  • Integration testing.
  • Regression checks.

Pre-Release

  • Performance testing.
  • Security testing.
  • Final quality assessment.

Define which failures should block a merge or deployment.

This ensures that API quality becomes part of the development process rather than a last-minute activity.

  1. Reporting and Defect Management

Finally, define how testing results will be reported.

Your plan should identify:

  • Test execution status.
  • Passed and failed test cases.
  • Defect severity and priority.
  • Outstanding risks.
  • Test coverage metrics.
  • Release readiness status.

Clear reporting helps stakeholders make informed release decisions.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Creating an API Test Plan

Even experienced QA teams can make mistakes while planning API testing.

Here are some common ones:

  1. Testing only successful scenarios

Happy-path testing isn't enough. Include invalid inputs, missing parameters, unauthorized requests, and unexpected responses.

  1. Ignoring API contract changes

Changes in request or response structures can break existing consumers. Include contract validation and backward compatibility checks.

  1. Using unrealistic test data

Unrepresentative data can hide important defects. Include boundary values, invalid data, and different user roles.

  1. Not defining measurable exit criteria

Without clear release conditions, teams may disagree about whether testing is complete.

  1. Keeping testing separate from CI/CD

Manual-only testing can slow down feedback. Automate repeatable checks and integrate them into the development pipeline.

How API Test Planning Supports Shift-Left Testing

Shift-left testing means moving testing activities earlier in the software development lifecycle.

Instead of discovering problems just before production, teams validate API quality during development.

A well-defined API test plan supports this approach by establishing:

  • API contract validation before deployment.
  • Automated tests during pull requests.
  • Early detection of breaking API changes.
  • Continuous regression testing.
  • Consistent quality gates across releases.

When testing is planned around API specifications, developers and QA engineers can identify potential issues before they become expensive production defects.

Final Thoughts

An effective API test plan is more than a document. It's a practical framework that helps development and QA teams deliver reliable, secure, and maintainable APIs.

By defining testing scope, methodologies, environments, test data, risk priorities, coverage targets, and CI/CD quality gates, teams can make API testing more predictable and efficient.

If you're building or improving your API testing process, having a reusable template can save significant planning time.

Want a ready-to-use starting point?

Check out the detailed API Test Plan Template by Total Shift Left.

It includes fill-in sections for testing scope, environments, entry and exit criteria, risk assessment, coverage targets, test data, tools, CI quality gates, and reporting, along with a practical worked example.

Use it as a starting point and customize it for your next API release.

What does your API testing process look like? Do you maintain a formal API test plan, or do you manage testing activities directly through test cases and CI/CD pipelines?

Share your experience in the comments!

title: Why have a Security Operations Centre (SOC)?
description:
As businesses continue to digitise, they will begin to heavily utilise cloud services, web-based applications, remote working capabilities and complex networks.Whilst these can increase efficiency within an organisation, they can also introduce new vulnerabilities to exploit.

In order to detect and act upon advanced cyber threats in a timely manner, businesses should ensure that they are constantly monitored, threats are detected quickly, and incidents are managed effectively. This is where a Security Operations Centre can be beneficial.

What Is a Security Operations Centre?

A Security Operations Centre (SOC) is a group of people, processes and technologies that work together to monitor, detect, investigate and manage cyber security threats. The SOC ensures that the digital infrastructure of businesses is secure.

Within the Security Operations Centre, activity on networks, devices, servers, cloud services and applications within an organisation are constantly monitored. If suspicious activity is detected, the security analysts will investigate and respond appropriately to reduce further damage.

Depending upon an organisations needs, a SOC can be provided by internal staff, by an external Cyber security provider, or a mixture of both.

Why do Businesses Need a SOC?

Cyber attacks can occur at any time. If monitoring is not implemented within the organisation, suspicious activity may not be identified in a timely manner, causing significant damage.

Benefits of having a SOC include the following.

  • Continuous Monitoring

Security analysts within the SOC continuously monitor an organisations IT infrastructure. Information from various systems is gathered and investigated to detect unusual activity, unauthorised access and possible vulnerabilities.

By performing continuous monitoring, suspicious activity can be detected quickly in order to reduce the risk of large scale issues.

  • Threats Detected Quickly

By detecting threats early in their lifecycle, the impact they could cause to your organisation can be minimised. Within a SOC, security monitoring tools, threat intelligence and behaviour analysis can be used to detect signs of compromise.

Detection of threats early means that phishing attacks, malware, ransomware and unauthorised access to accounts can be identified and responded to quickly, preventing attackers from affecting many systems.

  • Quick Incident Response

If cyber threats are identified in good time, businesses should respond to them quickly.

Analysts within the SOC will investigate alerts, and determine how severe an incident is. Based on this, predefined responses to incidents will be performed. This may include isolating infected devices, disabling suspicious accounts, blocking malicious connections and resetting credentials.

By having defined incident responses in place, disruption within businesses can be minimised and threats prevented from spreading throughout businesses systems.

  • Reduce Risk and Disruption

Cyber incidents can lead to financial loss, disruption to operations, damage to reputation and exposure of confidential information.

Having a SOC in place can reduce this risk. By identifying vulnerabilities, monitoring suspicious activity and improving incident responses, the risk of incidents occurring can be reduced. Performing regular security assessments and continuous monitoring within the organisation can improve overall security.

  • Improved Compliance

Many industries have specific security and data protection requirements. Having a SOC in place can improve compliance within businesses. By recording security data, logging incidents, monitoring access and creating reports, compliance can be improved.

This can allow businesses to be better prepared for security assessments, and prove that they have good security management in place.

  • Key Tools within a SOC

There are several key tools that can be utilised within a Security Operations Centre to improve threat visibility and response.

  • Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)
    – SIEM tools allow security log data to be collected from various systems. This enables security teams to determine suspicious patterns of activity, and investigate possible incidents.

  • Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)
    – EDR tools monitor devices such as laptops, desktops and servers. They can detect malicious activity and assist with investigation and containment.

  • Security Orchestration Automation and Response (SOAR)
    – SOAR tools automate repetitive security tasks and streamline incident response processes within businesses. Security analysts can then focus on more complex security investigations.

  • Threat Intelligence
    – Threat intelligence tools give insight into new cyber threats, malicious IP addresses, types of attacks and vulnerabilities.

Using these tools enables SOC teams to better understand threats, prioritise alerts and respond to incidents efficiently.

NOC vs SOC

Although both Security Operations Centres and Network Operations Centres monitor IT infrastructures within businesses, they have different roles.

While a SOC aims to protect systems from cyber threats, a NOC focuses on ensuring networks operate with optimum availability, performance and stability.

Within a SOC, suspicious logins and potential malware will be investigated. Within a NOC, network outages, connection issues and performance issues with servers will be investigated.

Both NOCs and SOCS support business continuity, however they focus on different priorities.

Should SMES have a SOC?

Small and medium sized enterprises hold valuable customer data, finances, applications and confidential company data. However, creating an internal SOC may be expensive as it requires substantial investment in infrastructure, tools and skilled staff.

To help alleviate this issue, businesses can use Managed Security Services or SOC as a service.

This means that businesses can benefit from expert cyber security support, security monitoring, threat detection and incident management without having to employ large numbers of staff in security.

Depending on the infrastructure, requirements and budget of the business, businesses can choose which method of security monitoring they would like to use.

Best Practices

To improve the effectiveness of an SOC, the following Best Practices should be taken into consideration.

  • Ensure continuous monitoring of critical systems.
  • Implement appropriate SIEM and endpoint security tools.
  • Create procedures for managing incidents.
  • Regularly review security alerts, and investigate any unusual activity.
  • Train staff to be aware of phishing/social engineering attacks.
  • Perform vulnerability testing and audits.
  • Measure performance using metrics, such as Mean Time to detect and Mean Time to respond.
  • Regularly update security procedures and policies.

By doing this, businesses can have a more proactive approach to security.

Conclusion

A Security Operations Centre is an important feature within modern cyber security strategies. They allow businesses to monitor their digital environment, detect threats, manage incidents and reduce the risk of cyber attacks.

As businesses become increasingly digital, it is no longer optional to implement proactive security monitoring. Whether internally or with a managed security provider, having an efficient Security Operations Centre in place can help organisations protect valuable assets, and ensure business continuity.

To learn more about the key roles, tools within SOC operations and business benefits, take a look at this guide: Security Operations Centre in modern Cybersecurity

title: How I built a browser-local batch image workflow with Canvas and ZIP
description:
Preparing product images is rarely one operation. You may need to fit every image into the same canvas, choose a background color, convert formats, rename the files, and download the set. Repeating those steps for each file is tedious.

I built a batch product image workflow for PNGDock to put those operations in one browser session. This post covers the implementation choices and the limits I had to make explicit. The workflow is free to try without an account. Its image processing and ZIP creation happen in the browser; the selected images are not uploaded for this workflow.

Start with limits, not the processing loop

The tool accepts PNG, JPEG, and WebP files. At present, it caps a batch at 20 files, 12 MB per file, 80 MB of source files in total, and 32 megapixels per image. It also caps the combined output size for a ZIP at 150 MB.

Those limits are part of the design. A compressed source file can decode into a much larger bitmap, and a browser may hold the decoded image, canvas, encoded output, and ZIP data at different points in the workflow. A file-size check alone cannot protect memory usage.

Each candidate file is checked before entering the queue. The tool verifies its extension and reported MIME type, tries to decode it, reads its dimensions, and rejects images above the pixel limit. Browser-side validation is still not a security boundary for a server, but here it keeps the local workflow from accepting inputs it is unlikely to handle well.

Decode and process one image at a time

The processing loop is sequential. For each file, it creates an ImageBitmap when the browser supports it, with an image-element fallback. It draws the decoded image into a target-size canvas, encodes the result, then releases the bitmap and clears the canvas dimensions.

The core fit calculation is small:

const scale = fit === "cover"
  ? Math.max(targetWidth / image.width, targetHeight / image.height)
  : Math.min(targetWidth / image.width, targetHeight / image.height);

const drawWidth = image.width * scale;
const drawHeight = image.height * scale;

context.drawImage(
  image,
  (targetWidth - drawWidth) / 2,
  (targetHeight - drawHeight) / 2,
  drawWidth,
  drawHeight
);

cover fills the canvas and crops the overflow. contain keeps the whole image visible and may leave empty space around it. The user can keep that space transparent or fill it with white or a chosen color. For JPEG output, a transparent choice becomes white because JPEG has no alpha channel.

One important distinction: a canvas background is not background removal. If the source photo contains a wall or a tabletop, choosing white does not cut the subject out. The page says this plainly, because the two operations are easy to confuse.

Encode according to the selected format

The browser's canvas.toBlob() handles the initial PNG, JPEG, or WebP encoding. A quality control applies to JPEG and WebP. PNG output gets an additional pass through an OxiPNG WebAssembly module, and the tool keeps the optimized file only if it is smaller than the initial PNG.

This still does not guarantee that every output will be smaller than its input. Dimensions, image content, format, and the source file's existing compression all matter. The interface shows source and result sizes so the user can compare them.

I also invalidate previous results when an export setting changes. Otherwise, a queue could silently contain files rendered with different dimensions or formats while presenting them as one batch.

Build the ZIP locally

Each successful result can be downloaded separately. For the whole set, the tool builds a ZIP in the browser. It writes ZIP local file headers, CRC-32 checksums, a central directory, and an end-of-central-directory record, then creates a Blob for download.

The ZIP entries use the already encoded image bytes. ZIP does not need to compress those bytes again, which is useful because PNG, JPEG, and WebP are already compressed formats.

Generated names are sanitized, length-limited, and made unique even when two source files would produce the same output name. A failed image stays visible in the queue and can be retried without discarding successful results. The user can also stop after the image currently being processed.

What browser-local actually means

The image bytes stay in the browser for this particular workflow. That does not mean the site makes zero network requests: it still loads the application code, and ordinary site analytics may send non-image events. It means this workflow does not send the selected image content to an image-processing server.

There are trade-offs. A large batch can still consume substantial memory, processing speed depends on the user's device, and a browser tab can be closed before export. The current limits and sequential loop are deliberate ways to keep those risks manageable, not claims that the browser can process arbitrarily large collections.

If you build similar tools, I would test the failure paths early: a corrupt file in the middle of a batch, two names that collide after sanitization, a PNG whose optimized version is larger, and a ZIP that crosses the output cap. The happy path is only half of the experience.

The live workflow and source repository are available if you want to inspect or try the implementation. I would be interested in hearing which browser-side failure cases or memory constraints you have run into with batch image tools.

Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against the PNGDock project source. Please review the implementation details and wording before publishing.

title: How to add a contact form to a static site without Formspree or Netlify Forms
description:
A static site is easy until someone needs to write to you.

mailto: leaks your address to scrapers. A Google Form looks like a Google Form. And the usual next step — Formspree, Basin, Netlify Forms, a serverless function plus a database — is either a monthly bill or a small project of its own.

You can host a tiny form backend yourself. This post walks through a working setup: a plain HTML form, a Node.js endpoint with no npm dependencies, a honeypot, and an inbox that is just a file on disk.

The finished starter is called Formbox Lite. It is free and MIT licensed. You can follow along and write it yourself, or clone the repo at the end and run node server.js.

1. The form on your site

No JavaScript required:

<form action="https://forms.yourdomain.com/f/contact" method="POST">
  <label>Name <input type="text" name="name" required></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required></label>
  <label>Message <textarea name="message" required></textarea></label>

  <input type="text" name="_gotcha" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off"
         style="position:absolute;left:-8000px" aria-hidden="true">

  <input type="hidden" name="_next" value="/thanks.html">
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

The _gotcha field is a honeypot. People never see it. A lot of bots still fill every input they find. If that field is not empty, the server should pretend the submit worked and then throw the message away.

_next is where the browser goes after a successful HTML submit. The server must only redirect to a path on your own origin, or you have built an open redirect.

2. A server that only does one thing

You do not need Express for this. Node's built-in http module is enough:

  • POST /f/contact accepts application/x-www-form-urlencoded or application/json
  • Reject an empty body
  • Reject the honeypot (with a fake success)
  • Rate-limit by a hash of the client address — do not store raw IPs
  • Append a JSON object to data/submissions.jsonl
  • Redirect to /thanks.html, or return { ok: true, id } if the client asked for JSON

JSON Lines is an underrated database for a contact form. You can read it with any editor, back it up by copying one file, and grep it when you need to. You only outgrow it when you have many forms, search, or notifications — not on day one.

3. An inbox you can actually open

A raw .jsonl file works, but a /inbox page is nicer when you are testing. On localhost it can be open. In production, put a password in front of it and serve it over HTTPS.

That is the whole product for a personal site: form, endpoint, file, inbox.

4. What this does not do (yet)

A one-form starter will not:

  • email you when a message arrives
  • post to Slack or a CRM
  • run captcha or a serious spam model
  • manage ten forms for ten sites

If you need those, you are in "real form backend" territory. I also make a fuller kit for that. For a single contact page, the lite server is enough.

5. Run it 

# download the zip from the link above and unzip it
cd formbox-lite
node server.js

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000, send a message, then open /inbox. There is a short go-live checklist in the README (HOST, PUBLIC_URL, ALLOWED_ORIGIN, INBOX_PASSWORD, a persistent disk).

Download (free, pay-what-you-want): https://richestcountry.gumroad.com/l/formbox-lite

If you want the multi-form dashboard, spam filtering, SMTP and signed webhooks: Formbox Kit ($19).

Questions and patches are welcome. Tell me what broke when you put it in front of a real site.

title: Convert Time Columns into Rows and Pivot into a New Cross Table
description:
Problem Description

The table tb can be seen as a cross table: the combination of the ID and PartNum fields forms the row header, the three field names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime form the column header, and the cells hold time points. Neither the content nor the number of the row headers is fixed. Now the table has to be turned around: the original cells (the time points) become the row header of the new table, the original row header (the combination of PartNum and ID) becomes the column header of the new table, and the original three column headers are replaced by the strings ENTERED, PICKED and DELIVERED, which are filled into the cells.

Source Data

Expected Result

The column header is the combination of PartNum and ID, the row header is the time point, and the cells hold the action names:

The first row 2024-03-28 08:59:13.727 falls in the column 50A_100 with the value ENTERED, which means it is the entered time of the record with ID=100 and PartNum=50A. Further down the same column the rows PICKED and DELIVERED appear, which are the picked time and the delivered time of that record. In other words, the three time points that used to lie side by side in one row are now stacked vertically in one column.

The records with ID=171 and ID=211 have only an entered time, while the picked and delivered times are empty, so the columns 50A_171 and 70B_211 each contain a single ENTERED and no PICKED or DELIVERED. Empty values have to be filtered out first, otherwise the new table would contain two meaningless time point rows.

The number of columns of the new table equals the number of "row header combinations" in the source data (4 in this example), and the number of rows equals the total number of non-empty values in the three time columns (6 plus 2, that is 8, in this example). Neither direction is fixed, which is why this problem cannot be solved by hard-coding the column names.

SQLazy Step-by-Step Implementation

The essence of this problem is pivoting twice. The first pivot turns the three time columns into rows, so that every time point occupies a row of its own and carries the action it belongs to; the second pivot turns the rows back into columns, using the combination of PartNum and ID as the new column names. Both pivots use the pivot action: the first one uses its inverse mode (column-to-row) and the second one uses the default mode (row-to-column). Two small things happen in between: filtering out the empty time points, and replacing the action field names with the short names the problem asks for.

[Click to run this example online]

The steps are explained below.


Step 1: Turn the three time columns into rows

pivot group ID, PartNum; name action_type; value t_stamp; inverse

This is the first key action of the problem. The pivot action turns rows into columns by default, and adding the inverse parameter switches it to column-to-row: the two grouping columns ID and PartNum stay unchanged, the other three time columns are expanded into rows, the original column names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime become the values of the new column action_type, and the original column values (the time points) become the values of the new column t_stamp.

After this step one wide record becomes three long records: the record with ID=100 turns into three rows carrying the three action names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime together with their time points. How many row header combinations and how many column headers there are does not affect this action, so an unfixed number of row headers is not a problem.

Step 2: Filter out the empty time points
filter (t_stamp notnull)
In the source data the records with ID=171 and ID=211 have only an entered time, while the picked and delivered times are empty. Column-to-row also expands the empty values into rows, and those rows are meaningless, so they are filtered out first. The test for an empty value uses the not-null function, and the whole condition is written inside the parentheses of the filter action.

Step 3: Replace the action names with the short names the problem asks for
compute if(action_type = “EnteredOn” then “ENTERED”, action_type = “PickedTime” then “PICKED”, action_type = “DeliveredTime” then “DELIVERED”) as status
The problem requires the cells to hold ENTERED, PICKED and DELIVERED, while column-to-row produces the original column names, so a computed column with the condition function performs the mapping: when the action name equals EnteredOn it becomes ENTERED, when it equals PickedTime it becomes PICKED, and when it equals DeliveredTime it becomes DELIVERED. The result goes into the new column status. The condition function can test several conditions in turn and return the matching value, which suits this kind of mapping with several equality branches.

Step 4: Build the column names of the new table
compute concat(PartNum, “_”, ID) as col_name
The column header of the new table is the combination of PartNum and ID joined by an underscore, such as 50A_100. The concat function joins the two fields and the underscore in between into one string, which is written into the new column col_name. The column names are not known in advance but computed from the data, which is the other reason this problem cannot hard-code them.

Step 5: Keep only the three columns that are needed
derive t_stamp, col_name, status
The previous steps leave intermediate columns such as ID, PartNum and action_type. The second pivot needs only the time point, the column name and the action name, so the derive action picks those three out.

Step 6: Turn the rows into columns
pivot group t_stamp; name col_name; value status; header ‘50A_100’,‘60B_125’,‘50A_171’,‘70B_211’
The second pivot does not write a calculation method and uses the default row-to-column mode: group by t_stamp, let every value of col_name become the name of a new column, and fill the values of status into the matching cells. One row and one column occur only once in the data (a time point belongs to the action of a single record), so no aggregation algorithm has to be specified and the default of taking the first record in the group is enough.
No inverse parameter is written here, which is the opposite of step 1: step 1 turns columns into rows and this step turns rows into columns, and the two pivots together turn the whole table around.

Generated SQL

After confirming the logic of the above 6 steps, the SQLazy compiler automatically generates native SQL (MySQL syntax used here):

WITH t1 AS (
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'EnteredOn' AS action_type, EnteredOn AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
        UNION ALL
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'PickedTime' AS action_type, PickedTime AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
        UNION ALL
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'DeliveredTime' AS action_type, DeliveredTime AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
    ),
    t5 AS (
        SELECT t_stamp
            , concat_ws('', PartNum, '_', ID) AS col_name
            , CASE
                WHEN action_type = 'EnteredOn' THEN 'ENTERED'
                WHEN action_type = 'PickedTime' THEN 'PICKED'
                WHEN action_type = 'DeliveredTime' THEN 'DELIVERED'
                ELSE NULL
            END AS status
        FROM t1
        WHERE t_stamp IS NOT NULL
    ),
    t5_2 AS (
        SELECT t_stamp, col_name, status
            , FIRST_VALUE(status) OVER (PARTITION BY t_stamp, col_name ORDER BY NULL) AS FIRST_1
        FROM t5
    )
SELECT t_stamp
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '50A_100' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `50A_100`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '50A_171' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `50A_171`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '60B_125' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `60B_125`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '70B_211' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `70B_211`
FROM t5_2
GROUP BY t_stamp

SQLazy lets you describe logic in business language instead of writing nested SQL queries. Each of the two pivots in this problem is expressed by a single pivot statement: the first uses the inverse mode to expand the three time columns into rows and the second uses the default mode to turn the rows back into columns, so the two steps "columns to rows, then rows to columns" are obvious at a glance and there is no need to hand-write UNION ALL and hard-coded CASE branches in SQL.

The two modes of the pivot action are the key to this problem. One and the same action switches direction depending on whether the inverse parameter is present, and both directions share the same wording of grouping column, name column and value column, so the business statement "which field becomes the new column name and which field becomes the new value" can be copied straight into the parameters without first working out whether SQL needs CASE or UNION.

When the new column names come from the data itself (PartNum joined with ID), SQL can only hard-code them in the statement, and the statement has to be edited whenever the data changes. SQLazy treats building the column name as an ordinary computed column, so the names are generated from the data and neither a change in the number of row headers nor in the number of column headers requires a code change.

Step-by-step calculation lets every step be inspected on its own: after step 1 you can see the expanded long table, after step 2 you can see that the empty values are gone, and after step 4 you can see the finished column names, so when something goes wrong there is no need to run the whole statement and then guess which part is at fault.

Official Links

SQLazy Online Experience: sqlazy.com (free, no registration required)

SQLazy Repository: github.com/SPLWare/SQLazy

title: Drift Is the Audit Finding: Detecting Network Configuration Drift Across Clouds Before an Auditor Does
description:
Every multi-cloud estate has two networks. One lives in code: the route tables, security groups, firewall rules, DNS zones, and interconnect settings declared in Terraform, Pulumi, or a pile of reviewed change tickets. The other lives in the clouds themselves, and it changes a little every week. Someone opens a port during an incident and forgets to close it. A console fix solves an outage and never makes it back into code. A vendor adds a route during a maintenance window. None of it feels like a security event at the time. Months later, in a SOC 2 observation window, it becomes one: the estate cannot show that the network running today is the network that was approved.

Drift is rarely dramatic. That is exactly why it survives. The work is not finding one bad rule. The work is building a routine that notices small differences early, while they are still cheap to explain.

Decide what counts as the baseline, per cloud

A drift check is only as good as the baseline it compares against, and a multi-cloud baseline cannot be one flat list. The same intent, say "only the application tier may reach the database tier on the database port", is enforced by security groups in one cloud, network security groups in another, and firewall policies in a third, each with different defaults and different ways of expressing a deny.

Start from intent, then record the expected enforcement in each cloud in that cloud's own terms. For each cross-cloud segment, write down the expected routes, the expected allowed flows, the expected DNS answers, and the expected logging state. Keep that record in version control next to the code that creates it. When a reviewer asks why a rule exists, the answer should be in the record, not in the memory of whoever was on call.

Avoid baselining everything. An estate wide comparison against every default and cosmetic setting produces thousands of harmless differences and trains everyone to ignore the report. Baseline the controls that matter: ingress and egress paths, route advertisements, encryption settings on interconnects, private endpoint exposure, DNS resolution for internal names, and whether flow logs are actually being delivered.

Read the live estate on a schedule, not on request

Drift detection that runs only when someone remembers is not detection. Poll each cloud's network configuration on a fixed cadence, daily for high change environments and at least weekly otherwise, using read only credentials scoped to that job. Store each snapshot with a timestamp, so a difference can be placed in time rather than argued about later.

Compare in both directions. Code that was applied but never took effect is as much a finding as a manual change nobody declared. A rule that exists in code and not in the cloud may mean a failed apply, a later console edit, or a resource recreated outside the pipeline. Each explanation has a different fix, and the snapshot history is usually what separates them.

Normalise before comparing. Cloud APIs return the same rule in different orders, with different generated identifiers, and with defaults made explicit in one cloud and implied in another. A comparison that flags ordering noise as drift will be muted within a month. Sort, strip generated fields, expand defaults, and compare the normalised form. Reserve human attention for differences that change who can reach what.

Give every difference an owner and an expiry

A drift report with no workflow behind it becomes a weekly guilt email. Route each confirmed difference to one of three outcomes, and record which one was chosen.

First, accept and codify: the change was right, so update the code and the baseline, with the same review a planned change would get. Second, revert: the change was temporary or wrong, so remove it in the cloud and confirm the next snapshot is clean. Third, exception: the difference must stay for a stated reason, for a stated period, with a named owner. Exceptions without an expiry date are just undocumented architecture, and auditors treat them that way.

Incident fixes deserve a special path, because they are the largest honest source of drift. When a responder changes a network control during an outage, the incident ticket should carry a drift task that cannot be closed by the incident itself. The fix stays in place while the incident is open. Within a few days, someone either codifies it or reverts it, and the snapshot history shows both steps.

Watch the quiet controls, not just the rules

The most valuable drift findings are often not in the rules at all. Flow logs that stopped being delivered after a storage change. An interconnect whose encryption setting reverted during a provider migration. A private DNS zone that is no longer associated with one of the networks it serves, so internal names resolve over a public path in one cloud only. A route that is still advertised but no longer preferred, leaving a failover path untested and effectively absent.

Include those states in the baseline: logging delivery, encryption posture, DNS association, route preference, and health check targets. A network can match its rule baseline perfectly and still have lost the evidence trail an auditor needs, or the failover path an incident will need. SOC 2 readiness is about whether controls operate over time, and quiet controls are where operating over time fails first.

Turn snapshots into evidence without extra work

If snapshots are timestamped, normalised, and kept with the decisions made about each difference, the audit conversation changes shape. Instead of reconstructing the past from tickets and memory, a team can show the baseline, the snapshot history, the differences found, and how each one was resolved. That is the shape of change management evidence: not a claim that nothing ever drifted, but a record that drift was looked for, found, and handled.

Keep retention aligned with the observation window. Snapshots deleted after thirty days cannot support a review covering six months. Store them cheaply, in object storage with versioning, and test a restore once. Evidence that cannot be retrieved is a finding waiting for the worst possible moment to announce itself.

A short checklist for cross-cloud drift control

  1. One intent record per segment, expressed per cloud in that cloud's own terms.
  2. Baseline only what matters: paths, flows, encryption, DNS, and logging delivery.
  3. Scheduled, read only snapshots in every cloud, kept with timestamps.
  4. Normalised comparison, so ordering and defaults never masquerade as drift.
  5. Every difference codified, reverted, or excepted with an owner and an expiry.
  6. Incident fixes carry a follow up drift task that outlives the incident.
  7. Quiet controls checked too: log delivery, DNS association, route preference.
  8. Snapshot retention matched to the audit observation window, with a tested restore.

No estate stays identical to its code forever, and pretending otherwise is what turns routine change into audit risk. The estates that pass cleanly are the ones that notice their own drift first, explain it while the context is fresh, and keep the receipts as a byproduct of normal operations. That discipline, applied to private connectivity and zero trust controls across clouds, is part of the SOC 2 readiness work described at cloudverg.com, where VergShield and VergMesh are used to keep multi-cloud network controls consistent and observable.

Drift will happen either way. The only choice is who finds it first.

title: IP44 Socket vs IP67: Which Rating Fits Your Site?
description:
Quick Answer

An IP44 socket is a socket rated to keep out solid objects larger than 1.0 mm and water splashed against it from any direction. An IP67 socket adds 30 minutes of temporary immersion at 1 m depth. Each rating is tested in one defined condition, so IP44 will not survive a hose jet and IP67 will not survive a pressure washer.

This guide compares what each digit actually proves, how the mated pair changes the answer, and where each rating belongs on a working site.

What Do the Two Digits in IP44 and IP67 Measure?

An IP code is a two-digit ingress protection rating published in IEC 60529, the international standard for enclosure sealing. The first digit covers solid objects, from a fingertip to fine dust. The second digit covers water, from vertical drips to high-pressure jets. Each digit is tested separately, on a defined sample, in a defined state.

On an industrial socket the code describes the product, not the installation. It says nothing about the cable, the gland, the panel cutout or the way the socket was mounted. Those parts decide whether the rating is still true after the first winter outdoors.

What the First Digit Covers for a Socket

Level 4 is the usual baseline for indoor industrial sockets. A 1.0 mm diameter probe pushed with 1 N of force must not reach live parts, and the enclosure must stop solid objects of 1.0 mm and above. Level 5 adds dust protection with limited ingress, and level 6 is dust tight. Most splash-proof sockets stop at 4, while watertight versions usually reach 6.

What the Second Digit Covers for Water

The water digits step up through different test rigs. Splash, jet and immersion are not variations of one test; they load the seal from different directions, at different pressures and for different times. A socket that passes a splash test can still take water the moment someone rests a hose against the lid.

Water digit Test condition Where it usually belongs
IPX4 Splashing water from any direction, 10 min at roughly 10 L/min Covered workshop, plant room, under a canopy
IPX5 6.3 mm nozzle, 12.5 L/min at 30 kPa, 3 min from about 3 m Open loading bay, edge of a wash area
IPX6 12.5 mm nozzle, 100 L/min at 100 kPa, 3 min from about 3 m Deck wash, jet cleaning a few metres away
IPX7 Temporary immersion, 30 min with the lowest point 1 m under water Open yard socket, pit, slab that can flood
IPX9K 80 °C water at 80 to 100 bar, 14 to 16 L/min, four angles Food and beverage washdown zones

Where Does IP44 Stop Working?

An IP44 socket handles rain, a mop splash and condensation running down a wall. It stops working when water arrives with speed. A garden hose at close range already delivers something closer to the IPX5 jet than to the IPX4 splash, and a washdown lance is two digits further away again.

Driving rain on an exposed wall is the other weak case. The test sprays from any direction for 10 minutes, but it does not reproduce wind pushing water into a lid lip for a full season. Sites that leave sockets facing the weather usually move those positions to IP67 even when the covered positions stay at IP44.

What Does an IP67 Socket Actually Survive?

IP67 makes two claims at once: dust tight at digit 6, and 30 minutes of immersion at digit 7. The immersion test puts the lowest point of the sample 1 m below the surface for 30 minutes, with no spraying and no pressure applied. Water may enter, provided it does not reach a harmful quantity or affect operation.

What the Immersion Test Does Not Cover

It does not cover 3 m, 8 hours, or water arriving at 80 bar. Continuous immersion is IP68, where depth and duration are agreed between buyer and maker rather than fixed by the standard. High-pressure cleaning is IP69K. An IP67 socket standing in a flooded pit for a week has left its test envelope, even though the label still reads IP67.

Does the Rating Apply to the Socket, the Plug or the Pair?

This is the most common source of field failures. A manufacturer tests and publishes a rating for one defined condition, and for a panel socket that condition is often the closed lid. For a plug and socket together it is the mated pair, and usually the pair from the same series.

IEC 60309-1 splits industrial plugs and sockets into splash-proof types, rated IP44, and watertight types, rated IP67. A watertight socket with a splash-proof plug in it is a compromise, not a rated assembly. Match both halves, and read the datasheet for the exact state that was tested.

The unmated state is the weak point. An IP67 socket with the lid hanging open is a funnel, and a spring that has lost tension defeats the seal without leaving a mark. This is why tethered lids and spare gaskets belong on the maintenance list, not in a drawer.

Which Rating Fits Which Location?

Most sites do not need one rating everywhere. The differences are modest per unit and significant per installation, so the practical method is to grade the location and match the socket to it. The table below is a starting point, not a substitute for the project specification.

Location Minimum rating Reason
Indoor workshop, dry floor IP44 Splash only; quick service access matters
Covered yard, canopy edge IP44 to IP65 Wind-driven rain reaches the lid
Open yard, no shelter IP67 Standing water and pooled rain
Washdown bay, food line IP67, with IP69K where jets are aimed Pressure and temperature, not volume
Construction site distribution IP44 minimum, IP67 at ground level IEC 60364-7-704 treats these as a special case

Construction and demolition sites deserve a separate note. IEC 60364-7-704 handles socket outlets on such sites as a special case and commonly sets IP44 as the floor for the assembly. Units that sit on the ground or in a puddle are still better served by a watertight version, because the rating was never meant to survive standing water.

Why Do Sealed Sockets Still Fill With Water?

Water inside a sealed enclosure rarely comes past the gasket. It usually travels down the cable, through a gland that does not match the jacket, or condenses out of the air pocket when the temperature drops overnight.

What Cable Entry Does to the Rating

A socket is rated with its own entry, and once a gland is fitted the assembly inherits the gland's seal and the installer's torque. A jacket diameter outside the clamping range leaves a path along the sheath, and water follows it by capillary action into the terminal chamber. Measure the jacket rather than the conductor, and check the gland range before ordering.

Why Condensation Forms Inside a Sealed Socket

A sealed enclosure that warms by day and cools at night pulls moisture out of the cable and the trapped air. No IP rating addresses that. A drain point, a breather membrane or a desiccant does, and the same failure path is covered in our review of the common causes of industrial connector failure in harsh environments.

What Do You Lose by Specifying IP67 Everywhere?

Watertight construction is not free. Gaskets, tighter tolerances, heavier lids and higher insertion force all add cost and time, and every service visit ends with a lid that has to be re-seated correctly. A torn gasket turns an IP67 socket into an unrated one with no visible warning.

There are practical losses too:

  • Sealed sockets hold moisture in as effectively as they keep it out, so a wet assembly stays wet.
  • Usable cable range narrows as the entry gets tighter.
  • Inspection takes longer, because the state of the seal is hidden under the lid.
  • Every service visit ends with a lid that must be re-seated, and a torn gasket is invisible.

Where a location is genuinely dry, an IP44 socket is easier to live with, and the budget is better spent on the positions that face water. The same logic applies to the plug on the cable: a watertight plug on a splash-proof cordset does not raise the rating of either part.

How Should the IP Requirement Be Written on a Drawing?

Two digits on a drawing are ambiguous. They say nothing about the state tested, the standard applied, or the cable entry the socket must accept. A supplier can meet that line item exactly and still deliver something that fails in service, so the requirement needs the surrounding conditions attached.

The IP Rating Requirement Checklist

  • Rating and standard: state IP44 or IP67 to IEC 60529, not the digits alone.
  • Tested state: closed lid, mated pair, or unmated with the cap fitted.
  • Cable entry: gland type and thread, plus the jacket diameter range the socket must accept.
  • Environment beyond water: UV exposure, salt spray, wash chemicals and ambient temperature.
  • Evidence: the test report, or at minimum the state and duration that were tested.
  • Service items: tethered lid, spare gaskets and expected mating cycles per shift.

Housing material belongs on the same list. A polyamide that absorbs water or ages under UV will loosen its grip on the gasket long before the contacts wear, which is why material choice decides long-term reliability as much as the rating does.

Which Evidence Should a Supplier Provide?

Ask for the test state before the test number. A report that shows IP67 on a closed lid tells you the gasket works; it does not tell you the socket stays sealed with a plug inserted in the rain. Ask which sample was tested, whether it was mated, and how long the sample had been in service before the test.

For the wider picture, our guide to how IP67, IP68 and IP69K affect application selection covers the upper end of the scale, and the comparison of IP65 to IP69K housings shows what changes inside a product when the second digit rises.

WEIPU has manufactured circular and industrial connectors since 1996, and the TYP range carries the same IEC 60309 pin configurations in splash-proof and watertight builds. Treat the catalogue as an evaluation starting point: verify the part number, the tested state behind the rating, and the gland range against the current datasheet before the socket goes on a drawing.

Conclusion

IP44 and IP67 answer different questions. IP44 says the socket tolerates splashing from any direction; IP67 says it tolerates 30 minutes under 1 m of still water. Neither says anything about jets, cable entries, condensation or the state of the lid. Grade the site, write the tested condition on the drawing, match plug to socket, and measure the cable before choosing the gland. Then check the report rather than the two digits.

Related Products for Outdoor and Washdown Sockets

The TYP range splits the same IEC 60309 pin configurations into splash-proof IP44 and watertight IP67 builds, so a site can be graded without changing the plug convention between areas. The four parts below cover the two most common split points: plugs on the cable side, and panel sockets where the water actually arrives.

  • The 16 A 3-pin IP44 cable plug by TYP231 is the splash-proof half for covered bays and indoor distribution.
  • The 16 A 3-pin IP67 cable plug by TYPR171 adds a sealed shell and cap for open yards and wet slabs.
  • The 32 A 3-pin IP44 angled panel socket by TYP3801 suits panel edges that see splashes but never jets.
  • The 63 A 5-pin IP67 angled panel socket by TYP3924 covers three-phase positions exposed to standing water.

Each part exists in several current ratings and pin counts, so confirm the contact layout and the tested state of the rating against the datasheet before ordering. The full range of IP44 and IP67 plugs and sockets, with the tested state written on each datasheet, is listed on the TYP IEC 60309 connector page.

Discuss Your IP44 Socket Requirements

Send the working conditions and we will reply with specific part numbers plus the evidence behind each rating, rather than a generic catalogue page. The more of the following you can supply, the shorter the review loop:

  • Installation: indoor, covered or exposed; panel position and mounting height.
  • Cable: jacket outer diameter, conductor cross-section, and whether a gland is already specified.
  • Electrical: current, voltage, pin count, and any three-phase or neutral requirement.
  • Environment: target IP rating, cleaning method and pressure, UV, salt and ambient temperature.

For drawings, samples or a rating review, contact the WEIPU engineering team and describe the socket position you are working on.
