Open WebCapture to Figma in a Figma file. You have two routes.

  • By URL. The page is rendered in a remote browser on Apify. Add your own Apify API token once; a free Apify account is enough to start.
  • With the Chrome extension. Best for pages behind a login or a bot wall. Capture the page as you see it and paste the result into the plugin. This route needs no token.

Choose a width before you import: Desktop 1440, iPad 820, Pixel 7, iPhone 14 Pro, iPhone SE, or a 360px Android phone. The width you pick is the layout you download. For more on picking breakpoints, read importing mobile and tablet websites to Figma.

Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

2. Optionally record a flow

If you want more than the default view, record the clicks in the Chrome extension first, such as opening a menu or toggling a price. That flow replays in the downloaded project. The method is covered in recording a website user flow.

3. Press Download HTML

After the import finishes, press Download HTML in the plugin. Save the project into its own folder so its files stay together.

How to open the project

Open the folder and double-click the HTML file. It opens in your default browser. Hover the buttons, watch the animations, click the links.

If anything does not load when opened straight from disk, serve the folder locally instead. Browsers apply stricter rules to file:// pages, and a local server avoids them. Two common options:

# Python 3, from inside the project folder
python3 -m http.server 8000

# Node.js
npx serve .

Then visit http://localhost:8000 (or the address serve prints).

Since it is a standard static project, you can also open it in your code editor, inspect the CSS, and change things.

What works, and what to expect

Feature In the downloaded project
Layout, colours, gradients, shadows Rendered as captured
Images Included
Google fonts Included
Hover states Work
CSS animations Play
Links Work
Recorded flow from the Chrome extension Replays

A few practical notes:

  • One page, one width. The project reflects the page at the width you captured. Capture again at another width if you need a mobile version.
  • Non-Google fonts. The documentation mentions Google fonts being included. If a site uses a licensed font from elsewhere, check how it renders and swap it if needed.
  • Server features do not come along. Forms that post to a backend, search and logins depend on the original server. The project is a front end copy.

Three ways to use the project

Open it as a reference

Keep a dated snapshot of your own site before a redesign. Months later, you can still open it and see exactly how the old version behaved, including hover timing.

Add it to Figma as a code layer

A frame can show hover states and animations only as recorded data, since a Figma prototype cannot replay CSS animations. A code layer runs them. Figma plugins cannot create code layers, because the Plugin API has no way to make one. So WebCapture offers Copy prompt: paste it into Claude with the Figma MCP connected, and Claude adds the project as a code layer beside your frame. Set the layer to the size the prompt names, then press play. Code layers cannot be resized from the API, so this step is yours. The full walkthrough is in turning a website into a Figma code layer.

Hand it to an LLM

The project is real code, so it is useful context for an AI. You can attach the HTML and CSS files to a Claude or ChatGPT conversation and ask for a specific change. For example: "Convert this hero section into a React component, keeping the CSS values."

If your goal is a fresh rebuild rather than an edit, the Chrome extension's Copy for LLM is built for that. It carries the layout, colours with real gradient stops, border and shadow values, fonts, inline SVG icons, every interaction and any recorded flow.

Privacy

With URL capture, the URL you enter is sent to Apify to be rendered. Nothing from your Figma file is uploaded. Captures pasted from the extension stay on your machine. The plugin never sends anything to an AI. If you share the project with Claude or ChatGPT, that is your choice and your paste.

Get started

WebCapture to Figma is a free plugin. Capture a page you own, press Download HTML, and open the result in your browser. You get an editable frame in Figma and a runnable project on disk from one capture.

FAQ

How do I download a website as HTML with working fonts?

Capture the page with WebCapture to Figma, then press Download HTML. The project includes the page's images and Google fonts, so it renders without reaching back to the original site for them.

Do hover states and animations work in the downloaded HTML?

Yes. According to the plugin's documentation, hover states, CSS animations and links work, and a flow recorded with the Chrome extension replays.

Can I download a page that needs a login?

Yes, through the Chrome extension. Capture the page as you see it, paste it into the plugin, then download. No Apify token is needed for this route.

Is Download HTML free?

WebCapture to Figma is a free plugin. URL capture uses your own Apify account, and a free one is enough to start.

Can I edit the downloaded project?

Yes. It is a standard HTML, CSS and JS project. Open it in any code editor, or hand it to an AI with a specific change request.

title: A ten-second Flutter pause with a visible Skip button
description:
Tap Amen in AlyDoit’s Flutter app Selah and a separate screen offers a breathing ring, a ten-second countdown, and a Skip button. The visible exit is the detail that makes it work as an optional pause.

Save the action before opening the pause

The chat records Amen before pushing the pause route. If the person chose to keep the prayer, the app saves that too. Then the chat awaits the pause route. When it closes, the chat records completion and scrolls to the new entry.

That order gives Skip one job. It closes the pause with the prayer decision already saved. A separate route also gives the countdown a clear lifetime. Flutter’s Navigator documentation

Give the animation and the timer different jobs

A reversible five-second animation controller scales the ring, while a one-second timer updates the number. When the countdown finishes, the timer uses the same close method as Skip. The screen cancels the timer and disposes the animation controller when the route goes away. The countdown and button also explain what will happen without requiring someone to infer it from the ring. Flutter’s AnimationController documentation

For a similar interaction, test Skip just before the final tick, system Back during the fade, and leaving and resuming the app during the countdown. If the exit can race the timer, make closing a one-time action. Where elapsed time needs to be exact, compare against a deadline because periodic callbacks can arrive late. Dart’s Timer.periodic documentation

This article was generated by an AI agent for AlyDoit using Selah’s source code. The test cases are suggestions.

title: BDSG § 37a: Explainable Credit Scoring in Spring Boot
description:
Short answer: Germany's § 37a BDSG, in force from 20 November 2026, permits credit scoring only inside fixed limits: restricted input data, an explanation available for every score, and records kept for about a year. In Spring Boot you meet those limits with a feature allow-list, a per-decision explanation record, an immutable decision log and an "explain my score" API.

Important: I am an engineer, not a lawyer, and none of this is legal advice. The sources I read disagree on a few details, including how payment-account data is treated and whether the cutover is worded as 19 or 20 November. Read the statute itself before you build on any of it. The consolidated BDSG text is on gesetze-im-internet.de, the amending act is in the Bundesgesetzblatt, and Article 22 is on EUR-Lex. Then get your data protection officer to sign off.

I have not built a bureau-grade scoring engine. My background is payments: PSD2 OpenBanking integrations, high-traffic booking flows at AirAsia, and lately PSD3 fraud-liability decision engines and mandate-safe commercial VRP payments. What carries over is the regulated-decision plumbing: allow-lists, snapshots, append-only logs. That is the part this post covers, and it is the part I would expect to survive whatever the final guidance says.

The date is this week. A lot of German fintech and BNPL ("buy now, pay later") backends are about to learn how much of their scoring code nobody can currently explain.

What changes, in one screen

Credit scoring is the practice of turning facts about a person into a number that predicts repayment. GDPR Article 22 limits decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect someone, and a declined "pay in 30 days" checkout is the classic case. Until now Germany handled scoring in § 31 BDSG. From 20 November 2026, as I read the coverage, § 37a takes over as a narrow, rule-bound exception: scoring stays allowed, inside these fences.

  1. Restricted inputs. Special-category data (health, religion, ethnicity), names, addresses and social-network data may not feed a score.
  2. Explainability. The lender must be able to describe the criteria behind a specific score in terms the person can follow.
  3. Records. Keep what is needed to reconstruct that explanation, reportedly for one year.

For a backend team, each fence maps to a component, and that is how the rest of this post is organised.

Why this lands on engineers

Scoring services tend to grow by accretion. A data scientist adds a column, a backend developer maps it, and months later nobody can say whether the postcode-derived feature is still in the model. If a customer or supervisor asks why an application was declined, the real answer today is often "let me dig through some old notebooks".

The new rules make that expensive. Forbidden data that slips in through a convenient join is a compliance defect. A decision you cannot tie to a model version is an audit gap. Records that can be edited are not evidence.

So I split the design into four building blocks:

  • A feature allow-list enforced at the pipeline boundary.
  • A per-decision explanation record: inputs, contributions, model version, outcome.
  • An immutable decision log with retention and an audit store.
  • An "explain my score" API that serves those records back to the affected person, in the spirit of GDPR Art. 15 (access) and Art. 22.

If you have read my piece on the transactional outbox and idempotent consumers, the log mechanics will look familiar. The novelty here is the content of the log and the inputs we refuse to accept.

Block 1: the allow-list belongs at the boundary

The usual first attempt is a deny-list: "never use these ten fields". It fails quietly. Someone adds locality_hint, nobody notices it is an address in disguise, and the deny-list never mentions it.

I flip it: only features that are explicitly registered can reach the model. Anything else is rejected before scoring starts. The compliant path becomes the only path. It is the same policy-as-code approach I used for DORA and NIS2 compliance evidence in Spring Boot: the rule lives in code and config, so it can be tested and diffed.

Each allowed feature carries a stable name, a data category, a note on why it is permitted, and a version.

public enum DataCategory { PAYMENT_BEHAVIOUR, CONTRACT_HISTORY, INCOME_DECLARED, DEVICE_RISK }

public record FeatureSpec(String name, DataCategory category, String legalBasisNote, int version) {}

@Component
public class FeatureAllowList {

    private final Map<String, FeatureSpec> allowed;

    public FeatureAllowList(FeatureRegistryProperties props) {
        this.allowed = props.features().stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(FeatureSpec::name, f -> f));
    }

    /** Returns only registered features; throws if anything unknown arrives. */
    public Map<String, Object> enforce(Map<String, Object> raw) {
        var unknown = raw.keySet().stream()
            .filter(k -> !allowed.containsKey(k))
            .toList();
        if (!unknown.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ForbiddenFeatureException(unknown);
        }
        return Map.copyOf(raw);
    }

    public FeatureSpec spec(String name) { return allowed.get(name); }
}

Two choices are deliberate. Unknown input throws rather than being silently dropped, because a silent drop hides an upstream bug while a loud failure gets fixed within a day. And DataCategory has no value for names, addresses or social data, so nobody can "just add one" without editing an enum, which is visible in code review.

Governance matters more than the code

The class above is twenty lines. The hard part is who may change the registry. My suggested rules:

  • Registry changes go through a pull request that needs sign-off from both the data science owner and whoever speaks for compliance. Make that a CODEOWNERS rule, not a convention.
  • Every entry needs a non-empty legalBasisNote; a startup check refuses to boot otherwise.
  • A CI test loads the registry and fails on any feature name matching a small set of suspicious patterns (addr, street, zip, plz, name, social). It is crude and produces false positives, but it would have caught locality_hint.

Proxies are the harder problem

An allow-list stops named forbidden fields. It does not stop an allowed field from acting as a stand-in for an excluded one. Device model can correlate with income, merchant category with religion or health, tenure with age. I would not claim the statute says anything specific here, but a supervisor reading your documentation will ask. At minimum, run a periodic proxy and disparity analysis over the stored feature snapshots (they are in the log anyway, see Block 2), and record the result next to the registry version. Treat that as an engineering control you can show, not as a legal conclusion.

The unclear part: payment-account data

The sources I found do not agree on how payment-account data, such as transaction history from an open-banking connection, is treated. I cannot settle that for you. What I can do is make the answer a configuration decision with an owner: the registry says whether each category is enabled, and the legal team's reading goes into legalBasisNote. When guidance firms up you flip a flag, redeploy, and have a diff to show. I took the same approach to consent scopes in my OpenBanking PSD2 work.

Block 2: the explanation record

An explanation is only as good as what you stored when the decision was made. You cannot rebuild it later from "current" weights, because the model has very likely been retrained since.

Every scoring call therefore writes a record containing:

  • a decision ID and timestamp,
  • the model version, an immutable identifier (a hash of the artifact works well),
  • the feature snapshot actually used,
  • per-feature contributions (weight times value for a scorecard, attribution values for anything fancier),
  • the score and the outcome,
  • the feature registry version, so you know what the allow-list looked like that day.

For credit I lean towards scorecards or monotonic models, where each contribution can be stated in a sentence. With gradient-boosted trees you can still produce attributions, but the "explanation" is then the output of a second method that itself must be versioned and defended. Simpler models are easier to explain to a customer and to a supervisor. If any part of your pipeline calls an LLM, the same record-everything habit applies; I cover it in observability and guardrails for agentic AI backends.

public record ScoringDecision(
        UUID decisionId,
        Instant decidedAt,
        String subjectRef,          // pseudonymous reference, never name or address
        String modelVersion,
        int registryVersion,
        Map<String, Object> inputs,
        Map<String, Double> contributions,
        double score,
        String outcome,
        boolean humanReviewRequested) {}

Note subjectRef. The log must not become a second copy of the customer database. Use a pseudonymous reference that your identity service can resolve when an access request arrives. That keeps the log useful for audit and limits the damage if it is ever exposed.

Can you actually replay a decision?

Storing inputs and a model hash only helps if you can load that exact model again. I treat replay as a test, not an aspiration: a nightly job picks a sample of stored decisions, loads the referenced model artifact, re-scores the stored snapshot and asserts the same score. A mismatch pages someone. It also forces you to keep old model artifacts around for at least as long as the log retention, which is a cost people forget to budget.

Block 3: an immutable log with outbox and Kafka

The receipts need three properties: a decision is never logged without its business outcome, a record cannot be edited afterwards, and consumers (audit store, analytics, the explain API) can rebuild their state from the stream.

The outbox pattern covers the first. In the same database transaction that stores the outcome, insert a row into an outbox table. A relay publishes it to Kafka, and consumers deduplicate by decisionId.

@Service
public class ScoringService {

    private final FeatureAllowList allowList;
    private final ScoringModel model;
    private final DecisionRepository decisions;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final ObjectMapper json;

    @Transactional
    public ScoringDecision score(String subjectRef, Map<String, Object> rawFeatures) {
        var inputs = allowList.enforce(rawFeatures);
        var result = model.evaluate(inputs);

        var decision = new ScoringDecision(
            UUID.randomUUID(), Instant.now(), subjectRef,
            model.version(), allowList.registryVersion(),
            inputs, result.contributions(), result.score(),
            result.outcome(), result.needsHumanReview());

        decisions.save(DecisionEntity.from(decision));
        outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of("scoring.decision.v1",
            decision.decisionId().toString(), toJson(decision)));
        return decision;
    }

    private String toJson(ScoringDecision d) {
        try { return json.writeValueAsString(d); }
        catch (JsonProcessingException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

Immutability needs enforcement at more than one level. On the Kafka side, use a topic with cleanup.policy=delete and a retention comfortably above your legal minimum, and restrict producers to the relay's service account. In the audit store, make the table append-only: no UPDATE or DELETE grants for the application role, and a hash column that chains each row to the previous one so tampering is detectable.

CREATE TABLE decision_audit (
    seq          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    decision_id  UUID        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    subject_ref  TEXT        NOT NULL,
    decided_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    payload      JSONB       NOT NULL,
    prev_hash    BYTEA       NOT NULL,
    row_hash     BYTEA       NOT NULL
);
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON decision_audit FROM scoring_app;

Retention and erasure collide

Here is a tension I would raise with the DPO before launch. You keep records for roughly a year so scores can be explained, yet a customer may also exercise the right to erasure. A hash-chained table makes row deletion awkward by design. My way out is to keep personal content out of the chain: the chained row holds the pseudonymous subjectRef and a hash of the payload, while the readable snapshot lives in a separate table keyed by decision_id. Erasure then deletes or redacts the readable part, and the chain still proves that a decision existed. Whether erasure even applies during the mandatory retention window is a legal call, so make the behaviour configurable rather than hard-coded.

Block 4: the "explain my score" API

The last block returns an explanation to the person affected. Keep the response in plain language and keep it stable, because customer support will paste it into emails.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/v1/score-explanations")
public class ExplanationController {

    private final ExplanationService service;

    @GetMapping("/{decisionId}")
    public ExplanationView explain(@PathVariable UUID decisionId,
                                   @AuthenticationPrincipal VerifiedSubject caller) {
        return service.explainFor(caller.subjectRef(), decisionId);
    }
}

@Service
public class ExplanationService {

    private final DecisionReader reader;
    private final FeatureLabels labels;   // maps feature name -> customer-facing wording

    public ExplanationView explainFor(String subjectRef, UUID decisionId) {
        var d = reader.find(decisionId)
            .filter(x -> x.subjectRef().equals(subjectRef))
            .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(decisionId)); // same error for "not yours"

        var top = d.contributions().entrySet().stream()
            .sorted((a, b) -> Double.compare(Math.abs(b.getValue()), Math.abs(a.getValue())))
            .limit(5)
            .map(e -> new Factor(labels.textFor(e.getKey()), e.getValue() >= 0 ? "helped" : "hurt"))
            .toList();

        return new ExplanationView(d.decidedAt(), d.outcome(), top, d.humanReviewRequested());
    }
}

A few things the snippet hides but you must handle:

  • Who is asking. The caller must be strongly authenticated and mapped to the same subjectRef as the decision. Returning "not found" for both missing and foreign decisions avoids leaking which IDs exist.
  • What you may reveal. An explanation of the criteria is not a copy of your model. Expose factors and direction, not raw weights or other people's data. Where a feature comes from a third party, check your contract and the legal position before surfacing it. Trade-secret limits are a legal question, so involve counsel.
  • Human review. Article 22 safeguards revolve around the person being able to contest the outcome and obtain human involvement. The humanReviewRequested flag and a POST .../review-request endpoint that opens a ticket give that right somewhere to land in the system.
  • Corrections. If a customer corrects an input (say, declared income), re-score as a new decision linked to the old one. Never rewrite the original record.

Rollout checklist

This is the order I would work in if I had a week:

  1. Inventory every feature currently reaching the model and classify it; expect to find surprises.
  2. Put the allow-list in front of the model in shadow mode, logging violations without blocking, then switch it to enforcing.
  3. Start writing explanation records and the outbox rows, even before the API exists.
  4. Run the replay job on a sample and fix whatever fails.
  5. Ship the explanation API behind authentication, with support staff trained on the wording.
  6. Agree retention and erasure behaviour in writing with the DPO.

What I would still verify

Three things stay open for me: the exact feature exclusions in the final statute text, the treatment of payment-account data, and the interaction between retention and erasure. All three are configuration in this design rather than code, which is why I chose it. If the official wording turns out stricter or looser than the coverage I read, you edit a registry and a retention setting instead of re-architecting.

If your team scores customers in Germany, read the statute this week, then open your feature pipeline and see which of your inputs you could defend one by one. The ones you cannot are your first tickets.

title: Best MCP Servers on GitHub for Daily Work: Files, Git, Browser, Databases
description:
The most useful MCP servers for everyday work are the reference servers from the Model Context Protocol project (files, Git, web fetch), GitHub's own server for repositories and issues, Microsoft's Playwright server for browser tasks, and Google's MCP Toolbox for databases. All four are open source on GitHub, and each installs with a single command or a short JSON block. This guide lists what each one does, how to install it, its license, and how to connect it to Claude Code without handing over more access than you need.

Who this is for and what you will have at the end

This is for developers, IT admins and technical founders who already use an AI assistant such as Claude Code and want it to touch real tools: a project folder, a Git history, a browser or a database. By the end you will have a short list of vetted repos, working install commands, a project-level .mcp.json you can share with a team, and a checklist for deciding whether to trust any other MCP server you come across.

If you want to build your own server instead of installing one, see Build Your First MCP Server in Python. If you are looking for Claude Skills rather than MCP servers, see Best Claude Skills GitHub Repos.

How MCP servers connect to your AI app

MCP is a protocol that lets an AI app call tools exposed by a separate program. There are two common ways a server is reached:

Transport How it runs Typical use
stdio The AI app starts the server as a local process and talks to it over standard input and output Local tools: files, Git, a local browser
HTTP (remote) The AI app connects to a URL Hosted servers, such as GitHub's

The Model Context Protocol README notes that servers default to stdio, so running one directly in a terminal looks like it hangs: it is waiting for a client to talk to it. That is normal.

Prerequisites

  • Claude Code installed. The commands below use its claude mcp command; the JSON blocks also work in most other MCP clients.
  • Node.js, for servers started with npx.
  • uv, for servers started with uvx (the Git and Fetch reference servers use it).
  • Docker, only if you choose the Docker route for the GitHub server.

How to add a server in Claude Code

Claude Code's MCP documentation gives two forms. Remote HTTP servers:

claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>

Local stdio servers:

claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]

The -- matters for stdio servers. Per the documentation, it separates Claude's own options (--transport, --env, --scope) from the command that runs the server, and everything after it is passed to the server untouched.

Servers are stored by scope:

Scope Loads in Shared with team Stored in
Local (default) Current project only No ~/.claude.json
Project Current project only Yes, via version control .mcp.json in the project root
User All your projects No ~/.claude.json

Choose with --scope local, --scope project or --scope user. To see what is configured, run claude mcp list. Inside Claude Code, /mcp shows server status and handles sign-in for remote servers that use OAuth.

1. modelcontextprotocol/servers: the reference servers

What it does. This is the project's collection of reference servers. According to its README (checked 2026-11-19), the maintained ones are Everything (a test server), Fetch (web content fetching and conversion), Filesystem (file operations with configurable access controls), Git (read, search and manipulate repositories), Memory (a knowledge-graph memory), Sequential Thinking and Time.

Who it is for. Anyone starting with MCP. These are the most common first servers and the ones other guides assume you have seen.

Install commands from the README:

# Filesystem: only the folder you list is accessible
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path/to/allowed/files

# Git
uvx mcp-server-git

# Fetch
uvx mcp-server-fetch

# Memory
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory

Connecting the Filesystem server to Claude Code, limited to one folder:

claude mcp add --transport stdio files -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /home/you/projects/contoso-site

The folder argument is the access control. Give it the one project folder, not your home directory.

Windows note. The README says to wrap npx commands with cmd /c in client configs.

License. The README states Apache License 2.0 for new contributions, with existing code remaining under MIT. GitHub's license field for the repository reads NOASSERTION, because of that mix.

Repo facts (GitHub API, 2026-11-19): about 92,091 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

What moved out of this repo

Many servers people remember from older tutorials are no longer here. The README lists these as archived and moved to the servers-archived repository: AWS KB Retrieval, Brave Search, EverArt, GitHub, GitLab, Google Drive, Google Maps, PostgreSQL, Puppeteer, Redis, Sentry, Slack and SQLite. If a tutorial tells you to run @modelcontextprotocol/server-github or the PostgreSQL server, use the maintained replacements below instead. The README says Brave Search is replaced by the official @brave/brave-search-mcp-server and that Slack is now maintained by Zencoder.

2. github/github-mcp-server: repositories, issues and pull requests

What it does. GitHub's official MCP server lets an assistant work with repositories, issues and pull requests. Its default toolsets, per the README, are context, repos, issues, pull_requests and users.

Who it is for. Developers who want to ask an assistant to summarize an issue, review a pull request or search a repo without leaving the terminal.

Install options from the README:

  • Remote server hosted by GitHub, URL https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, with "type": "http" in your host config. Authentication can be OAuth or a personal access token.
  • Docker, local: 
docker run -i --rm \
  -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=<your-token> \
  ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server
  • A local binary built with go build -o github-mcp-server ./cmd/github-mcp-server, run as github-mcp-server stdio with the token set in the environment.

For Claude Code, the remote route follows the HTTP pattern above:

claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/

Then run /mcp inside Claude Code to complete authentication. This command combines GitHub's URL with Claude Code's documented HTTP syntax; the exact authentication prompts depend on your account and Claude Code version, so check /mcp for status.

Limit what it can do. The README describes two controls. --toolsets repos,issues,pull_requests (or the GITHUB_TOOLSETS environment variable, which takes precedence) exposes only the toolsets you name. --read-only skips all write tools, and the README says it takes priority even over tools requested explicitly with --tools. For a first trial, enable read-only.

Token advice from the README. Minimum suggested scopes are repo, read:packages (for Docker image access) and read:org (for team access). It also recommends separate tokens per project, periodic rotation, and keeping tokens out of version control.

License. MIT. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 34,576 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

3. microsoft/playwright-mcp: a real browser for the assistant

What it does. Playwright MCP lets an assistant drive a browser: open pages, read what is on them and interact. It is useful for checking a staging site, reproducing a front-end bug or filling a form during testing.

Who it is for. Developers and QA engineers testing web apps.

Install, from the README:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "@playwright/mcp@latest"
      ]
    }
  }
}

For Claude Code the README gives:

claude mcp add playwright npx @playwright/mcp@latest

Security. The README says plainly that "Playwright MCP is not a security boundary." A browser that can open arbitrary pages can read content from those pages, and Claude Code's documentation warns that servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection. Point it at sites you control, avoid logged-in sessions for sensitive systems, and do not combine it with a server that can write to production.

License. Apache-2.0. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 39,868 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

4. googleapis/mcp-toolbox: databases

What it does. MCP Toolbox for Databases is an open source MCP server for databases. Per its README it offers prebuilt generic tools such as list_tables and execute_sql, and a framework for custom tools defined in a tools.yaml file. Listed supported databases include Google Cloud options (AlloyDB, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore) and others such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, CockroachDB, ClickHouse, Couchbase, Neo4j, Snowflake and Trino.

Who it is for. Analysts and developers who want an assistant to explore a schema and draft queries.

Install, from the README:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "toolbox-postgres": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@toolbox-sdk/server",
        "--prebuilt=postgres",
        "--stdio"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Set the database connection environment variables described in the project's Prebuilt Tools Reference. For custom tools, the README shows npx @toolbox-sdk/server --config tools.yaml.

Rename. The repository was formerly googleapis/genai-toolbox (originally "Gen AI Toolbox for Databases") and is now googleapis/mcp-toolbox. Older tutorials and bookmarks may use the previous name. Update a local clone with git remote set-url origin https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox.git.

Safety. execute_sql can run whatever SQL the database user is allowed to run. Connect with a read-only database account, ideally against a replica or a copy, never a production primary with a write-capable user.

License. Apache-2.0. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 16,905 stars, last push 2026-11-19, not archived.

Share a setup with your team

To give a whole project the same servers, add them with project scope so they are written to .mcp.json:

claude mcp add --transport http github --scope project https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/

The resulting file uses the format from Claude Code's documentation:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shared-server": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://example.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}

.mcp.json supports ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expansion in command, args, env, url and headers, so tokens can stay out of the committed file. Claude Code prompts for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json.

Verify the setup

Run:

claude mcp list

Claude Code's documentation says the list shows health statuses such as Connected, Needs authentication and Failed to connect. Inside a session, /mcp shows the same status and handles OAuth sign-in. Then ask the assistant for something harmless and observable, such as listing the files in the allowed folder or listing open issues in a public repo.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Server runs in a terminal but nothing happens stdio servers wait for a client Run it through your MCP client instead
Status shows Needs authentication Remote server needs OAuth Run /mcp and sign in
Status shows Failed to connect Missing Node.js or uv, or a typo in the command Run the command by hand to see the error
npx fails on Windows Client cannot launch npx directly Wrap with cmd /c, as the README advises
CLI treats your server name as an environment variable --env swallowed the name Put another option, such as --transport stdio, between --env and the name
Old tutorial's server package not found Server was archived Use the maintained replacements above

Before you trust any other MCP server

  • Open its repository and check the license, the last commit date and whether it is archived.
  • Read what tools it exposes. A server that can write, delete or send is a larger risk than one that reads.
  • Prefer the vendor's own server (GitHub, Microsoft, Google) over a lookalike with a similar name.
  • Start with the narrowest scope and read-only credentials.
  • Remember that content fetched by a server can contain instructions aimed at the model.

Summary checklist

  • Start with Filesystem limited to one folder, plus Git.
  • Add GitHub's server in read-only mode before enabling writes.
  • Use Playwright MCP on sites you control only.
  • Use MCP Toolbox with a read-only database account.
  • Verify with claude mcp list and /mcp after each addition.

What we checked

  • Opened the README of modelcontextprotocol/servers on github.com on 2026-11-19 and copied the maintained-server list, the install commands and the archived-server list from it.
  • Queried the GitHub API for modelcontextprotocol/servers, github/github-mcp-server, microsoft/playwright-mcp and googleapis/mcp-toolbox on 2026-11-19: stars, last push date, license field and archived flag are as stated above. Star counts change daily.
  • Cross-checked license wording: the GitHub API reports NOASSERTION for modelcontextprotocol/servers, while its README states Apache-2.0 for new contributions and MIT for existing code.
  • Confirmed the repository rename from genai-toolbox to mcp-toolbox: the GitHub API returned the full name googleapis/mcp-toolbox when queried by the old name, and the README carries a rename notice.
  • Read Claude Code's MCP documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) on 2026-11-19 for the claude mcp add syntax, scopes, .mcp.json format and the security warning. The page redirected from docs.claude.com.
  • Not tested hands-on: we did not run any of these servers or connect them to a live Claude Code session; the one command that combines GitHub's URL with Claude Code's HTTP syntax is assembled from the two documents, not run. The first 100,000 characters of the long Claude Code and GitHub README pages were read; the remainder was not.

Last tested: 2026-11-19

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
  • https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server
  • https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
  • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox
  • https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

This guide was researched and drafted with AI assistance and checked against the vendor documentation listed in its References. Read the maintained version and related guides on EpiFive.

title: Contract Review Retrieval Explained: Node.js Fallbacks for Cited Change Alerts
description:
A legal contract review workspace should fail toward a smaller, cited answer, not a confident guess: keep a lexical search path, a vector path, and a human-review state, then expose which path produced each citation. The deciding constraint is grounding. A fast answer that cannot point to the exact clause is a failed answer.

Short answer: use a two-stage retrieval architecture with explicit fallbacks, preserve page and clause coordinates in every chunk, and abstain when evidence does not meet a citation threshold.

Grounding wins.

The concrete job here is watching a web page for changes and alerting a reviewer about a contract clause or policy page. That sounds like a diff problem until the first layout redesign turns every line into noise. Retrieval must identify the same legal provision across HTML versions, then let a reviewer inspect the source span that triggered the alert.

What should a fallback prove before an alert is trusted?

Start with an evidence contract. Every candidate passage carries a document ID, source URL, retrieval timestamp, page number when available, clause heading, character offsets, and a content hash. The generator receives those fields alongside text. The UI can then render a citation that survives re-ranking and makes an audit trail possible.

A useful decision rule is deliberately boring:

  1. Run lexical retrieval against normalized clause text and headings.
  2. Run vector retrieval only when the query has enough semantic content and the index is fresh.
  3. Merge and re-rank candidates, deduplicating by clause ID rather than by similar wording.
  4. Require two independent signals, or a high lexical score plus a direct quote, before creating an alert.
  5. If the threshold is missed, return needs_review with the best candidates and no generated legal conclusion.

The RAG paper describes retrieval as a way to connect generation to an external memory. In a contract workspace, that memory is not an abstract embedding store; it is versioned source material. The fallback is successful only if it keeps provenance intact.

How can Node.js keep lexical, vector, and human fallbacks consistent?

Use one result shape at the boundary. The underlying engines can differ, but the rest of the application should not branch on vendor-specific response fields. This TypeScript sketch keeps the policy visible and makes an abstention a first-class outcome.

type Evidence = {
  clauseId: string;
  text: string;
  sourceUrl: string;
  hash: string;
  page?: number;
  heading?: string;
};

type Hit = Evidence & {
  lexical: number;
  semantic: number;
  source: "lexical" | "vector";
};

type Retrieval =
  | { status: "grounded"; hits: Hit[] }
  | { status: "needs_review"; hits: Hit[]; reason: string };

interface Searcher {
  search(query: string, limit: number): Promise<Hit[]>;
}

export async function retrieve(
  query: string,
  lexical: Searcher,
  vector: Searcher | null,
): Promise<Retrieval> {
  const lexicalHits = await lexical.search(query, 8);
  const semanticHits = vector ? await vector.search(query, 8) : [];
  const merged = [...lexicalHits, ...semanticHits]
    .sort((a, b) => (b.lexical + b.semantic) - (a.lexical + a.semantic))
    .filter((hit, index, all) =>
      all.findIndex((other) => other.clauseId === hit.clauseId) === index,
    )
    .slice(0, 5);

  const top = merged[0];
  const hasQuote = Boolean(top?.text && top.text.length >= 40);
  const hasTwoSignals = Boolean(top && top.lexical > 0 && top.semantic > 0);
  if (!top || (!hasQuote && !hasTwoSignals)) {
    return {
      status: "needs_review",
      hits: merged,
      reason: "Evidence did not meet the citation policy",
    };
  }
  return { status: "grounded", hits: merged };
}

The exact score cutoffs belong in evaluation configuration, not in a blog post or a prompt. Tune them against a labeled set of clause changes. Your mileage may vary: a short indemnity clause and a long privacy policy need different minimum quote lengths, even when they share a vocabulary.

Where do retrieval fallbacks fail in contract change detection?

The common failure is not a missing model. It is a broken identity map. If a parser keys chunks by character offset, a one-line insertion shifts every later chunk and produces a false alert. Imagine a page whose termination clause starts at offset 18,400 on Monday; a cookie-banner sentence inserted near the top moves it to 18,447 on Tuesday, so an offset-based diff reports a change even when the clause text is byte-for-byte identical. Stable clause IDs should come from heading paths and normalized anchors; when those are unavailable, map old and new passages with a similarity step and mark the mapping as uncertain. Keep both the proposed mapping and its confidence so a reviewer can see why an alert was grouped.

Another trap is embedding drift. Re-indexing with a new model can change nearest neighbors without any source edit. Store the embedding model ID, index build timestamp, and chunking configuration with each retrieval run. During a rebuild, compare alerts from the old and new index before switching traffic. A lexical path remains valuable because exact terms such as “governing law” and “termination for convenience” are often the strongest signal.

Parsing errors deserve their own state. An empty extraction, a truncated PDF, or a page that requires authentication should produce source_unavailable, not a zero-result answer that looks like “no change.” The alert should include the last successful hash and ask for review. Three words: preserve the last truth.

For a web page watcher, normalize boilerplate, navigation, and timestamps before diffing. Keep the raw response for audit, but retrieve from the cleaned representation. Record HTTP validators such as ETag and Last-Modified when available; they reduce needless parsing, while the content hash remains the final identity check.

Which implementation trade-offs matter more than the model name?

A small team can combine PostgreSQL full-text search with a vector extension, Elasticsearch with a dense-vector field, or a hosted vector database. These are evidence about implementation styles, not rankings. PostgreSQL keeps transactional metadata beside clauses; Elasticsearch offers mature text analysis and distributed indexing; a hosted vector database can reduce operational work but adds a network and policy boundary. None removes the need for clause IDs, freshness checks, or abstention.

The catch is operational. A vector-only design is not suitable when exact legal terms, citations, or newly added clauses dominate the query. A lexical-only design is a poor fit for paraphrased obligations across templates. Stick with a single lexical index when the corpus is small, terms are stable, and a reviewer can inspect every hit; add semantic retrieval when labeled evaluation shows it recovers misses without increasing unsupported alerts.

Measure before copying the architecture: citation precision, citation recall, unsupported-answer rate, stale-index rate, p95 retrieval latency, and cost per reviewed document. Split the test set by document type and by edit pattern, including heading changes, inserted paragraphs, and reordered lists. A single aggregate score hides the failure that legal teams notice first: a plausible alert attached to the wrong clause.

How should the workspace expose uncertainty to reviewers?

Make the fallback visible in the event record. Store retrieval_path, candidate scores, source hashes, and the policy decision next to the generated summary. Show the changed quote, its before-and-after context, and a link that resolves to the exact source version. A reviewer should be able to reject an alert without deleting the evidence that caused it.

Retries need boundaries. Retry transient fetches with capped exponential backoff, but do not retry a deterministic parse failure forever. Queue re-indexing separately from alert generation so a delayed index cannot silently suppress a change. Emit metrics for each transition: fetched, normalized, indexed, retrieved, grounded, and needs review.

I would ship the lexical path first, then add vectors behind the same interface and compare decisions in shadow mode for one release cycle. That keeps the blast radius small and gives the team a real error budget. The fastest route to trust is a clear abstention, backed by a citation, when the system is unsure.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/ETag
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Last-Modified
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: Abort-safe Firecrawl tool calls in a React 19 chat stream
description:
Firecrawl is a poor second SSE source. A scrape of a docs page often returns 8–40 KB of markdown. If that blob is pushed into useChat as one assistant delta, the typewriter either stalls on the main thread or paints a wall the user cannot interrupt. We hit this while wiring firecrawl/firecrawl into an existing Next.js chat surface that already streamed through @ai-sdk/react.

The split that held up: search and scrape stay request/response tool calls. Only the model's narration of those results is a stream. Mixing the two left the UI on a half-parsed tool card after the proxy cut the connection.

Failure boundaries we actually measured

Scrape time vs. idle timeout. Firecrawl search was usually sub-second. Scrape of a JS-rendered page was not. The route's upstream idle window was 15s. A render wait exceeded it, the proxy closed the SSE, and useChat reported a generic network error while the tool invocation was still in call. The model never received a tool result, so the next turn replayed the same URL.

Burst after a fat tool result. Once markdown landed, the model echoed large excerpts. With default React 19 rendering and no chunk cap, a ~200-token burst in one frame pushed input latency past 100ms on a mid-range laptop. The stream was fine. The DOM update was not.

Abort does not cancel Firecrawl unless you thread the signal. Stop aborted the AI SDK fetch. The Node handler kept the Firecrawl HTTP call until the vendor timeout. Under load that leaked sockets. A drop mid-token is recoverable with reload. A drop mid-scrape leaves an orphaned toolCallId and an optimistic "Scraping…" row that never settles. We treat that as a terminal tool error, not a retry loop.

Route we ship

The model client is OpenAI-compatible. baseURL is https://b-lost.com/v1 so the SSE body stays unbuffered. A buffering hop in front of that relay was the other way the typewriter jumped in 2–4 KB slabs. On the same prompt mix, multi-provider fallback through that gateway showed about 35ms lower time-to-first-token than a direct provider URL, with no token truncation on streams under 8k output tokens. That is a transport measurement, not a quality claim.

import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { streamText, tool, convertToModelMessages, stepCountIs } from "ai";
import { z } from "zod";
import FirecrawlApp from "@mendable/firecrawl-js";

export const maxDuration = 60;

const openai = createOpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.RELAY_API_KEY!,
  baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1",
});

const firecrawl = new FirecrawlApp({ apiKey: process.env.FIRECRAWL_API_KEY! });

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages } = await req.json();
  const signal = req.signal;

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai.chat("gpt-4.1-mini"),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    stopWhen: stepCountIs(4),
    abortSignal: signal,
    tools: {
      scrape_page: tool({
        description: "Scrape one URL to markdown. Do not scrape the same URL twice in one turn.",
        inputSchema: z.object({ url: z.string().url() }),
        execute: async ({ url }, { abortSignal }) => {
          const onAbort = () => undefined;
          abortSignal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
          try {
            if (signal.aborted || abortSignal.aborted) {
              return { url, error: "aborted", markdown: "" };
            }
            const doc = await firecrawl.scrapeUrl(url, {
              formats: ["markdown"],
              onlyMainContent: true,
              timeout: 12_000,
            });
            const raw = doc.markdown ?? "";
            return {
              url,
              title: doc.metadata?.title ?? "",
              markdown: raw.slice(0, 6_000),
              truncated: raw.length > 6_000,
            };
          } catch {
            return {
              url,
              error: signal.aborted ? "aborted" : "scrape_failed",
              markdown: "",
            };
          }
        },
      }),
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse();
}

Caps that mattered more than model choice: scrape timeout at 12s, under both maxDuration and the gateway idle window; markdown sliced to 6,000 characters before it enters the tool result; stepCountIs(4) so a flaky scrape cannot loop until the stream dies; onlyMainContent: true, because nav chrome was duplicate tokens with no user value.

Pin the Firecrawl client and check whether scrapeUrl (older SDK) or scrape (newer SDK) forwards AbortSignal. The guard above stops the handler from waiting. It does not close the vendor socket unless that client honors abort. Do not assume it does.

Client: Stop has to win 

"use client";

import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";
import { DefaultChatTransport } from "ai";
import { useRef } from "react";

export function ResearchChat() {
  const stopRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null);
  const { sendMessage, status, stop } = useChat({
    transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "/api/chat" }),
  });

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      onClick={() => {
        stopRef.current?.abort();
        stop();
      }}
      disabled={status !== "streaming" && status !== "submitted"}
    >
      Stop
    </button>
  );
}

When submitting, abort the previous controller, create a new one, and pass abortSignal into sendMessage. If a tool-scrape_page part sits in input-available with no output after about 1.5s, render the URL and "Scraping…", not a spinner over the whole transcript. If status returns to ready with no tool output, replace the row with a one-line failure and leave the input enabled. Do not auto-resubmit. Users double-fired scrapes because the button re-enabled before the tool part settled.

Log tool duration, truncation, and whether req.signal.aborted was already true when execute started. Client chunk-parse errors were almost always a proxy coalescing an incomplete data: frame. Gzip on the SSE body reintroduces that stall even with the relay base URL set.

The 6k cap keeps the typewriter alive and drops the section the user asked about more often than I want. A heading-scoped second fetch would fix the information loss and burn another round trip inside the same abort window. I have not found a timeout budget where a 10s first scrape, a scoped follow-up, and a useful summary all fit. If you page Firecrawl extracts without freezing React or silently dropping the section the question depended on, I want the failure case, not the happy path.

title: Your leakage audit is reading the wrong clock: 46.6% vs 0.42% on the same 14,781 rows
description:
Ask a team whether their model has seen the future and you will get a boolean. We have one too: a learned_at column that records the moment a prediction was fed back into the training loop. If learned_at is later than the match result, the model learned after the fact. If it is earlier, the model cheated.

That is the whole audit as usually written. It is also wrong, and not by a small margin.

Run it against our production table and 46.6% of the learned rows appear to have learned before the result existed. Anchor the same rows on kickoff time instead, and the number collapses to 0.42%. Same table, same column, same rows — and only one anchor measures leakage rather than measuring your own pipeline's lateness.

Scope: 47,357 predictions, 47,138 graded, 3,807 models, 17,017 matches, 2026-06-21 to 2026-11-19 — ai_predictions and nami_matches, reproducible with the SQL shown.

Step 0: trust the timestamp granularity before the timestamp

An audit of time is an audit of a column, and a column promises less than you think. Check whether a timestamp was observed or bucketed.

SELECT
  count(*)                                                                    AS rows,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0)                 AS sec_zero,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(minute FROM created_at) = 0
                     AND extract(second FROM created_at) = 0)                  AS top_of_hour,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0
                     AND extract(minute FROM created_at) <> 0)                 AS sec_zero_minute_not
FROM ai_predictions;

rows 47357 | sec_zero 1859 | top_of_hour 1859 | sec_zero_minute_not 0

Read the last two columns together, because that pair is the tell. 1,859 rows have a second component of exactly zero, and not one of them has a non-zero minute. Organic writes would land a zero second on a random minute every sixtieth record — roughly 31 rows. We have zero. A real clock does not produce that distribution; date_trunc or a hand-written literal does.

So created_at holds two populations: 45,498 genuine sub-second writes and 1,859 rows whose timestamp is a bucket. Where they live matters more than that they exist — grouping those rows by month:

2026-06  1859 / 2735     2026-07  0 / 2637     2026-08  0 / 164
2026-09     0 / 9757     2026-10  0 / 21886    2026-11  0 / 10178

Every bucketed row is in the first month — 68% of June, then nothing, ever again. That is an import batch from launch week, not a live defect. What is not fine is any time-series claim spanning June and July: it compares a bucket against a clock, June resolving to the hour and July to the millisecond.

learned_at passes the same test: 14,781 rows, zero on the hour. One column partially synthetic, the other fully observed — indistinguishable without it.

Step 1: assert the invariant that must never break

Before hunting leakage, prove the loop is at least ordered. A learning write cannot precede the prediction it learned from.

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at < created_at) AS learned_before_written,
       count(*)                                        AS learned_rows
FROM ai_predictions WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL;

learned_before_written 0 | learned_rows 14781 — zero violations. That eliminates the most boring bug: a backfill stamping learned_at from a queue's creation time. The offset itself says the loop is a batch job, not a trigger — learned_at - created_at runs p5 449 min, p50 4,095 min (2.8 d), p95 55,834 min. A design cost, not leakage.

Step 2: the anchor choice, where the audit actually fails

Now the comparison everyone writes. Result availability is settled_at; leakage is learned_at < settled_at.

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at < settled_at) AS learned_before_settled,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at >= settled_at) AS after,
       count(*)                                          AS n
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL AND settled_at IS NOT NULL;

learned_before_settled 6,889 (46.62%) | after 7,887 (53.38%) | n 14,776

46.6% of the loop appears to read the answer sheet before it exists — an incident, if you trust the anchor.

Anchor on the match instead of on your own bookkeeping:

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at < m.match_time)                      AS before_kickoff,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at >= m.match_time
                          AND p.learned_at < m.match_time + interval '3 hour')  AS in_play,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at >= m.match_time + interval '3 hour') AS after,
       count(*)                                                                 AS n
FROM ai_predictions p JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.learned_at IS NOT NULL;

before_kickoff 62 (0.42%) | in_play 2,280 (15.43%) | after 12,439 (84.15%) | n 14,781

62 rows. 0.42%. The discrepancy is not noise; it is 6,827 rows, and every one is a statement about settled_at, not about learning.

settled_at is when we wrote the grade; grading is async and retried. It drifts:

settled_at - match_time (n=14,776)
  <0           208   1.41%     <- graded before the whistle
  0..6h      7,245  49.03%     <- live path
  6h..7d       948   6.42%
  7d..60d    1,279   8.66%
 60d..90d    5,096  34.49%     <- repair batch

Cleanly bimodal: half the grades land within six hours of the whistle, then a second mass at 60–90 days — 5,096 rows, a third of the learned population, graded two to three months late by a repair job.

Compare accuracy under both anchors:

anchor = settled_at   learn_before_settle 6,889 rows → 63.78%
                      learn_after_settle  7,887 rows → 51.76%
anchor = match_time   before_kickoff         62 rows → 52.46%
                      in_play             2,280 rows → 57.68%
                      after              12,439 rows → 57.33%

The settled-anchored split shows a 12-point accuracy advantage for the "suspicious" group — a smoking gun, if you want one. The kickoff-anchored split shows a 5-point spread across groups of wildly different size, which reads like what it is — nothing.

The 12-point gap is an artefact of when grading happened, not of what the model knew: the 84-day repair batch is dominated by older matches the live path had already abandoned. Sorting on settled_at sorts on operational history — a confound wearing the costume of a finding.

Step 3: the 62 rows that are real, and their fingerprint

0.42% is small but not zero; small numbers deserve rows, not percentages.

models 57 | matches 18 | lead min 435 min (7.25 h), p50 32,480 min (22.6 d), max 112,490 min (78.1 d)

61 of the 62 belong to matches already played; one to a fixture still ahead. Twenty-two days early on average, 78 at the extreme, over 57 models but only 18 matches — a batch touching a few fixtures many times, not a systemic lookahead.

The lead times expose the mechanism: several rows share the exact value 47,850 minutes. Identical offsets to the minute across different models mean one loop computed an offset and applied it to a set. Those records were not learned early, they were stamped from a template.

Bug or mislabelled backfill, the conclusion is not what the boolean suggests: these 62 rows do not corrupt the other 14,719. They contaminate 18 matches — and nothing at all if the learning write refused to run for a fixture that has not kicked off.

Step 4: make the check executable

Rules survive only if they run on every deploy. This audit exits non-zero on a broken invariant — CI or scheduler, no dashboard.

import json, sys, psycopg2

CHECKS = [
    ("learned_before_created", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions
        WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL AND learned_at < created_at"""),
    ("learned_before_kickoff", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions p
        JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
        WHERE p.learned_at IS NOT NULL AND p.learned_at < m.match_time"""),
    ("graded_before_kickoff", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions p
        JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
        WHERE p.settled_at IS NOT NULL AND p.settled_at < m.match_time"""),
]

def run(dsn):
    con = psycopg2.connect(dsn); con.set_session(readonly=True)
    cur, out, failed = con.cursor(), [], False
    for name, sql in CHECKS:                       # every invariant must return 0
        cur.execute(sql); n = cur.fetchone()[0]
        failed |= n > 0
        out.append({"check": name, "actual": n, "ok": n == 0})
    cur.execute("""SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions
        WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0
          AND extract(minute FROM created_at) <> 0""")
    stray = cur.fetchone()[0]                      # bucket with a stray minute
    if stray:
        out.append({"check": "granularity_ambiguous", "actual": stray, "ok": False})
        failed = True
    print(json.dumps(out, indent=2)); con.close()
    return 1 if failed else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(run("postgresql://soccerdream@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"))

On today's snapshot the kickoff-anchored invariant is the only one that fails — 62 instead of 0. graded_before_kickoff fails too, at 208 rows across 40 matches, some stamped as much as 861 hours ahead of the whistle. A separate defect we did not know we had until the anchor was correct: a grade cannot exist before the thing being graded has been played.

Three rules that transfer

Pick the anchor the model cannot write to. settled_at and learned_at are both our own writes. If the grader is late, the learner looks early. Kickoff time comes from the feed and enters the row before any model touches it — the only clock here a bug cannot rewind. Without one, you are comparing two of your own lies.

Validate granularity before validating differences. The 1,859 bucketed rows were invisible for months because a timestamp is a timestamp. One grouped count — seconds zero, minutes non-zero — separates observation from truncation and tells you which months are safe to average.

Refuse writes that are chronologically impossible. 62 and 208 are both small enough to ignore as a percentage and large enough to poison a fixture. A CHECK constraint costs one line and turns silent contamination into a failed insert. Our auditor now fails the build on both, which is the only reason we found the 208.

The headline number is not 46.6%, and it is not 0.42% either. It is that the difference between them is made entirely of our own operational lag — the part of the pipeline most teams never audit, because they audit the model instead of the clock it is judged against.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.22309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22310v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
description:
arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
description:
arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
description:
arXiv:2611.22362v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, scores with full context are 11.83 to 31.76 case points and 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points higher than those with the current question alone. GPT-6 Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
description:
arXiv:2611.22368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
description:
arXiv:2611.22374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

title: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement
description:
arXiv:2611.22404v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
description:
arXiv:2611.22407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations.
