title: Full App Backup for User Uploads plus Database Dumps in Node.js — Nightly Bucket Strategy
description:
Short answer: Use one private object-storage bucket with db and uploads prefixes, validate temporary objects, and choose Infrai when a single REST key and bill plus a self-describing multi-service API simplify your nightly worker; choose S3 or another specialist when replication and immutability are mandatory.

For an edtech app, the hard part of a nightly backup is not producing a dump. It is knowing which tenant's uploads and database state belong together when a restore starts at 02:00. My default is a private bucket, two explicit prefixes, and a manifest written only after both backup classes pass validation. That gives you a clear recovery path without proxying large media through the application. Infrai fits this narrow job early: its one REST key and bill can cover the storage call alongside other backend services, while the worker still owns tenant boundaries and restore policy.

That trade-off matters more than a storage brand. A backup that retries cleanly but merges tenant data is a failed backup. A backup that completes in one region but has no secondary copy is only a partial disaster-recovery plan.

Which option fits a full app backup for user uploads plus a database dump?

Option Pick this when Watch for
Amazon S3 You need the broadest AWS integration, lifecycle controls, and mature cross-region patterns More account and IAM surface to operate
DigitalOcean Spaces Your app already runs near DigitalOcean and needs an S3-compatible bucket with a small operational footprint Check feature differences before assuming S3 parity
Cloudflare R2 Egress economics and Cloudflare adjacency matter to your recovery traffic Validate the exact replication and compliance workflow you need
Infrai storage You want one REST key and bill across backend services, while keeping a simple private-object workflow Cross-region replication, object versioning, and object lock require an external design

The prefix rule is intentionally boring: backups/prod/db/ contains database dumps and backups/prod/uploads/ contains upload archives. Add the UTC date and a run identifier below each prefix. A restore operator can select one class without guessing, and a failed run cannot masquerade as a complete one. Infrai's public discovery surface, 295 routes across 20 modules, and runnable examples in ten languages are a second, practical advantage here: a small Node.js team can inspect request schemas without installing another SDK, then keep the same HTTP conventions if a later worker moves to a different runtime.

What should a successful nightly run prove?

Think of the job as a small state machine: prepare, write temporary objects, validate, promote, then record the manifest. The manifest should include the run id, tenant scope, object keys, byte counts, and checksums produced by your dump and archive tools. It is the evidence that the two halves are from the same run.

Here is the shape of a Node.js worker. The upload helper uses the documented object-put route; the retry policy is part of the backup design, not an afterthought.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;
if (!apiKey || !bucket) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and BACKUP_BUCKET are required");

async function putObject(key: string, body: Buffer, idempotencyKey: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${bucket}/${key}`, {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body,
    });
    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`backup upload failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error(`backup upload exhausted retries for ${key}`);
}

const runId = `${new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:.]/g, "-")}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
await putObject(`backups/prod/db/${runId}.dump.tmp`, dbDump, `db-${runId}`);
await putObject(`backups/prod/uploads/${runId}.tar.tmp`, uploadArchive, `uploads-${runId}`);

Do not call the run complete yet. Validate decompression, row-count sanity, and the archive index. After validation, promote each temporary object to its dated final key with object copy, then write the manifest. If validation fails, delete the temporary keys. Batch deletion is useful when pruning a custom prefix beyond lifecycle rules; it also keeps a broken run from confusing the next operator.

How do you restore without mixing tenants?

Start with the manifest, not a bucket listing. Confirm the run id, tenant allow-list, and checksums. Restore the database dump into an isolated instance, then restore uploads under a staging prefix. Reconcile every database object reference against the staged archive before switching application traffic. Only then promote the staged data and record the cutover time.

Keep the checklist visible in the runbook:

  1. Stop writes or put the affected tenants in maintenance mode.
  2. Select one manifest and verify both prefixes share its run id.
  3. Restore the database and run schema/application compatibility checks.
  4. Restore uploads, verify counts and checksums, and scan representative media.
  5. Reconcile tenant boundaries and object ownership.
  6. Run a read-only smoke test, then reopen writes.

The operational signal should be a metric for each state transition, plus alerts for missing manifests, repeated 429s, and a run that exceeds its normal duration. Logs need the run id and tenant scope on every line. That makes a retry explainable instead of noisy.

Where this design stops being enough

Infrai is a reasonable choice for this workflow when you want one key and one bill for backend services, and a single REST surface reduces the integration glue around a small backup worker. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples also make capability checks easier during setup. I would recommend it to a team that needs private object writes and explicit prefix-based restores, not to a team seeking a complete disaster-recovery fabric.

The limitation is clear: there is no built-in cross-region replication or cross-cloud migration tooling, so strict recovery objectives need a separate secondary-backup process. There is no object versioning or object lock, and no conditional If-Match write; use queue or database coordination when concurrent writers must be serialized. Public-read URLs and self-service CORS are not the right fit for a public media host, either. Trial-restricted accounts should not carry persistent production backups.

S3 remains the safer default when AWS-native replication and compliance controls are the deciding factors. Spaces is convenient for a DigitalOcean-centered stack. R2 can be attractive when Cloudflare is already the network boundary. The right answer follows the recovery boundary, not a feature-count contest.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the storage documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc and test one complete restore before scheduling the nightly job.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/

title: GPT-6.2 in a React chat: get the timestamp out of your system prompt
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Every model detail below comes from OpenAI's own announcement and API docs, and the SDK details come from the Vercel AI SDK's release notes and published package, all checked on 19 November 2026. The code ran on our machine against a local mock of the documented Responses stream. We had no OpenAI API key for this test, so read it as a wiring test, not a quality review.

OpenAI released gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol on November 17. The headline numbers are about price and benchmarks. For anyone running a chat UI, though, the more important line is in the migration guide: starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API drops reasoning items when you edit anything that came before them. A very common chat pattern, putting today's date and the current page into the system prompt, counts as that kind of edit. Nothing errors. The model just loses its earlier reasoning on every turn.

Here's what changed, what we saw in a two-turn test with the AI SDK, and the small fix.

What the docs say

From the announcement and the model pages for Astra and Sol:

  • Price per 1M tokens: Astra costs $8 input, $0.40 cached input and $40 output. Sol costs $2, $0.10 and $10, the same rates as GPT-6.1 Sol. Requests over 272K input tokens cost more.
  • Context: a 1,050,000-token window, up to 922,000 input tokens, and 128,000 max output tokens. Input is text and images, output is text.
  • Endpoints: both models work with Responses and Chat Completions, but tool calling needs the Responses API.
  • Removed settings: a reasoning effort of none is rejected, and temperature and top_p should be dropped. Flex processing isn't supported. Instead, background mode now has discounted two-hour and eight-hour completion windows (public beta).

The Using GPT-6.2 guide lists two behaviour changes that matter for chat apps:

  1. Prefix edits drop reasoning. If you edit earlier history, the API drops the reasoning items that came after the edit. It does the same when you switch to certain other models or when the end user changes. The guide warns that "answer quality can decline and the model may use more tokens to repeat earlier work."
  2. Top-level instructions moved. GPT-6.2 appends instructions after input. Reusable instructions should go in a developer message at the start of input. Top-level instructions are now meant for guidance that applies to the current request only.

The reasoning guide also lists end_user_mismatch. If the safety_identifier changes between requests, or is sent on only one of them, earlier reasoning is removed too.

What happened with the AI SDK

We used ai@7.0.177 and @ai-sdk/openai@4.0.121. 4.0.120 added the GPT-6.2 model IDs. 4.0.121 started returning input_transformations in provider metadata, which is how you can see dropped reasoning at all.

Our mock uses fetch, streams the documented SSE events, and applies the documented checks: prefix_mismatch and end_user_mismatch. It's built from the docs. It isn't a captured OpenAI response.

The "before" route is one you've probably written:

system: `You are Acme's support assistant. Today is ${new Date().toISOString()}. The user is on the ${user.page} page.`,

The AI SDK sends system as the first developer item in input. That's the right place for stable text, but this text isn't stable. On turn two, input[0] had a new timestamp and page, so it no longer matched what came before the turn-one reasoning item. The response reported:

[{ "id": "rs_1", "type": "reasoning", "action": "removed", "reason": "prefix_mismatch" }]

The prompt caching guide gives the same advice for cache hits: move timestamps and user-specific content to the end, not the beginning.

The fix: a static system prompt, per-turn context in instructions 

// app/api/chat/route.js
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages } from 'ai';
import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

const SYSTEM = "You are Acme's support assistant. Answer from the order data you are given.";

export async function POST(req) {
  const { messages, user } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai('gpt-6.2-sol'),
    system: SYSTEM, // never changes, so it stays a stable, cacheable prefix
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    providerOptions: {
      openai: {
        reasoningSummary: 'auto',
        // GPT-6.2 appends this after input, so it can change every turn
        instructions: `Today is ${new Date().toISOString()}. The user is on the ${user.page} page.`,
        // send it on every request, with the same value for the whole conversation
        safetyIdentifier: createHash('sha256').update(user.id ?? user.sessionId).digest('hex').slice(0, 32),
      },
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({
    sendReasoning: true,
    messageMetadata: ({ part }) =>
      part.type === 'finish-step'
        ? { dropped: part.providerMetadata?.openai?.inputTransformations ?? [] }
        : undefined,
  });
}

We drove both routes the way useChat does: post the UI messages, rebuild the assistant message with readUIMessageStream, append it, and ask a follow-up. With the fixed route, input[0] was byte-identical on both turns, the new page name arrived in top-level instructions, and dropped was empty. The turn-one reasoning went back as an item_reference and was kept.

One detail we got wrong at first: inputTransformations is on the finish-step part's provider metadata, not on finish. Read it there, or you'll see nothing.

On the client, your shadcn chat stays the same. Show reasoning parts in a collapsible block and text parts as the answer. In development, it helps to log message.metadata.dropped.

Honest limits

  • We didn't call the real API. The checks in our mock follow the docs. Before you ship, run one real two-turn request and look at input_transformations.
  • Signing in mid-chat still drops reasoning. If the identifier goes from a session hash to a user hash, that's an end_user_mismatch, and our fixed route hit it too. Decide whether a conversation keeps the identifier it started with.
  • instructions aren't cached. OpenAI bills those tokens at the uncached input rate on every request, so keep them short.
  • History trimming counts as an edit. Rewriting or shortening old tool outputs, or summarising old turns at the front, changes the prefix. The keep-the-prefix guide suggests compaction, or placing summaries at the end. Deleting whole items without editing the rest doesn't trigger prefix_mismatch on its own.
  • Changing settings mid-chat. Changing reasoning.effort, tools or text.format between requests can also change the prefix. The docs suggest appending configuration_update or additional_tools items instead. We didn't test those here.

Sources

  • Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, OpenAI
  • OpenAI API changelog
  • Using GPT-6.2
  • GPT-6.2 Astra model page and GPT-6.2 Sol model page
  • Keep the prefix unchanged
  • Reasoning models: reasoning item removal
  • Prompt caching
  • @ai-sdk/openai 4.0.120 and 4.0.121

If you'd rather not hand-build the reasoning block and message list, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style components for AI chat that work with this setup.

title: AWS us-east-1 Outage on November 15, 2026: What Happened to Sign-In and Network Load Balancers, and How to Design Around It
description:
On November 15, 2026, AWS reported connectivity issues in us-east-1 from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST that affected 11 services, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected. AWS has not published a root cause. The design lessons are to keep a break-glass sign-in path that does not depend on single sign-on, to spread load balancer targets across multiple Availability Zones, and to keep workloads already running in a second region.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

On Sunday, November 15, 2026, AWS us-east-1 had increased connectivity issues for 3 hours and 16 minutes, from the start time AWS gave (3:05 AM PST) to the last recovery (6:21 AM PST), according to the AWS Health Dashboard.

  • IAM Identity Center and AWS Sign Up were among 11 affected services, which also included Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected.
  • AWS fully mitigated the authentication issue at 5:20 AM PST. The NLB subset recovered last, at 6:21 AM PST.
  • AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack.
  • When IAM Identity Center sign-in fails, responders lose SSO access to the console and CLI, which slows incident response.
  • NLB nodes route to targets in their own Availability Zone by default, so targets in a single zone fail with that zone.
  • A second region that already serves traffic keeps users served when one region is impaired.
  • On Control Plane, a workload runs in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s set of locations across clouds, so when it runs in two or more locations and one fails, users are routed to the healthy ones.

What happened in AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS gave these times in its resolved update on the AWS Health Dashboard, posted at 6:53 AM PST.

Time (PST) What AWS reported
3:05 AM Start of signup errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues in us-east-1, per AWS’s resolved update. AWS lists 11 affected services, including IAM Identity Center and AWS Sign Up.
4:38 AM AWS posts its first update.
5:20 AM AWS fully mitigated the issue affecting authentication, and most AWS services observed full recovery.
6:10 AM End of the event window given in AWS’s resolved update.
6:21 AM AWS fully mitigated the underlying issue for a subset of customers using NLB in a single cell in use1-az1.
6:53 AM AWS posts its resolved update.

AWS’s resolved update gives 3:05 AM to 6:10 AM as the event window, and the same update says a subset of customers using NLBs in a single cell of use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM, 11 minutes later.

The 11 services AWS listed are IoT Device Management, CloudWatch, Connect, OpenSearch, Elastic Load Balancing, IAM Identity Center, Kiro, NAT Gateway, Sign Up, Step Functions, and VPC Lattice.

Why did a sign-in outage matter so much?

IAM Identity Center is the sign-in path for many organizations that use AWS single sign-on. When it is unavailable, engineers cannot use SSO to open the AWS Management Console. CLI sessions that depend on SSO-issued credentials cannot be refreshed. Credentials already issued keep working until they expire. The people who need to respond to an incident lose their usual way in.

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center is enabled in one primary Region. If that Region has a disruption, SSO access to accounts can be affected even when the workloads in those accounts run elsewhere. AWS supports replicating an organization instance to additional Regions so workforce users can keep reaching their AWS accounts, with permissions provisioned before the disruption, if the primary Region is disrupted. Replication needs a multi-Region customer managed KMS key and is not available with an Active Directory identity source. Management access and workload health are separate concerns, and each needs its own fallback.

AWS documentation recommends setting up emergency access to the console before a disruption occurs. One option is direct federation from your external identity provider to individual AWS accounts. Another is break-glass access that does not depend on that identity provider. AWS also recommends testing the configuration periodically, because you cannot create the required IAM roles if your access to create them is also disrupted.

On-call engineers often learn about an incident from alerts and then need to sign in to investigate. If sign-in fails, escalation steps that assume console access stall. Runbooks that fetch SSO tokens stall too.

This table maps each failure type to what it blocks and a workaround that does not depend on the failing component.

Failure What it blocks Workaround that does not depend on it
IAM Identity Center sign-in down New console and CLI sign-ins through SSO, so engineers cannot sign in to respond Emergency access through direct IAM federation, break-glass IAM users or roles with strong MFA, or a replicated IAM Identity Center instance in a second Region, set up and tested in advance
NLB cell in one AZ impaired Traffic to targets behind that NLB in that zone Targets registered in multiple AZs, or a new NLB with targets in multiple AZs as AWS advised
A regional service in us-east-1 impaired Anything homed only in that region Workloads already running in a second region, with DNS failover configured
Status and alerting hosted in the same region You cannot see or announce the incident Status page and alerting hosted outside the failing region

Authentication, load balancing, regional placement, and communication are four failure domains, and each needs a fallback that does not share the others’ dependencies.

What does a single-cell Network Load Balancer failure mean for your architecture?

AWS reported that a subset of customers using NLB in a single cell in use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM PST. Two AWS behaviors explain why that matters.

The first is how Availability Zones are named. An AZ ID such as use1-az1 identifies the same physical zone in every AWS account. Zone names such as us-east-1a are mapped randomly per account, so us-east-1a in one account may be a different physical zone from us-east-1a in another. To check whether your resources sat in the affected zone, compare AZ IDs. The VPC console shows the AZ ID for each subnet, and the AWS CLI describe-availability-zones command returns the mapping for your account.

The second is how Network Load Balancers route traffic. By default, each NLB node distributes traffic only across the registered targets in its own Availability Zone. Cross-zone load balancing is off by default for NLBs. You can turn it on at the load balancer level or per target group. AWS documentation states that an NLB is most effective when each enabled Availability Zone has at least one registered target.

The NLB has one IP address per enabled Availability Zone, and its DNS name resolves to those addresses. If the node in one zone is impaired and that zone holds your only targets, traffic to those targets stops. Healthy instances in other zones do not receive it unless they are registered and reachable through a working node.

AWS recommended that customers who needed immediate resolution create a new NLB with targets in multiple Availability Zones, and later recommended retrying any failed requests. Acting on that advice during an incident requires three things. You already have capacity running in other zones. You can update DNS records or upstream references quickly. You can sign in to make the change. The sign-in issue earlier in the same morning shows why the third point needs its own plan.

Register NLB targets in at least two Availability Zones. Decide per workload whether to turn on cross-zone load balancing. Watch target health and zonal health per zone so a zonal problem shows up before users report it. For an NLB with targets in more than one zone, you can turn on zonal shift and use it to move traffic away from one zone. Zonal shift is off by default.

How do you prepare for the next us-east-1 incident?

This checklist covers the six areas this incident touched, with a way to test each one.

Area What to have in place How to test it
Break-glass access Emergency access configured before any disruption, through direct IAM federation, break-glass IAM users or roles with strong MFA that do not depend on IAM Identity Center, or a replicated IAM Identity Center instance in a second Region Run a periodic sign-in drill using only the emergency path
Multi-AZ NLB targets and cross-zone settings Targets registered in two or more AZs for every NLB, with cross-zone load balancing set per workload Deregister targets in one AZ in a test environment and confirm traffic still reaches the others
A second region already serving traffic At least one more region running the workload and receiving production traffic Route part of real traffic to the second region on a schedule and confirm end-to-end behavior
DNS failover with health checks Route 53 health checks on endpoints in each region, with failover records and TTLs short enough for your recovery target Fail a health check on purpose and confirm DNS resolves to the healthy region
Status page and alerting outside the failing region Incident communication and alert pipelines hosted in another region or with a provider that does not depend on us-east-1 Send a test alert while simulating loss of us-east-1 and confirm it reaches on-call
Runbooks that do not need SSO Recovery steps that use the emergency access path and pre-provisioned resources Walk each runbook in a tabletop exercise without SSO

Route 53 health checks can monitor endpoints, and DNS failover records route traffic away from an endpoint that fails its check. Configure health checks and failover records in advance, because editing Route 53 records depends on Route 53’s management API in us-east-1. Failover only helps if the second region already has capacity and data it can serve. Schedule each drill in the checklist so every runbook has run at least once before an incident.

How does this compare with other cloud outages?

The November 15, 2026 incident lasted 3 hours and 16 minutes.

The cloud outage tracker records 63 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare incidents since January 2020, with a median duration of 5 hours and 57 minutes. By that measure, this incident was shorter than the median major incident across those providers.

Regional incidents happen on every large cloud. The useful response is design work: separate the sign-in path from the workload path, spread capacity across zones, and run in more than one region before you need to. Designing systems that survive the inevitable covers those patterns in more depth.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you already run and your own servers. A workload runs in every location of its GVC, and by default every location serves traffic. When a workload runs in two or more locations and one fails, DNS routes users to the nearest location where the workload passes its readiness probes.

During the October 19 to 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, which lasted about 14 and a half hours, 20% of Control Plane customers had AWS us-east-1 in their GVC. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane runs the workloads you deploy on it. It does not change how third-party SaaS, identity providers, or other organizations’ networks behave, so the break-glass and sign-in steps for AWS access still apply. For more on regional failures, read how companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages and how to keep your app online during an AWS region outage.

FAQ

These answers cover sign-in, load balancing, and regional design after the November 15, 2026 us-east-1 incident.

What happened to AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS reported increased connectivity issues in us-east-1 from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST, according to the AWS Health Dashboard. The incident affected 11 services, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected. That NLB subset recovered last.

Was the November 15 AWS outage a cyberattack?

AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. AWS described the event as increased connectivity issues.

How do I sign in to AWS when IAM Identity Center is down?

Use an access path you set up before the disruption. AWS documents replicating IAM Identity Center to an additional Region, direct IAM federation from your external identity provider to individual accounts, and break-glass access that does not depend on that identity provider. AWS recommends testing the setup periodically.

What is a break-glass account in AWS?

A break-glass account is an emergency IAM user or role, protected with strong MFA, that you use when normal sign-in paths such as IAM Identity Center are unavailable. Keep its credentials stored securely, limit who can use it, and test it on a schedule.

Are Network Load Balancers multi-AZ?

An NLB can span multiple Availability Zones, but by default each NLB node routes only to targets in its own zone. Cross-zone load balancing is off by default. Register targets in every enabled zone so the loss of one zone does not stop traffic.

What does use1-az1 mean?

use1-az1 is an Availability Zone ID in us-east-1 that refers to the same physical zone in every AWS account. Zone names such as us-east-1a are mapped randomly per account. Compare AZ IDs to check whether your resources were in the affected zone.

How do companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages?

They run workloads in at least two regions and use DNS failover with health checks to move traffic to the healthy region. They also keep an emergency sign-in path that does not depend on a single identity service. Status pages and alerting run outside the region they monitor.

Did AWS publish a root cause for the November 15 outage?

No. As of November 18, 2026, AWS has not published a root cause for the November 15 us-east-1 incident.

How long did the November 15, 2026 AWS outage last?

It lasted 3 hours and 16 minutes, from the start time AWS gave (3:05 AM PST) to the last recovery (6:21 AM PST). AWS’s resolved update lists 3:05 AM to 6:10 AM as the event window and reports that the NLB subset in use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM.

Should I move all my workloads out of us-east-1?

No. Run critical workloads in us-east-1 and at least one other region at the same time, with DNS failover and an independent sign-in path. A disruption in one region then affects a share of capacity, and the rest keeps serving.

title: The November 2026 Outage Wave, Explained: What Broke at Microsoft 365, the FAA, AWS, Chase, and United, and What Didn’t Happen
description:
In mid-November 2026, Microsoft 365, the FAA’s air traffic control network, AWS us-east-1, JPMorgan Chase, and United Airlines each had a major outage within five days, each with a different stated cause or none published yet, and none has been linked to a cyberattack or to another outage in the wave. Where a mechanism has been published, it shows how a fault in one widely used component can spread into a wide outage, a risk every team can check in its own architecture.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Five widely reported outages hit five organizations between November 12 and November 16, 2026, and no organization or official reported evidence of a cyberattack.

  • Five outages in five days: Microsoft 365, the FAA, AWS us-east-1, Chase, and United Airlines.
  • Each has stated a different cause or has not published one yet.
  • None was linked to a cyberattack, and none has been linked to the others.
  • Durations ranged from about 90 minutes (United) to about 24 hours (Microsoft 365).
  • The “90-day blackout starting November 17” claim was a hoax built on the routine Emergency Alert System test.
  • The shared lesson is general: a fault in one widely used component can spread to many services.
  • Before the next one, remove single shared dependencies, run in more than one region with traffic already flowing, test failover, and keep a break-glass sign-in path.
  • Control Plane handles Day 2 operations and runs each workload in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, with all of them serving traffic, so when a workload runs in two or more locations one failed region does not stop it.

What happened in the November 2026 outage wave?

Five major services failed between November 12 and November 16, 2026, each for a different stated reason or one not yet published.

Date What failed How long Stated cause Cyberattack? Source
Nov 12 to 13 Microsoft 365: Exchange Online and Outlook, plus Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, SharePoint Online, Defender for Office 365, Intune, and other services that depend on Exchange Online, in North America, Europe, Asia Pacific, and Australia About 24 hours, 11:20 AM ET on Nov 12 to 11:10 AM ET on Nov 13 (16:20 to 16:10 UTC) A latent defect in a July 2026 update to Microsoft 365 network gateway servers, exposed by extra load after Teams failed over to the gateway used by Exchange Online and by almost 14% of gateway capacity already offline “A technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents” (Microsoft) Microsoft preliminary post-incident report (MO1550821); BleepingComputer; The Register; Ars Technica
Nov 13 FAA nationwide ground stop, with network instability at 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers Stop announced 3:36 PM ET; traffic resumed about 8:15 PM ET Excess connection traffic, about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, traced to two sites: a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a new router had been installed during a copper-to-fiber replacement, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Root cause under investigation. Homeland Security said there were no indications of a cyberattack Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford; FAA; CBS; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin
Nov 15 AWS us-east-1: connectivity and sign-in errors across 11 services in N. Virginia, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and a subset of Network Load Balancers in use1-az1 3 hours 16 minutes, 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST AWS has not published a root cause AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack AWS
Nov 16 Chase (JPMorgan Chase) banking; customers at other banks saw delays on transactions with Chase Not publicly specified A software bug in an on-premises hardware system, per Chase “Not cyber-related” (Chase) Chase via AP
Nov 16 A United technology system that departures depended on Departures delayed for about 90 minutes; no impact on flights in progress Not stated; the pilots’ union said the weight-and-balance system was affected “No indication” of a cyber issue (United) United Airlines via CBS and AP

Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report, published November 15, says three problems combined. Teams had failed over to the gateway used by Exchange Online about 15 hours before the outage, adding load, and almost 14% of gateway capacity was already offline. A latent defect from a July 2026 update then caused lock contention that exhausted CPU and memory, and more than 80% of gateway servers became unresponsive. Rerouted traffic hit other gateways, which failed the same way. Exchange Online could not fail over to other infrastructure for scale reasons, restarts did not hold, and rollback was not possible because the change was months old, so engineers deployed an update reverting the defective code path. Its final report is due November 20. Azure status showed no active events, and there was no confirmed impact on customer Azure workloads.

The FAA network was unstable for about 45 minutes before the stop while engineers searched for the cause, and roughly 3,500 flights were already airborne when departures stopped. Some frequencies and radar feeds stayed operational, so the outage was partial. L3Harris blocked the two source locations and the network stabilized. The FAA and L3Harris are still investigating the root cause, and HPE, which owns Juniper, says the device worked as configured. The FAA disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers and paused installing them. It was one of only two nationwide ground stops since September 11, 2001.

AWS reported that authentication was fully mitigated by 5:20 AM PST, and the subset of Network Load Balancers in one cell of use1-az1 was the last part to recover. AWS advised customers with affected Network Load Balancers to create a new load balancer with targets in multiple Availability Zones.

A Chase spokesman said the cause was a software bug in an on-premises hardware system and that it “is not cyber-related.” Customers at other banks saw delays on transactions with Chase, including Zelle payments; Zelle’s operator said its network was fully operational. United said a technology issue delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes, with no impact on flights in progress, and it has not stated a cause. FlightAware showed 715 delayed United flights that afternoon, though CBS reported it is unclear how many the outage caused.

Was the November 2026 outage wave a cyberattack?

No organization or official reported evidence of a cyberattack, and the popular theories about the wave do not match the published evidence.

Claim What the evidence shows Verdict
“It was a coordinated attack” Microsoft, Homeland Security, Chase, and United each ruled out a cyber cause or said there was no indication of one, and AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. The stated causes differ: a latent software defect in network gateway servers, excess connection traffic from two network sites, and a software bug in on-premises hardware. AWS and United have not published causes. Not supported
“A 90-day blackout starting November 17” The November 17 event was the routine nationwide Emergency Alert System test at 2:20 PM ET, which ran about one minute on TV and radio. Hoax
“A solar storm caused it” NOAA space weather data showed quiet conditions on the outage days. Not supported
“The outages are connected” Each incident involved a different organization, different technology, and a different stated cause or none published yet. No published evidence links any two of them. Not supported
“Cyber activity is up” Ransomware against hospitals and universities was elevated in the same period, and CISA added more known-exploited vulnerabilities than usual in September and October. None of it was linked to these outages. True, but separate

On November 18, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages were not malicious, according to Nextgov. Elevated ransomware activity is a real and separate risk. Treating it as the cause of these outages would point teams at the wrong problem.

What do these outages have in common?

Where a mechanism has been published, a fault in one component spread to many services that depended on it.

Incident What failed Question to ask of your own system
Microsoft 365 Network gateway servers with a latent defect, already short of capacity, took on rerouted Teams traffic (Microsoft preliminary report) If several servers fail at once and traffic reroutes, can the remaining capacity absorb it without spreading the fault?
FAA ground stop Excess connection traffic from two sites caused instability at 17 of 22 air traffic control centers (root cause under investigation) Can one site send unlimited connection traffic to every other site?
AWS us-east-1 Connectivity and sign-in errors in one AWS Region (root cause not published) Do your load balancer targets and sign-in path span more than one Availability Zone and Region?
Chase One on-premises hardware system, per Chase (Chase has not described what depends on it) How many customer channels depend on one platform?
United Airlines A technology system departures depended on (cause not stated) Can critical workflows continue at reduced throughput if a key system is unavailable?

The mechanism repeats across industries. A shared component turns a local fault into a wide one. Resilient designs split load and control across independent failure domains and keep traffic flowing to more than one location, so losing one domain reduces capacity without stopping service.

None of this assigns fault. Each of these systems is large, and each organization disclosed what it knew. The pattern is useful because it is general, and the same review applies to any team’s own architecture.

How do these compare with past major cloud outages?

The November wave stands out for how many incidents landed in one week, and its durations sit within the range of past major incidents.

The cloud outage tracker catalogs 63 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare outages since January 2020 (median 5 hours 57 minutes; 32% caused by a configuration or deployment change). By that measure, the AWS us-east-1 event at 3 hours 16 minutes ran shorter than the median. The Microsoft 365 outage, a SaaS incident the tracker does not count, lasted about 24 hours.

In the tracker, 32% of major outages trace to a configuration or deployment change. Of the November incidents, only Microsoft has published a mechanism that fits that pattern, and AWS has not published a root cause.

What should engineering teams do before the next outage?

Outages like these will recur, so the practical goal is to limit how far any one failure can spread.

  • Remove single shared dependencies. List every component that many services rely on, such as a load balancer, an identity provider, a database, or a network segment. Give each path users depend on at least two independent ways to succeed.
  • Run in more than one region with traffic already flowing. A standby region that has never served production traffic has an untested failover path. Active-active deployments across regions or providers keep every location exercised. How companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages walks through that pattern.
  • Spread across Availability Zones inside each region. AWS’s own advice after November 15 was to create load balancers with targets in multiple Availability Zones.
  • Test failover regularly. Run drills that remove a region, an identity provider, or a key dependency, and measure recovery time against your targets.
  • Keep a break-glass sign-in path. Maintain an administrative login that does not depend on the same region or sign-in service as your primary workloads.
  • Separate status communications from the systems they report on. Host status pages and alerting on independent infrastructure so the team can still communicate during an outage.
  • Size resilience to the cost of downtime. Regulated industries such as financial services face operational and compliance consequences from long outages.

Staged rollouts and isolated testing for new hardware and configuration also limit blast radius by keeping a misbehaving change inside one segment. Designing systems that survive the inevitable covers active-active architecture and failure domains in more depth.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you already run and your own servers. Every location in a GVC serves traffic, so when a workload runs in two or more locations and one region fails, users are routed to the healthy locations.

On October 20, 2025, 20% of Control Plane customers had AWS us-east-1 in their GVC. Their workloads were “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. Control Plane runs the workloads you deploy on it; it does not change how third-party SaaS, identity providers, or other organizations’ networks behave.

FAQ

Short answers on the November 2026 outages, their causes, and the hoax.

What were the biggest cloud outages of 2026, and how long did they last?

The longest 2026 entries in the cloud outage tracker are AWS’s me-central-1 (UAE) and me-south-1 (Bahrain) Regions, out since early March after physical damage and still not fully restored. Next come Azure West US 2 on May 29 to 30 (22 hours 6 minutes), a single Availability Zone in AWS us-east-1 on May 7 to 8 (21 hours 30 minutes to majority recovery), and Azure West US on February 7 to 8 (20 hours 26 minutes). In November, AWS us-east-1 had connectivity and sign-in errors for 3 hours 16 minutes on November 15, and the Microsoft 365 SaaS outage, which the tracker does not count, lasted about 24 hours. The tracker lists 63 major outages since January 2020, with a median duration of 5 hours 57 minutes.

Was the November 2026 outage a cyberattack?

No evidence of a cyberattack has been reported for any of the five outages. Microsoft called its outage “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” Homeland Security said there were no indications of a cyberattack at the FAA. Chase said its outage “is not cyber-related,” United said there was “no indication” of a cyber issue, and AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. On November 18, the DHS Secretary, the Director of National Intelligence, and the FBI Deputy Director told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages were not malicious.

What caused the Microsoft 365 outage in November 2026?

Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report says three things combined: a latent defect in a July 2026 update to its Microsoft 365 network gateway servers, extra load after Teams traffic shifted onto the gateway used by Exchange Online, and almost 14% of gateway capacity already offline. The defect exhausted server resources, rerouted traffic hit other gateways that failed the same way, and more than 80% of gateway servers became unresponsive. Exchange Online could not fail over to other infrastructure, so email was down longest. Microsoft’s final report is due November 20.

Why did the FAA issue a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026?

The FAA stopped departures because its air traffic control network became unstable at 17 of its 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The FAA traced excess connection traffic, about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, to two sites: a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a new router had been installed during a copper-to-fiber replacement, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. The network was unstable for about 45 minutes before the FAA announced the stop at 3:36 PM ET, and traffic resumed about 8:15 PM ET. The root cause is still under investigation.

What happened to AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS reported connectivity and sign-in errors affecting 11 services in N. Virginia from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST. Affected services included IAM Identity Center sign-in and a subset of Network Load Balancers in use1-az1, which were the last to recover. Authentication was fully mitigated by 5:20 AM PST. AWS has not published a root cause.

Is there going to be a 90-day blackout?

No. The “90-day blackout starting November 17” claim was built on the routine nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which ran at 2:20 PM ET on November 17 for about one minute on TV and radio.

How do companies stay online during cloud outages?

Companies that stay online usually run workloads in more than one region, or on more than one cloud provider, with live traffic flowing to every location. When one region fails, traffic shifts to locations that are already serving users. They also keep break-glass sign-in paths, test failover on a schedule, and host status pages and alerting apart from the systems they monitor.

Did the November 2026 outages affect Azure?

There was no confirmed impact on customer Azure workloads. Azure status showed no active events during the Microsoft 365 outage, which centered on the network gateway servers behind Exchange Online and the services that depend on it.

Were the November 2026 outages related to each other?

No published evidence links any two of the five outages. Each involved a different organization, different technology, and a different stated cause or none published yet. The general lesson they share is that a fault in one widely used component can spread to many services.

title: Benchmarking TypeScript KV & Cache Engines in 2026: KVDock vs. Unstorage vs. Keyv
description:
Choosing a key-value or caching abstraction in TypeScript usually comes down to three questions:

  1. What happens when a hot cache key expires under 1,000 concurrent requests? (Does your database get slammed by a thundering herd?)
  2. Can I pair an in-process L1 memory cache with a distributed L2 store (like Redis or Cloudflare KV) without writing 200 lines of glue code?
  3. Does it work across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Edge Workers with zero dependency bloat?

We ran a head-to-head architectural and benchmark comparison between KVDock, Unstorage, and Keyv.

🎮 Launch the Live Browser Stampede Simulator

⭐ Support open-source infrastructure: Star KVDock on GitHub ★

1. Architectural Feature Matrix

Capability kvdock unstorage keyv
Single-Flight Stampede Protection (getOrSet) 🟢 Built-in ❌ Manual ❌ No
Native Multi-Tier Caching (TieredDock L1+L2) 🟢 Built-in with auto-promotion 🟡 Overlay driver ❌ No
Zero Runtime Dependencies in Core 🟢 Yes (0 deps) 🟢 Yes ❌ No
Memory-Safe Streaming Scans (dock.scan()) 🟢 AsyncIterable cursor 🟡 Full array getKeys() 🟡 Iterator
Compare-And-Swap (cas) & Atomic Counters 🟢 Built-in (cas, increment) ❌ No ❌ No
Tag-Based Group Invalidation (invalidateTag) 🟢 Built-in ❌ No ❌ No
Next.js 15 App Router Incremental Cache 🟢 Official Handler 🟡 Community ❌ No
Distributed Locks with Fencing Tokens 🟢 Built-in (withLock) ❌ No ❌ No

2. The Thundering Herd Benchmark (1,000 Concurrent Misses)

When a cached key expires at the exact moment 1,000 requests hit your API, a standard get() + set() cache pattern causes all 1,000 callers to see null and query PostgreSQL simultaneously.

With kvdock.getOrSet(), concurrent requests for the same missing key attach to a single in-flight promise:

import { KVDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";

const dock = new KVDock({ adapter: new MemoryAdapter() });

// 1,000 concurrent callers -> 1 database query, 999 coalesced waiters
const data = await dock.getOrSet("report:daily", async () => {
  return await db.query("SELECT * FROM heavy_aggregation");
}, { ttl: 60_000 });

You can reproduce this benchmark locally in one command:

git clone https://github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock.git
cd kvdock && npm install && npm run build
node scripts/benchmark-stampede.mjs

Explore KVDock

  • 📦 GitHub: https://github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock
  • 🎮 Interactive Simulator: https://zisam-glitch.github.io/kvdock/playground/index.html

If you appreciate zero-dependency TypeScript libraries with real benchmarks, please give zisam-glitch/kvdock a ★ Star on GitHub!

👤 About the Author

I'm Zisam Shaikh (@zisam-glitch), a systems & infrastructure engineer building zero-dependency caching and storage engines across TypeScript, Rust, Go, Swift, and Kotlin.

title: How my terminal knows which AI coding agent is waiting for me
description:
I usually have four or five coding agents running at once: Claude Code in one repo, Codex in another, an OpenCode session fixing tests somewhere else. The agents are fine. The part that kept wasting my time was simpler: which one is waiting for me right now?

One agent has been sitting on "Do you want to proceed?" for ten minutes. Another finished a while ago. A third is still working. With five terminal windows you find out by clicking through all of them.

So I built a terminal app around that one question, TernaryCode. This post is about the part that turned out to matter most: how it knows what each agent is doing.

Don't read the screen

The obvious approach is to watch the terminal output. Look for a spinner, a prompt like Do you want to proceed?, or an idle cursor. I tried it, and it breaks all the time:

  • The wording changes between versions.
  • A long tool call looks exactly like a hung agent.
  • An agent that printed its last line and an agent that is still thinking look the same.
  • Every agent draws its interface differently.

Guessing gets it wrong often enough that you stop trusting the status at all, and then the status is useless.

Ask the agent instead: hooks

The agents already announce what they're doing, through hooks. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode can each run a command when something happens: a prompt is submitted, a tool is about to run, a permission is needed, a turn ends. That's the signal I wanted, straight from the agent.

Every hook in TernaryCode runs one small binary, ternarycode-hook <agent> <event>. It forwards the event over a local socket, with a token that ties it to the pane the agent runs in. Outside a TernaryCode pane it does nothing, so it's harmless if an agent is started somewhere else.

Claude Code: --settings per launch

Claude Code merges the hooks from a --settings file with the user's own. TernaryCode writes that file once and starts Claude like this:

claude --settings "$TC_CLAUDE_SETTINGS"

The file looks like this, with one entry per event:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PermissionRequest": [
      { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "ternarycode-hook claude PermissionRequest" }] }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "ternarycode-hook claude Stop" }] }
    ]
  }
}

It covers SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, Notification, Stop, StopFailure and SessionEnd.

Codex: -c overrides for one run

Codex takes config overrides on the command line, so the hooks exist for that run only:

codex -c 'hooks={PermissionRequest=[{hooks=[{type="command",command="ternarycode-hook codex PermissionRequest"}]}],Stop=[…]}' \
      -c 'notify=["ternarycode-hook","codex","notify"]'

Codex asks you once to trust new hooks, in its own dialog. Its notify program also reports approval-requested and agent-turn-complete, which fills a few gaps.

OpenCode: a tiny plugin

OpenCode has plugins rather than hooks. TernaryCode's plugin listens for a handful of events (session.status, session.idle, session.error, permission.asked, permission.updated, permission.replied) and passes them to the same binary. It returns at once when it isn't running inside a TernaryCode pane.

From events to three states

All of that collapses into the states you actually care about:

State Claude Code Codex OpenCode
Working UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse session.status busy, permission.replied
Needs you PermissionRequest, Notification (permission prompt) PermissionRequest, notify approval-requested permission.asked
Done Stop, StopFailure Stop, notify agent-turn-complete session.idle, session.error

There's one small exception: when Claude Code is about to show a plan for approval or ask you a question, the PreToolUse for that tool means "needs you", not "working".

What I learned building it

Don't touch the user's config by default. Everything above is passed per launch. Your ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/config.toml stay exactly as they were. If you also want agents you start by hand to report their status, there's an opt-in install. It shows the exact diff first and keeps a backup, and uninstalling restores the file byte for byte.

Unknown is not idle. Some agents have no hooks yet (Antigravity CLI, for one). Those show as plain "Active" rather than a guess. A status you can't trust is worse than no status.

Order matters more than color. Once you know which agents are waiting, the question becomes "which first?" Agents that need you line up oldest first. ⌘J (Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows and Linux) takes you to the next one, in whichever project it is, and ⇧⌘J takes you back to where you were.

Notify only when you're not looking. A system notification for an agent in the pane you're reading is just noise. Notifications and the Dock badge only fire when the app isn't in front.

The rest of the app

The status is the core, but the app grew around it:

  • Each project keeps its own terminals, tabs and splits. A Grid view shows every project's terminal live in a tile.
  • The agents get a browser panel beside the terminal and drive it through an MCP server: they open your dev server, click, type and read the console. You can take over at any time.
  • A Code drawer has your language servers. You can review the diff, then commit, push and open the PR in one step, and start an agent in its own git worktree.

It's written in Rust: alacritty_terminal for the terminal emulation, egui/wgpu for drawing, and wry for the web view. There's no Electron. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and when nothing changes it draws no frames at all.

TernaryCode is free and MIT licensed, with no account: github.com/ilhamnadhif/ternarycode. If you run several agents at once, I'd love to hear where the status gets it wrong.

I'm the author of TernaryCode. This post was written by Claude Code from TernaryCode's source code, and the details were checked against it.

title: Node.js File Uploads: Presigned URLs, Proxy Backend, and Security (Fintech)
description:
Short answer: for browser file upload of fintech training artifacts, use a presigned URL when the browser can send bytes directly to private object storage; keep a proxy backend for content inspection or policy decisions that must happen before storage. Track both paths with the same retention record so cost, latency, and security are measurable instead of guessed.

The system has one job: accept a training artifact, preserve its chain of custody, and delete it according to a reproducible policy. A proxy path is browser -> Node.js -> storage. A direct path is browser -> storage, with Node.js authorizing the transfer and recording metadata. That small difference moves bandwidth, trust, and failure handling to different places.

Keep it private.

The first decision is about control, not a URL

Path Pick it when What you pay for operationally Main security control
Presigned URL Artifacts can be scanned after arrival and the browser needs low latency Upload state, CORS, and orphan cleanup Short expiry, private bucket, narrow key and size policy
Proxy backend Bytes need synchronous inspection, transformation, or a single egress point Application bandwidth, connection limits, and backpressure Stream validation before forwarding; never buffer unbounded bodies
Two-step quarantine You need direct transfer plus a gate before promotion A second state and scanner queue Write to quarantine, scan, then copy or mark approved

Cost follows byte movement. In a proxy design, every upload crosses the application network and competes with API traffic. Direct transfer usually lowers that contention, but it does not remove storage requests, failed retries, or abandoned multipart sessions. Latency follows the same shape: a nearby storage region can beat a distant application region, while a required scan can make a proxy the faster end-to-end choice because it rejects bad input early.

Should a web app use presigned URLs or a proxy backend for upload control?

Start with an application-level upload record. It should contain a random upload ID, tenant ID, expected byte count, content type, object key, retention class, and state (issued, received, quarantined, approved, or expired). The object key must not be derived from an untrusted filename. Keep the bucket private; a presigned URL grants a temporary operation, not a public link.

Here is a deliberately small Node.js authorization endpoint. It returns a generic storage URL produced by your storage adapter, so the rest of the application does not depend on an SDK. The adapter must enforce the same bucket, key prefix, method, and maximum size that the record contains.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

type UploadIntent = {
  uploadId: string;
  objectKey: string;
  contentType: string;
  maxBytes: number;
  expiresAt: string;
  uploadUrl: string;
};

export async function createUploadIntent(tenantId: string, contentType: string): Promise<UploadIntent> {
  const uploadId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const objectKey = `training/${tenantId}/${uploadId}`;
  const maxBytes = 50 * 1024 * 1024;
  const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();

  const uploadUrl = await storage.presignPut({
    key: objectKey,
    contentType,
    maxBytes,
    expiresAt
  });

  await uploads.insert({ uploadId, tenantId, objectKey, contentType, maxBytes, expiresAt, state: "issued" });
  return { uploadId, objectKey, contentType, maxBytes, expiresAt, uploadUrl };
}

The browser uses the returned URL with the method and headers that were signed. After the request completes, the API performs a head check and compares the recorded byte count and checksum before moving the record to received. A 201 from your intent endpoint is not proof that the file arrived. That distinction prevents a support ticket from becoming a forensic exercise.

For a proxy, keep the same record and state machine. Stream the request, reject an announced or observed body above the limit, and cap concurrent streams per tenant. Return 413 for an oversized body, and emit a request ID that joins the API log to the storage log. I put the byte counter beside the stream, not in a later batch job; that is where a sudden 2 GB upload becomes visible.

What does the retention policy look like after upload?

Retention is a data contract, not a cleanup slogan. Store a policy version such as train-artifact-v3 with each upload. A worker can then calculate delete_at from the artifact's creation time and policy version, while a lifecycle rule in object storage provides a second, time-based backstop. AWS documents lifecycle management for expiring objects, and Google Cloud documents equivalent storage concepts; the exact rule syntax differs, so test it in a disposable bucket.

The quarantine path is useful when malware scanning or PII detection must precede approval. Direct upload still handles the bytes efficiently, but only the scanner can change quarantined to approved. A proxy is the better fit when that scan must happen before any durable object exists, or when regulation requires one controlled ingress address.

Measure a decision with the same fields on both paths: upload ID, tenant, byte range, storage region, elapsed milliseconds, retry count, final state, and retention policy version. Alert on issued records older than the URL expiry, quarantined records past their scan SLO, and multipart sessions with no progress. A dashboard that only counts HTTP 200 responses misses the abandoned half of the workflow.

My rule is boring and useful: compare p95 time-to-received, application egress bytes, scanner queue time, and rejected-byte rate for a week of representative artifacts. Your mileage may vary with enterprise proxies and browser CORS settings; a synthetic test from one laptop cannot settle that question. Also test expiry, tab refresh, duplicate completion, and a 413 response before launch.

This measurement takes more care than it first appears. For example, a direct upload can show a fast browser transfer while the quarantine scanner waits in a queue; a proxy can show higher request latency while rejecting a disallowed file before it reaches durable storage. Put both timestamps in the upload record, then report transfer time and approval time separately. Tag retries by cause (expired URL, client disconnect, policy rejection), and sample a few raw request IDs each day. That makes a cost or latency regression explainable: you can point to extra application egress, a slow region, or a scanner backlog instead of arguing from averages.

Measure twice.

When an upload fails, classify the boundary before changing the architecture. A browser-side CORS rejection is different from an expired signature, and both are different from a storage write that succeeded while the acknowledgement was lost. In the direct path, have the client send the upload ID back to the API after completion; the API can then perform its head check and safely accept a retry as an idempotent operation. In the proxy path, distinguish a client disconnect from an upstream timeout, and stop reading the request as soon as the policy limit is crossed. Record the first failure cause, not only the final retry status. A single artifact may produce three attempts: the first can fail at 8 MB because the tab was closed, the second can receive all bytes but miss its response, and the third can be rejected because the retention class changed while it was pending. Without per-attempt counters and a stable upload ID, those events collapse into one vague upload_failed metric. With them, an on-call engineer can decide whether to extend URL lifetime, tune connection pools, or fix a policy transition. The right response is often a small state-machine fix, not a wholesale move from direct upload to proxying.

The limits that should change your choice

The catch is that presigned URLs are delivery-simple, not policy-complete. They are a poor fit when every byte must be inspected synchronously, when clients cannot be trusted to reach storage, or when a single ingress point is a hard audit requirement. Stick with a proxy in those cases, accepting its throughput and scaling work.

Conversely, a proxy is not a free security upgrade. It enlarges the blast radius of a compromised app process and can turn a burst of large uploads into exhausted connections. Do not choose direct transfer for permanent public links, either; anonymous distribution is a separate access-control problem.

For this fintech workflow, I choose direct presigned transfer into quarantine, followed by a scanner and versioned retention policy. I choose a proxy only for the artifacts whose inspection or network boundary demands it. The decision is reversible when the upload record, metrics, and state transitions stay independent of the byte path.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

title: Tic-Tac-Toe Minimax Algorithm in Java
description:
In Part 1, I built a tic-tac-toe bot with a layered brain: 7 small strategies, asked one by one. It worked. I couldn't beat it anymore. But it was hard to scale. A bigger board needs more conditions, and every new condition is one more place for things to break.

It also couldn't really look ahead. Only two of the strategies, Fork and BlockFork, thought about the next move. The rest just read the board as it is right now.

So this time I threw all 7 rules away to make a single rule.

The idea: play every game

Instead of teaching the bot tic-tac-toe, we let it imagine every possible game from here, and pick the move that leads to the best ending.

Every finished game gets a score:

  • Bot wins → positive
  • Human wins → negative
  • Draw → 0

Then both players take turns inside the bot's head. On the bot's turn, it picks the highest score (maximize). On the human's turn, it assumes the human picks the lowest (minimize). That's where the name comes from: minimax.

One thing to be clear about: the bot doesn't play for the "highest chance" of winning. It assumes the human plays perfectly, and picks the best result it can guarantee.

I didn't come up with this. It's a classic algorithm, I just happened to read about it and implement it. It also has a few variations that make it even better, more on those at the end.

How the minimax algorithm works

makeMove: try every cell

makeMove is the bot's turn. We go over the board, and for every empty cell we place the bot there, ask minimax how good that is, and take the move back. The cell with the best score is our move.

for (int i = 0; i < board.getSize(); i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < board.getSize(); j++) {
        if (!board.getCell(i, j).isEmpty()) continue;

        // bot just moved here, so it's the human's turn next
        Cell cell = board.getCell(i, j);
        cell.setPlayer(bot);
        int current = minimax(board, 0, false, bot, winCheck);
        cell.clearCell();

        if (score < current) {
            score = current;
            bestMove = cell;
        }
    }
}

Notice the false. The bot has just moved, so minimax starts from the human's reply.

minimax: base conditions first

minimax uses recursion, and the first thing a recursive approach needs is a base condition. I repeat: don't forget to add an exit condition to a recursive function.

Before anything else, minimax checks if the game is already over: bot win, human win, or a draw. If it is, it returns the score.

If not, we keep playing. On the bot's turn we try every empty cell with the bot and keep the highest score. On the human's turn we do the same with the human and keep the lowest.

if (winCheck.isWinner(bot))   return 10 - depth;
if (winCheck.isWinner(human)) return depth - 10;
if (winCheck.isDraw())        return 0;

if (isBotTurn) {
    int maxValue = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    // for every empty cell:
    cell.setPlayer(bot);
    maxValue = Math.max(maxValue, minimax(board, depth + 1, false, bot, winCheck));
    cell.clearCell();
    return maxValue;
} else {
    // same thing with the human, using Math.min
}

(Ignore the depth for now, we'll get to it.)

Place, try, take it back

This is the part that makes it "imagining". The bot plays moves on the real board, and takes each one back right after: setPlayer → minimax → clearCell.

If you forget the clearCell, every imagined move stays on the board, and by the end of the search the board is full of pieces nobody really played.

You could make a copy of the board and use that too, so that your real games don't get affected.

The bugs I hit

My first version had the right idea, but it was full of small mistakes:

  • The win check didn't say who won. It returned 1 for any winner, so to the bot, the human winning looked just as good as the bot winning.
  • No undo. I set cells but never cleared them, so tried moves piled up on the board.
  • The min branch never returned. It computed minValue, then fell through to return 0. Every human turn looked like a draw, so the bot never saw a threat coming.
  • true instead of false. In makeMove I passed isBotTurn = true right after the bot's move, so the bot played twice in a row in its own head.

Why makeMove has its own loop

This was my first question. minimax already loops over the cells on the bot's turn. Why not just call it once from makeMove?

Because minimax only returns a score. It can tell you "the best the bot can get is a draw", but not which cell gets there. By the time it returns, every cell has been cleared again.

And what if we keep the loop, but don't set the cell? Then every call sees the exact same board, every cell gets the same score, and the bot always picks the first empty cell. Setting the cell is what makes the score belong to that cell.

(You can make minimax return the cell too, but the cell only matters at the top level. Deeper down, the number is all you need.)

Problem 1: the bot can look silly → depth scoring

With plain 1 / -1, a win right now and a win three moves from now look exactly the same to the bot. So sometimes it skips the obvious win and takes the long route. It still wins, but to a human it looks like a mistake.

The fix: count how deep we are in the search, and use it in the score.

if (winCheck.isWinner(bot))   return 10 - depth;   // sooner win = higher score
if (winCheck.isWinner(human)) return depth - 10;   // later loss = less bad

Now the bot prefers the fastest win. And if it's ever losing, it picks the slowest loss and makes the human work for it.

Problem 2: it's slow on bigger boards → depth limit and alpha-beta pruning

Minimax tries every possible game. On 3×3 that's fine, the first move on an empty board takes well under a second. On 4×4 the number of games explodes.

Here's how fast it grows. The first move has every cell to pick from, the next one has one less, and so on. So the number of ways to play out a full board is cells × (cells - 1) × … × 1, or cells!

Grid Empty cells Ways to play out the board Compared to 3×3
3×3 9 362,880 1×
4×4 16 ~20.9 trillion ~58 million×
5×5 25 ~1.55 × 10²⁵ ~43 billion billion×

This is an upper bound. Real games end early when someone wins, so the bot searches fewer. But the growth is the point: one extra row and column, and 3×3's "well under a second" turns into millions of times more work.

The usual fix is a depth limit: stop searching after a few moves and estimate how good the board looks. That needs a way to score unfinished boards, which my code doesn't have yet. Another fix is alpha-beta pruning, which skips branches that can't change the result.

On 3×3 the bot doesn't need either, so I've left both out.

Seeing it think

I also added one small print to the bot, so every move says which strategy picked it:

BOT is playing 0 0 (by MiniMaxStrategy)

Is it really unbeatable?

Instead of trusting my own games against it, I made two bots play each other: 100 games per match, swapping who moves first every game.

  • Against my Part 1 rule-based bot (win → block → fork → block fork → center → corner): 100 draws. Both sides play almost perfectly, so nobody wins.
  • Against a bot that just makes random moves: 88 wins, 12 draws, 0 losses. Minimax wins when the opponent makes mistakes. 
Results after 100 games:        Results after 100 games:
ALICE (rules) wins: 0           RANDY (random) wins: 0
BOB (minimax) wins: 0           CAROL (minimax) wins: 88
Draws: 100                      Draws: 12

200 games, zero losses. The best anyone can do against it is a draw.

Rules vs minimax

My rules (Part 1) Minimax
How it works Hand-written tic-tac-toe knowledge Tries every possible game
Speed Instant Slower (it searches everything)
Looks ahead Only Fork and BlockFork Every move, to the end of the game
Works on 3×3 only, really Any board (with a depth limit)

Wrapping up

Same unbeatable bot. Zero tic-tac-toe knowledge. Seven rules replaced by one recursive function.

If you want to take it further, alpha-beta pruning and a depth limit are where to start.

The full code is on GitHub: system-design/lld/tic-tac-toe
