title: What a Hex Code Taught Me: A Freelancer's Notes on Using Invert Image Tools for Dark Palettes
description:
Last spring a client asked me for a dark theme on a site that had only ever been light. They gave me four brand colors, a deadline, and one request: "make it feel the same, just dark." I did what many freelancers do in a hurry. I opened a tool, typed in the hex codes, and started to invert image swatches to see what came out. This post is about what that shortcut gave me, and where it let me down.

The shortcut

The idea is simple. Inversion subtracts each channel from 255. A light cream becomes a deep brown, a bright blue becomes a soft orange. The result is not a design, but it is a fast way to see what an "opposite" palette looks like.

For hex codes I used the hex inverter on the invert image page. You type a hex value, read the inverse and copy it. No account, no watermark, and as far as the page says, nothing leaves the browser for local files. For a quick sanity check on a client's palette, that is about as light as tools get.

What worked

It showed me contrast relationships. When a cream background became a dark brown, I could see immediately which text colors would likely stay readable. It gave me a first draft for surfaces in minutes.

It started a conversation. I showed the client two swatch sheets: the original and the flipped version. They pointed at the flipped orange and said, "that is actually closer to our old logo." I would never have tried that color myself.

It was a good test of my assumptions. I thought the dark theme would need only a couple of changes. The flipped swatches made me look at every color in the palette, and I found two accents that were too close together in the dark version.

What did not work

A pure inversion is not a dark theme. A bright blue button turns orange, which can break the meaning your client has attached to the color. A green "success" tone turns magenta. Grey text stays grey, but at the wrong contrast. If you ship the raw numbers, the interface will feel wrong even if each color is technically the opposite.

So I treated the flipped colors as raw material. I moved them toward the brand hues by hand, then checked contrast ratios with a proper accessibility checker. The inverter gave me a starting point, not an answer.

Using the same idea on images

The same tool also handles images, so I tried it on the client's hero illustration and some flat screenshots in their docs. The tool accepts JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC and TIFF up to 20 MB, and exports PNG, JPEG or WebP at the original pixel size. For the screenshots, PNG kept the transparency and edges clean. For the hero illustration, a partial flip using the strength slider felt closer to the brand than a full one. When I had a stack of small assets, the batch page took up to 30 images and gave me a ZIP, so I did not spend my evening clicking.

Three rules I follow now

  1. Treat inversion as a sketch. Use it to explore, never to ship.
  2. Keep meaning-carrying colors by hand. Success, error and warning colors should be chosen on purpose.
  3. Show the client both versions. A flipped palette is a cheap way to ask a better question.

A short note on professionalism

Clients do not pay me to press a button; they pay me to know when a button is not enough. If you use a shortcut, say so, and say what you did afterward. My client appreciated seeing the rough flipped swatches next to the final palette, because it explained the thinking.

If you work with palettes, I would like to hear what quick checks you rely on. When it comes to the humble invert image trick, I find it most useful as a conversation starter, and the final colors always need a human to decide.

title: Gin Go Tutorial: Build Fast APIs With Very Little Code
description:
Quick answer

Gin is a web framework for Go that turns a handful of routes into a working JSON API with almost no boilerplate. This post builds a small orders API with it: list orders, create an order, and fetch one order by id, with real requests and real responses.

A small online shop in Karachi takes orders through a chat app, and the owner copies each one into a spreadsheet by hand, until two customers order the same last kurta and both get a yes. The owner needs a small API: a list of orders anyone on the team can read, a way to add one, and a way to fetch one by number. Just three endpoints that answer in JSON. Go fits: it compiles to one binary and starts fast, and Gin keeps the routing and JSON work to a few lines. This post builds exactly that API and breaks it once, so you see what a bad request looks like.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the API is small enough for Gin to stay simple. Three endpoints, JSON in and JSON out, is exactly where Gin shines: one file, one router, three handlers. If the project needs HTML pages, sessions, and an admin panel, look at a bigger framework. The Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast post covers the language underneath.

My second check is the Go version. Gin v1.12.0 needs Go 1.25 or later, and the demo ran on Go 1.25.0. An older toolchain refuses to build it. Check go version first.

My third check is how the API handles bad input. Gin binds JSON into a Go struct and validates it with struct tags, but the default error messages are written for developers, not for API users. The demo returns those messages as they are, which is fine for learning. For a real client, translate them into a short message naming the field.

My fourth check is where the data lives. The demo keeps orders in a slice in memory, so every restart wipes the shop. That is fine for learning, and the wrong design for a shop that takes real money. Decide early whether the next step is a database; a demo that forgets is not a service that remembers.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Gin when you want a small, fast JSON API in Go and the team is comfortable with the language. Skip it when the project needs a full-featured framework, or when the team does not write Go. The recommendation flips the moment the API grows past simple CRUD.

Three orders, one API, and a wrong total

Three orders belong to one small shop: Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet for Rs 5,400. The first two are seeded; Hina's arrives through the API.

One file holds the whole API: the Order struct carries json tags for the field names and binding tags so a missing field fails validation, three handlers cover the three routes, and gin.Default() adds logging and panic recovery.

// Orders API for The Practical Developer (Gin demo).
//
// A small online shop exposes three endpoints with Gin:
//   GET  /orders      list all orders
//   POST /orders      create an order (JSON body, all fields required)
//   GET  /orders/:id  fetch one order by id
//
// Run from this folder:
//   go run main.go            (listens on http://localhost:8080)
//   curl http://localhost:8080/orders
package main

import (
    "net/http"
    "strconv"

    "github.com/gin-gonic/gin"
)

type Order struct {
    ID       int      `json:"id"`
    Customer string   `json:"customer" binding:"required"`
    Items    []string `json:"items" binding:"required"`
    Total    float64  `json:"total" binding:"required"`
}

var orders = []Order{
    {ID: 101, Customer: "Ayesha", Items: []string{"kurta", "dupatta"}, Total: 12400},
    {ID: 102, Customer: "Bilal", Items: []string{"sneakers"}, Total: 7800},
}

var nextID = 103

func listOrders(c *gin.Context) {
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, orders)
}

func getOrder(c *gin.Context) {
    id, err := strconv.Atoi(c.Param("id"))
    if err != nil {
        c.JSON(http.StatusBadRequest, gin.H{"error": "order id must be a number"})
        return
    }
    for _, order := range orders {
        if order.ID == id {
            c.JSON(http.StatusOK, order)
            return
        }
    }
    c.JSON(http.StatusNotFound, gin.H{"error": "order not found"})
}

func createOrder(c *gin.Context) {
    var order Order
    if err := c.ShouldBindJSON(&order); err != nil {
        c.JSON(http.StatusBadRequest, gin.H{"error": err.Error()})
        return
    }
    order.ID = nextID
    nextID++
    orders = append(orders, order)
    c.JSON(http.StatusCreated, order)
}

func main() {
    gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode)
    router := gin.Default()
    router.GET("/orders", listOrders)
    router.GET("/orders/:id", getOrder)
    router.POST("/orders", createOrder)
    router.Run(":8080")
}

Here is the real output: the list returns the two seeded orders, creating Hina's order returns it with id 103, and fetching order 101 returns Ayesha's order alone. The server log agrees.

$ go run main.go
$ curl http://localhost:8080/orders
[{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400},{"id":102,"customer":"Bilal","items":["sneakers"],"total":7800}]

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":5400}'
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":5400}

$ curl http://localhost:8080/orders/101
{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400}

[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 200 | 81.272µs | ::1 | GET      "/orders"
[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 201 | 211.888µs | ::1 | POST     "/orders"
[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 200 | 61.141µs | ::1 | GET      "/orders/101"

Hina's order goes wrong twice. First, the total is missing, so the required tag fires and Gin answers 400. Then it arrives as the text "5400" instead of the number 5400, and Go's decoder refuses it because the struct field is a float64. Neither request touches the orders list: bad data is rejected at the door, not stored and discovered later.

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"]}'
{"error":"Key: 'Order.Total' Error:Field validation for 'Total' failed on the 'required' tag"}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":"5400"}'
{"error":"json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field Order.total of type float64"}

The fix is on the client side: send every field, and send numbers as numbers. The server side already handles it: ShouldBindJSON returns the error to the handler, so the handler shapes the response. The Node.js REST API post builds the same three endpoints in JavaScript, where a missing field slips through unless you check for it, and the FastAPI post shows Python doing the same validation with Pydantic.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, using BindJSON when you want to control the error. The symptom is a plain-text 400 written by Gin itself, with no JSON body to parse. The fix is ShouldBindJSON, as the demo uses: it returns the error, and the handler decides the response.

Second, sending numbers as strings in JSON. The symptom is json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field Order.total of type float64, for a request that looks right at a glance. The fix is to send 5400, not "5400": Go types the field as a number, and JSON must match.

Third, reading the wrong path parameter name. The symptom is a 400 saying the order id must be a number, even for /orders/101. The fix is to match them: the route says /orders/:id, so the handler must call c.Param("id"), not c.Param("orderId").

Fourth, trusting the in-memory slice with real data. The symptom is orders that vanish after a restart, because the slice is rebuilt from seed data on every start. The fix is to store orders in a database; the slice is a demo only.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Gin part of Go itself? No. Gin is a third-party module, github.com/gin-gonic/gin, added with go get like any other dependency. Go's standard library serves HTTP on its own; Gin adds routing, binding, and middleware.

Do I need to know Go well before trying Gin? Basic Go is enough: structs, slices, functions, and error handling. If main.go reads clearly, you are ready; the Go Explained post fills in the language basics.

How is Gin different from the standard library net/http package? The standard library gives you a server and a handler, and you write the routing and JSON parsing yourself. Gin adds a router, JSON binding with validation, and middleware, so the same API takes less code.

Does Gin work with a database? Gin does not care where the data lives. The demo handlers read a slice, and the same handlers can query Postgres or SQLite instead. The framework handles HTTP; storage stays your choice.

What to remember

  • Gin maps a route to a handler in one line.
  • Struct tags declare the JSON shape and validation rules together.
  • ShouldBindJSON returns the error to your handler.
  • Numbers in JSON must be numbers: "5400" is text, and Go refuses it.
  • The in-memory slice is for learning; real orders need a database.

Where this leaves you

Gin earns its place the moment you want a JSON API in Go without writing your own router and JSON checks by hand. The demo proved what matters: the API listed, created, and fetched real orders, bad data was rejected with a clear 400 instead of stored, and the whole server fit in one file of about eighty lines. Start with three endpoints and an in-memory list, add a database when the orders matter, and keep the binding tags honest so bad requests fail loudly at the door.

Further reading

  • Gin docs, https://gin-gonic.com/docs/
  • Gin docs, model binding and validation, https://gin-gonic.com/en/docs/binding/binding-and-validation/
  • Go tutorial, Developing a RESTful API with Go and Gin, https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/web-service-gin
  • Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/go-explained-simple-code-that-runs-fast.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Hono: One Small API That Runs Almost Anywhere, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/hono-one-small-api-that-runs-almost.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Axum Tutorial: Build a Rust API Without the Boilerplate
description:
Quick answer

Axum is a Rust web framework built on Tokio: you describe routes with small handler functions, and Axum turns them into a fast async HTTP server. This post builds a small orders API with three routes, lists two seeded orders, creates a third, and fixes a real 422 error when the JSON body forgets a field.

A small shop in Karachi takes orders over the phone and writes each one in a paper notebook. When a customer calls to ask where an order is, someone flips pages. A simple web API would fix that: list the orders, add a new one, fetch one by number. Rust suits that little service because the compiler catches whole classes of bugs before the code runs, and the finished binary starts fast and uses little memory. Axum turns that Rust code into a server without much ceremony. The rest of this post builds that API, with real output.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the team already writes Rust. Axum is a thin layer, and most of the work is still Rust: ownership, borrowing, and async code with Tokio. A team that already ships Rust will feel at home, while a team new to Rust will spend its first week fighting the compiler. If Rust is new to everyone, the Rust Explained: Memory Safety Without the Garbage Collector post is the place to start.

My second check is whether the API needs async. Axum is async-first, and every handler runs on Tokio. That suits an API that waits on databases and other services. For a script that runs once and exits, async is machinery with no payoff. The Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express post shows the same three routes in Node.js.

My third check is how far the API needs to grow. Axum stays out of the way: routes, extractors, and shared state, with no database layer or admin panel. That suits a focused JSON API, and leaves a gap when the project needs auth and an admin screen on day one.

My fourth check is error handling. Rust makes the team decide what every failure returns: a missing order is a 404, a bad body is a 422, and the compiler refuses to let an error go unhandled. That discipline is what an API needs, though it makes the first version slower to write.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Axum when the team writes Rust and the API answers JSON. Skip it when nobody on the team knows Rust yet. The recommendation flips the moment the API needs an admin panel and auth.

Three orders, one API, and a missing total

Three orders arrive at the same small shop. Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet. The first two are seeded when the server starts; Hina's arrives later, through the API.

One file holds the whole server. An Order is what the API returns, a NewOrder is what a client sends, and the orders live in a vector behind a Mutex, shared through Axum state. Three handlers cover the routes: list them all, fetch one by id, or create one and return a 201.

// Shop orders API for The Practical Developer (Axum demo).
//
// A small online shop exposes three routes with axum and tokio:
//   GET  /orders       list every order
//   POST /orders       create an order from a JSON body
//   GET  /orders/{id}  fetch one order by id
//
// Orders live in memory, behind a Mutex, so the demo needs no
// database. A create request that forgets the total is rejected
// with 422, because the NewOrder struct requires that field.
//
// Run from this folder:
//   cargo run            (listens on http://127.0.0.1:3000)
//   curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders
use axum::{
    extract::{Path, State},
    http::StatusCode,
    routing::get,
    Json, Router,
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::{
    net::SocketAddr,
    sync::{Arc, Mutex},
};

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
struct Order {
    id: u32,
    customer: String,
    items: Vec<String>,
    total: u32,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct NewOrder {
    customer: String,
    items: Vec<String>,
    total: u32,
}

type Orders = Arc<Mutex<Vec<Order>>>;

async fn list_orders(State(orders): State<Orders>) -> Json<Vec<Order>> {
    Json(orders.lock().unwrap().clone())
}

async fn get_order(
    State(orders): State<Orders>,
    Path(id): Path<u32>,
) -> Result<Json<Order>, StatusCode> {
    let orders = orders.lock().unwrap();
    match orders.iter().find(|o| o.id == id) {
        Some(order) => Ok(Json(order.clone())),
        None => Err(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND),
    }
}

async fn create_order(
    State(orders): State<Orders>,
    Json(input): Json<NewOrder>,
) -> (StatusCode, Json<Order>) {
    let mut orders = orders.lock().unwrap();
    let id = orders.iter().map(|o| o.id).max().unwrap_or(100) + 1;
    let order = Order {
        id,
        customer: input.customer,
        items: input.items,
        total: input.total,
    };
    orders.push(order.clone());
    (StatusCode::CREATED, Json(order))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let orders: Orders = Arc::new(Mutex::new(vec![
        Order {
            id: 101,
            customer: "Ayesha".to_string(),
            items: vec!["kurta".to_string(), "dupatta".to_string()],
            total: 12400,
        },
        Order {
            id: 102,
            customer: "Bilal".to_string(),
            items: vec!["sneakers".to_string()],
            total: 7800,
        },
    ]));
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/orders", get(list_orders).post(create_order))
        .route("/orders/{id}", get(get_order))
        .with_state(orders);
    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([127, 0, 0, 1], 3000));
    println!("Axum server listening on http://{addr}");
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(addr).await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}

Here is the real output. The two seeded orders list cleanly, and then Hina's order goes wrong: the first POST forgets the total.

$ ./target/debug/shop-api
Axum server listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders
[{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400},{"id":102,"customer":"Bilal","items":["sneakers"],"total":7800}]

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"]}'
Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: missing field `total` at line 1 column 48
HTTP status: 422

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}'
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}
HTTP status: 201

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders/103
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}
HTTP status: 200

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP status: %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders/999
HTTP status: 404

The thing that went wrong is the missing total. Axum hands the JSON body to serde, which looks for a field the struct requires, and the request is rejected with 422 before the handler runs. Nothing half-created sits in the orders list. Send the total, and the same request returns 201 with order 103. The FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed post shows the same idea in Python, where a missing field also fails validation, and the Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast post shows the same three routes in Go. If a field is optional, make it Option in the struct instead of sending a made-up number.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, putting the Json extractor before State in a handler. The symptom is a compile error, E0277, saying the handler trait is not satisfied. The fix is to keep State first: body extractors must come last, so Json goes after State, as create_order does.

Second, writing a route with the old :id syntax. Axum 0.8 changed captures to braces, so /orders/:id compiles and then panics at startup with "Path segments must not start with :". The fix is to write /orders/{id}, as the demo does.

Third, forgetting the Content-Type header on a POST. The symptom is a 415 response with "Expected request with Content-Type: application/json", even though the body is valid JSON. The fix is to send that header with every POST.

Fourth, locking the Mutex and then awaiting while holding it. The symptom is a server that slows down under load, because one handler holds the lock while it waits and every other request queues behind it. The fix is to copy what the handler needs out of the lock, drop the lock, and only then await.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need Tokio to use Axum? Yes. Axum is built on Tokio, and #[tokio::main] starts the runtime the server runs on.

How is Axum different from Actix Web? Both are fast Rust frameworks, but Axum is built on Tokio and Tower, while Actix Web runs on its own runtime.

Can Axum serve HTML as well as JSON? Yes. A handler can return Html for a page, or Json for an API response. The demo returns JSON only.

What happens when a client asks for an order that does not exist? The handler returns a 404, as the curl for order 999 showed. Returning a proper status beats a 200 with an error hidden inside the body.

Do I need a database to start with Axum? No. The demo keeps orders in a vector behind a Mutex, which is enough to learn routing and state. A database comes later, when orders must survive a restart.

What to remember

  • Axum routes are small handler functions, and Tokio runs them.
  • State comes before the body extractor; Json always goes last.
  • Route captures use braces in Axum 0.8, /orders/{id}, not :id.
  • A missing required field fails with 422 before the handler runs.
  • Return proper statuses: 201 for a created order, 404 for a missing one.

Where this leaves you

Axum earns its place the day a small JSON API needs to be fast, correct, and hard to break by accident. The demo proved the three things that matter: two seeded orders listed as JSON, a bad request rejected with a 422 that named the missing field, and a fixed request creating order 103 with a 201. The compiler and the framework did the checking, not the developer's memory. Start with three routes and an in-memory list, then add a database when the orders must survive a restart. A small API that answers honestly beats a big one that guesses.

Further reading

  • Axum docs, https://docs.rs/axum
  • Axum docs, routing, https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/routing/index.html
  • Tokio docs, https://tokio.rs/
  • Axum examples, https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/tree/main/examples
  • Rust Explained: Memory Safety Without the Garbage Collector, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/rust-explained-memory-safety-without.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/go-explained-simple-code-that-runs-fast.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Browser Upload Storage Explained: R2, S3, and Wasabi (A 3-Option Guide)
description:
Cloudflare R2 is the best starting point for a customer-support SaaS that uploads product images directly from the browser, mainly because free egress keeps the delivery side simple; AWS S3 is the safer choice when global coverage and fine-grained controls matter more, while Wasabi needs a closer look at its egress rules.

That is the short answer. The real decision is not just storage per gigabyte. It is the cost of moving an image from a support agent's browser to a tenant's bucket, then back to a browser, without turning credentials and CORS into a second product.

Infrai belongs on the shortlist when the application wants one REST contract across storage and other backend capabilities. It is less useful as the component that must let each tenant configure browser CORS by itself.

The awkward part is CORS.

Should I choose cloud storage with CORS support for direct browser uploads?

What changed the decision for me

In a one-person SaaS, every infrastructure decision competes with a feature that could ship this week. I care about revenue per hour, so I outsource undifferentiated storage work. I do not want to build an upload proxy merely to avoid configuring a bucket.

The useful boundary is a presigned upload. The application authorizes a short-lived operation on the server; the browser sends the image to object storage; the application keeps the tenant and object key in its own database. The image does not pass through the application server twice.

For example, when a support agent attaches product.png to ticket 8f2e, the service can derive a key under tenant 42, check that the request belongs to that tenant, and return a presign for that one object. The browser uploads the bytes directly. The ticket record stores the key, not a public URL and not a storage credential. If another tenant guesses the key, guessing does not grant authorization to obtain a read presign. This is the small design choice that keeps the storage layer useful without asking it to become the application database.

Ship the boundary, not the bucket.

R2 fits this browser-first path well: it has low storage costs, free egress, and CORS support for direct uploads through presigned URLs. S3 provides the broadest operational menu and granular configuration, at somewhat higher pricing. Wasabi can be attractive for stored data, but its significant restrictions on native egress can complicate a workflow where support agents repeatedly view images in the browser.

Do the traffic math before picking a bucket. A low storage bill does not rescue a design that downloads every thumbnail through a costly or restricted path.

The first useful result should be boring: one authorized image in the right tenant prefix.

The storage surface currently lists 22 routes, but a long route list is not the same thing as a browser-ready upload product.

Which option fits a tenant-scoped image workflow?

Option Where it is strong Friction to check first Best fit
Cloudflare R2 Low storage cost, free egress, and CORS support for presigned direct uploads Confirm the controls and compatibility your application actually needs Browser-heavy media uploads and downloads
Amazon S3 Global coverage and granular configuration More configuration and somewhat higher pricing Systems with detailed AWS policy, region, and lifecycle requirements
Wasabi Object storage for teams that can keep access patterns predictable Native egress restrictions can complicate browser delivery Workloads where download behavior is controlled and well understood
Infrai storage One REST contract and one credential across backend capabilities It does not expose a self-service CORS configuration route A unified backend surface when CORS is handled elsewhere

The last row needs an honest reading. A stable contract can reduce integration friction: the storage provider behind the capability can move while application code keeps its boundary. One key and a shared API surface can also remove a pile of SDK and credential setup when storage is one part of a larger backend.

That does not make it the right answer to every direct-upload problem. The current storage capability has no self-service CORS configuration route. Its bucket model contains CORS-related data, but the route is not exposed for configuring it. If your acceptance test is “a new tenant can upload from its browser after my service creates a bucket,” a storage specialist with direct CORS controls is the better fit.

My explicit recommendation is: try Infrai for tenant-scoped storage when your service already has a separate, managed CORS boundary and you value one integration contract; choose R2 when direct browser upload and browser delivery are the primary workflow. That split keeps the recommendation useful instead of turning a platform abstraction into a pretend specialist.

How does the smallest upload path work?

The browser should receive a presigned URL, not a storage secret. The server should create an object key that includes the tenant boundary, such as tenant_42/tickets/8f2e/product.png, and should validate the content type and size before issuing the URL. The object key is an application decision, not a trust boundary by itself; authorization still belongs in the service that creates the presign.

Here is the server-side presign call and the browser side of the flow. The API call uses the verified storage route, while the returned URL remains provider-neutral. The route's path carries the bucket and object key, so this example deliberately sends no invented request fields.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

export async function createProductImagePresign(
  bucket: string,
  objectKey: string,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (!apiKey) {
    throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
  }

  const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket))
    .replace("{key}", encodeURIComponent(objectKey));
  let delayMs = 250;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Idempotency-Key": `presign-${bucket}-${objectKey}`,
      },
    });

    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(
          `Presign failed with HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`,
        );
      }
      return response;
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    await new Promise((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : delayMs),
    );
    delayMs *= 2;
  }

  throw new Error("Presign failed after rate-limit retries");
}

export async function uploadProductImage(
  uploadUrl: string,
  file: File,
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(uploadUrl, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": file.type,
    },
    body: file,
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Image upload failed with HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }
}

After the upload, persist the tenant ID, object key, content type, and any application-level label. Fetching the object later should be another authorization decision, usually followed by a read presign or an application-controlled response. Do not mistake Content-Disposition for access control; it describes how a user agent should handle a response, while authorization must be decided before the response is issued.

For a unified backend surface, the relevant storage operation is a presign route under /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. The contract stays in the application while the implementation behind it can change. That is a good integration property. It is not a replacement for a CORS policy.

What would I change at scale?

At a small volume, a tenant-scoped key and a short-lived presigned URL are enough to make the workflow understandable. At larger volume, I would make the object record explicit and test the failure paths: an upload can finish after the ticket tab closes, a key can be reused accidentally, and a browser can retry after a network timeout.

I would also separate upload completion from image processing. The support UI can show a pending attachment, while a worker validates the object and generates any derived thumbnail. That avoids making the ticket save depend on image work.

The trade-offs become sharper here. The storage capability does not provide object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls. It also does not provide If-Match conditional writes, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. Strict concurrency needs coordination in a database or queue. Financial-grade immutability needs an external design.

Lifecycle is another small detail with a large operational effect: the shortest lifecycle is one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not server-side searchable; listing supports prefix filtering. Those limits are manageable for support images when the application owns the index, but they are poor matches for a system that expects the bucket to be its query engine.

I would measure three things before expanding the design: upload completion rate by browser, download volume by tenant, and the percentage of objects that are never attached to a ticket. The first finds CORS and network problems. The second tests the egress assumption. The third pays for cleanup work before it turns into a storage habit.

The practical choice

For browser-based product-image uploads, start with R2 when direct delivery and egress are central to the product. Pick S3 when the application needs AWS's global footprint and detailed controls enough to justify more setup. Consider Wasabi only after mapping the actual read path and its egress constraints, not from its storage line item alone.

Use a unified storage API when it removes real integration work across a broader backend and the missing specialist controls are already supplied by your architecture. Keep the provider boundary small. Keep tenant authorization in your application. Keep the browser on a presigned URL.

If that boundary fits your system, the storage capability and its request schemas are documented at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • GDPR Article 20: Right to data portability
