title: Azure AI Models, CLI Agents, Rust Ports, and Java/Nginx Patches
description:
As of November 19, 2026, five Azure-adjacent signals deserve attention: model selection, agent-operated CLIs, incremental Rust rewrites, and two runtime vulnerabilities.

The common theme is verification. Whether you are switching models, granting an agent command-line access, porting an endpoint, or deploying a patch, the safe approach is the same: define the expected behavior, make the change in a controlled environment, and compare the result.

If you operate either affected Java or Nginx runtime, start with the patching sections rather than the experiments.

Five practical Azure engineering workflows

1. Compare seven models in Azure AI Foundry

  • What it is: The Azure AI Foundry catalog provides access to the seven models announced at Microsoft Ignite 2026, with workflows for evaluating and calling them.
  • Why now: The Ignite 2026 announcement reached 470 points on Hacker News. More model choices do not remove selection work; they make repeatable evaluation more important.
  • Tutorial angle: Run one representative workload through all seven models and compare task quality, schema adherence, latency, token usage, and estimated cost. Keep the prompt, model settings, and input data identical. Run each case multiple times to separate model behavior from one-off output, then deploy the winner gradually.
  • Difficulty: Intermediate.

A useful benchmark sheet contains:

  • Correct task completion
  • Required output fields or structure
  • p50 and p95 latency
  • Input and output token counts
  • Published rate-card cost
  • Failure and retry rates
  • Notes about hallucinations or unsupported claims

For workloads with deterministic answers, automate the correctness check. For open-ended outputs, use a small rubric and save every response for later review. After selecting a winner, canary it against the current production model rather than switching all traffic at once.

  • Start today: Open https://ai.azure.com, select one of the newly announced models, and paste the same smoke-test prompt into its playground.

2. Give an Azure CLI coding agent a safe contract

  • What it is: CLI-Anything is an open-source approach to making command-line software agent-native. In this case, it can expose Azure CLI operations to a coding agent while keeping command discovery, execution, and verification explicit.
  • Why now: The November 19 GitHub Trending snapshot attributed 389 stars to CLI-Anything for the day and 59,886 stars overall. That interest reflects a practical problem: agents often understand the intent of an az command but invent flags, skip confirmation, or fail to explain what changed.
  • Tutorial angle: Build a small Azure CLI interface, deliberately submit a malformed command, and confirm that it fails with a useful error. Then implement a plan → apply → verify workflow against a disposable resource group.
  • Difficulty: Intermediate.

The agent should not receive unrestricted access to a production subscription. Give it a constrained workflow:

  1. Discover valid operations and parameters.
  2. Produce an executable plan without changing resources.
  3. Require approval before applying it.
  4. Capture the commands and expected changes.
  5. Read the resulting state and verify it independently.

A disposable resource group is essential for the first run. For example, create a test group, let the agent deploy a small resource, and require the agent to show az group show output before considering the task complete. If the malformed command succeeds—or if verification does not match the plan—the interface is not ready for broader use.

  • Start today: Open the CLI-Anything repository search and identify the canonical repository.

3. Port .NET to Rust with differential tests

  • What it is: rust-anything is an open-source workflow for rewriting an application incrementally in Rust while comparing the rewritten components against the original application's recorded behavior.
  • Why now: The repository accumulated 3,547 stars in roughly three days after being created on November 16, making it the strongest new-repository signal in the research report.
  • Tutorial angle: Port one .NET endpoint rather than an entire service. Record the original endpoint's request and response fixtures, implement the Rust version, and run both implementations against the same test corpus. Any material mismatch should fail the migration and trigger review or rollback.
  • Difficulty: Intermediate.

Good fixtures should cover more than successful responses. Include:

  • Different HTTP methods and status codes
  • Missing and malformed parameters
  • Authentication and authorization failures
  • Empty, large, and Unicode payloads
  • Database or downstream-service errors
  • Response headers and content types
  • Stable ordering and timestamps

Normalize values that are expected to change between runs, such as timestamps and generated identifiers. Everything else should match exactly or through an explicitly documented transformation.

The rewrite should remain reviewable as a sequence of small changes. A pull request that replaces an endpoint with a Rust service, adds its fixtures, and demonstrates a passing differential test is much safer than a repository-wide conversion.

  • Start today: Run gh search repos "rust-anything" --limit 5 and open the result that describes the incremental migration workflow.

4. Triage and patch Java4Shell on Azure App Service

  • What it is: The Java4Shell advisory describes an unauthenticated remote-code-execution vulnerability associated with OpenJDK Base64 processing. Azure App Service hosting does not automatically make an application vulnerable; the deployed JDK, reachable code path, and runtime configuration determine exposure.
  • Why now: The disclosure received 1,156 points and 321 comments on Hacker News during the previous seven days. That makes runtime identification and patching more urgent than another general Azure feature update.
  • Tutorial angle: Inventory the actual JDK used by each App Service deployment, compare it with the advisory, update the tested base image, run a benign Base64 compatibility regression, and rehearse a safe redeployment and rollback.
  • Difficulty: Intermediate.

Start with deployment metadata rather than the Java version shown in an old configuration file. For App Service, record:

  • The container image and digest
  • The output of java -version inside that image
  • Whether the application uses a built-in Java stack or its own container
  • The App Service configuration and deployment slots
  • Internet exposure and relevant authentication settings

A useful inventory command is:

az webapp list --query "[].{name:name,javaVersion:javaVersion,linuxFxVersion:linuxFxVersion,windowsFxVersion:windowsFxVersion}" -o table

Treat this as a starting point, not proof of the running version. Verify the actual image or runtime. Patch a staging deployment first, exercise normal Base64 encoding and decoding with non-sensitive fixtures, and confirm that application behavior is unchanged. Do not attempt exploit payloads against a production application.

  • Start today: Run java -version inside the same JDK image used by your Azure build and save the output beside the deployment manifest.

5. Patch the Nginx HTTP/2 RCE exposed through Azure workloads

  • What it is: The Nginx HTTP/2 advisory describes an unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw affecting certain Nginx versions. The risk applies when your workload actually exposes an affected Nginx build, potentially including an Azure App Service deployment using Nginx as a proxy or container.
  • Why now: The advisory was the Hacker News front-page leader in the research snapshot, with 1,193 points and 532 comments.
  • Tutorial angle: Identify the deployed Nginx version, compare it with the fixed release, rebuild from a patched image, run nginx -t, perform a benign HTTP/2 smoke test, and rehearse rollback through an App Service deployment slot.
  • Difficulty: Intermediate.

The application UI may show an Azure stack name without revealing the exact Nginx build. Inspect the container image and run nginx -v inside the same runtime used in production. Also confirm whether HTTP/2 is enabled and reachable from untrusted networks.

After updating the image:

  1. Run nginx -t before sending traffic.
  2. Verify that the server starts with the expected configuration.
  3. Test ordinary HTTP/2 requests with curl --http2.
  4. Check application logs for startup or proxy errors.
  5. Shift a small amount of traffic to the patched deployment.
  6. Keep the previous image available for rollback.

Do not expose a vulnerable build merely to reproduce the advisory. Inventory, patching, and defensive validation are enough for the first remediation pass.

  • Start today: Run az webapp list --query "[].{name:name,linuxFxVersion:linuxFxVersion}" -o table to identify App Services that may need an image-level Nginx inspection.

Building in public: my lead-gen engine

Today's run of my Hong Kong SME lead-gen engine discovered 1,776 leads, enriched 201, and recorded 231 contacts. Because the contact count is higher than the enrichment count, these totals should not be interpreted as a strict same-cohort funnel without shared cohort IDs. Publishing the counters makes it easier to identify where the pipeline needs better instrumentation.

  • Discovered: 1,776
  • Enriched: 201
  • Contacted: 231
  • Next measurement improvement: join enrichment and contact records with a shared lead or campaign ID

Start with this today

Open https://ai.azure.com, choose one of the seven newly announced models, and paste this exact prompt into its playground:

Write a TypeScript function named chunk<T>(items: T[], size: number): T[][].
Split the array into groups of the requested size while preserving order.
Throw a RangeError when size is not greater than zero.
Return only code.

Use the result as the first fixture in your seven-model comparison sheet. Keep the prompt unchanged when you repeat it across the catalog.

Picks of the week

  • Model selection: Benchmark one real workload instead of choosing from a leaderboard.
  • Agent-operated CLIs: Make plan, apply, and verify separate, observable stages.
  • Incremental Rust ports: Record the old behavior before rewriting the component.
  • Runtime patching: Inventory the actual deployed version; the Azure resource name is not a version.

Which would you tackle first: a measured model switch, an agent-safe Azure CLI, a behavior-tested Rust port, or an urgent Java/Nginx patch?

Connect

If this kind of post is useful, the easiest way to support the work is to:

  • Star / follow on dev.to (you're already here 🙂)
  • Follow on X: @devkingov
  • Reach out for HK-based dev work — .NET / Azure / system integration / IT security: studio.resurrects.co or email devkingov@gmail.com
  • Subscribe to weekly HK tech posts → studio.resurrects.co/blog (one email a week, no spam)

title: Snowflake vs Databricks: How to Compare Them
description:
Snowflake and Databricks started in different places, one as a managed cloud SQL warehouse and one as a managed Spark platform, and have spent years adding each other's strengths. In 2026, both run SQL warehouses for BI, both run Python, both load streams, both govern open table formats, and both sell AI features. So comparing them by slogans, such as "Snowflake is for BI, Databricks is for ML", is out of date and will not survive an interviewer's follow-up question.

What still differs is the default shape of each platform: where data lives by default, how compute is provisioned and billed, which language is first-class, and how much you tune versus how much is managed for you. Those defaults decide which platform fits a given team and workload.

Architecture

Snowflake has three layers. Table data is stored once in Snowflake-managed storage as compressed columnar micro-partitions; virtual warehouses are independent compute clusters that read it; and a cloud services layer handles metadata, optimisation, transactions and security. You do not see the files. Apache Iceberg tables are the exception: their Parquet files live in your own bucket, with either Snowflake or an external catalog as the Iceberg catalog.

Databricks splits a Databricks-run control plane (UI, notebooks, scheduler, APIs, Unity Catalog) from a compute plane that runs Spark and SQL either on VMs in your cloud account (classic) or on Databricks-managed serverless capacity. Table data is files in your object storage, by default Delta Lake tables, governed by Unity Catalog.

Snowflake Databricks
Where table data lives Snowflake-managed storage (native tables); your bucket for Iceberg tables Your object storage (Delta by default, Iceberg supported)
Compute unit Virtual warehouse (T-shirt sizes; multi-cluster for concurrency) plus serverless features Clusters (all-purpose, jobs), serverless compute, SQL warehouses
Engine Snowflake's SQL engine; Snowpark pushes DataFrame code down to it Apache Spark plus Photon (vectorised engine)
What you tune Warehouse size, clustering keys, auto-suspend Compute type and size, runtime version, file layout, Spark settings (less on serverless)

The practical consequences: Snowflake needs less tuning knowledge to get good SQL performance, because it manages files, statistics and most layout; Databricks gives more control over storage and compute and lets other engines read the same files without copying, at the cost of more decisions.

Workloads

Workload Snowflake Databricks
SQL analytics and BI Core strength: warehouses, result cache, high concurrency with multi-cluster SQL warehouses (serverless, pro, classic) with Photon; competitive for BI on Delta
SQL ELT with dbt Very common; dbt runs on a warehouse Common; dbt runs on a SQL warehouse
Large Python or Scala transformations Snowpark DataFrames (translated to SQL), Python UDFs and stored procedures Native PySpark and Scala on clusters; the most flexible option for complex code
Incremental and streaming Snowpipe and Snowpipe Streaming, Streams and Tasks, Dynamic Tables (target lag) Structured Streaming, Auto Loader, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines
Machine learning Snowpark ML, Snowflake ML features, Cortex AI functions MLflow, feature engineering on Spark, model serving, Mosaic AI features
Data sharing Secure Data Sharing and Marketplace (zero-copy within Snowflake) Delta Sharing (open protocol, also to non-Databricks clients) and Marketplace

Low-latency sub-second streaming is not the default strength of either; both target seconds to minutes. Both vendors have also added managed PostgreSQL offerings for operational data (Snowflake Postgres and Databricks Lakebase); as of October 2026, check each one's availability and limits before relying on them in a design.

Pricing model concepts

Neither vendor publishes a single price that applies to everyone, so compare models, not numbers.

Snowflake bills in credits. A running virtual warehouse consumes credits per second at a rate set by its size (each size up roughly doubles the rate), with a 60-second minimum each time it starts. Serverless features (Snowpipe, Automatic Clustering, Search Optimization, serverless tasks, Dynamic Table refreshes on serverless compute and others) consume credits on their own meters. Cloud services usage is billed only when it exceeds a share of daily warehouse usage. Storage is billed per terabyte per month of compressed data, and Time Travel and Fail-safe retention add to it. The price per credit depends on edition, cloud, region and contract.

Databricks bills in Databricks Units (DBUs), consumed per hour at a rate that depends on the compute type (all-purpose, jobs, SQL warehouse, serverless, pipelines) and the pricing tier. On classic compute you also pay your cloud provider for the VMs; serverless rates include the infrastructure. Storage is paid directly to your cloud provider because the files are in your account.

What this means when you estimate:

  • Cost follows compute time × rate on both. Idle compute (a warehouse that never suspends, an all-purpose cluster left running) is the most common waste on both.
  • Make the comparison on the same workloads, implemented idiomatically on each, and include serverless meters and cloud VM bills, not just the headline unit.
  • Count people cost: time spent tuning clusters, files and pipelines is real money.

The cost lessons go deeper: Snowflake cost optimization and the compute section of Databricks workspace and jobs.

Governance

Snowflake Databricks
Model Role-based access control: privileges to roles, roles to users and roles; object owners Unity Catalog: privileges on securables (catalog, schema, table, volume) to users, groups and service principals, inherited downwards
Fine-grained access Masking policies, row access policies, tag-based masking, projection and aggregation policies Row filters, column masks, tag-driven ABAC policies
Classification and tags Object tags, sensitive data classification Governed tags, data classification
Lineage and audit Access history and lineage views (edition-dependent), ACCOUNT_USAGE views Automatic table and column lineage, system tables for audit and billing
Open catalog Horizon catalog; Apache Polaris (open-sourced from Snowflake) as an Iceberg REST catalog Unity Catalog (open-sourced version available); Iceberg REST catalog API

Both are capable. The difference in practice is scope: Snowflake governs data inside Snowflake very tightly; Unity Catalog is designed to govern files and tables in your storage that several engines may touch. Either way, design roles or groups per function, give pipelines their own service identities and protect PII with policies rather than copies. See Snowflake security and Unity Catalog governance.

Open table formats and Iceberg

Open table formats are where the two platforms have converged most, and where interviewers like to probe.

  • Snowflake Iceberg tables store Parquet data and Iceberg metadata in your external volume (your bucket). With Snowflake as the catalog, Snowflake manages writes and maintenance, and other engines can read the tables. With an external catalog (through a catalog integration, for example AWS Glue or an Iceberg REST catalog), another system usually owns the table. Snowflake can read it, and can also write to tables in a remote Iceberg REST catalog; a catalog-linked database keeps their namespaces in sync. Native Snowflake tables remain the default and are not readable as files by other engines.
  • Databricks defaults to Delta Lake. Delta tables can expose Iceberg metadata so Iceberg clients can read them (Delta UniForm, which the Databricks docs now call Iceberg reads). Unity Catalog can manage Iceberg tables and serve them through an Iceberg REST catalog API. It can also read foreign Iceberg tables from other catalogs. Feature status (preview or GA) has been changing during 2025 and 2026.
  • The decision that matters in a design is which system is the writer and owner of each table, and which catalog is authoritative. Two engines writing the same table through different catalogs is how you corrupt it.

Background on the formats themselves: Delta vs Iceberg vs Hudi and Lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse.

When to choose which

If your situation is mostly... Leaning Why
Analysts and analytics engineers writing SQL and dbt; BI concurrency; small platform team Snowflake Least tuning for good SQL performance; warehouses isolate workloads simply
Large Python or Scala pipelines, complex transformations, streaming from Kafka, ML on the same data Databricks Spark is native; full control over compute and code
Requirement that data stay in open formats in your own storage, read by several engines Either, designed deliberately Delta on Databricks, or Iceberg tables on Snowflake; decide the owning catalog
Sharing data with many external partners Either Snowflake sharing is zero-copy inside Snowflake; Delta Sharing reaches non-Databricks clients too
Existing estate and skills strongly on one side The existing one Migration and retraining cost usually outweighs feature differences

Many companies run both: Databricks for engineering and ML, Snowflake for BI, connected through open tables or sharing. That is a legitimate answer if you can name the integration cost (two governance models, two bills, data movement or a shared catalog).

How to run a fair evaluation

  1. Pick three to five real workloads: a large transformation, a dashboard query set under concurrency, an incremental or streaming load, and an ML feature job if relevant.
  2. Implement each idiomatically on both platforms rather than porting one platform's design to the other (for example, a Dynamic Table on Snowflake versus a declarative pipeline on Databricks).
  3. Measure runtime, total cost (including serverless meters and cloud VMs), developer effort and operational steps (deploys, monitoring, failure recovery).
  4. Include governance: access control, masking, lineage and auditing for your compliance requirements, and how each fits your identity provider.
  5. Write down assumptions, because both platforms will have shipped new features before the contract renews.

Common mistakes

  1. Choosing from vendor benchmarks or marketing comparisons instead of your own workloads.
  2. Comparing the price of a credit with the price of a DBU directly; the units measure different amounts of work.
  3. Forgetting the cloud VM bill on classic Databricks compute, or serverless feature meters on Snowflake.
  4. Ignoring team skills and hiring.
  5. Assuming "open format" means "any engine can write it safely"; one catalog must own each table.
  6. Repeating out-of-date generalisations (no Python on Snowflake, no BI on Databricks).

In an interview

If asked "Snowflake or Databricks?", give a framework (workloads, where data lives, users and skills, operations, cost model, governance) and then a recommendation for the scenario stated. A good shape: "For a team of analysts doing SQL ELT and dashboards, I would lean towards Snowflake because... If the same company also has heavy streaming and ML, I would consider Databricks for those workloads. I would share gold tables through Iceberg or sharing, and accept two governance models."

Expect follow-ups on cost (credits versus DBUs plus VMs), Iceberg interoperability, and how you would run a proof of concept. Practise with Q49 in the Top 50 Databricks interview questions and the Top 50 Snowflake interview questions.

Key takeaway

Both platforms now cover SQL, Python, streaming, governance and open tables. Choose by workload mix, where the data must live, team skills, operational appetite and measured cost on your own workloads, and be explicit about which system owns each table if you run both.

Originally published on DataDank, a free Data Engineering learning site with a 90-day interview plan and 900+ interview questions.

title: Gaming Reports at Scale: Node.js Multipart Upload and Sharp Thumbnail Backpressure
description:
A customer opens a generated gaming report and sees a broken image. The page says delivery is behind, completed uploads are rising, and the thumbnail queue is old. The tempting response is to add Sharp workers. That can make the incident worse if the real constraint is upload completion, object-store throughput, or derivative delivery.

Short answer: use multipart upload for each large original, acknowledge it only after completion, then let a bounded Node.js and Sharp worker pool create thumbnails under separate private keys. Page on customer-visible report readiness, but diagnose with upload age, completion rate, queue age, derivative failures, and presigned-delivery errors.

This order matters. A thumbnail job must never race an incomplete multipart object, and a retry must never overwrite the original. For a team already operating several backend capabilities, Infrai can fit the storage boundary because one key and one bill cover the wider platform instead of adding another credential and invoice. I would try it for private report originals and derivatives when reducing control-plane sprawl matters; its plain REST surface and public, self-describing discovery also remove an SDK dependency from the integration.

How should a large image upload, multipart Node.js Sharp thumbnail pipeline, and S3-compatible private storage interact?

Treat multipart completion as the commit record. Before that event, parts are transport state, not an image that Sharp may consume. After completion, enqueue a thumbnail command containing the tenant, report ID, immutable original key, derivative specification, and a deterministic operation ID. The worker reads the completed object, validates it as an image, resizes it, and writes every output to its own key. Both original and derivative delivery use short-lived presigned URLs.

A practical key layout is tenants/{tenant}/reports/{report}/original/{content-id} for the source and tenants/{tenant}/reports/{report}/thumb/{spec}/{content-id} for a derivative. The exact names are application policy; the important property is separation. A retry for 320x180-webp then converges on the same derivative key and cannot corrupt the source. Keep the bucket private.

The sequence is small enough to put in a runbook:

  1. Create the multipart upload for the private bucket.
  2. Presign and transfer each part, retaining every returned part identifier in durable application state.
  3. Complete the upload only after all intended parts are present.
  4. Commit the report-image record and enqueue the deterministic thumbnail command.
  5. Let the bounded Sharp pool produce distinct derivative keys.
  6. Mark the report image ready only when the required derivatives can be served with presigned URLs.
  7. Abort a failed multipart session; orphaned parts are not removed by lifecycle rules.

No completion, no resize.

The browser-direct variant needs an extra decision. Infrai's bucket model mentions CORS rules, but self-service CORS configuration is not an available capability boundary, so don't assume a web client can be enabled from this API. Put an application upload relay in front, or choose a direct storage control plane that supplies the browser-origin controls your design requires. This is a capability choice, not an incident workaround.

Work backward from the report-delivery page

The primary page should describe the failed customer promise: authenticated customers cannot view required images for generated reports within the service objective. It should not merely say that a worker process is busy. A busy worker can be healthy under a burst, while a quiet worker can be disastrous if completion events stopped arriving.

Work backward. First inspect readiness lag by report cohort and tenant. Then split that lag into four intervals: multipart creation to completion, completion to queue admission, queue admission to derivative write, and derivative write to successful presigned delivery. This turns one vague page into a location. If the first interval grows, adding Sharp concurrency is noise. If queue age grows while completed originals arrive normally, worker capacity or image complexity deserves attention. If writes finish but authenticated delivery fails, inspect signing and expiry policy rather than upload throughput.

The earlier signal should normally be sustained queue age or a falling completion-to-ready rate, not raw queue depth. Depth has no units of customer delay. One thousand tiny thumbnails may clear before ten unusually large originals; age and completion rate expose that difference. Break the signals out by derivative specification because a large report preview and a small list thumbnail consume different work.

Use HTTP status families as diagnostic dimensions, with 429 handled as backpressure: honor Retry-After when present and apply exponential delay. Don't turn a rate limit into a tight retry storm. Surface 4xx response bodies to the operator because they carry the reason, but keep authentication data and presigned query strings out of logs. The OWASP upload guidance is also a useful floor: allow-list expected extensions, validate the actual file type, rename stored files, set size limits, and keep uploads away from a public path.

This is where the alert becomes actionable. The page links to the oldest affected report IDs, the four latency intervals, current worker concurrency, input-byte rate, output-byte rate, 429 rate, and abort rate. An operator can reduce admission, increase a bounded pool, or stop a bad producer based on evidence. A chart called thumbnail_errors_total by itself offers no such choice.

Instrument the completion boundary and the worker budget

Throughput planning starts with bytes, pixels, and concurrency, not requests. Model a hypothetical peak before choosing a provider or worker count. Suppose an hour brings 400 report images averaging 120 MB, and each completed original produces three private derivatives. That is 48,000 MB of source input per hour before retries, plus derivative writes and later customer egress. These are planning inputs, not benchmark results; replace them with the p50, p95, and maximum from your own accepted uploads.

The longest paragraph in the runbook should explain overload behavior because this is where duplicate work hides. Set a maximum number of simultaneous Sharp transforms from measured memory per transform and the container memory budget, then reserve headroom for the Node.js process, download buffers, and transient output buffers. Admission should stop before the process is forced into repeated restarts. Each queue delivery checks the report-image state and deterministic derivative key before doing expensive work. If the derivative is already committed, acknowledge the delivery. If another worker owns an unexpired lease, release or defer it. If neither is true, acquire coordination in the application's database or queue, render to a temporary destination, and promote the result through the application's state transition. Infrai has no If-Match conditional write, so strict mutual exclusion belongs in that coordinator. This is deliberate duplication control — standard retries alone are not a lock.

Before wiring the full uploader into Node.js, this small Go preflight verifies the create-and-abort lifecycle against a private bucket. It is deliberately narrow. The production uploader adds part presigning, part transfer, completion, and a presigned read URL only after discovery schemas have been checked.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type createResponse struct {
    UploadID string `json:"upload_id"`
}

func call(client *http.Client, method, endpoint string, body []byte, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 6; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, endpoint, res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("request remained rate-limited after 6 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("REPORT_BUCKET")
    if key == "" || bucket == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and REPORT_BUCKET")
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{
        "key":          "preflight/report-original.png",
        "content_type": "image/png",
        "acl":          "private",
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    createURL := baseURL + "/storage/multipart/create/" + url.PathEscape(bucket)
    data, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, createURL, payload, "report-upload-preflight-v1")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    var created createResponse
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &created); err != nil || created.UploadID == "" {
        panic("create response did not contain upload_id")
    }
    abortURL := baseURL + "/storage/multipart/abort/" + url.PathEscape(created.UploadID)
    if _, err := call(client, http.MethodDelete, abortURL, nil, ""); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("multipart create-and-abort preflight passed")
}

The sample sends the bearer key only to the API. A returned presigned URL is already authorized and must never receive that header. The stable idempotency key protects the create retry, while the explicit abort proves the application owns fragment cleanup.

Your mileage may vary sharply with image dimensions, codec, Sharp settings, cache behavior, and customer download patterns. I'm not sure which interval will dominate in a given production system until those byte and duration histograms exist; that uncertainty is exactly why the page should expose the intervals separately.

Instrument aborted sessions too. Multipart helps large transfers survive unstable connections, but lifecycle policies cannot clean multipart fragments automatically here, and lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum. The application therefore owns an upload-session ledger and an abort sweep. Track sessions created, completed, explicitly aborted, and older than the application's deadline. A rising gap between created and completed sessions should warn before storage residue becomes an invoice surprise.

Compare the full operating bill, not one storage rate

The effective bill has at least six lines: original ingress handling, retained originals, derivative writes, retained derivatives, authenticated delivery, and compute for decode and resize. Add engineering and on-call costs for credentials, vendor SDK upgrades, upload-session cleanup, concurrency coordination, observability, and invoice reconciliation. A unit storage rate cannot represent those costs. Nor can this article supply a measured winner without your workload and contract.

Option Operational fit for this pipeline The catch
Infrai Fits teams that value one key and one bill across backend services, plus a consistent REST and discovery surface No public ACL, object versioning, object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration; browser CORS is not self-service
AWS S3 direct Evaluate when direct provider controls and a specialist storage relationship are the deciding requirements Adds a separate vendor credential, integration, and billing boundary to this comparison
Cloudflare R2 direct Evaluate when the team wants to own the R2 relationship and control plane directly The team also owns that separate operational boundary
DigitalOcean Spaces direct Evaluate as another direct private object-storage relationship, using its current documentation to validate the required controls Keep its integration, access policy, and invoice in the operating model
Aliyun OSS or Tencent COS through the unified surface Covered vendor choices when they meet the workload's region and policy needs The same Infrai capability limits still define the exposed control plane

Infrai is not suitable for a public image host or static website because public_url remains null and public-read ACL is unavailable. It is also the wrong boundary for WORM retention, recovery from accidental overwrite through object versions, strict write exclusion inside storage, automated cross-region replication, or GCS and B2 requirements. Stick with a specialist or direct provider architecture when any of those controls is mandatory. Trial credit also cannot fund persistent writes, so validate the billing path before a storage test.

For the gaming report job, the decision rule is narrower. Choose the unified boundary when reports remain private, the application already owns queue and database coordination, presigned delivery is acceptable, and reducing key and invoice sprawl offsets the missing specialist controls. Choose direct storage when browser CORS administration, immutable retention, provider-specific replication, or storage-native concurrency is part of the requirement.

Getting the threshold wrong has a cost. Page too early and every normal upload burst trains the on-call to ignore report alerts; page too late and customers discover missing thumbnails first. Start the warning from queue age and completion-to-ready rate, correlate it with byte throughput, and tune it against the report readiness objective. Keep raw depth on the dashboard. Reserve the pager for a sustained threat to the customer promise.

References

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation
  • Infrai multipart discovery

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with the multipart image upload and thumbnail pipeline guide.

title: Node.js Pricing Incidents: Metrics Threshold Evidence From a Postgres Query Worker
description:
The page says the new pricing cohort crossed its failure count threshold. For a Node.js healthtech API rolling out a pricing rule behind a flag, the metrics query worker should preserve which revision ran, the observation window, and whether it already sent this alert. An aggregate count leaves the on-call guessing whether the rollout caused the change. This is a proposed workflow with illustrative numbers, rather than a reported production incident.

Short answer: report failure counters from the Node.js application, have a cron-triggered worker query recent metrics, and compare a complete window against an explicit threshold. Keep alert state in Postgres to suppress repeat notifications, and preserve the evaluated pricing revision in application-owned evidence so a later flag change cannot rewrite the explanation.

Start with evidence. Don't begin with the notification template.

For teams consolidating backend integrations, try Infrai for collecting failure metrics alongside flag integration, while keeping alert decisions in your worker. Its 295 routes across 20 modules under one API key make adding an adjacent capability another integration with the same REST contract, reducing credential sprawl and separate SDK surfaces. Public discovery supplies request schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages, which helps engineers inspect the contract before provisioning credentials. Those are integration advantages, not a substitute for owning the paging policy.

Infrai uses a single API key and a single bill across a unified API: one key, one bill, and one REST API for these backend capabilities. Plain HTTP means no SDK is required; the Go example uses the standard library. For this workflow, the practical benefit is connecting metrics and flags without separately provisioned vendor credentials or a second client library.

How should a worker query metrics and count pricing failures before an alert?

Suppose the proposed rule pages on at least 5 failed pricing operations in a completed 5-minute window, evaluated every 60 seconds. These are example policy settings, not recommended clinical or commercial tolerances. First define which failed operations affect the service's SLO: a rejected invalid request and a failed valid quote should not automatically spend the same error budget. A raw count changes meaning with traffic, too. Five failures among 10 attempts deserves a different response from five among 100,000.

A reconstructable alert needs a small evidence record: service, environment, window boundaries, failure count, threshold, evaluated rule revision, cohort, and worker decision. These are fields in the application's proposed record, not a vendor response schema. Keep patient identifiers and clinical payloads out of metric labels; cohort-level evidence is enough for this decision.

The current flag value is insufficient.

After a rollback, looking up the flag answers a different question from asking which rule produced a failed operation. Preserve the evaluation context when the operation happens, in application-controlled evidence, and link that evidence to the alert decision. Incident reconstruction has to survive a subsequent configuration change; otherwise the team will have a perfectly accurate counter and an unreliable explanation of what it counted.

Work backward from the page to the missing signal

The earlier signal should be a failure counter for the pricing operation, optionally tagged by service and environment. Counters such as job_failures, api_5xx, and payment_failures are useful categories; choose semantics that match the operation rather than counting every alarming log line. An API error counter describes application responses. RFC 5424 defines log severity semantics, but severity alone does not identify the user operation whose SLO is at risk.

Do not equate a query result with a window total until the aggregation contract is clear. Cumulative counters require deltas and reset handling; independent increments require summation; overlapping observations can double-count a failure. The metrics adapter should produce one documented value for one completed window and retain its boundaries. A later investigation cannot reconstruct a decision from a number whose time range has been lost.

Polling adds another clock.

With the illustrative 5-minute window and 60-second schedule, detection depends on alignment, metric visibility, and worker execution. No measured latency is implied. Capacity planning should include service and environment combinations, active revisions, and revisited windows; otherwise a small polling job becomes an expanding query workload. Keep unbounded request identifiers in evidence records rather than metric dimensions.

A quiet counter is ambiguous if the worker never ran. Assign the worker a separate heartbeat check, using a tool such as Healthchecks, so observer silence has its own owner.

Verify the query before wiring it to a threshold

Instrument the application outcome once, define how retries count, and preserve the pricing revision in corresponding evidence. Then establish the metrics observation contract. Infrai supports metrics reporting and querying, but its discovery surface does not declare exact query filter parameters. An integration acceptance test must establish the selected window and aggregation semantics before the adapter drives a page. Guessing parameter names would make an example look complete while weakening its correctness.

The following Go program makes the smallest authenticated query without inventing filters or response fields. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the process environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with go run main.go. It prints the returned body for contract inspection; it does not pretend that an unfiltered response is a verified five-minute total. Use synthetic telemetry for this first check, and avoid placing returned operational data in shared terminal logs.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1 << attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                suggested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                if suggested > delay {
                    delay = suggested
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if suggested := time.Until(deadline); suggested > delay {
                    delay = suggested
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("metrics query returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("query attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is a read, so retries do not create duplicate writes. It explicitly checks status codes and honors Retry-After on rate limiting while retaining exponential backoff. The finite attempt count limits request retries; a production worker also needs a scheduling deadline and cancellation policy, especially if the server requests a long delay.

Once the observation adapter is verified, compare its count against the threshold and persist the decision. With a 15-minute cooldown, a second above-threshold observation should record evidence without sending another page. Decide whether recovery followed by rapid reopening starts a fresh incident or remains suppressed: suppressing it reduces chatter but can delay notification of a separate episode. That is policy, not a harmless implementation detail.

Serialize decisions in Postgres for each rule, service, environment, and cohort. Reject already processed or out-of-order windows. Within one transaction, store the observation, update alert state, and insert a uniquely identified notification intent into an outbox. A delivery worker can retry that intent using the destination's supported deduplication mechanism. Persisting only the state risks losing a page if the process crashes between committing its decision and sending the notification. Preserve delivery failures separately from pricing failures, or the observer can end up alerting recursively on itself.

Buy versus build depends on who owns the reconstruction

The comparison is setup work versus investigation and on-call responsibilities left with the platform team. These are architectural selection criteria, not measured setup times or a feature-parity benchmark.

Option Setup and first useful result Work retained by the platform team Appropriate boundary
Infrai plus a scheduled worker Inspect public schemas and Go examples; connect metrics and flags through one REST contract Thresholds, cooldown state, notification delivery, and historical rollout evidence Consolidated backend integrations with an application-owned alert policy
Prometheus with Alertmanager Establish collection, alert rules, and notification routing Operating the selected deployment and connecting rollout evidence A specialist metrics and alerting stack with an operational owner
Grafana Cloud Evaluate a managed observability and alerting workflow with application telemetry Instrumentation, access setup, and rollout evidence correlation Managed alert investigation instead of a custom polling policy service
Datadog Evaluate its monitoring workflow against the pricing operation and incident response requirements Agent or integration setup, monitor design, and evidence linkage Teams seeking a broader managed monitoring workflow
Healthchecks Establish a heartbeat for the scheduled worker Business failure counting and pricing investigation Detecting the silent failure where the observer stops running

Choose a specialist when alert management itself is the work you need to buy. Infrai leaves thresholds, cooldowns, and notification channels with the worker; Prometheus with Alertmanager, Grafana Cloud, or Datadog deserves priority if the team does not want those responsibilities. Healthchecks complements either approach rather than replacing failure metrics.

The limitation is explicit: this polling design is not suitable for a team seeking a managed alert engine with notification routing. Its trade-off is less integration sprawl in exchange for application-owned alert state and delivery.

Keep investigation boundaries visible, too. Stored trace and span identifiers are correlation handles rather than a distributed span-tree investigation interface. Own historical flag-evaluation evidence in the application instead of relying on flag change auditing or evaluation statistics. If investigation requires crash symbolication or session replay, evaluate a specialist for that requirement. Aggregate alerting can still be useful, provided the page does not promise evidence the chosen system cannot supply.

Close the loop without exhausting the on-call budget

A threshold of 5 sounds precise.

Review it against normal traffic, low-volume cohorts, retries, and the SLO before enabling paging. Increasing rollout exposure increases opportunities to fail, so a fixed count can trigger even when the failure ratio stays unchanged. Retain a count guard where useful, but inspect the attempt denominator during incident review and avoid treating every threshold crossing as proof that the pricing revision caused the failure.

The false-positive cost is operational: somebody stops other work, examines the evidence, and may halt a healthy rollout. An excessively permissive threshold allows affected operations to continue while the worker stays quiet. Record suppressed transitions as well as delivered notifications so the next review can distinguish a noisy policy from a delivery problem. The first useful result is one reconstructable decision from a complete window; production readiness also requires understood recovery and observer-liveness behavior.

Further reading

References for the design and alternatives:

  • Martin Fowler, Feature Toggles
  • RFC 5424, log severity semantics
  • Prometheus alerting overview
  • Grafana Cloud alerting documentation
  • Datadog monitoring documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this integration boundary fits your system, start with the first-party metrics failure alerting guide and verify the observation contract before enabling notifications.

title: Correct tables, wrong answer: the hidden defaults that make two calculators disagree
description:
In short. My wire-size app had the right code tables and still put a kitchen range on the wrong breaker, because one default belonged to a different kind of job. Calculators rarely disagree because of the math; they disagree because of defaults the user never sees. One 50 A electrical circuit, run through those defaults, comes out as four different wire sizes. If your app computes anything, put the assumptions next to the answer.

I make Electrician Calc, a phone app that sizes wire and breakers by the US National Electrical Code (NEC) or the international IEC 60364. Getting the tables right was the easy part. The hard part was everything around them.

The bug that wasn't in the math

Before the US launch I ran a user test: an AI agent played a licensed residential electrician, read only the store page and tried a real job. A 40 A kitchen range, 240 V, 60 ft away, on NM-B cable (Romex).

Every number it checked was correct. The answer was still wrong: the app put the range on a 50 A breaker.

The cause was two defaults. "Continuous load" was on, so the app multiplied the current by 1.25, which the code requires for loads that run at full current for 3 hours or more, such as EV chargers. A range is not one of those: its elements cycle. And the wire type defaulted to THHN in conduit, which is commercial wiring. Both settings were reasonable for a commercial job and wrong for a house.

Nothing in the code was broken. The defaults described someone else's job.

One circuit, four wire sizes

To see how far defaults alone can move an answer, take one circuit: 50 A at 240 V, copper, 130 ft one way, say a welder outlet in a detached shop. The code tables are fixed. Only the assumptions change:

What the calculator assumes Answer Why
75 °C column, not continuous, no voltage drop check 8 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG is 50 A at 75 °C
The same, with a 5% voltage drop limit 8 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG drops 4.2%
The same, with a 3% voltage drop limit 6 AWG, 50 A breaker 6 AWG drops 2.7%
60 °C column (NM-B cable) 6 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG is only 40 A at 60 °C
Continuous load, 75 °C column 6 AWG, 70 A breaker 50 × 1.25 = 62.5 A
Continuous load, 60 °C column 4 AWG, 70 A breaker 6 AWG is 55 A at 60 °C
130 ft typed as a 260 ft round trip, 3% limit 3 AWG, 50 A breaker The voltage drop doubles

Ampacities are from NEC Table 310.16; voltage drop is the usual K-factor formula with K = 12.9 for copper.

Every row except the last follows the code for the conditions it assumes. The last one is a typing mistake that looks exactly like a result. A user who compares two apps sees 8 AWG in one and 6 AWG in the other and concludes one of them is broken.

The defaults that matter

These are the settings that changed the answer, and most calculators show few of them:

  • Which column of the table. The code table has 60, 75 and 90 °C columns. Which one applies depends on the terminals and the cable type, not on the wire's own rating.
  • Continuous or not. A 1.25 multiplier that some tools apply to everything and some to nothing.
  • Voltage drop limit. 3%, 5% or no check at all, and checked at the breaker rating, the load, or 80% of the breaker.
  • Voltage drop method. Resistance at 20 °C instead of operating temperature reports about 20% less drop, enough to move a borderline run one size.
  • One-way or round-trip length. The formula already doubles the length for the return wire. Type the round trip and it doubles twice.
  • Material and wire type. Copper or aluminum, conduit or cable.
  • Special rules. Derating for heat and crowded conduits, an 83% rule for house services, motors and air conditioners sized from their nameplates.

None of these is exotic. Each one is a legitimate input, and each one, hidden, turns into "the app is wrong".

What I changed

  • Defaults for the audience. In US mode the app now starts residential: not continuous, NM-B cable. The continuous-load switch sits next to the current field, off by default, so the 1.25 is a visible decision instead of a silent one.
  • Assumptions on screen. Column, wire type and voltage drop limit are inputs you can see, not settings three menus away.
  • The working with every answer. Each result lists its steps: the column it read, the 1.25 if applied, the derating, the voltage drop and the ground wire. A user can check it, and an electrician can show it to the inspector.
  • Wording that cannot be read as an instruction. One step used to say "voltage drop ≤ 3% first met by 10 AWG". It was a lower bound and read like "install 10 AWG". It now says "10 AWG or larger keeps the voltage drop within 3%", and a final step names the size to install.

The general lesson

If your app calculates anything (a dose, a loan payment, a paint quantity, a wire size), your users will compare it with another tool. When the answers differ, they will not open your settings to find out why. They will decide which app is wrong.

  1. Every default is a claim about who the user is. Pick it for the audience the store page speaks to.
  2. Put the assumptions that change the answer next to the answer.
  3. Show the working. A number with its steps is something people trust and share; a bare number is something they argue with.
  4. Test with someone playing your actual user on a real task, not with your own test data. My tables passed every unit test; the range on a 50 A breaker only showed up when someone tried to wire a house.

The full electrician version, with the code sections for every row, is here: 8 AWG or 6 AWG for 50 amps? Why two wire size calculators give different answers. The other guides in the set (voltage drop, wire sizing step by step, the 125% rule, conduit and box fill) are at zhukovskyi.space/blog/guides. The app is Electrician Calc, on Google Play and the App Store; Wire Size and Voltage Drop are free.

Originally published at zhukovskyi.space.

title: Como corrigir Java4Shell no Ubuntu e reiniciar serviços Java
description:
Builds corrigidos do OpenJDK por versão do Ubuntu

A Canonical publicou em 18 de novembro de 2026 avisos de segurança com pacotes corrigidos para Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade identificada como CVE-2026-114938. A versão necessária depende da edição do Ubuntu e da versão principal do OpenJDK instalada; nas edições mais antigas, a correção requer Ubuntu Pro.

Confira os builds corrigidos na tabela e compare-os com os pacotes instalados. Os números correspondem às versões principais do OpenJDK disponíveis em cada edição, e os avisos de segurança indicam que os pacotes para Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04 são distribuídos por meio do ESM Apps.

UbuntuOpenJDK 17OpenJDK 21OpenJDK 2526.1017.0.21.1+2-1~26.10.121.0.13.1+2-1~26.10.125.0.5.1+2-1~26.10.126.0417.0.21.1+2-1~26.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~26.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~26.04.124.0417.0.21.1+2-1~24.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~24.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~24.04.122.0417.0.21.1+2-1~22.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~22.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~22.04.120.0417.0.21.1+2-1~20.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~20.04.1Não empacotado18.0417.0.21.1+2-1~18.04.1Não empacotadoNão empacotado

No Ubuntu 26.10, o aviso USN-9158-1 também corrige o OpenJDK 27 para a versão 27.0.1.1+4-1~26.10.1. Ubuntu 20.04 oferece pacotes corrigidos para OpenJDK 17 e 21, enquanto o 18.04 oferece apenas o 17; ambos requerem Ubuntu Pro e ESM Apps.

Em Ubuntu 22.04 ou posterior, os builds vulneráveis terminam em .0.3 e os corrigidos em .1. Como as duas versões podem aparecer nas fontes do apt, confira a versão candidata e o repositório de segurança, em vez de se orientar apenas pelo número instalado.

Verifique se o processador alcança o código vulnerável

A falha está em uma rotina Base64 que usa AVX-512 e depende da presença conjunta de quatro flags do processador. A verificação ajuda a priorizar a manutenção, mas não elimina a necessidade de aplicar a correção nos sistemas afetados.

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Se a saída não listar as quatro flags, o processador não alcança esse caminho vulnerável. A atualização continua recomendada: máquinas virtuais podem migrar entre famílias de processadores, grupos de autoscaling podem mudar de instância e imagens de contêiner podem rodar em hosts diferentes dos usados na compilação.

Localize todos os pacotes OpenJDK instalados

O Ubuntu permite manter várias versões principais do OpenJDK no mesmo sistema. Como java -version mostra somente a versão selecionada pelo update-alternatives, consulte os pacotes registrados pelo dpkg para identificar instalações paralelas que também precisam do patch.

dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n' 'openjdk-*-jre-headless' | grep -v ' $'
apt-cache madison openjdk-17-jre-headless openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-25-jre-headless

O primeiro comando lista os pacotes de runtime conhecidos pelo dpkg; o segundo mostra as versões disponíveis nos repositórios configurados. Se a versão vulnerável continuar listada em updates após a correção, confira a candidata: o apt escolhe a versão mais alta, que deve vir do repositório de segurança.

Uma versão candidata vulnerável pode indicar que o sistema está fixado ao repositório de updates ou usa um espelho que não inclui o repositório de segurança. Essa checagem ajuda a identificar por que uma atualização não aparece antes de tentar instalar o pacote novamente.

Instale as atualizações de segurança

Nas versões 26.04, 24.04 e 22.04, os pacotes corrigidos estão no repositório de segurança padrão. A atualização seletiva abaixo limita a mudança aos pacotes OpenJDK 17, 21 e 25, sem executar uma atualização geral do sistema.

sudo apt update
sudo apt-get install --only-upgrade 'openjdk-17-' 'openjdk-21-' 'openjdk-25-*'

No Ubuntu 26.10, acrescente 'openjdk-27-*' ao comando se essa versão estiver instalada. O apt-get rejeita a operação se um padrão não corresponder a nenhum pacote disponível, por isso Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04 precisam de comandos próprios, conforme os majors empacotados para cada edição.

O cliente pro pode indicar quais avisos afetam os pacotes instalados. Uma simulação com --dry-run pode exibir que a CVE está resolvida antes de instalar qualquer pacote; trate essa mensagem como previsão do resultado da operação, não como comprovação de que a atualização foi aplicada.

sudo pro fix CVE-2026-114938 --dry-run

Comprove a atualização e reinicie os serviços

Após a instalação, confira a versão reportada por cada JVM e procure o identificador da CVE nos changelogs dos pacotes. A segunda checagem associa o build instalado ao aviso de segurança, em vez de depender apenas da comparação visual entre números de versão.

for d in /usr/lib/jvm/java-??-openjdk-amd64; do echo "== $d"; $d/bin/java -version 2>&1 | head -1; done
for n in 17 21 25; do echo -n "openjdk-$n: "; zgrep -c CVE-2026-114938 /usr/share/doc/openjdk-$n-jre-headless/changelog.Debian.gz; done

Em Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04, retire o número 25 do segundo laço porque essas edições não têm esse pacote. As duas verificações examinam arquivos no disco; elas não confirmam que processos Java já em execução deixaram de usar o código vulnerável carregado antes da atualização.

Os avisos recomendam reiniciar as aplicações Java após a atualização, pois uma JVM mantém bibliotecas e dados carregados durante a execução. Em algumas configurações, o needrestart reinicia os serviços durante a atualização; no modo de listagem, ele apenas informa quais unidades precisam ser reiniciadas.

Para localizar serviços pendentes em lote, consulte o needrestart. Em uma máquina de teste, três sinais apontaram que um processo ainda usava o build antigo: a versão mostrada pelo jcmd no processo ativo, mapas de arquivos excluídos em /proc/PID/maps e a unidade listada pelo needrestart.

sudo needrestart -b -r l | grep NEEDRESTART-SVC

O comando jcmd acompanha o JDK e pode não estar instalado em servidores que tenham somente o runtime. A inspeção de /proc/PID/maps também funciona nesses sistemas; depois de identificar a unidade pendente, reinicie o serviço para que a JVM carregue os arquivos corrigidos.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/como-corrigir-java4shell-no-ubuntu-e-reiniciar-servicos-java/
