title: Every Vibe-Coded Site Looks the Same. I Wrote a Linter for the Default Look.
description:
A post went around X this week that just said every website UI is vibe coded now. Nobody in the replies argued. Around the same time, a demo got passed around of an MCP server that feeds a coding agent curated designs from real websites, so the agent has something better to copy than its own defaults. People shared it because they already have the problem it fixes. You open a new SaaS landing page and you can tell what made it before the page finishes loading.

I build with these tools every day, and I don't think the issue is that AI-generated sites are ugly. Most of them look fine. The problem is that they all look the same kind of fine, and visitors notice. A page that looks like a template reads like a weekend project, even when the product behind it is good.

"It looks AI-made" is a vibe, and you can't review a vibe in a pull request. So I tried to turn it into something you can check: a small linter that looks for the default look in a project's HTML, JSX, CSS and Tailwind classes, prints what it found, and gives a score.

The fingerprints

These are my observations from looking at a lot of generated marketing pages, plus my own first drafts. I haven't measured any of this. It's a pattern list, and you'll recognize most of it:

  • One font, and it's Inter. Or system-ui, or Tailwind's font-sans with nothing set. No display face, no contrast between headings and body text.
  • A purple-to-blue gradient hero. from-purple-600 via-indigo-600 to-blue-500, or the same colors written as a CSS linear-gradient.
  • Glassmorphism. backdrop-blur on bg-white/10, usually on the sticky nav and a "Now with AI" pill.
  • Three rounded cards in a row. md:grid-cols-3, rounded-2xl, a soft border, a hover lift.
  • Emoji or lucide icons as the card art. ⚡ for speed, 🔒 for security, 📈 for insights.
  • A grey "Trusted by" logo bar. grayscale opacity-60, often showing logos the company has no relationship with.
  • A centered hero with two buttons. "Get started" and "Learn more", side by side.
  • Launch copy that could describe any product. Supercharge, unlock, seamless, effortless, empower, elevate, all-in-one, streamline.
  • The same spacing everywhere. Every section gets py-24, so the page has no rhythm. It's just one block after another.
  • Testimonials that look made up. "Sarah Johnson, CEO at Acme", a pravatar.cc avatar, five star glyphs.

None of these is wrong on its own. Inter is a great typeface, and three cards are sometimes the right layout. The fingerprint is all of them showing up together, because together they mean nobody made a design decision.

The fixture

I didn't scan anyone's real site. I wrote a fixture for a made-up invoicing tool called Ledgerly, the way a coding agent tends to write it when you prompt "build a modern landing page for an invoicing SaaS" and give it nothing else: an index.html with Tailwind classes, a small styles.css, and a src/Testimonials.jsx component. I put the fingerprints in on purpose, so the "before" score below is expected to be high. The useful part is what happens after.

sameness-lint

It's one Python file, stdlib only, about 140 lines. Each rule has a weight, and the weights add up to 100. A rule adds its weight once if it finds anything. Buzzwords cost 3 points each, up to the rule's 12-point cap. Here's the core:

RULES = {  # id: (weight, label)
    "default-font":   (12, "Only Inter/system sans in the whole project"),
    "purple-gradient":(14, "Purple-to-blue gradient"),
    "glass":          (8,  "Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)"),
    "card-grid-3":    (10, "Three-up rounded card grid"),
    "icon-cards":     (8,  "Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art"),
    "logo-bar":       (8,  "Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar"),
    "centered-hero":  (10, "Centered hero with two CTAs"),
    "buzzwords":      (12, "Generic launch copy"),
    "same-rhythm":    (8,  "Every section uses the same vertical padding"),
    "stock-proof":    (10, "Placeholder-looking testimonials"),
}

# gradients: Tailwind stops, or CSS hex stops that all sit in the violet/blue band
for m in re.finditer(r"from-(purple|violet|indigo|fuchsia)-\d+[^\"']*?to-(blue|indigo|cyan|sky|purple|pink)-\d+", low):
    add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
for m in re.finditer(r"linear-gradient\(([^)]*)\)", low):
    hs = [hue(h) for h in re.findall(r"#[0-9a-f]{6}\b|#[0-9a-f]{3}\b", m.group(1))]
    if len(hs) >= 2 and all(200 <= h <= 300 and s > 0.4 for h, s in hs):
        add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))

# centered hero: text-center near the <h1>, and at least two generic CTAs after it
for m in re.finditer(r"<h1\b", low):
    before, after = low[max(0, m.start() - 500): m.start()], low[m.start(): m.start() + 1500]
    if "text-center" in before + after[:200] and len(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))) >= 2:
        add("centered-hero", m.start(), "text-center h1 + ...")

# rhythm: if 75%+ of <section>s share one py-* value, the page has no rhythm
if sections >= 3 and len(where) / sections >= 0.75:
    hits["same-rhythm"].append(f"{len(where)}/{sections} sections use {py}")

The font rule collects every font-family declaration and every Google Fonts family= in the project. If all of them are in the default sans set (Inter, system-ui, Roboto, Helvetica, Arial and friends), it flags the project. The buzzword rule strips tags and class attributes first, so class="seamless-grid" doesn't count and visible copy does. A file can opt out of a rule with a sameness-lint-disable <rule> comment. That's on purpose: the opt-out shows up in the diff, where a reviewer can push back on it.

Full sameness_lint.py (about 140 lines, stdlib only) 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sameness-lint: flag the "AI default" look in a marketing site's HTML/JSX/CSS.
Heuristics, not taste. Each rule is a fingerprint you see a lot in generated sites."""
import re, sys, json, colorsys
from pathlib import Path

EXTS = {".html", ".htm", ".jsx", ".tsx", ".js", ".ts", ".vue", ".svelte", ".css", ".scss"}
SKIP = {"node_modules", ".git", "dist", "build", ".next"}
DEFAULT_FONTS = {"inter", "system-ui", "-apple-system", "blinkmacsystemfont", "sans-serif",
                 "ui-sans-serif", "segoe ui", "roboto", "helvetica", "arial", "helvetica neue"}
BUZZ = ["supercharge", "unlock", "seamless", "effortless", "revolutioni", "empower", "elevate",
        "next-level", "game-chang", "cutting-edge", "all-in-one", "streamline", "unleash",
        "transform your", "10x", "at scale", "like never before"]
CTA = r"(get started|start (?:for )?free|try (?:it )?free|book a demo|learn more|see how|watch demo)"
STOCK = r"(i\.pravatar\.cc|randomuser\.me|ui-avatars\.com|\bjohn doe\b|\bjane doe\b|\bacme\b|lorem ipsum|★★★★★)"
EMOJI = re.compile("[\U0001F300-\U0001FAFF\u2600-\u27BF]")

RULES = {  # id: (weight, label)
    "default-font":   (12, "Only Inter/system sans in the whole project"),
    "purple-gradient":(14, "Purple-to-blue gradient"),
    "glass":          (8,  "Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)"),
    "card-grid-3":    (10, "Three-up rounded card grid"),
    "icon-cards":     (8,  "Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art"),
    "logo-bar":       (8,  "Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar"),
    "centered-hero":  (10, "Centered hero with two CTAs"),
    "buzzwords":      (12, "Generic launch copy"),
    "same-rhythm":    (8,  "Every section uses the same vertical padding"),
    "stock-proof":    (10, "Placeholder-looking testimonials"),
}

def files(root):
    for p in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*")):
        if p.is_file() and p.suffix in EXTS and not SKIP & set(p.parts):
            yield p

def line_of(text, idx):
    return text.count("\n", 0, idx) + 1

def visible(text):  # strip markup but keep newlines so line numbers still work
    keep = lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n") + " "
    t = re.sub(r"<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>", keep, text, flags=re.S | re.I)
    t = re.sub(r"\{/\*.*?\*/\}|className=\"[^\"]*\"|class=\"[^\"]*\"", keep, t, flags=re.S)
    return re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", keep, t)

def hue(hexstr):
    h = hexstr.lstrip("#")
    if len(h) == 3: h = "".join(c * 2 for c in h)
    r, g, b = (int(h[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (0, 2, 4))
    hh, l, s = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(r, g, b)
    return hh * 360, s

def scan(root):
    hits = {k: [] for k in RULES}
    fonts, rhythm = set(), {}
    for p in files(root):
        rel, text = str(p.relative_to(root)), p.read_text(errors="ignore")
        low = text.lower()
        off = set(re.findall(r"sameness-lint-disable ([\w-]+)", text))  # per-file opt-out, reviewed in PR
        def add(rule, idx, ev, src=text):
            if rule in off: return
            item = f"{rel}:{line_of(src, idx)}  {ev.strip()[:70]}"
            if item not in hits[rule]: hits[rule].append(item)
        # fonts: CSS font-family, Google Fonts links, Tailwind font config
        for m in re.finditer(r"font-family\s*:\s*([^;}{]+)", low):
            fonts |= {f.strip(" '\"") for f in m.group(1).split(",") if f.strip(" '\"") and "var(" not in f}
        for m in re.finditer(r"fonts\.googleapis\.com/css2?\?([^\"']+)", low):
            fonts |= {f.split(":")[0].replace("+", " ") for f in re.findall(r"family=([^&\"']+)", m.group(1))}
        # gradients: Tailwind stops or CSS hex stops in the violet/blue band
        for m in re.finditer(r"from-(purple|violet|indigo|fuchsia)-\d+[^\"']*?to-(blue|indigo|cyan|sky|purple|pink)-\d+", low):
            add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"linear-gradient\(([^)]*)\)", low):
            hs = [hue(h) for h in re.findall(r"#[0-9a-f]{6}\b|#[0-9a-f]{3}\b", m.group(1))]
            if len(hs) >= 2 and all(200 <= h <= 300 and s > 0.4 for h, s in hs):
                add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"backdrop-blur[\w-]*|backdrop-filter\s*:\s*blur", low):
            ctx = low[max(0, m.start() - 200): m.end() + 200]
            if re.search(r"bg-white/\d+|rgba\(255,\s*255,\s*255,\s*0?\.\d+\)", ctx):
                add("glass", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"(?:md:|lg:)?grid-cols-3", low):
            if low[m.end(): m.end() + 1500].count("rounded-2xl") + low[m.end(): m.end() + 1500].count("rounded-3xl") >= 3:
                add("card-grid-3", m.start(), m.group(0) + " + rounded-2xl cards")
        for m in re.finditer(r"from ['\"]lucide-react['\"]|data-lucide=", low):
            add("icon-cards", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"<(?:h3|div|span)[^>]*>\s*(" + EMOJI.pattern + ")", text):
            add("icon-cards", m.start(), "emoji icon " + m.group(1))
        for m in re.finditer(r"(trusted by|loved by|used by teams at|backed by)", low):
            if re.search(r"grayscale|opacity-(?:[1-6]0)|text-(?:gray|slate|zinc)-[34]00", low[m.start(): m.start() + 1200]):
                add("logo-bar", m.start(), m.group(0) + " + greyed logos")
        for m in re.finditer(r"<h1\b", low):
            before, after = low[max(0, m.start() - 500): m.start()], low[m.start(): m.start() + 1500]
            if "text-center" in before + after[:200] and len(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))) >= 2:
                add("centered-hero", m.start(), "text-center h1 + " + ", ".join(sorted(set(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))))))
        if p.suffix != ".css":
            vis = visible(text).lower()
            for w in BUZZ:
                for m in re.finditer(re.escape(w), vis):
                    add("buzzwords", m.start(), f'"{w}"', vis)
            for m in re.finditer(r"<section\b[^>]*class(?:name)?=\"([^\"]*)\"", text, re.I):
                pys = re.findall(r"\bpy-\d+\b", m.group(1))
                if pys: rhythm.setdefault(pys[-1], []).append(f"{rel}:{line_of(text, m.start())}")
            for m in re.finditer(STOCK, low):
                add("stock-proof", m.start(), m.group(0))
    if not fonts or fonts <= DEFAULT_FONTS:
        hits["default-font"].append("font stack: " + (", ".join(sorted(fonts)) or "none declared (Tailwind font-sans)"))
    sections = sum(len(v) for v in rhythm.values())
    for py, where in rhythm.items():
        if sections >= 3 and len(where) / sections >= 0.75:
            hits["same-rhythm"].append(f"{len(where)}/{sections} sections use {py}")
    return hits

def score(hits):
    s = 0
    for k, (w, _) in RULES.items():
        n = len(hits[k])
        if k == "buzzwords": s += min(w, 3 * n)          # 3 points per phrase, capped
        elif n: s += w
    return s

def main():
    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
    root = Path(args[0] if args else ".")
    limit = int(next((a.split("=")[1] for a in sys.argv if a.startswith("--max=")), 101))
    hits = scan(root); total = score(hits)
    if "--json" in sys.argv:
        print(json.dumps({"score": total, "hits": hits}, indent=2)); return
    print(f"sameness-lint  {root}\n")
    for k, (w, label) in RULES.items():
        if hits[k]:
            print(f"✗ {label}  [{k}, {len(hits[k])}]")
            for ev in hits[k][:3]: print(f"    {ev}")
            if len(hits[k]) > 3: print(f"    … +{len(hits[k]) - 3} more")
    clean = [k for k in RULES if not hits[k]]
    if clean: print(f"✓ clean: {', '.join(clean)}")
    print(f"\nsameness score: {total}/100  (lower is more yours)")
    if total >= limit:
        print(f"FAIL: score {total} >= --max={limit}"); sys.exit(1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run 1: the default look

Here's the real output on the fixture, run with --max=30 the way it would run in CI:


$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/before --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/before

✗ Only Inter/system sans in the whole project  [default-font, 1]
    font stack: -apple-system, inter, sans-serif, system-ui
✗ Purple-to-blue gradient  [purple-gradient, 2]
    index.html:19  from-purple-600 via-indigo-600 to-blue-500
    styles.css:2  linear-gradient(135deg, #7c3aed 0%, #4f46e5 50%, #3b82f6 100%)
✗ Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)  [glass, 3]
    index.html:12  backdrop-blur-md
    index.html:21  backdrop-blur
    styles.css:3  backdrop-filter: blur
✗ Three-up rounded card grid  [card-grid-3, 1]
    index.html:42  md:grid-cols-3 + rounded-2xl cards
✗ Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art  [icon-cards, 7]
    index.html:14  emoji icon ✨
    index.html:21  emoji icon 🚀
    index.html:44  emoji icon ⚡
    … +4 more
✗ Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar  [logo-bar, 1]
    index.html:32  trusted by + greyed logos
✗ Centered hero with two CTAs  [centered-hero, 1]
    index.html:22  text-center h1 + get started, learn more
✗ Generic launch copy  [buzzwords, 17]
    index.html:6  "supercharge"
    index.html:22  "supercharge"
    index.html:23  "unlock"
    … +14 more
✗ Every section uses the same vertical padding  [same-rhythm, 1]
    5/5 sections use py-24
✗ Placeholder-looking testimonials  [stock-proof, 6]
    index.html:34  acme
    src/Testimonials.jsx:4  acme
    src/Testimonials.jsx:4  i.pravatar.cc
    … +3 more

sameness score: 100/100  (lower is more yours)
FAIL: score 100 >= --max=30
[exit 1]

All ten rules fired, so the fixture scored 100 out of 100. Again, that's by design. I wrote the fixture to hit every rule. The evidence lines are the useful part: 17 buzzword hits (five of them in the testimonial quotes), three placeholder avatars, and all five sections using py-24.

The scanner also over-counts in one place. The ★★★★★ string matched twice: once as "stock proof" and once as an "emoji icon", because U+2605 falls in the symbol range I scan for emoji. The score doesn't change, because each rule only adds its weight once, but don't treat the hit counts as precise measurements.

The fix: write the brief before the first prompt

What actually changed the output wasn't a better prompt. It was a file the agent reads before it writes any markup. I keep a DESIGN.md in the repo root and point the agent at it in the first message ("Read DESIGN.md. Do not use anything it bans."). Here's the template, filled in for Ledgerly:

# DESIGN.md — Ledgerly marketing site

## Who it's for
Freelancers and two-to-five person studios who invoice 5–40 clients a month
and hate chasing late payments. Not "modern teams". Not enterprises.

## Type
- Display: Fraunces 600, optical size on, tight tracking (-0.02em) at 48px+
- Body/UI: IBM Plex Sans 400/500, 17px base, 1.55 line height
- Numbers: IBM Plex Mono for amounts, dates, invoice IDs
- Never: Inter, system-ui as the only stack

## Palette (no gradients on backgrounds)
| Role        | Hex     |
|-------------|---------|
| Paper (bg)  | #F6F1E7 |
| Ink (text)  | #1B1B18 |
| Ledger green (primary) | #1F5C4A |
| Stamp red (overdue, one accent per screen) | #C8452B |
| Rule lines  | #D8CFBE |

## Spacing and rhythm
8px base. Sections do not share one padding: hero 112/64, proof 48, features 96,
closing 64. Content column 680px for prose, 1040px for layouts.
Corners: 4px on inputs and buttons, 0 on the invoice. No rounded-2xl cards.

## Signature move
The hero *is* an invoice: a ruled, left-aligned paper document with a real
line-item table and a red "OVERDUE 14 DAYS" stamp, next to the headline.
Every other section borrows the ruled-line motif. No floating blobs, no glass.

## Components
- One primary CTA per screen. Secondary actions are text links.
- Features as a numbered list with a one-line outcome each, not icon cards.
- No emoji. Icons only when they label a control.

## Voice
- Say what happens: "Ledgerly emails the reminder on day 3, 7 and 14."
- Use the customer's nouns: invoice, client, retainer, late fee.
- Numbers only if we can source them. No invented stats.
- Banned: supercharge, unlock, seamless, effortless, empower, elevate,
  revolutionize, game-changer, cutting-edge, all-in-one, streamline,
  next-level, "for modern teams", "like never before".

## Social proof
Real customer, real name, permission on file, or no testimonial section.
No placeholder avatars, no five-star glyphs, no fake logo bars.

## References (look at these, don't copy them)
- A paper invoice from an actual accountant
- Stripe's docs for table density
- A newspaper classifieds page for ruled-line rhythm

The section that does the most work is the signature move. Fonts and hex codes stop the page from looking generic, but one specific layout idea tied to the product (here, "the hero is an overdue invoice") is what makes the agent stop reaching for a centered hero. If you can't name one, look at real sites in your category before you prompt. A list of real business website examples is a better starting point than "make it modern". If you're using a references MCP server like the one in that demo, give it two or three sites you actually like and tell the agent what to take from each one: the density, the type contrast, or the way the proof section is laid out. Don't ask it to copy the whole page.

The other section that earns its place is Social proof. The before fixture had invented testimonials because the prompt asked for a "complete" page. If you don't have a real quote yet, leave the section out. A page with no testimonials looks more honest than one with Sarah Johnson from Acme.

Run 2: after the brief

I rebuilt the page against the brief. The hero is now a left-aligned Fraunces headline next to a ruled invoice with the stamp. The logo bar became a plain mono strip of facts (reminders on day 3/7/14, card or SEPA, CSV export). Features became a numbered list, and section padding varies. Then I added a src/Pricing.jsx component the way it usually arrives: generated in a separate session that never saw the brief.


$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/after --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/after

✗ Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art  [icon-cards, 1]
    src/Pricing.jsx:1  from "lucide-react"
✗ Generic launch copy  [buzzwords, 1]
    src/Pricing.jsx:7  "seamless"
✓ clean: default-font, purple-gradient, glass, card-grid-3, logo-bar, centered-hero, same-rhythm, stock-proof

sameness score: 11/100  (lower is more yours)
[exit 0]

The score went from 100 to 11, and both remaining hits are in the component that never saw DESIGN.md. That's the most useful thing this run showed. The brief works on the session that reads it, and new sessions start from defaults again.

The two hits aren't equally important:

  • "seamless" in a pricing bullet is a real regression. I rewrote it as "Nightly CSV push to your accountant's inbox", which says what the feature does.
  • The lucide-react import is arguable. Those Check icons mark list items in a pricing table, which the brief allows ("icons only when they label a control"). So the file gets a sameness-lint-disable icon-cards comment with the reason next to it, and a reviewer can disagree in the PR.

After both changes:

$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/after-review --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/after-review

✓ clean: default-font, purple-gradient, glass, card-grid-3, icon-cards, logo-bar, centered-hero, buzzwords, same-rhythm, stock-proof

sameness score: 0/100  (lower is more yours)
[exit 0]

A 0 doesn't mean the page is good. It means the page avoids ten specific defaults. Taste is still your job, and the linter can't tell you whether the invoice hero actually works for a freelancer. It just stops the easy defaults from slipping back in.

Make it a pre-merge check

Linters only help if they run without anyone remembering to run them. Mine runs on every PR that touches the marketing site:

# .github/workflows/sameness.yml
name: sameness-lint
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["site/**"]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - run: python3 tools/sameness_lint.py site --max=30

A few things I'd tell anyone copying this:

  1. Set the threshold from your own baseline. Run it on your current site first. If you score 40, set --max to 45 and tighten it over time. 30 is just what I picked for this fixture.
  2. Tune the rules to your brief. If your brand really does use Inter, delete that rule. The rules should enforce your DESIGN.md, not my taste.
  3. Add your agent's tics. Every model has its own favorite phrases. When you catch a new one in review, add it to BUZZ and the brief's banned list in the same commit.
  4. Keep the opt-out visible. A per-file disable comment shows up in the diff. A global config flag doesn't.

Where this fits

It doesn't matter much whether the site comes from Cursor, Claude Code or an AI website builder. The first draft will lean toward the average of everything the model has seen. That's what "default" means. That's true of every tool, PolyDraft included, which is why the brief matters more than the prompt. If you're comparing tools, generate a page from the same brief in each one and run a check like this on the output. It's a useful extra row on a list of what to check when evaluating an AI website builder. And if your "site" is really one page right now, decide whether it should stay a landing page or grow into a website (the difference matters for what you build next) before you write the brief.

What's the tell you spot first on an AI-built site? I'll add good ones to the rule list.

title: npm ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree: 4 fixes
description:
npm install stops before writing anything, and instead of a package list you get a tree dump:

npm error code ERESOLVE
npm error ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree

npm error While resolving: my-app@1.0.0
npm error Found: react@18.3.1
npm error Could not resolve dependency:
npm error peer react@^19.0.0 from chart-lib@2.4.0

The line that matters is always peer … from …: the project already decided one version, a dependency's peerDependencies excludes it, and npm refuses to guess.

Why it happens at all

Since npm 7, peer dependencies are installed automatically and a conflicting peer range is a hard error. npm 6 installed peers only with a warning, so this class of failure did not exist before. npm builds one tree per project, and each package name resolves to exactly one directory — node_modules/react cannot be two versions.

A four-line reproduction in an empty directory:

mkdir eresolve-demo && cd eresolve-demo
npm init -y
npm pkg set dependencies.react="^18.3.1"
npm pkg set dependencies.chart-lib="^2.4.0"   # this version peers on react@^19 
npm install
# npm error code ERESOLVE

Read the tree before you pick a flag

Line npm prints What it tells you
While resolving: the package whose dependencies are being resolved
Found: the version already chosen for that name, and who asked for it
Could not resolve dependency: the package whose peer range excludes that version 
npm ls react                              # which versions exist, and who requires them
npm explain chart-lib                     # why the package is in the tree at all
npm view chart-lib peerDependencies --json
npm view chart-lib versions --json | tail -20

That last pair is the cheapest fix path: if a newer patch widened the peer range, upgrading beats every override you could write.

Four strategies, in the order worth trying

Strategy What it changes Lockfile Take it when
Upgrade the dependent its peerDependencies range clean a release accepts your version — always first
overrides resolution for the whole tree clean and reproducible a transitive package lags behind
--legacy-peer-deps skips peer installation (npm 6 behaviour) records the skipped peers plugin ecosystem, migration in progress
--force installs anyway, may duplicate can hold duplicates and broken peers never in CI; a local unblock only

npm install --strict-peer-deps is the inverse: it refuses to auto-pick when ranges conflict, which is what you want in CI when failing is better than drifting.

overrides that actually apply 

{
  "dependencies": { "react": "^19.1.0", "chart-lib": "^2.4.0" },
  "overrides": { "chart-lib": { "react": "$react" } }
}
  • $react means "the version the root manifest resolves", so the pin follows your own dependency instead of being copied in and going stale.
  • The field applies to the entire tree, including packages you never import directly.
  • In a workspace, overrides inside a package's own package.json is ignored. Only the root counts: 
npm pkg set 'overrides.react=$react' -w .    # writes the root manifest
npm install --workspaces

If two workspaces genuinely need different React majors, they need separate lockfiles and separate installs. No override makes one node_modules hold two Reacts safely.

When the tree is already installed

npm reuses an existing node_modules, so an overrides edit can silently fail to reach a nested copy:

rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install

A merge that combined two lockfiles can raise ERESOLVE on a manifest that is perfectly fine. Inspect before deleting anything:

npm ls --all 2>&1 | grep -i "invalid\|peer\|ERR"
npm install --package-lock-only    # does the manifest resolve at all?

--package-lock-only is the safe first move after a merge: it answers the question without destroying a working node_modules you may still need. npm ci is the only command that promises "exactly this lockfile or nothing".

The traps in the containment strategies

  • --legacy-peer-deps typed once in one terminal is recorded nowhere. The next person's npm ci fails the same way — put it in .npmrc or remove the need for it.
  • --force silences the error by installing conflicting copies. The failure then reappears at runtime as two React instances, a dead context, or an invalid hook call.
  • peerDependenciesMeta: { optional: true } means npm 7+ does not fail when the peer is absent, so an ERESOLVE naming an optional peer usually points at a second, real conflict above it in the tree.
  • A yarn.lock beside a package-lock.json produces two disagreeing resolutions. Commit one, delete the other.
  • Node 20 ships npm 10 and Node 18 ships npm 9; the error text and resolution details differ. Pin the Node version in CI and in .nvmrc.
  • A global install has no overrides field to edit. Use npx some-cli@latest or npm exec --package=some-cli@latest -- some-cli --help for one-off tools instead.

Version cheat sheet

npm Peer dependencies Conflict result
6 warnings only, not installed npm WARN, working tree
7 installed automatically ERESOLVE (introduced here)
8 installed automatically, overrides supported ERESOLVE, fixed by overrides
8.3+ $package references inside overrides pin to the root's own version
9 / 10 / 11 same rules, npm error prefixes richer Could not resolve text

A package-lock.json generated by npm 6 will not reproduce on npm 10, because npm 6 never recorded the peers it skipped.

The longer version, with the workspace and lockfile cases in full, is on my site: npm ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree: 4 fixes.

title: Best UI kit marketplaces in 2026: price, license and code compared
description:
Where you buy a UI kit decides what you can do with it: the license, whether code comes with it, and whether you pay once or every month. I put six places side by side, with every fact linked to the page it comes from. One of them is ours, so read that row with that in mind.

The best UI kit marketplace depends on how you build. UI8 sells 6,428 UI kits plus coded templates, Envato Elements unlimited downloads by subscription, Creative Market single kits, Untitled UI one design system with React code, Figma Community free kits, and mebius.design 35 Figma kits with shadcn code.

How do the six compare?

Price, license and code, checked on each site on 17 Nov 2026.

UI8, Envato Elements, Creative Market and Figma Community are marketplaces with many authors; Untitled UI is one design system, and mebius.design is one studio’s catalog (ours). Each label links to the page its fact comes from.

  • UI8. Price: per product, or All Access at $188 / 3 months, $368 / year or $570 once (Pro $112, Pro+ $220 and Lifetime $399 in a Black Friday sale that day). License: personal, commercial and client use, one person per license or pass; no reselling the files or making kits from them. Code: 456 coded templates in many stacks; the UI8 MCP with All Access.
  • Envato Elements. Price: Core from $8.99 a month, Plus from $39, Ultimate from $168, all with unlimited downloads. License: one license per project, client work included; finish the end product while you subscribe; no redistributing items in a tool or template. Code: admin, site and landing page templates in a separate Website Templates section.
  • Creative Market. Price: per product and license; one CRM UI kit was $45 Personal, $120 Commercial and $220 Extended Commercial. License: Commercial covers up to 5,000 end products for sale, but not use in a website, app or game, which needs Extended Commercial, one title per license. Code: themes and templates for WordPress, Shopify, Wix, Bootstrap, HTML and more, sold separately.
  • Untitled UI. Price: paid once; Figma PRO $149 and React PRO $499 for one user ($129 and $349 on sale that day), plus free tiers. License: unlimited end products for you or your clients; no kits, templates or design systems made from it for others. Code: free MIT React components (React 19.3, Tailwind CSS v4.3, React Aria); React PRO adds 5k+ components.

  • mebius.design (ours). Price: $19 per item or $259 for all items, paid once. License: personal, commercial and client work with every purchase, one person; the Agency license (custom quote) adds handing files to clients, white-label products and resale templates. Code: 19 of the 35 kits have React + Tailwind v4 code in shadcn registry format, installed with the shadcn CLI or over MCP; code for the rest is added free when it’s ready.

UI8’s figures match our mebius vs UI8 comparison. Prices and counts move on every site, so open the linked page before you buy.

Is UI8 good for UI kits?

6,428 UI kits from many authors, plus code and AI tools.

Yes, especially if you buy more than UI kits. UI8 lists 14,852 products: UI kits, 3D, illustrations, icons, mockups, fonts and 456 coded templates in stacks such as Next.js, Astro, SwiftUI and Flutter, with files for Figma, Sketch and Framer. All Access covers every product, with up to 40 downloads a day, the UI8 MCP and Design DNA for AI coding tools.

Pro and Pro+ renew until you cancel; Lifetime is paid once, and each pass is for one person. Sales are final, but a single product that doesn’t work as described is fixed or refunded if you report it within 7 days.

Is Envato Elements worth it for UI kits?

Unlimited downloads of 30+ million assets, licensed per project.

It can be, if you also use stock video, music, photos or fonts: one plan from $8.99 a month covers them all, and its UI kits come for Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD and more. Each download licenses one project, client work included, and the project has to be finished while you subscribe. Once finished, it stays licensed after you cancel. More in Envato Elements alternatives for UI kits.

What does Creative Market sell?

Single kits from independent shops, under three licenses.

Creative Market lists 4,206 UI kits, each sold on its own by an independent shop, so you pay only for the kit you need, with no subscription. A membership saves up to 25% across the catalog.

Pick the license with care. Commercial covers up to 5,000 end products for sale, but its terms rule out use in a website, application or video game. That needs Extended Commercial: one website, app or game per license, up to 250,000 end products.

Is Untitled UI a marketplace?

No: one large design system in Figma and React, paid once.

No. It’s one design system, sold by its makers, so every component shares one style. Untitled UI’s Figma PRO kit has 10k+ components and variants and 420+ page examples, with lifetime updates. Its free React components are MIT-licensed, and React PRO adds 250+ page examples. Its Standard License covers client work; Studio, Business and Enterprise tiers cover teams.

Are Figma Community UI kits free?

Figma Community lists 4,770+ free UI kits, among them Apple’s iOS and iPadOS 26 kit and the Material 3 Design Kit, which makes it the first stop for platform kits. Free files are CC BY 4.0: share and adapt them for any purpose, commercial included, as long as you credit the creator.

The kits are design files. Matching code, where it exists, lives in its own project, as shadcn/ui’s does for the community shadcn kits.

Where does mebius.design fit?

Ours: Figma kits with React + shadcn code, paid once.

Which one should you pick?

  • Many asset types, a pass, Sketch or Framer files, or code in other stacks: UI8.
  • Stock video, music, photos and fonts on top of UI kits, for one monthly price: Envato Elements.
  • One kit for one project without a subscription: Creative Market, with Extended Commercial if it goes into a website or app.
  • One design system with free MIT React components: Untitled UI.
  • Free platform kits from Apple, Material Design and others: Figma Community.
  • A product dashboard, mobile app or website in Figma, with React + shadcn code in the same style: mebius.design. Start with the dashboard UI kits or the free shadcn charts.

FAQ

What is the best UI kit marketplace?

It depends on how you build. UI8 suits buyers of many asset types and coded templates, Envato Elements heavy downloaders who also need stock media, Creative Market one-off purchases, Untitled UI teams that want one design system with React code, Figma Community free platform kits, and mebius.design React + shadcn projects whose Figma file and code should match.

Which UI kit marketplaces include code?

UI8 lists 456 coded templates in many stacks. Envato Elements and Creative Market sell website templates and themes as separate items. Untitled UI has free MIT React components and a paid React PRO library. Figma Community’s kits are design files. mebius.design ships React + shadcn code with 19 of its 35 kits.

Can I use marketplace UI kits in client projects?

UI8, Untitled UI and mebius.design cover client work with every purchase. Envato Elements covers it per project, if you finish the work while you subscribe. On Creative Market, a website or app needs the Extended Commercial license. Free Figma Community files allow any use with credit to the creator.

Are there good free UI kits?

Yes. Figma Community lists 4,770+ free UI kits, including Apple’s and Material Design’s. Untitled UI has a free Figma kit and MIT React components, and UI8 has 2,500 free assets for anyone with an account. mebius.design gives away 62 charts and 128 forms with code, free with an account.

Is a subscription or a one-time payment better for UI kits?

A subscription pays off when you download a lot across asset types: Envato Elements, or UI8’s Pro and Pro+ passes. A one-time payment suits a few kits you keep using: single products on UI8 or Creative Market, Untitled UI’s PRO tiers, UI8’s Lifetime pass, or mebius.design at $19 per item or $259 for all items.

title: When does reserved GPU capacity beat on-demand pricing?
description:
Reserved GPU capacity beats on-demand once your utilization over the term exceeds the reserved rate divided by the on-demand rate: 63.0% of all hours for an 8 x NVIDIA H100 machine on a 1-year Amazon EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Nodus lists the H100 SXM at $2.60/hr on its pricing page, a GPU rate below even AWS's 3-year plan per GPU-hour, and Nodus Reserved Compute (Beta) quotes dedicated capacity for a steady floor. Commit only the GPUs that stay busy above the line and run the rest on demand.

How do you calculate the break-even utilization for reserved GPUs?

Divide the reserved rate by the on-demand rate you would otherwise pay. The answer is the fraction of the term's hours you must actually use for the commitment to cost less.

The reasoning is short. A commitment bills every hour of the term, used or not. On-demand bills only the hours you run. So reserved wins when reserved rate x all hours < on-demand rate x used hours, which rearranges to:

break-even utilization = reserved rate / on-demand rate
effective reserved rate = reserved rate / your utilization

The second line is the one people skip. A $4.33 commitment that you use half the time really costs $8.67 per hour of work. That is more than the $6.88 on-demand rate it was meant to beat.

We worked this on AWS because it publishes every commitment rate for the same machine. From the official AWS price list for us-east-1, a p5.48xlarge costs $55.04 per hour on demand, or $6.88 per GPU-hour.

The 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with no upfront payment is $34.6752 per hour, or $4.33 per GPU-hour. The break-even is 34.6752 / 55.04 = 0.630. We re-checked it the other way: 55.04 x 0.63 = 34.6752.

Option (8 x H100, AWS us-east-1) Per instance-hour Per GPU-hour Break-even utilization
On-demand $55.04 $6.88 n/a
EC2 Capacity Block $47.757 $5.97 86.8%
Compute Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront $43.344 $5.42 78.8%
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront $34.6752 $4.33 63.0%
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 3 years, no upfront $23.77728 $2.97 43.2%

Prices checked November 18, 2026 (this applies to every price in this post). AWS rates come from the AWS EC2 on-demand price list, the AWS Compute Savings Plans price list file for us-east-1 (which also carries EC2 Instance Savings Plan rates) and the EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing page. Per GPU-hour is the instance rate divided by 8, rounded to cents. Linux, no operating system fee.


The deeper the discount and the longer the term, the less of the year you need to fill.

What does a year of one 8 x H100 machine cost at each utilization?

A commitment is a flat line and on-demand is a slope, so the only question is where your real usage lands. A full year is 8,760 hours (AWS defines a Savings Plan year as 365 days). The 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan costs $34.6752 x 8,760 = $303,754.75 for the year. The 3-year plan costs $23.77728 x 8,760 = $208,288.97 per year, for three years.

Utilization over the year On-demand cost 1-year plan 3-year plan, per year
0% $0.00 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
20% $96,430.08 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
40% $192,860.16 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
60% $289,290.24 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
80% $385,720.32 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
100% $482,150.40 $303,754.75 $208,288.97

On-demand is $55.04 x 8,760 x utilization. At 60% the machine is still cheaper on demand, by $14,464.51. At 80% the 1-year plan saves $81,965.57.


On-demand crosses the 1-year line at 63.0% utilization and the 3-year line at 43.2%.

Utilization here means hours of the whole year, nights and weekends included. A team that runs a training box 10 hours a day on weekdays uses 50 of 168 weekly hours, which is 29.8%. That team should not sign either plan for that machine.

Should you reserve your peak or your floor?

Reserve the floor. Split your fleet into tiers by how busy each GPU is across the term, commit only the tiers above break-even, and run the rest on demand or on spot.

Here is a worked example with the AWS per-GPU rates above. A team serves a model on 8 H100s around the clock. It adds 8 more H100s for weekday business hours, 10 hours a day, 5 days a week. The second tier runs 8 x 8,760 x 50 / 168 = 20,857.14 GPU-hours a year.

Strategy First 8 GPUs (100% busy) Second 8 GPUs (29.8% busy) Year total
Everything on demand $482,150.40 $143,497.14 $625,647.54
Reserve all 16 (1-year plan) $303,754.75 $303,754.75 $607,509.50
Reserve the floor, peak on demand $303,754.75 $143,497.14 $447,251.89
Reserve the floor, peak on Nodus at $2.60 $303,754.75 $54,228.57 $357,983.32

The floor tier saves $178,395.65 by committing. The peak tier would waste $160,257.61 if you committed it too, which is why reserving everything barely beats paying list price. The last row prices the peak hours at the H100 SXM rate listed on the Nodus pricing page: 20,857.14 x $2.60. GPU rates only; the AWS rate includes the instance's CPUs, memory and networking, so treat that row as a rate comparison, not a like-for-like quote.


Committing the always-busy floor saves money; committing the peak gives most of it back.

Is reserved capacity always cheaper per hour than on-demand?

No. Some reservations cost more per GPU-hour than the same vendor's on-demand rate, because you are buying guaranteed, co-located capacity for fixed dates rather than a discount.

Lambda's pricing page lists 1-Click Clusters of 16 H100s for terms of 2 weeks to 1 year at $6.16 per GPU-hour, while an on-demand 8 x H100 instance is $4.59 per GPU-hour.

That ratio is 134.2%, so on rate alone the cluster never breaks even. You buy it for a cluster of 16 or more GPUs held for a fixed term, not for a lower rate. The AWS Capacity Blocks documentation describes the same trade: blocks are for GPUs "for days or weeks at a time", placed close together in EC2 UltraClusters. The Capacity Blocks pricing page adds that the reservation fee is charged up front when you schedule it.

Lambda also says on that page to contact them "for reserved capacity at our lowest prices". Runpod's pricing page and the Nebius prices page likewise route reserved and commitment pricing through sales. Their long-term rates are not published, so we have not priced them here.

What is the difference between spot instances and reserved instances?

They sit at opposite ends of the same trade. Spot is the cheapest per hour with no commitment, but the provider can take the machine back. Reserved costs a commitment and bills every hour, but the capacity is yours for the term.

AWS advertises Spot Instances at up to 90% off on-demand prices. Spot fits interruptible work that checkpoints, such as training and batch inference.

Reserved fits the always-busy floor: production inference, a long training run with a fixed start date. On-demand covers the space between. Our spot vs on-demand guide works through the rework math for spot, so we do not repeat it here.

Which AWS commitment should you pick for GPUs?

Pick the one whose flexibility matches what you might change. AWS's Savings Plans guide says EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit you to one instance family in one region, while Compute Savings Plans apply regardless of family, size or region. For p5 that flexibility is priced in: the 1-year Compute plan breaks even at 78.8%, against 63.0% for the instance plan.

A 3-year plan drops the line to 43.2%, but it locks one GPU generation for three years. Sign it only if you are confident you will still want that hardware in year three. If you mostly want to stop overpaying AWS list rates, our cheaper AWS alternatives post compares on-demand H100 rates across platforms.

Where does Nodus fit for steady and bursty load?

We cover both halves of the floor-and-peak split. For the peak, Nodus Jobs run your command on demand, with logs, outputs, spending limits and recovery, and the H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page. That is below the $2.97 per GPU-hour of AWS's 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, so for GPU rate alone no AWS commitment in the table beats it at any utilization.

For the floor, Nodus Reserved Compute (Beta) supplies dedicated GPU capacity for your configuration and reservation window. You describe the GPU model, quantity, duration, location and start timing. Nodus reviews each request and sends a proposal covering availability, price, access and delivery. Submitting a request does not reserve hardware or authorize payment.

The Reserved Compute page also shows a planning index built only from providers' published reservation rates for the exact term you select, with the range and provider count.

It is a Beta and a quote, not a self-serve checkout. If you need a price this minute, use the published commitments above.

FAQ

How do I measure my utilization before committing?

Take at least a few weeks of billing or scheduler data for the exact GPU type, and divide GPU-hours used by GPU-hours in the period. Count nights and weekends. If the number moves a lot week to week, commit only to the lowest steady level.

Does paying upfront change the break-even?

Yes, slightly. In the same AWS file, the 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for p5.48xlarge is $34.6752 per hour with no upfront. It drops to $33.024 partial upfront and $32.36352 all upfront, so more cash up front lowers the line a little.

Can I request a single GPU through Nodus Reserved Compute?

Yes. The Reserved Compute guide says you can request a single GPU, and the final offer confirms how GPUs are arranged across servers. The console request form accepts durations up to 365 days.

What if my load grows after I commit?

Growth is the easy case: the commitment keeps covering the floor and new load runs on demand until it proves steady. Shrinking is the costly case, because the commitment bills every hour whether or not you use it. Our cost per finished job post shows how idle hours inflate the real bill.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Node.js Image Thumbnail Uploads to S3-Compatible Storage: Presigned Private Downloads
description:
Short answer: keep originals and resized thumbnails under separate prefixes in a private S3-compatible bucket, then return short-lived presigned GET URLs. Generate the thumbnail in the application or a worker after the upload is durably recorded. This keeps a marketplace user's private image private without making the browser responsible for bucket policy.

That decision is a control-plane decision as much as a storage one. The failure I care about is a thumbnail that looks fine in a test but becomes a public object, a duplicate after a retry, or an overwritten original during a replacement. Those are paging events, not cosmetic bugs.

How can a Node.js example implement image thumbnail uploads to private S3-compatible storage?

Use a key layout that makes an incident legible at a glance: originals/{userId}/{assetId}.jpg for the source and thumbs/{size}/{userId}/{assetId}.jpg for derivatives. The predictable prefixes make listing and cleanup practical, while the asset ID prevents two requests for the same user file from racing on a friendly filename.

Sharp is a reasonable choice for the resize step in a Node.js worker. Put the original first, enqueue a thumbnail job with the source key and requested sizes, and make the worker idempotent. A retry should either observe the existing derivative or write the same deterministic derivative key; it must not create thumb-1, thumb-2, and leave the database guessing.

The bucket stays private. Since public-read ACLs are not available in this setup, delivery is a short-lived presigned GET URL or an application proxy. Do not put a permanent object URL in a listing response. A URL lifetime of a few minutes is usually enough for an image detail page; your threat model and client caching policy should set the exact value.

No exceptions.

For a team already operating several backend integrations, Infrai gives the storage worker one API key and one bill across backend capabilities, and its REST API works over plain HTTP without a storage SDK. Its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which is useful when a runbook has to be reproduced months later.

Keep it boring.

Which upload failure belongs in the thumbnail reliability runbook?

The first useful signal is not average upload speed. It is a mismatch between the database pointer and the object set: a row says a thumbnail exists, but the object is absent; or an old object is still serving after a replacement. Alert on that reconciliation count, on presign requests that return expired URLs, and on multipart debris older than your cleanup window. Those checks catch privacy and correctness failures before a customer reports a broken image.

Here is the small part of a Go worker I use to make the storage calls explicit. The same sequencing applies to a Node.js service using fetch or an S3 client. The API key comes from the environment, and a deterministic idempotency key makes a retry safe.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func call(method, path string, body []byte, idem string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        if idem != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem) }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            d := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if v := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); v != "" { d = 2 * time.Second }
            time.Sleep(d)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data) }
        return data, readErr
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    bucket, key := "marketplace-private", "originals/u_42/a_9.jpg"
    if _, err := call(http.MethodPut, "/storage/object/put/"+bucket+"/"+key, []byte("image bytes"), "upload-a_9"); err != nil { panic(err) }
    // The presign request returns a short-lived GET URL; send its JSON payload per discovery.
    if _, err := call(http.MethodPost, "/storage/object/presign/"+bucket+"/"+key, []byte(`{"expires_in":300,"method":"GET"}`), "presign-a_9"); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The production version sends the actual image bytes, records content type and dimensions, and validates the returned URL before handing it to the client. The sample deliberately checks every status: a 4xx response is an actionable reason, not a successful upload.

What does the reproducible evaluation measure?

Run the same four-step test against each candidate: upload a representative original, resize it to the largest thumbnail your feed needs, request a presigned download, and repeat the upload request once with the same idempotency key. Record p50 and p95 upload time, thumbnail completion time, download success after expiry, and whether the retry creates exactly one logical object.

Pass means the largest test file meets your marketplace latency budget, the URL is unusable after its configured expiry, and the repeated write leaves one database record and one key. Fail the candidate if it requires public ACLs, if metadata must be searched server-side, or if replacement correctness depends on an unavailable conditional If-Match write.

Keep the test data fixed: three image dimensions, two file sizes, and the same concurrency ramp. I am not claiming a benchmark result here; the point is a decision rule your team can rerun after a vendor or Sharp upgrade. Your mileage may vary with region and network, so publish the raw timings beside the pass/fail decision.

Where do S3, R2, B2, and a unified API differ?

The storage primitive is familiar, but operational boundaries differ. Amazon S3 has the broadest surrounding ecosystem and mature versioning and lifecycle controls. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when egress economics and Cloudflare placement dominate. Backblaze B2 is a straightforward object store with a clear pricing page. Infrai is useful when the same service already calls several backend capabilities: one key and one bill remove credential and invoice sprawl, and its REST API can be called from any language without installing a storage SDK.

Option Strong fit Trade-off to test
Amazon S3 Deep AWS integration, versioning, lifecycle tooling More IAM and account surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 Cloudflare-centric delivery and object storage Check feature parity and egress assumptions
Backblaze B2 Simple object storage and transparent pricing Validate region, latency, and migration tooling
Infrai storage One REST key across storage and other backend services No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

For this workflow, try Infrai when consolidating credentials and API integration is worth more than specialist storage controls. Its discovery endpoint documents request and response schemas, which helps a small team keep the Go worker and Node.js service aligned. Choose S3 when object versioning, object lock, or the AWS-native ecosystem is a hard requirement; choose R2 or B2 when their network and regional characteristics win your measured test.

That is the gate.

Rollout and rollback for private thumbnail delivery

Start with a private bucket and a canary user. Verify that a listing response contains keys, not public URLs; fetch through the presigned URL; then wait past expiry and confirm the fetch is rejected. Check that the object metadata records width, height, and content type, while the searchable index remains in your database because metadata is not server-searchable.

Don't promote the canary because the happy-path image rendered once. The rollback trigger is any pointer/object mismatch, duplicate logical asset, or URL that remains usable after its deadline — freeze new writes, keep reads on the last committed pointer, and drain the resize queue before retrying the rollout.

Replacement deserves its own alarm. There is no conditional If-Match write, so do not overwrite a live key in place when two edits can arrive together. Create a new asset key, commit the pointer in a transaction, and garbage-collect the old key only after readers have moved. In a busy marketplace this means the database transaction owns the state change: the upload worker can finish twice, but only one committed pointer becomes current, and a sweeper can safely remove the previous object after a grace period. If strict ordering matters, coordinate through the database or a queue.

Lifecycle rules can remove abandoned originals and old thumbnails, but the shortest lifecycle is one day and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. Set an explicit abort job and keep a metric for orphaned keys. A failed resize should be retried from the original; it should never make the original public as a fallback.

The catch is important: private, presigned delivery is not suitable for a permanent public gallery, static website hosting, or a workload that needs WORM retention. Stick with a specialist or add an external immutability and replication layer for those cases. That is a capability boundary, not a reason to hide the constraint in a launch checklist. If the boundary fits, start with the storage presign contract at https://docs.infrai.cc/storage/object/presign and run the canary before changing the default bucket.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing
  • https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/

title: Go Checkout Rollback — Idempotency Bounds Feature Flag Retries and Duplicate Writes
description:
For checkout feature flag retries, use idempotency to make duplicate writes preserve the desired kill-switch state. Treat a lost response as an unknown outcome until reconciliation establishes the state; otherwise a second toggle can undo the rollback that the first request already completed.

TL;DR: Feature flag retries need idempotent backend logic, a stable operation identity, and verification of the observed state. For an e-commerce AI agent loop, keep rollback control separate from the latency and cost measurements that decide whether the loop should continue. A successful write response alone is insufficient evidence that every checkout worker has adopted the new state.

How can feature flag retries turn duplicate writes into a rollback reversal?

A toggle describes a transition relative to whatever state exists when the backend executes it. Suppose a checkout agent is enabled, the rollback request flips it off, and the response disappears. Retrying the toggle flips it on again. Two accepted writes can therefore leave the operator looking at the original state, even though the backend executed both requests correctly; an integration error seen by the caller does not establish that a write failed.

Preserve the intent.

The operational distinction is between “invert the flag” and “make agent execution disabled.” Repeating the second instruction preserves the target value, provided the backend implements deterministic set semantics. Read the current state first to establish a baseline, then use an explicit set or rollout value, but do not mistake that preliminary read for concurrency control: another operator can change the flag between the read and the write. Serialize changes through a controller or require a backend concurrency mechanism whose actual contract has been verified.

For checkout, a dedicated kill switch should stop admission of new agent work at the boundary chosen by the application. Decide separately what happens to work already running and to purchase mutations already committed. A flag cannot retract an order.

Bound the control loop before sizing telemetry

Measure agent-loop latency and accumulated call cost under a shared operation identity, and record retry attempts separately from logical operations so that repeated delivery does not inflate the apparent number of shopper actions. The decision record should preserve the desired flag value, the controller generation, the time of observation, and the observed value. These are application-owned record fields, not a proposed vendor request schema. Keep shopper content out of that record unless it is necessary.

Use explicit SLOs for both checkout behavior and control propagation. As an illustrative planning exercise, a team might choose a 2-second observation interval and a 30-second rollback verification deadline; those are proposed operating parameters, not measured service performance or a vendor guarantee. With 600 workers polling independently every 2 seconds, budget for 300 reads per second before retries, dashboard queries, or ordinary traffic. A shared controller can reduce upstream reads, but it also adds a distribution path whose failure and propagation delay belong in the rollback SLO.

Budget retries too.

The latency of a retried agent step includes time waiting between attempts, while the cost accounting must include every billable attempt associated with the logical action. Do not add a cumulative total to the same ledger twice. Keep raw attempt records and derive the operation total from distinct attempts; retain the operation's end-to-end elapsed time separately from individual call duration. Otherwise a rollout can appear faster merely because the slow attempts disappeared from the aggregate.

Infrai fits teams that want one REST API and a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, with unified billing on one bill; the application-facing contract stays stable when the vendor behind a capability changes. Its specified per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata supports attribution inside the agent loop. Sharing a credential across backend capabilities reduces credential configuration for a controller that observes flags alongside agent activity. The trade-off is a broader credential boundary, so scope access to the controller's operational role. That contract is useful only if the application still owns the rollback policy and verifies the semantics of the particular write capability, rather than assuming that a platform idempotency convention makes every operation safe.

Implement one intent and replay its result

Start with a read-only observation of the actual flag. This standalone Go program reads the versioned API base URL from INFRAI_API_BASE_URL, the credential from INFRAI_API_KEY, and the flag key from FLAG_KEY. Configure the base URL for the intended deployment, including its version prefix. The program prints the response without guessing its schema; production reconciliation must validate the documented response and compare its state with the durable intent. A read cannot authorize a write.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func observe() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key, flag := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("FLAG_KEY")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" || key == "" || flag == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("configure an HTTPS versioned base URL, credential, and flag key")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            base+"/flags/get/"+url.PathEscape(flag), nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 1<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 { return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit delay exceeds observation budget") }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(when)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("flag read status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("observation attempt budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := observe(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The following Go program is a local, deterministic demonstration of a write that commits before its response is lost. It uses no network and exercises no vendor API. Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain. The operation identity stays fixed across the retry, and the ledger refuses reuse of that identity with a different target.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

var errLostResponse = errors.New("response lost after commit")

type controller struct {
    enabled bool
    intents map[string]bool
}

func (c *controller) set(id string, desired, loseResponse bool) error {
    if previous, exists := c.intents[id]; exists {
        if previous != desired {
            return errors.New("operation identity reused with different intent")
        }
        return nil
    }
    c.enabled = desired
    c.intents[id] = desired
    if loseResponse {
        return errLostResponse
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    c := controller{enabled: true, intents: make(map[string]bool)}
    const operation = "checkout-agent-disable-42"
    err := c.set(operation, false, true)
    if errors.Is(err, errLostResponse) {
        err = c.set(operation, false, false)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if c.enabled {
        panic("rollback target not observed")
    }
    fmt.Println("rollback target observed: agent disabled")
}

This intentionally small example has one process and one writer. In production, persist the operation record and state update atomically, serialize competing generations, and define record retention to cover the full retry horizon; an in-memory map cannot provide those properties across a restart. If an old disable operation is replayed after a newer enable operation, return its historical result without silently executing it again, then reconcile against the latest authorized generation. Historical success and current state are different observations.

Transport retries also need a deadline, bounded backoff, and handling for rate limits that honors Retry-After when present. An exhausted retry budget leaves an unresolved operation for reconciliation. It must not trigger a toggle as a recovery shortcut.

Buy or build the controller boundary?

A feature management product and an analytical store answer different questions. Buying a flag service can move control-plane work out of the platform backlog; building the controller gives the team direct ownership of intent ordering, at the expense of storage, concurrency, recovery, and on-call responsibility. Compare the following candidates using the same lost-response and stale-generation tests before making a procurement decision. The acceptance requirements below are evaluation criteria, not claims that every product implements them.

Option Proposed role in this checkout design Acceptance boundary and trade-off
LaunchDarkly Candidate external flag control plane Verify explicit desired-state updates, adoption visibility, and recovery evidence; an external control plane adds a dependency to the rollback path.
Unleash Candidate flag control plane evaluated against the platform's operating model Verify the chosen deployment's polling behavior and ownership of recovery; include operational work in the buy-versus-build review.
Flagsmith Candidate flag control plane evaluated against the same rollback contract Verify concurrent edits, stale callers, and repeated desired-state writes; a familiar flag UI does not establish retry semantics.
Application-owned controller Implement operation ordering and a durable intent ledger Offers direct control over reconciliation policy; the team must implement and operate persistence and recovery.
ClickHouse Analytical storage candidate for attempt and decision records Useful to evaluate separately from flag control; choosing an analytical store leaves the write controller and its SLO as distinct responsibilities.
Sentry Candidate for the error-review side of the workflow Evaluate how an ambiguous write appears to the responder; error review alone cannot establish the desired flag state.
Datadog Candidate for the latency and operational-review side Evaluate correlation of agent attempts with controller decisions; require a separate acceptance test for rollback control.
Grafana Candidate for the SLO-review side Evaluate whether the selected data sources expose attempt totals and adoption delay; a dashboard cannot replace a durable intent ledger.

There is no winner from a feature checklist alone. Keep the external candidates in the comparison until a representative integration demonstrates the required behavior, and require a build proposal to survive the same exercise instead of giving internal code a free pass. An analytics choice should not decide who is allowed to re-enable the checkout agent.

Verify adoption, then release the rollback

Before rollout, exercise three synthetic cases: a committed write with a lost response, a repeated request carrying the same operation identity, and an old generation delivered after a newer one. Include a controller restart in the durable implementation. Verify both the stored intent and the state observed by the checkout admission path; a ledger that says “disabled” is not sufficient if workers are still admitting new agent work.

Keep the kill switch asserted while investigating latency or cost regressions. Re-enable through a new, authorized desired-state operation after the verification criteria pass, then reconcile any explicit rollout value against the intended cohort. A timeout is a reason to investigate propagation and observation, not permission to alternate the flag until a response looks reassuring.

The telemetry boundary needs an equally explicit acceptance review. Use application-owned change records rather than assuming flag history is available, and measure adoption directly rather than assuming evaluation statistics exist. Plan for polling clients. Arrange threshold notifications and missed-job detection in the operating design, and do not infer a distributed span tree from trace identifiers carried by log records. Where the workflow requires replay, symbolication, per-user erasure, export, or configurable retention, verify that requirement separately before sending production data. These are selection gates, not promises supplied by a generic observability label.

The release condition is concrete: the latest authorized target is observed at the admission boundary, unresolved writes have an owner, and the agent-loop measurements account for retries. Until then, leave the rollback intent intact.

References

  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • ClickHouse documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation

title: RagePal: making an upward flick and a downward drag feel different
description:
We’re AlyDoit, the team behind RagePal, a short mobile game about a cloth doll that keeps making excuses. In the November iPhone update, we shipped a mode called Hear Excuses. Swipe an excuse away and the doll tries another. Pull it down far enough and you accept a fictional IOU due the next day.

Both choices move the same card along the same axis. The choice between them affects what the game does next, so we gave the gestures different ways to finish.

A flick ends on release

The code measures travel from the start of the gesture. On an 844-pixel-tall viewport, an upward movement of more than 70 CSS pixels dismisses an excuse on release. A quick gesture can dismiss it after 35 pixels if it takes under half a second. Both distances scale with viewport height.

This lets a deliberate push and a short flick end in the same action. When the gesture falls short, the card settles back so the player can try again.

A drag commits after it travels far enough

The card follows the finger. Once it moves down by more than 110 CSS pixels on the same reference viewport, the game accepts the deal while the finger is still down. The later release has no additional effect because the scene has already marked the action as finished.

There’s one more detail in the input handler. It starts by treating the movement as undecided. It switches to a card gesture once the vertical movement clears a small threshold and exceeds the horizontal movement. That gives the doll’s sideways interaction room to work in the same scene.

What I’d like feedback on

With the game in your hand, is it clear when pulling down actually accepts the IOU? I’m curious whether you’d want the card to show a progress cue as it follows your thumb, or a short confirmation when the threshold is crossed.

RagePal is available on iPhone and Android. To try the gesture, open Hear Excuses after the first ritual. Official game page and store links

This post was generated by an AI working on AlyDoit’s publishing task. The gesture details were checked against the game’s source code.

title: Go PDF Job Polling and Terminal States (Before Support Contract Signing)
description:
A customer-support contract must stop occupying the rendering stage before the signing stage can make a defensible decision. TL;DR: when a PDF job appears stuck in progress forever, read its current job status, check that the poller handles terminal failure, and put a deadline on the local waiting state. Most apparently stuck jobs finished badly and nobody looked. Preserve the last observed status alongside the local outcome so the audit trail explains why signing did or did not proceed.

For a bounded production design exercise, I would follow one support settlement contract from approved terms through PDF rendering to server-side signing, with a 30-second observation budget chosen for the example rather than presented as a provider guarantee. Suppose the provider reports failure while the application still displays “in progress.” The postmortem question is immediate: what page fired when the contract stopped advancing? If the only answer is a green request dashboard, the application has measured the wrong thing.

Stop signing there.

This is a hypothetical failure in the application's state handling, not an incident report about a rendering service. Its lesson is an invariant: every local wait must end in an explicit local outcome, including when the remote outcome remains unknown. A renderer's failure and an observer's expired deadline are different evidence, even when both block the next workflow step.

What page fires when a PDF job never leaves progress?

Start with the last observed status, not another render request. A poller that recognizes success but keeps waiting after failure can leave its database row in progress indefinitely; a poller that never gives up can do the same when observations stop arriving. These cases look alike to a support agent waiting to send a contract, but they need different responses, and blindly recreating the job makes the subsequent audit harder to explain.

I would record the contract reference, renderer job identifier, observation time, last provider status, local state, and local reason as separate fields in the application's audit record. These are proposed application fields, not a vendor response schema. Keep the distinction explicit: “deadline exceeded” explains why this observer stopped, while the last remote observation explains what it actually knew. Neither proves that a remote operation was canceled.

That distinction also makes a portability boundary useful. Infrai puts backend capabilities behind one REST API, so a change in the vendor behind a capability can stay behind the application-facing contract instead of forcing vendor-specific calls into the support workflow. I recommend that support teams try Infrai for the PDF rendering integration when they want that stable boundary, while keeping polling deadlines and permission to advance into signing in their own application. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which removes a concrete setup chore: teams can inspect the integration contract before distributing production credentials.

Infrai uses one API key across 295 routes and 20 modules. For this integration, that means the team can use a single API key for supported backend capabilities instead of adding a separate secret for each service; access-control requirements still determine whether sharing that credential is appropriate. The recommendation is limited. The API interface does not establish the legal sufficiency of a signed support agreement, and a rendering result alone should never be treated as evidence of signer authorization. Establish those requirements independently before selecting the signing system.

Treat the contract as an artifact, not a dashboard color

The useful postmortem timeline has at least three boundaries: render requested, render observed complete, and signing authorized. An HTTP request finishing belongs in that timeline, but it cannot stand in for completion of an asynchronous PDF job. The status reader must interpret the renderer's documented response and translate it into application states, including a terminal failure branch that stops the wait immediately.

Keep unknown values visible. If an adapter receives a status it cannot interpret, recording “still running” conceals the very evidence needed to repair the integration. My preferred policy is to stop automatic advancement, retain the unrecognized status, and require investigation; another team might tolerate a bounded observation interval, but it still needs a deadline and an alertable outcome. That is an explicit operational trade-off, not a claim that every provider shares a status vocabulary.

For the support contract, fidelity versus render cost belongs at this boundary too. Choose representative approved terms, a long customer name, and a signature area that crosses a page boundary, then inspect the resulting artifact before allowing a template into production. Those are suggested fixtures, not measured defects. A faster render that moves the signature area away from its terms fails this workflow's acceptance criteria; demanding unnecessarily elaborate layout for every internal draft consumes rendering work without improving the agreement the customer signs.

No dashboard settles that trade-off.

Compare who owns rendering and who owns the waiting

Evaluate setup by the first useful result: an acceptable contract artifact accompanied by an explainable terminal outcome. A successful sample request is a smaller milestone. For a fair comparison, these are the alternatives I would include in the evaluation, with their own official documentation as the starting point rather than an asserted performance ranking.

Option Integration boundary to evaluate Where it earns a place in this workflow
