Playwright Browser automation, including page-to-PDF generation; the application owns the surrounding job lifecycle. Evaluate it when control over the browser page and contract layout matters enough to own browser operation.
Puppeteer Browser automation with a PDF interface; rendering code remains close to browser behavior. Evaluate it when the team wants to express rendering through browser APIs and can operate that dependency.
Gotenberg A document-conversion service boundary instead of a browser library inside the application. Evaluate it when the team prefers to operate a dedicated conversion service and define its own workflow adapter.
Infrai PDF capabilities within a shared backend API, with publicly discoverable schemas and examples. Evaluate it when a stable capability contract and less separate credential setup matter across the support workflow.

Playwright and Puppeteer deserve a serious look when browser-level control is the reason for the project. Gotenberg deserves one when a dedicated conversion boundary fits the deployment model. Infrai's breadth is useful when the integration would otherwise accumulate separate service credentials and SDK surfaces, but breadth does not establish superior contract fidelity; inspect the actual output and the documented capability contract before choosing.

None of these choices relieves the application of deciding what to do when it stops receiving useful observations. Compare template fidelity first, then count the operating responsibilities needed to keep that result repeatable. There is no measured latency or render-cost ranking here.

Make the preventative path executable

The following Go program demonstrates the local state boundary with synthetic observations. It is a runnable state-machine example, not an Infrai client: the names complete, failed, and working belong to this application, and a real adapter must map documented provider responses into them. There is deliberately no invented response payload or remote status enumeration.

Save it as main.go and run go run main.go. The second observation represents a terminal rendering failure; the program retains it and refuses to authorize signing. Change that observation to working to exercise the separate deadline outcome. The tiny example uses a 30-second deadline and a 2-second interval as local design choices, not recommended service limits.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    State string
    Raw   string
}

type Audit struct {
    ContractID string    `json:"contract_id"`
    State      string    `json:"state"`
    LastStatus string    `json:"last_status"`
    Reason     string    `json:"reason"`
    ObservedAt time.Time `json:"observed_at"`
}

func main() {
    row := Audit{ContractID: "support-settlement-42", State: "waiting"}
    deadline := time.NewTimer(30 * time.Second)
    defer deadline.Stop()
    ticker := time.NewTicker(2 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    observations := []Observation{
        {State: "working", Raw: "synthetic rendering observation"},
        {State: "failed", Raw: "synthetic terminal failure observation"},
    }
    index := 0
    for row.State == "waiting" {
        select {
        case <-deadline.C:
            row.State = "failed"
            row.Reason = "observation deadline; remote outcome unresolved"
        case <-ticker.C:
            if index >= len(observations) {
                continue
            }
            observation := observations[index]
            index++
            row.LastStatus = observation.Raw
            row.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
            switch observation.State {
            case "working":
            case "complete":
                row.State = "rendered"
            case "failed":
                row.State = "failed"
                row.Reason = "renderer reported terminal failure"
            default:
                row.State = "failed"
                row.Reason = "unrecognized adapter state"
            }
        }
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(row); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The important property is the separation between LastStatus and Reason: when the deadline fires, it changes the application's state without manufacturing a new remote observation. Even rendered authorizes only the next validation step. It is not a signed-contract state.

For the actual status read, use the following standalone program instead of the synthetic exercise. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and PDF_JOB_ID in the environment, save this version as main.go, and run go run main.go. It reads the existing job and prints the response without guessing any JSON field names; use the discovery response schema to implement the adapter above. Don't interpret a successful HTTP status as a completed render.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func readStatus(ctx context.Context, key, jobID string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/pdf/job/get/{job_id}", "{job_id}", url.PathEscape(jobID), 1)
    backoff := time.Second
    for {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "status 429: %s\n", body)
        wait := backoff
        value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if seconds > 30 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond observation budget")
            }
            if delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; delay > wait {
                wait = delay
            }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
            if delay := time.Until(date); delay > wait {
                wait = delay
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
        if backoff < 8*time.Second {
            backoff *= 2
        }
    }
}

func main() {
    key, jobID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("PDF_JOB_ID")
    if key == "" || jobID == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and PDF_JOB_ID")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := readStatus(ctx, key, jobID)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

This is a read of an existing job, so retrying it does not create another contract. The reader backs off on HTTP 429, honors Retry-After, surfaces error bodies, and stops at its context deadline. Keep its output in an appropriately restricted diagnostic destination: the audit trail needs job evidence, not unrestricted copies of customer data.

In production, persist the transition and its audit entry together, and make a failed local transition visible to the support queue. A network reader needs bounded request durations so an individual read cannot defeat the overall deadline, as the HTTP example enforces. Neither example performs remote writes or signing; those operations need their own documented idempotency behavior before automatic replay is safe.

Where the deadline advice stops

An observation deadline is a policy for the application, not a remote cancellation mechanism. If the remote job completes later, reconcile that evidence against the original job identifier before permitting a new signing attempt, and preserve both events rather than rewriting the earlier deadline as though it never occurred. A contract with an unresolved rendering outcome should remain blocked from automatic signing.

The local timer is also insufficient across process restarts. Persist an absolute deadline with the workflow record and enforce it when observation resumes; otherwise every restart grants another waiting period and recreates the “forever” problem. Page on the contract's failure to advance with its last status attached. Request charts can help investigate afterward.

For a browser-specific layout requirement, start with the browser specialists. For a conversion service you intend to operate directly, evaluate that deployment boundary. If the shared capability contract fits your support workflow, start with the API documentation and verify the PDF status schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

References for the API contract, PDF specification, and alternatives discussed above:

  • Infrai documentation
  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Playwright PDF API
  • Puppeteer PDF API
  • Gotenberg documentation

title: Animate Popover API entry and exit without JavaScript delays
description:
A popover can animate in cleanly after showPopover() yet disappear immediately on close. The problem is not that showPopover() ignores animations. It changes the popover’s browser-managed state and top-layer participation; CSS still needs to preserve a paintable element during the closing transition.

Build the styling around the browser state rather than a separate JavaScript flag. Give the base popover selector the closed visual state, such as reduced opacity and a compressed transform. Give :popover-open the fully visible state. With both endpoints explicit, the same transition can run in either direction.

For entry, add @starting-style for the open selector. This supplies a deterministic first frame when the element becomes visible, instead of relying on an implicit initial state.

The important lifecycle detail is the transition list. Include display and overlay with allow-discrete in addition to visual properties like opacity and transform. Opacity and transform describe the motion, but display and overlay allow the browser to keep the popover rendered and in the top layer long enough for that motion to be seen on exit. Without them, the close can effectively remove the popover before its visual transition finishes.

Keep JavaScript focused on state commands. Before opening or closing, check :popover-open so code does not request showPopover() for an open popover or hidePopover() for a closed one. The script decides whether state should change; CSS owns the visible choreography.

This pattern solves a specific problem: preserving the visible exit transition for a browser-managed popover. It does not turn a popover into a modal dialog, provide complete focus management, or animate an element that your application removes from the DOM. Browser support and timing details should also be considered for the environments you support.

Working example 

// This module provides a small, testable popover transition helper.
// It models the article's working idea: JavaScript should only guard state,
// while CSS supplies the transition configuration that keeps the popover
// visible long enough to animate out.

const REQUIRED_PROPERTIES = new Set(['opacity', 'transform', 'display', 'overlay']);
const DISCRETE_PROPERTIES = new Set(['display', 'overlay']);

export function buildPopoverTransition({ durationMs = 700, properties } = {}) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(durationMs) || durationMs <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError('durationMs must be a positive finite number');
  }

  const selected = properties ?? ['opacity', 'transform', 'display', 'overlay'];

  if (!Array.isArray(selected) || selected.some((property) => !REQUIRED_PROPERTIES.has(property))) {
    throw new TypeError('properties must contain only supported popover transition properties');
  }

  for (const required of REQUIRED_PROPERTIES) {
    if (!selected.includes(required)) {
      throw new Error(`Missing required popover transition property: ${required}`);
    }
  }

  return Object.freeze({
    durationMs,
    properties: Object.freeze(
      selected.map((property) => Object.freeze({
        property,
        allowDiscrete: DISCRETE_PROPERTIES.has(property),
      })),
    ),
  });
}

export const popoverAnimationCss = `
[popover] {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: scaleX(0);
  transition:
    opacity 700ms,
    transform 700ms,
    display 700ms allow-discrete,
    overlay 700ms allow-discrete;
}

[popover]:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: scaleX(1);
}

@starting-style {
  [popover]:popover-open {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: scaleX(0);
  }
}
`;

export function createPopoverCommands(popover) {
  if (
    !popover ||
    typeof popover.matches !== 'function' ||
    typeof popover.showPopover !== 'function' ||
    typeof popover.hidePopover !== 'function'
  ) {
    throw new TypeError('popover must provide matches(), showPopover(), and hidePopover()');
  }

  function isOpen() {
    return popover.matches(':popover-open');
  }

  return Object.freeze({
    isOpen,
    open() {
      if (isOpen()) return 'already-open';
      popover.showPopover();
      return 'opened';
    },
    close() {
      if (!isOpen()) return 'already-closed';
      popover.hidePopover();
      return 'closed';
    },
  });
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/popover-showpopover-exit-transition

title: Multipart Upload Selection for Large Private Documents from 100 MB to 1 GB Explained
description:
Short answer: choose multipart upload for large private customer-support documents, especially 100 MB to 1 GB PDF and ZIP files on unreliable connections; keep a single PUT for ordinary small PDFs and office files because it has fewer states to coordinate.

The deciding constraint isn't raw capacity. It's the failure unit. A failed single PUT restarts the whole object, while multipart lets the client retry one part. For a support portal, every upload also needs a tenant-owned object key, an expiring download link, and an application record that says who may retrieve it. Infrai is a reasonable option for teams that expect storage to sit beside other backend capabilities and want one consistent REST contract instead of adding another SDK and credential set. Its public discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules and includes runnable Go examples; that makes the time to a first verified request unusually concrete. I recommend trying it for the private upload boundary when reducing integration surface matters, while keeping authorization and upload state in your own application.

How do large PDF and ZIP retries expose the right multipart upload boundary?

Start with a policy, not a magic industry threshold. The 100 MB boundary below is an application decision for this example: files below it take the short single-request path, while files from 100 MB through the portal's 1 GB limit take the multipart path. Your mileage may vary if clients have stable office networks, or if mobile uploads dominate. Measure completion and retry behavior before moving the line. Multipart wins when restarting a full upload is expensive or likely. Each part is its own retry unit, so a brief connection loss doesn't throw away all prior progress. The catch is state: the service must remember the upload ID, accepted part numbers, checksums or provider-returned part identifiers, tenant ID, object key, and terminal status. Completion must consume one authoritative parts list. A retry must never create two logical attachments. Single PUT is still the right default for normal documents because it has one request, one success condition, and much less stale state. Don't make a 2 MB invoice follow a multipart state machine merely because the 700 MB diagnostic bundle needs one. Tenant isolation comes first: build object keys from an internal tenant identifier rather than a user-supplied folder, keep objects private or signed-only, and issue short-lived presigned download URLs only after an application authorization check. Never treat possession of an object key as permission. This storage boundary has no public/public-read ACL, which suits this workflow but rules out permanent public links and static website hosting.

Retry one part.

Treat credentials and upload state as one failure domain

The important comparison is where operational ownership lands. Direct providers expose their own account, credential, SDK, and feature surface. An aggregation layer narrows that surface, but its common contract may omit specialist controls. Here is the practical split for this workload:

Option Setup and credential shape Best fit Boundary to verify
AWS S3 Direct provider integration Teams that need provider-specific storage controls Your application still owns tenant authorization and upload state
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider integration Teams standardizing directly on R2 Validate the exact multipart and lifecycle behavior you plan to operate
Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct provider integration Teams already operating in the OSS ecosystem Account and SDK conventions remain provider-specific
Tencent Cloud COS Direct provider integration Teams already operating in the COS ecosystem Account and SDK conventions remain provider-specific
Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 Direct specialist integration Workloads committed to GCS or B2 Infrai doesn't cover these vendors
Infrai Plain HTTP under one key and one billing relationship Teams adding storage alongside other backend modules No object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or migration tool

Infrai's primary advantage here is breadth behind a consistent interface: adding another backend capability is another discovered REST operation, not a fresh SDK integration. The supporting benefit is inspectability. Discovery is public, needs no key, and returns request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so a team can confirm the contract before distributing a production credential.

That convenience isn't universal. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba OSS, or Tencent COS directly when a provider-specific control is part of your design. Choose Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 directly when either is a hard platform requirement. For regulated retention, use an external solution that provides object lock or WORM behavior; this storage surface has neither versioning nor object lock. FedRAMP requirements also need a separate compliance assessment rather than an inference from an API shape.

Make the policy and integration probe explicit in Go

The smallest safe example is the decision layer that runs before any provider call. It validates the tenant, normalizes the file name for display only, derives the storage key from trusted identifiers, and returns one of two modes. The threshold is configuration, so changing it doesn't rewrite upload code.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type UploadMode string

const (
    SinglePut UploadMode = "single-put"
    Multipart UploadMode = "multipart"
)

type Policy struct {
    MultipartAt int64
    MaximumSize int64
}

type UploadPlan struct {
    Mode        UploadMode
    ObjectKey   string
    DisplayName string
}

func getBucket(client *http.Client, apiKey, bucket string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/get/{bucket}",
        "{bucket}",
        url.PathEscape(bucket),
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("bucket lookup returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("bucket lookup remained rate limited after retries")
}

func planUpload(policy Policy, tenantID, attachmentID, fileName string, size int64) (UploadPlan, error) {
    if tenantID == "" || attachmentID == "" {
        return UploadPlan{}, errors.New("tenant and attachment IDs are required")
    }
    if size <= 0 || size > policy.MaximumSize {
        return UploadPlan{}, fmt.Errorf("file size %d is outside policy", size)
    }

    displayName := filepath.Base(strings.ReplaceAll(fileName, "\\", "/"))
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(tenantID + ":" + attachmentID))
    objectKey := fmt.Sprintf("tenants/%s/attachments/%s", tenantID, hex.EncodeToString(digest[:]))

    mode := SinglePut
    if size >= policy.MultipartAt {
        mode = Multipart
    }
    return UploadPlan{Mode: mode, ObjectKey: objectKey, DisplayName: displayName}, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BUCKET")
    if apiKey == "" || bucket == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BUCKET are required")
    }
    body, err := getBucket(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, apiKey, bucket)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bucket=%s\n", body)

    policy := Policy{MultipartAt: 100 * 1024 * 1024, MaximumSize: 1024 * 1024 * 1024}
    plan, err := planUpload(policy, "tenant_42", "attachment_9f2", "logs.zip", 734003200)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("mode=%s key=%s name=%s\n", plan.Mode, plan.ObjectKey, plan.DisplayName)
}

This program verifies the configured private bucket through a real Infrai call, then runs the provider-independent upload policy. Request bodies and completion fields should come from the selected provider's current schema, not from a copied blog snippet. Query the public capability discovery document and use its Go example. API calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY; uploads remain private, and that authorization header must not be forwarded to a returned presigned URL.

For multipart, persist the state transition before acknowledging it to the browser. Use a stable application attachment ID as the idempotency anchor, retry HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, and explicitly abort a failed multipart session. There is no automatic cleanup rule for abandoned fragments. This is where missed cleanup becomes a bill and a runbook entry — quiet failure, but still failure.

Overwrite protection needs the same discipline. Strict If-Match conditional writes aren't available, so serialize changes with a queue or guard them with a database transaction and generation field. A key should identify one immutable attachment attempt; publishing a replacement should point the support record at a new key rather than overwrite the old bytes.

Prove isolation before defining rollback

Verification should prove invariants, not just report a green response. In staging, upload one small PDF through single PUT and one large ZIP through multipart. Interrupt a part, resume it, and confirm that only that part is retried. Then attempt a download as the owning tenant, another tenant, and an unauthenticated client. The first gets an expiring link; the others don't.

Check four records after completion: the application attachment is terminal, the object key starts with the trusted tenant prefix, the reported size matches the accepted upload, and no active multipart state remains. Also exercise a client-visible 429 retry. A tight loop is an incident generator.

Rollback is boring by design. Disable new multipart starts with a feature flag, allow already-created sessions to complete for a bounded drain window, and abort the rest explicitly. Route files below the single-request limit back to PUT. Files above that limit should receive a retryable maintenance response from your application rather than silently switching to a full-object upload that clients may not be able to finish.

Don't delete completed objects during control-plane rollback. Detach the application record only after authorization and retention checks, and keep deletion as a separate, auditable operation. Lifecycle expiration can't provide minute-level rollback cleanup because its minimum is one day.

Draw the specialist boundary after the rollback drill

Use multipart for the 100 MB to 1 GB class when individual-part retries materially improve completion; use single PUT for the everyday support attachment. Keep tenant authorization, overwrite coordination, and cleanup in the application no matter which storage vendor receives the bytes.

For teams that value a small integration surface across several backend services, Infrai is worth evaluating for this private storage boundary. For teams that need public hosting, browser-direct CORS self-service, strict conditional writes, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 coverage, a specialist or direct provider is the better fit. If this boundary matches your system, start with the large-document upload guide.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • FedRAMP
  • Infrai storage lifecycle discovery

title: Cron Trigger Queue Worker Node.js Example: Scheduled Digest Enqueue Beyond 15 Minutes
description:
Short answer: let the cron trigger enqueue a small, repeatable command, then let a queue worker deliver each customer digest. A 15-minute scheduler limit is fine when no individual invocation owns the whole report. The useful guarantee is a recorded handoff, not a heroic timeout.

A small decision matrix for weekly delivery

Design What it can prove Where it fits Trade-off
Cron calls the report directly The process started A tiny, read-only task A timeout can hide partial work
Cron enqueues one batch The batch was handed off Uniform, short reports One poison item can delay the batch
Cron records a run and enqueues customer jobs Each customer has a traceable attempt Active-customer digests Requires a ledger and reconciliation

For a B2B SaaS digest, I use the third row. The trigger writes a run record, creates one message per active customer, and exits. A worker owns data fetching, rendering, and delivery. That split keeps the scheduler's execution window boring and makes the business result inspectable.

This is a revenue-per-hour decision. Queue mechanics are undifferentiated plumbing; I want them managed or isolated so one person can spend the week shipping product. The ledger is worth keeping in application code because it answers the question support actually asks: “Did Acme's Monday report send?”

What delivery guarantee does the queue really provide?

Most queues provide at-least-once delivery. A message may appear again after a worker has sent the email but before it has acknowledged the message. A FIFO queue can preserve ordering and, with a deduplication window, reduce duplicates, but it cannot make an external email provider exactly-once. AWS describes those FIFO properties and their limits in its queue documentation.

So I define two separate facts: enqueued means the scheduler committed a message, and sent means the delivery provider accepted the final payload. A retry changes attempts; it must not create a second business event. The idempotency key joins the scheduled run and customer ID, and the delivery adapter stores that key before acknowledging work.

There is a catch. A per-customer job is only safe if its inputs are stable enough to replay. Store the report version or a snapshot pointer in the message, rather than serializing a giant report into it. If the worker sees the same key, it returns the prior result. That behavior is more valuable than squeezing another minute out of the cron runtime.

How should a cron trigger enqueue Node.js work for long-running cleanup reports?

Use the trigger as a coordinator, not as the worker. This TypeScript example uses generic interfaces so the same state machine can sit over a hosted queue, a database-backed queue, or a self-managed broker.

type DigestJob = {
  runId: string;
  customerId: string;
  snapshotId: string;
};

async function scheduleDigest(now: Date): Promise<void> {
  const runId = `weekly:${now.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`;
  const customers = await customerStore.activeIds();
  await ledger.insertIfAbsent({ runId, status: "enqueuing", total: customers.length });

  for (const customerId of customers) {
    const snapshotId = await reportStore.freezeInputs(customerId, runId);
    await queue.send({ runId, customerId, snapshotId } satisfies DigestJob);
  }

  await ledger.markEnqueued(runId);
}

async function work(job: DigestJob): Promise<void> {
  const key = `${job.runId}:${job.customerId}`;
  if (await ledger.wasSent(key)) return;

  const report = await reportStore.render(job.snapshotId);
  await delivery.sendEmail(job.customerId, report, { idempotencyKey: key });
  await ledger.markSent(key);
}

The loop is intentionally plain. In production, enqueue in bounded pages and record the last successful page. A crash after page three should resume at page four, not silently claim that all customers were handled. The worker should renew its lease while rendering, cap retries, and move a repeatedly failing item to a dead-letter queue with the run ID attached.

Node.js is a good fit for this coordination because the trigger does little synchronous work. It is not a reason to keep a 40-minute report inside one process. Break expensive cleanup into retryable units, and make each unit observable.

Where do scheduled jobs fail after the trigger appears healthy?

The first failure mode is an apparently successful timeout. The scheduler waits 15 minutes, stops waiting, and the enqueue may already be committed. If an operator retries manually without checking the ledger, two weekly runs enter the queue. A deterministic run ID plus an insert-if-absent constraint turns that ambiguity into a visible state.

The second is a worker crash at the worst possible line: after the provider accepted an email, before the queue acknowledgement. The next delivery sees the same idempotency key and records a duplicate attempt without sending again. Test this exact point. It is a five-minute fault injection that exposes a whole class of expensive support tickets.

That is the contract.

The useful test matrix is wider than a happy-path unit test. Start a run with ten customers, kill the worker after rendering customer four, and let the lease expire. The replay should produce four recorded attempts, no second email for customer four, and six untouched messages. Then pause the delivery provider for twelve minutes and watch backlog age, retry count, and dead-letter movement. Finally, deploy a new message schema while an old worker is still draining; the old worker must reject or ignore fields it does not understand without marking the job sent. These checks cost less than a support incident because they exercise the boundaries where state changes hands. I keep the fixture data small and deterministic, so I can run the scenario locally before a weekly release and compare the ledger rows as plain text. It is not glamorous. It is the part that lets a solo operator trust an automated customer promise.

The third is stale membership. “Active customers” changes while a long enqueue loop runs. Freezing the customer set, or recording a membership version, gives the digest a defined population. Otherwise a customer can be absent simply because their subscription changed between page reads.

I once assumed a longer timeout would solve the handoff problem. It only made the failure harder to locate. Your mileage may vary with queue lease defaults, but the invariant stays the same: every customer has one run ID, one idempotency key, and a final state that can be queried.

When is a queue the wrong alternative?

Do not add a queue for a maintenance query that finishes in seconds, has no customer-visible side effect, and can be rerun safely. A direct cron call is easier to operate there. A hosted workflow scheduler is also reasonable when infrequent runs, retained logs, and a small delay matter more than per-customer throughput; GitHub's schedule event documentation is a useful example of that model.

The queue is not suitable when nobody watches backlog age, lease expirations, or dead-letter volume. Choose the simpler path, or make monitoring part of the same feature before shipping it. The operational burden is real: retries need backoff, schemas need versioning, and a replay tool needs authorization.

For a weekly digest, my decision rule is narrow: direct execution for bounded work, one queue message per independently retryable customer, and a ledger when a delivery dispute costs more than the ledger costs to maintain. That rule leaves room to change infrastructure later without changing the customer-facing contract.

Ship weekly. Keep the boring parts boring.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: Feeding GPUs in Another Cloud Without Moving the Dataset Twice: Data Gravity for Cross-Cloud Training
description:
The GPUs are available in one cloud. The training data lives in another. That mismatch is now routine: GPU capacity is scarce and unevenly distributed, while datasets were collected wherever the product happened to grow up. So a team books capacity where it exists, and then discovers the real project is not the training run. It is moving, and keeping moved, the data the training run feeds on.

The naive answer is a full copy before every run. Copy the dataset across, train, copy the results back, repeat next month with a slightly larger dataset. It works once. It fails as a habit, because most of the bytes never changed, the copy window grows faster than the training window, and egress charges quietly become a line item nobody budgeted for. Data gravity is not a metaphor to admire. It is an engineering constraint to design around.

Move the delta, not the dataset

The first fix is to stop treating the dataset as one indivisible object. A training dataset is a collection of items, most of them stable, some of them new, a few of them corrected or withdrawn. If the storage layer can describe the dataset as a manifest of items with content hashes, the cross-cloud question changes from "copy everything" to "which items are missing or different on the other side".

Sync by manifest. The receiving side lists what it already holds, compares hashes, and pulls only the missing or changed items. The first sync is still a full move, and there is no way around paying it once. Every sync after that is proportional to how much the data actually changed, which for most real datasets is a small fraction per training cycle.

Content addressing does quiet extra work here. If two datasets share items, and most training sets are revisions of earlier ones, the shared items transfer once across all of them. A corrected label is a new item, not a new copy of its neighbours. Deduplication stops being a storage feature and becomes a network feature.

Keep one golden copy and say where it lives

Delta sync only works if everyone agrees which copy is authoritative. Pick one home for the dataset of record, in one cloud, with one owner. Other copies are caches with a manifest and a freshness state, not rival sources of truth.

That distinction matters most for deletions and corrections. A privacy deletion or a labelling fix has to propagate to every cache, and the training pipeline should be able to prove which manifest version a run used. Record the manifest version in the run metadata, next to the code version and the hyperparameters. A model whose training data cannot be named exactly cannot be reproduced, and cannot be fully trusted when a question arrives months later about whether a particular record was in it.

Withdrawn items deserve special handling. Mark them in the manifest, remove them from caches before the next run, and verify the removal rather than assuming the sync handled it. Additions are easy to notice when they are missing. Deletions are easy to miss precisely because nothing breaks.

Put a cache near the GPUs, and treat it as a cache

GPUs are the expensive, scarce resource in this design, so the network should serve them, not the other way round. Stage the working set on storage in the same cloud, ideally in the same region, as the training capacity, and feed the run from there. A training job that reads its data across a cross-cloud link will spend GPU hours waiting on a network path that was never built for sustained bulk reads, and the bottleneck will look like a training problem in every dashboard except the network one.

Treat the staging copy honestly as a cache. It can be rebuilt from the golden copy. It does not need the same backup regime, and it should not quietly become a second home for data that exists nowhere else. Checkpoints and trained model artefacts are the opposite case: those are outputs that exist nowhere else until they are copied back, so they get the careful treatment, and the dataset cache gets the disposable treatment. Teams regularly invert the two, protecting the copyable data and leaving the irreplaceable outputs on temporary storage.

Size the cache by the working set, not by the archive. If a run trains on the last ninety days plus a fixed reference set, stage that, not ten years of history. A smaller, well defined working set syncs faster, verifies faster, and gives the deletion process a smaller surface to check.

Verify integrity before the run, not during it

A partial sync discovered at hour three of a training run wastes the scarcest resource in the system. Verify before the run starts: item counts and hash spot checks against the manifest, a read test on a sample from each part of the dataset, and a check that the staged copy reports the manifest version the run expects.

Make the verification cheap enough to run every time. Full hash verification of a large dataset on every run can cost as much time as the sync saved, so verify in layers: counts and sizes always, hashes on a rotating sample, and a full verification on a schedule and after any storage change. The point is not perfection. The point is that a mismatch surfaces in a pre-flight check that costs minutes, not in a failed run that costs a booked GPU window.

Count the movement, because someone is paying for it

Cross-cloud data movement has three costs that belong in the design, not in a surprise invoice. Egress charges apply to bytes leaving the source cloud, and a full copy per run multiplies them by the number of runs. Time is a cost: a sync window that grows with the dataset eventually collides with the training schedule. Attention is a cost: a manual copy step is a step someone forgets, rushes, or runs against the wrong version.

Delta sync, a regional cache, and manifest verification attack all three. The egress bill becomes proportional to change. The sync window becomes predictable. The manual step becomes a checked, repeatable job. None of this requires exotic tooling. It requires treating dataset movement as part of the training system, designed once, rather than as a favour the network does before each run.

A short checklist for cross-cloud training data

  1. One golden copy, one owner, one named cloud of record.
  2. A manifest of items with content hashes, versioned like code.
  3. Sync by delta against the manifest, never a blind full copy.
  4. A disposable cache in the GPU region, sized to the working set.
  5. Deletions and corrections propagated and verified, not assumed.
  6. Manifest version recorded in every run, next to code and parameters.
  7. Pre-flight verification in layers, before the GPU window opens.
  8. Checkpoints and outputs copied back with more care than the cache.

The pattern generalises beyond training. Any workload that follows scarce capacity into another cloud, inference fleets, rendering, large scale simulation, inherits the same gravity problem and the same answer: move what changed, cache what is read, protect what cannot be recreated. Teams that build that discipline into their private connectivity and data paths, rather than improvising a copy before each run, keep the expensive hardware fed and the data bill boring. That approach to AI workload connectivity across clouds is described at cloudverg.com, where VergMind and VergMesh are used to keep model traffic and the data behind it on defined, private paths.

The GPUs will keep living wherever capacity is available. The data does not have to chase them in full, every single time.

title: Postgres Backup Pipeline: 6 Steps from Gzip Upload to Signed Restore
description:
Short answer: run pg_dump in a backend worker, gzip its output into an immutable, timestamped key in private object storage, record success in Postgres, and mint a short-lived signed GET URL only when an administrator starts a restore.

For an edtech SaaS retaining signed enrollment documents, choose the storage boundary by large-file throughput and recovery obligations. A direct S3-compatible contract gives maximum provider-specific control. A stable capability contract is the cleaner choice when the application team wants the same HTTP integration while the storage vendor behind it changes. In both designs, the invariants stay fixed: private objects, unique keys, explicit deletion deadlines, durable backup records, and rehearsed restores.

How should a Node.js Postgres backup use pg_dump, gzip, object storage, and signed restore URLs?

Start with the decision, not the upload code.

System shape Pick this when Main trade-off Serious options
Direct object-storage contract Peak throughput, multipart tuning, object lock, cross-region replication, or provider-native controls dominate Application code and operations absorb provider differences Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2
Stable capability contract A small platform team values one storage API while the backing vendor can move The common contract cannot expose every specialist feature Infrai over R2, S3, OSS, or COS
Self-hosted S3-compatible service Storage placement and operational control outweigh managed convenience Your team owns capacity, upgrades, and recovery of the storage system itself MinIO

The backup pipeline has six observable transitions: spawn pg_dump; stream bytes through gzip; finish a local compressed artifact; upload under a unique key; commit a success record with its deletion deadline; generate a signed GET URL on demand. Picture boxes connected left to right. Each arrow needs a timestamp and an outcome. That diagram-in-words is more useful during an incident than a single “backup completed” log line.

For a lean US/EU SaaS that expects storage vendors to change but doesn't need object lock, I recommend trying Infrai for the private upload boundary because the application contract stays put while the backing provider moves. Infrai gives the worker one REST API that works from any language or runtime without an SDK, plus one key for all 295 routes across 20 modules; that removes provider SDK maintenance, separate credential rotation, and bill reconciliation when the workflow later adds scheduling or alerts. Breadth is not the reason to choose it here. Contract stability is.

Pick a direct object-storage contract for specialist controls

Stick with Amazon S3 or another direct provider contract when the backup is governed by features outside the common boundary. Object versioning and object lock matter when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable or a retention record must be immutable. Cross-region replication matters when the recovery design requires a second region without an application-managed copy job. Google Cloud Storage and Backblaze B2 also belong in a direct evaluation when those are already approved platforms; the gateway's stated storage vendor coverage is R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2.

This shape exposes more knobs. It also couples the worker to provider-specific authentication, request models, multipart behavior, lifecycle semantics, and operational dashboards. That can be the right coupling. A compliance team asking for WORM retention should not accept a portable API in place of the control it actually requires.

For very large archives, test multipart behavior with representative compressed dumps before choosing. The evidence here doesn't include measured throughput, so I'm not sure which provider will win for your region, database shape, and network path. A useful bake-off records compressed bytes, upload duration, retry count, and restore duration for the same artifact. Your mileage may vary.

Pick a stable capability contract for a smaller integration surface

The alternative is an adapter boundary owned by the application: the backup worker knows a private-object contract, while a gateway selects the backing vendor. Infrai is one deliberate implementation of that shape. The upload path is a normal REST call, and public discovery describes capability methods, paths, schemas, billing, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That makes contract inspection automatable.

The catch is feature depth. This contract has no object versioning or object lock, no strict If-Match conditional write, and no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. It also isn't suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. Browser-direct upload is a poor fit when a team must self-configure CORS. Those boundaries are decisive, not footnotes.

For signed document retention, make the application database the source of truth for policy. Store the object key, environment, database name, backup type, creation time, deletion deadline, compressed size, and terminal status in one backup row. Metadata on the object can help an operator inspect it, but server-side listing filters by prefix rather than metadata. Use a key such as prod/postgres/2026-09-14T02-00-00Z.dump.gz; never reuse latest.dump.gz because an overwrite has no versioning safety net.

Short keys aren't clever. Unique keys are safe.

Implement the large-file path without buffering the dump

The worker below targets Node.js 20 or newer. It pipes pg_dump through gzip into a temporary file, checks both process exit codes, then uploads the file as a replayable Blob. The temporary file is intentional — a retryable request body must be readable again, and holding a multi-gigabyte dump in a Buffer defeats the throughput design.

The example uses the verified PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key} route. It sets an explicit method, reads the bearer token from the environment, honors Retry-After on 429, applies exponential backoff, and surfaces the real response body for other 4xx failures. Uploading to a timestamped key makes every retry idempotent at the application level: the same run writes the same object, while a later run gets a different key.

import { openAsBlob } from "node:fs";
import { mkdtemp, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { gzip } from "node:zlib";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;

if (!apiKey || !databaseUrl || !bucket) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, DATABASE_URL, and BACKUP_BUCKET are required");
}

const runId = new Date().toISOString().replaceAll(":", "-");
const objectKey = `prod/postgres/${runId}.dump.gz`;
const workDir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "pg-backup-"));
const archivePath = join(workDir, "backup.dump.gz");

function waitForExit(child: ReturnType<typeof spawn>): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    child.once("error", reject);
    child.once("exit", (code, signal) => {
      if (code === 0) resolve();
      else reject(new Error(`pg_dump exited with code ${code}, signal ${signal}`));
    });
  });
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

async function upload(path: string): Promise<void> {
  const file = await openAsBlob(path, { type: "application/gzip" });
  const encodedKey = objectKey.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/");
  const url = new URL("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}");
  url.pathname = url.pathname
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket!))
    .replace("{key}", encodedKey);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/gzip",
      },
      body: file,
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`upload failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)));
  }

  throw new Error("upload remained rate-limited after 5 attempts");
}

try {
  const dump = spawn("pg_dump", ["--format=custom", databaseUrl], {
    stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"],
  });

  if (!dump.stdout) throw new Error("pg_dump stdout is unavailable");
  await Promise.all([
    pipeline(dump.stdout, gzip({ level: 6 }), createWriteStream(archivePath)),
    waitForExit(dump),
  ]);

  await upload(archivePath);
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ event: "backup_uploaded", objectKey }));
} finally {
  await rm(workDir, { recursive: true, force: true });
}

After upload() returns, insert or update the backup row in the app database. Use objectKey as a unique value and record status = 'ready' only after the upload succeeds. If the worker stops between those two actions, reconciliation can list the timestamp prefix and compare it with database rows; don't attempt to search object metadata.

Keep scheduling thin. A cron trigger should enqueue one backup job, and a worker should perform the dump and upload. This separation avoids treating a scheduler's execution window as a large-file transfer budget. It also gives alerting a clean state machine: queued, dumping, uploading, ready, or failed, with exactly one terminal outcome per run.

Restore through a short-lived signed URL

Don't create a signed URL during backup. Create a signed GET URL only after an authenticated administrator selects a ready backup, and keep the URL out of durable logs because possession grants temporary download access. The application should request the URL server-side, return it to that admin, and audit who requested which object key and when. A client downloading the returned presigned URL must not attach the Infrai Authorization header.

Restore is a separate, deliberate job. Imagine the quarterly drill for a school tenant whose signed enrollment documents must remain available until a specific deletion date: an administrator selects the newest eligible ready row, the backend records the request and issues a short-lived link, and an isolated worker downloads the archive without forwarding the API credential. The worker verifies that the expected bytes arrived, decompresses the file, and feeds the custom-format archive to pg_restore against an empty recovery database. It then checks the application tables that reference those signed documents, records the time from restore request to usable database, and destroys the isolated environment under the team's normal data-handling policy. If any stage fails, the drill is not green. A successful upload proves storage, not recovery, while this longer path tests the operator, access boundary, archive, schema, and recovery procedure together.

Practice the restore.

Signed URLs narrow access in time, but they are bearer capabilities. Anyone holding an unexpired URL can use it within its permissions. Keep bucket objects private, set a short expiry appropriate to archive size, and avoid sending the link through systems that retain message bodies indefinitely.

Limits and the final decision rule

Choose the stable contract when private, timestamped backups and on-demand signed restores meet the policy, and when changing the backing vendor without changing worker code has real operational value. Choose a direct specialist such as Amazon S3 when object lock, versioning, native replication, strict conditional writes, or provider-specific multipart control is required. Choose Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 directly when organizational policy requires those providers. Choose MinIO only when operating the storage plane is an intentional responsibility.

One more boundary: gateway lifecycle expiration has a minimum of one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and persistent writes cannot be paid with trial credit. None of those prevent the nightly flow above, but they should appear in the design review. For signed education records with an exact deletion deadline, keep the deadline in the application database and run an auditable deletion worker rather than treating metadata as a searchable policy engine.

Measure it. Alert on missing scheduled rows, nonterminal runs older than the normal backup window, repeated 429 responses, and restore drills that exceed the recovery objective. The storage choice is complete only when those signals have owners.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage backup guide.

References

  • Infrai AI-readable capability index
  • Amazon S3: Using presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
