title: Building Resilient Web Applications: Beyond Offline Loading (Part 2)
description:
Making web applications useful when the backend is unavailable.

Introduction: Loading Offline Is Only the Beginning

In Part 1, we explored the challenges of building web applications for unreliable networks and low-bandwidth environments.

We discussed bandwidth, latency, browser storage, Service Workers, the Cache API, and how to make an application's shell available offline.

By the end, our Resilient Task Board could load its application shell after it had been installed and its required resources cached.

But there was still a problem.

The application could open offline, but could it actually do anything useful?

Imagine opening a task management application without an internet connection. The interface loads successfully, but your tasks are missing because the application still depends on an API request to retrieve them.

You try creating a task, and the request fails because the backend is unreachable.

We have improved availability, but we haven't solved data availability or offline interaction.

This is where the next layer of resilience begins.

1. Understanding the Difference Between Application Availability and Data Availability

An application can be available without its data being available.

Consider these two scenarios:

  • Application availability: The user can open the application, navigate its interface, and access its basic structure.
  • Data availability: The user can access relevant information even when the backend cannot be reached.

Caching HTML, CSS, and JavaScript helps with the first problem. It does not automatically solve the second.

For our Task Board, we need a way to store and retrieve tasks locally.

That brings us to IndexedDB.

2. IndexedDB: Giving the Browser a Local Database

In Part 1, we introduced three important browser storage technologies:

  • LocalStorage
  • Cache API
  • IndexedDB

Each serves a different purpose.

LocalStorage is useful for simple key-value data such as preferences. The Cache API is designed to store network requests and responses. IndexedDB, however, gives us a structured, asynchronous database inside the browser.

It can store JavaScript objects, create indexes, and support transactions.

For our Task Board, this makes IndexedDB a suitable place to store task records locally.

Think of it as a database available to the application even when the network is unavailable.

Why not LocalStorage?

Although LocalStorage can store serialized objects using JSON, it is synchronous and does not provide the structured querying, indexing, and transaction capabilities we need for a more substantial offline data layer.

IndexedDB is better suited to this job.

Designing our local data store

Our application already has a Task type. We can use that model to define the records stored locally.

For example:

export interface Task {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
  completed: boolean;
}

We can create an IndexedDB database and an object store for tasks.

const DB_NAME = "resilient-task-board";
const DB_VERSION = 1;
const TASK_STORE = "tasks";

export function openDatabase(): Promise<IDBDatabase> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = indexedDB.open(DB_NAME, DB_VERSION);

    request.onupgradeneeded = (event) => {
      const db = (event.target as IDBOpenDBRequest).result;

      if (!db.objectStoreNames.contains(TASK_STORE)) {
        db.createObjectStore(TASK_STORE, {
          keyPath: "id",
          autoIncrement: true,
        });
      }
    };

    request.onsuccess = () => {
      resolve(request.result);
    };

    request.onerror = () => {
      reject(request.error);
    };
  });
}

A few things are happening here:

  • indexedDB.open() opens or creates the database.
  • DB_VERSION allows us to manage future database schema changes.
  • onupgradeneeded runs when the database is first created or its version changes.
  • createObjectStore() creates the equivalent of a collection or table for our task records.
  • keyPath tells IndexedDB which property identifies each record.

We now have a local database to work with.

Saving and retrieving tasks

Once the database is open, we can perform operations through transactions.

For example, retrieving all locally stored tasks:

export const getTasks = async (): Promise<Task[]> => {
  const db = await openDatabase();

  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const transaction = db.transaction(TASK_STORE, "readonly");
    const store = transaction.objectStore(TASK_STORE);
    const request = store.getAll();

    transaction.oncomplete = () => {
      db.close();
      resolve(request.result);
    };

    transaction.onerror = () => {
      db.close();
      reject(transaction.error);
    };

    transaction.onabort = () => {
      db.close();
      reject(transaction.error ?? new Error("Transaction aborted"));
    };
  });
};

Notice that we resolve the operation when the transaction completes, rather than assuming that an individual request succeeding means the entire transaction has committed.

That distinction matters when working with IndexedDB.

We can also save a task using a readwrite transaction and the object store's add() or put() method.

The important idea is that our application now has a local source from which it can retrieve data without depending on a network request.

3. Local-First Reads: Read From the Browser Before the Backend

Now that we have a local database, how should the application retrieve its tasks?

One approach is to always request data from the backend first and use IndexedDB only when the request fails.

But this still makes the user wait for the network whenever it is slow.

A better approach for our Task Board is a local-first read strategy.

The application reads from IndexedDB immediately, renders the available data, and then attempts to retrieve the latest data from the backend when connectivity is available.

The flow looks like this:

  1. The application requests tasks.
  2. It retrieves locally stored tasks from IndexedDB.
  3. The interface renders those tasks.
  4. It attempts to fetch the latest tasks from the backend.
  5. If the request succeeds, the local database is updated.
  6. The interface reflects the refreshed data.

This gives users a faster initial experience and allows them to see previously saved tasks even when offline.

There is an important distinction here: local-first does not mean the local database is always the source of truth.

In our architecture, MySQL remains the authoritative shared database. IndexedDB is the local copy used to support availability and interaction.

The two databases have different responsibilities.

Database Responsibility
MySQL Authoritative shared application data
IndexedDB Local data available to the current browser

This distinction becomes especially important when multiple users access the same application.

4. Offline Mutations: What Happens When Users Change Data?

Reading data offline is one challenge. Changing data offline is another.

Imagine a user creates a task while disconnected.

The browser cannot reach the backend, so the API request fails.

Should we simply display an error and ask the user to try again later?

That would mean the application is technically available offline but still not very useful.

Instead, we can allow the user to perform the operation locally and synchronize it with the backend when connectivity returns.

This is called offline mutation handling.

For example, when a user creates a task:

  1. Generate a unique identifier for the operation and a local identifier for the task.
  2. Save the task locally in IndexedDB.
  3. Record the operation as pending synchronization.
  4. Update the interface immediately.
  5. Attempt synchronization when the backend becomes reachable.
  6. Mark the operation as synchronized once the server confirms it.

The user does not have to wait for the backend before seeing the task appear.

Optimistic UI

This approach is closely related to a technique called optimistic UI.

Optimistic UI updates the interface before receiving confirmation from the server, based on the expectation that the operation will succeed.

For example, when a user marks a task as completed, the interface can immediately display it as completed.

But what if the request fails?

The application must have a recovery strategy. Depending on the operation and the application's data model, it can retain the pending change for retry or roll back the optimistic update.

Optimistic UI improves perceived responsiveness, but it does not guarantee that the server has accepted the change.

That distinction should never be ignored.

5. Building an Offline Mutation Queue

If users can perform several operations while offline, we need a reliable way to keep track of them.

This is where an offline mutation queue becomes useful.

Rather than sending an operation and forgetting about it when the request fails, we store it locally until the backend confirms that it has been processed.

A queue record might look like this:

interface PendingOperation {
  id: string;
  type: "CREATE_TASK" | "UPDATE_TASK" | "DELETE_TASK";
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  status: "pending" | "syncing" | "failed";
  createdAt: number;
  retryCount: number;
}

Each operation contains enough information for the application to attempt it again later.

For example, creating a task offline might produce this record:

const operation: PendingOperation = {
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  type: "CREATE_TASK",
  payload: {
    title: "Prepare workshop article",
    completed: false,
  },
  status: "pending",
  createdAt: Date.now(),
  retryCount: 0,
};

The operation is stored in IndexedDB alongside the locally available task data.

When connectivity returns, the application can process pending operations and send them to the backend.

A simplified synchronization flow looks like this:

User performs an action
        |
        v
Save change locally
        |
        v
Add operation to queue
        |
        v
Is backend reachable?
        |
    +---+---+
    |       |
   Yes      No
    |       |
    v       v
Send API   Keep operation
request    pending
    |
    v
Server confirms?
    |
  +---+---+
  |       |
 Yes      No
  |       |
  v       v
Mark as   Keep for
synced    retry/recovery

This gives us a controlled way to handle changes that cannot immediately reach the backend.

However, simply retrying every failed operation introduces another problem.

6. The Idempotency Problem: What If the Server Already Processed the Request?

Consider this scenario:

  1. A user creates a task.
  2. The browser sends the request.
  3. The backend creates the task successfully.
  4. The response gets lost because the network drops.
  5. The browser assumes the request failed.
  6. The application retries the request.

What happens?

Without additional protection, the backend may create the same task twice.

This is a classic distributed-systems problem: the client does not always know whether the server completed an operation when communication fails.

One solution is idempotency.

An operation is idempotent when repeating it produces the same intended result as performing it once.

For mutation requests, we can use an idempotency key: a unique identifier generated by the client and sent with the request.

For example:

POST /api/tasks
Idempotency-Key: 7c8f5d1a-...
Content-Type: application/json

The backend records the key and the result of processing the request.

If it receives the same key again, it can return the previously recorded result instead of creating another task.

This requires backend support. Generating an idempotency key in the browser alone does not prevent duplicate operations.

Retries without idempotency can create more problems than they solve.

7. Retry Strategies: Don't Attack the Backend

When a request fails, immediately retrying it repeatedly is usually a bad idea.

Imagine thousands of users reconnecting after a network outage and all their applications sending requests simultaneously.

The backend could become overwhelmed.

A better approach is to use exponential backoff.

Instead of retrying at fixed, very short intervals, the application progressively increases the delay between attempts.

For example:

Attempt Delay
1 1 second
2 2 seconds
3 4 seconds
4 8 seconds
5 16 seconds

In production systems, random jitter is often added to these delays to prevent many clients from retrying at exactly the same time.

We should also distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures.

A temporary network error may justify another attempt. A validation error, such as an invalid task title, will not be fixed by repeatedly sending the same request.

Retries should be intentional, bounded, and based on the type of failure.

8. Conflict Resolution: What If Local and Server Data Differ?

There is one more problem we need to consider.

Suppose a user edits a task offline. Meanwhile, another user edits that same task on a different device and successfully saves the change to the backend.

When the first user reconnects, both versions exist:

  • The locally modified version.
  • The newer server version.

Which one should win?

This is a data conflict.

There is no universally correct conflict-resolution strategy. The right approach depends on the application and the importance of the data.

Some common strategies include:

Last-write-wins: The most recent update takes precedence. This is relatively simple, but it can silently overwrite meaningful changes.

Version-based conflict detection: Each record has a version number. The server rejects an update if the client is editing an outdated version, allowing the application to resolve the conflict.

Manual conflict resolution: The user is shown the conflicting versions and decides which changes to keep.

For a simple task board, last-write-wins might be acceptable in some situations. For financial transactions, collaborative documents, or other sensitive data, blindly overwriting changes would be a dangerous design choice.

Conflict resolution should be a deliberate product and engineering decision.

9. Putting the Architecture Together

Let's bring these concepts together.

Our resilient Task Board now has several distinct responsibilities:

Component Responsibility
Service Worker Intercepts requests and supports offline application loading
Cache API Stores application resources and selected network responses
IndexedDB Stores local application data and pending operations
React application Renders data and handles user interactions
Backend API Processes application operations and coordinates shared data
MySQL Stores authoritative application records

The overall data flow becomes:

  1. The Service Worker helps the application load.
  2. The React application retrieves locally available data from IndexedDB.
  3. The user interacts with the application.
  4. Changes are saved locally and recorded for synchronization.
  5. When the backend is reachable, pending operations are sent.
  6. The backend validates and processes operations, using idempotency protection where appropriate.
  7. Confirmed changes are reflected in the local database.

This is the foundation of a resilient, offline-capable application.

It is not enough to cache a page and call the application offline-ready. We must also think about the data, user actions, synchronization, and recovery.

10. Final Thoughts: Resilience Is an Architectural Decision

Building for unreliable networks requires us to change how we think about web applications.

Instead of assuming that every user action can immediately reach the backend, we design for the possibility that communication will be delayed or interrupted.

Instead of treating network failure as an exceptional situation, we make it part of the application's expected operating conditions.

And instead of leaving users uncertain about whether their actions were successful, we design clear states for pending, synchronized, and failed operations.

The key lessons from this series are:

  • Use the Service Worker and Cache API to support application availability.
  • Use IndexedDB for structured local application data.
  • Consider local-first reads to reduce dependency on network response times.
  • Use optimistic UI carefully to improve perceived responsiveness.
  • Queue offline mutations instead of losing user operations.
  • Implement idempotency to make retries safer.
  • Use sensible retry strategies and account for conflicts.

A resilient application is not one that never experiences network failure.

It is one that remains useful, communicates honestly with its users, and recovers gracefully when the network eventually returns.

The network may be unreliable. Your application doesn't have to be.

Explore the Project

Follow along with the Resilient Task Board repository, starting from the original version before the resilience improvements discussed in this series.

Further Reading

  • MDN: Cache API
  • MDN: Service Worker API
  • MDN: Background Synchronization API
  • MDN: HTTP Semantics

title: TypeScript Contracts for React Email Tests
description:
Email tests become confusing when the UI, the test runner, and the delivery provider all speak different languages. A React component waits for a verification state, while a Node.js service waits for a message, and the test waits for both. When something is slow, the failure usually says only that a button never changed.

The fix I like is a small TypeScript contract between the application and its mail test adapter. It makes the boundary explicit, gives every scenario a stable identity, and lets the same React test move from a fast fake transport to a real disposable mail address when the delivery path needs coverage.

The boundary is the product of the test

An email test is not just an assertion about a message. It is a short workflow:

  1. Create a scenario with a unique ID.
  2. Submit an address through the React form.
  3. Wait for the backend to send a message.
  4. Read the message and extract a link or code.
  5. Return to the UI and assert the next state.

If each step exposes provider-specific details, the test becomes hard to read and harder to replace. A test should describe the user journey; the adapter should describe how a mailbox works. Its a small distinction, but it keeps product behavior visible.

This is also why a stable scenario ID is more useful than a random address alone. The ID can appear in logs, message metadata, and cleanup jobs. I keep that idea close to stable inbox scenario IDs, especially when several CI jobs run the same flow at once.

Define a small mail port

Start with the smallest interface the test actually needs. Do not copy an entire provider SDK into every browser test.

export type MailScenario = {
  id: string;
  address: string;
};

export type MailMessage = {
  id: string;
  subject: string;
  text: string;
};

export interface TestMailPort {
  createScenario(): Promise<MailScenario>;
  waitForMessage(input: {
    scenarioId: string;
    subject: string;
    timeoutMs: number;
  }): Promise<MailMessage>;
  dispose(scenarioId: string): Promise<void>;
}

The port has a lifecycle, not only a getLatestMessage function. That matters because an old message can make a flaky test look green. The scenario ID and subject become part of the lookup, while the timeout makes waiting a deliberate choice.

For local component tests, the fake implementation can resolve immediately. For an end-to-end run, the implementation can allocate an isolated mailbox. The React test does not need to know which one is active. A disposable mail address is useful here as a delivery boundary, but it should be owned by the scenario and cleaned up after the run.

Keep React states separate from transport states

The UI should not render provider states such as MESSAGE_POLLING or MAILBOX_RETRYING. Those are useful diagnostic states, but they are not product states. Map them at the test boundary into a small set of user-visible states:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "submitting" }
  | { kind: "check-inbox"; address: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

In React, this keeps the component focused on accessible labels, disabled buttons, and the next action. The test harness can still record transport timings and message IDs beside the browser trace. Mixing both models in one state object is a bit more easier at first, then expensive when the provider changes.

A useful contract test checks the adapter independently:

it("returns only a message for the requested scenario", async () => {
  const scenario = await mail.createScenario();
  await app.sendVerification(scenario.address);

  const message = await mail.waitForMessage({
    scenarioId: scenario.id,
    subject: "Verify your account",
    timeoutMs: 30_000,
  });

  expect(message.text).toContain("/verify");
});

The browser test can then verify that the React screen changes after the verification link is used. It doesnt need to prove mailbox filtering and accessible UI behavior in the same assertion.

Make failures carry evidence

Timeouts are inevitable in integration tests. Unexplained timeouts are optional. When waitForMessage fails, include the scenario ID, expected subject, elapsed time, provider request ID, and the last observed delivery event. Do not dump the entire message into CI logs; links and tokens can become credentials in the wrong place.

A failure such as “scenario signup-42 saw 0 matching messages after 30s” is actionable. “Expected text not found” is not. In practise, this evidence saves more debugging time than another retry.

Also check the boring details. A label containing tem email or tempail can hide a typo in a fixture name, so normalize scenario metadata at the adapter boundary and keep the canonical ID in every log line. Small naming mistakes are not a security issue by themselves, but they make searches and cleanup less reliable.

Where replay safety fits

Verification links should have explicit expiry and single-use behavior. The test adapter can help by recording which message ID and token were consumed, but the backend remains responsible for rejecting a replay. For a deeper backend design, see these replay windows for email change tokens.

This split keeps responsibilities clear: the mail port proves delivery and isolation, while the application proves authorization and token semantics. A passing inbox check must never be treated as proof that a token is safe to reuse.

Q&A: choosing the right level of testing

Should every React test use a real mailbox?

No. Use a fake port for component and most workflow tests. Reserve a real delivery adapter for a small end-to-end suite that covers rendering, sending, parsing, and cleanup. That gives fast feedback without pretending that a mock proves delivery.

Should message bodies be stored in test artifacts?

Usually only for a short-lived local debug bundle. Prefer subject, message ID, scenario ID, and a redacted extraction result in CI. Retaining full bodies can expose verification URLs.

What should the timeout be?

Set it from the delivery path you are testing, then make it visible in the test name or diagnostics. A fixed, justified timeout is better than an unbounded poll that hides a broken worker.

A short implementation checklist

  • Define one typed mail port with create, wait, and dispose operations.
  • Give every scenario a unique ID and include it in logs.
  • Keep React states independent from provider retry states.
  • Test adapter filtering and cleanup separately from UI assertions.
  • Record useful metadata without retaining secrets or full message bodies.
  • Verify token expiry and replay behavior in the backend.
  • Run a small real-delivery suite alongside fast fake-transport tests.

The result is a cleaner developer experience: React tests explain product behavior, TypeScript protects the seams, and delivery failures arrive with enough evidence to fix them. That boundary may be small, but it keeps email from turning every signup test into a mystery.

title: Has Your Company Been Audited for Oracle Java? Here's What You Need to Know
description:
Over the past 18 months, thousands of companies have received audit notices from Oracle about unlicensed Java installations. If you manage IT infrastructure at a company with 20+ staff, this matters to you.

The Problem

On September 20, 2026, Oracle JDK 21 moved from free (NFTC) to paid (OTN) licensing. If your company auto-updates Java on employee machines, any Oracle JDK 21 installed after the September update may trigger audit notices—even if nobody is actively using it.

Which Versions Are Free?

Free (no audit risk):

  • OpenJDK (GPL + Classpath Exception)
  • Eclipse Temurin (Eclipse Foundation)
  • Amazon Corretto (AWS-supported, free LTS)
  • Azul Zulu Community Edition
  • Oracle JDK 8 up to build 8u202 (January 2022)

Paid (audit risk):

  • Oracle JDK 8 after build 8u202
  • Oracle JDK 11, 17 (OTN-only after Sept 2026)
  • Oracle JDK 21 (free until Sept 2026, then OTN-paid)
  • Oracle JDK 22+ (OTN-paid immediately)

5-Step Audit You Can Run Right Now

  1. Find all Java installations on your fleet
  2. Extract vendor, version, and build number
  3. Cross-check the license against the roadmap
  4. Triage machines with paid versions
  5. Plan your replacement strategy

You're not doing anything wrong by having Java installed. The problem is that Oracle changed the licensing mid-year. Thousands of companies are in the same situation. Use this moment to clean up your Java footprint and move to free, well-maintained alternatives.

If you receive an audit notice from Oracle, consult your legal team. But first, knowing which machines have which Java versions is the first step to being in control.

title: mq: a small Kafka-style message queue in Go, built from scratch
description:
Kafka has a reputation for being complicated, and its vocabulary does not help: topics, partitions, offsets, segments, consumer groups, rebalances, generations. I used these words for a long time before I could explain why each one has to exist.

The quickest way I know to understand a design is to rebuild a small version of it. mq is a small Kafka-style message queue in Go, using only the standard library. It has topics split into partitions, an append-only segmented log per partition, consumer groups with committed offsets, retention, and a TCP protocol with a Go client. It is a single broker and a learning project. What it gave me is a clear picture of why a log sits at the centre of a message queue.

What it does

The code is four packages:

  • wal: the storage engine. Segment files with CRC-checked records, a sparse offset index, crash recovery that cuts off a torn tail, and retention by size and age.
  • broker: topics and partitions on top of wal, key-hash or round-robin partitioning, long-polling fetches, consumer groups (broker-side assignment, heartbeats, session expiry, generation-fenced commits) and the TCP server.
  • protocol: length-prefixed JSON frames. Each request has an ID, so a client can pipeline requests on one connection, and a parked long-poll does not block anything else.
  • client: a Go client with a producer API and a group Consumer that handles joining, heartbeats, rebalances and commits.

On disk, a topic looks like this:

data/
  topics/events/topic.json            {"Partitions": 3}
  topics/events/0/00000000000000000000.log    [len][crc32c][offset|ts|key|value] ...
  topics/events/0/00000000000000000000.index  [rel offset u32][file pos u32] every 4 KiB
  topics/events/0/00000000000000004211.log    next segment, named by its base offset
  offsets.json                        {"group/topic/partition": next offset}

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Why a log is the core. In this design a message is never "taken" from the queue. It is appended to a partition and gets an offset, which is just a position. Consumers keep their own position, and "acknowledging" a message is committing a number. Once you see that, most of the rest follows: several groups can read the same topic independently, and a consumer can go back and read again.

Storage details. Each record is framed with a length and a CRC-32C checksum. The index is sparse: one entry every 4 KiB, mapping a relative offset to a file position. That is enough, because a read does a binary search on the segments' base offsets, finds the index entry at or below the wanted offset, then scans a few KiB. Segments roll when they are full, and each new one is named by its base offset. Retention deletes whole segments instead of rewriting files, which is why it is cheap.

Crash consistency. A crash in the middle of a write leaves a torn record at the end of the active segment. On open, recovery scans the active segment, truncates at the first bad record and carries on with the right offsets. Sealed segments load their index and only check from the last index entry to the end. The important distinction: a torn tail in the active segment is expected and repaired, but corruption in a sealed segment is an error, not silent data loss.

Consumer group coordination. When a member joins, the group's generation number goes up and partitions are assigned round robin. A member whose heartbeat carries a stale generation is told to rebalance and rejoins. A member that misses heartbeats for the session timeout is expired, which triggers a rebalance. The generation works as a fencing token: a commit is refused unless the member, the generation and the partition ownership all match. So a consumer that missed a rebalance cannot commit over the new owner. This is also where you see why delivery is at-least-once.

A protocol that does not block. Fetches are long polls: the broker parks the request until data arrives, and a produce wakes the waiting fetches. Because every request carries an ID, a parked long poll and other requests can share one connection.

How to use it

Install the broker binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq/cmd/mq@latest

Add the Go client to your module:

go get github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq/client@latest

From a clone of the repository, the command line shows the whole flow:

go build -o mq ./cmd/mq
./mq serve -addr 127.0.0.1:9092 -data data &

./mq create  -topic events -partitions 3
seq 1 10 | ./mq produce -topic events
./mq consume -topic events -group printers     # Ctrl-C to stop
./mq topics

And from Go:

c, _ := client.Dial(ctx, "127.0.0.1:9092")
c.Produce(ctx, "events", -1, []byte("user-42"), []byte("signed up"))

k := c.NewConsumer("mailer", "events")
for {
    msgs, _ := k.Poll(ctx, time.Second)
    for _, m := range msgs { /* handle */ }
    k.Commit(ctx)
}

The loop is the usual one for this kind of system: poll, handle, commit. If the process dies after handling and before committing, the messages are delivered again. Your handler has to tolerate that.

How it is tested 

go test -race ./...

The wal tests cover appends and reads, segment rolling with reads across many segments, reopening, a lost index file being rebuilt, recovery from a torn write (the file is cut in the middle of the last record), trailing junk, a flipped byte in a middle record, refusing to open a damaged sealed segment, and retention by size and by age on a fake clock.

The broker tests cover key-to-partition stability, round robin, reloading topics after a restart, long polling, group assignment, rebalance on heartbeat, fenced commits from a stale generation or for another member's partition, session expiry, and offsets surviving a restart.

The client tests run over TCP on 127.0.0.1: two consumers sharing a 4-partition topic with every message delivered exactly once in steady state, a clean handover when one leaves, and an end-to-end crash-recovery test that stops the broker, truncates the last record on disk, restarts it and checks the data and the next offset.

Things to know

This is a learning project, and the README says what that means:

  • Single broker. No replication, no leader election, no cluster metadata. If the disk dies, the data is gone.
  • Durability is configurable but coarse. By default writes are flushed to the OS on each append and fsynced on segment roll and close. wal.Options.SyncEveryWrite fsyncs every record. A power loss can lose the last unsynced records, and recovery then drops any torn tail.
  • At-least-once delivery. During a rebalance, two consumers can briefly read the same partition; only the current owner's commit is accepted. There are no transactions or idempotent producers.
  • Assignment is done by the broker, not by a group leader as in Kafka, and a group consumes exactly one topic.
  • JSON framing is easy to debug but slow, and values are base64 on the wire.
  • No authentication or TLS. Bind it to localhost or a trusted network.
  • Offsets are stored by rewriting one JSON file per commit.

What I learned

The biggest change is in how I think about acknowledgements. I used to picture a queue as a list where messages are removed when handled. A log with offsets is simpler and stronger: the broker stores bytes in order, and each group stores one number per partition.

The second lesson is about fencing. Without the generation check, a slow consumer that wakes up after a rebalance would commit an old offset over the new owner's progress. A single integer that goes up on every rebalance closes that hole.

The third is that recovery code needs a rule about what damage is acceptable. A torn tail is normal after a crash. A bad record in the middle of a sealed file is not, and refusing to open is the honest answer.

Get the code

The source, the client and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq. It is MIT licensed. Start with the wal package: it is the part everything else stands on.

title: loadbalancer: an HTTP reverse-proxy load balancer in Go, built to learn
description:
A load balancer is easy to describe: requests come in, and you send each one to one of several backends. The interesting questions start right after that sentence. Which backend? How do you know one of them is dead? What do you do with a request that was already sent to a dead one? And how do you change the list of backends without dropping the traffic that is flowing right now?

loadbalancer is my learning project for those questions. It is an HTTP reverse-proxy load balancer in Go, using only the standard library and fsnotify. It has three balancing strategies, active health checks, a passive circuit breaker per backend, retries for idempotent requests, config hot reload and Prometheus metrics.

What it does

The request path is short enough to show in full:

request ─► pick(): candidates = healthy ∧ breaker ready ∧ not tried yet
              strategy.Pick(candidates) → breaker.Acquire()
         ─► forward(): ReverseProxy to the backend
              transport error → breaker.Failure(), retry if idempotent
              5xx             → breaker.Failure(), response is passed through
              otherwise       → breaker.Success()

A backend is a candidate only if the health checker says it is healthy, its circuit breaker is ready, and this request has not tried it yet. The strategy picks one of the candidates, and the request is forwarded through httputil.ReverseProxy.

Next to the proxy port there is an admin port with /metrics in the Prometheus text format and /status, a JSON view of the pool.

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Retries around httputil.ReverseProxy. By default, when the proxy cannot reach a backend, it writes a 502 to the client, and then it is too late to try another one. Here the error handler records the failure instead of writing a 502, so the request can still go to another backend. Retries are deliberately narrow: only GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE requests without a body, and only when the backend could not be reached, so nothing has been written to the client yet. A 5xx response is never retried; it is passed through.

Balancing algorithms. There are three strategies: round robin, weighted, and least connections with rotating tie-breaks. The weighted one is nginx's smooth weighted round robin. With weights 5, 1, 1, a naive implementation gives a a a a a b c: five requests in a row to the same backend. The smooth version gives a a b a c a a, which keeps the same proportions and spreads them out.

Two ways to detect a dead backend. Active checks probe a path such as /healthz on a timer. One goroutine probes every backend concurrently each interval, and thresholds stop one lost probe from making the pool flap. Passive checks watch real traffic, and they work even when the backend has no health endpoint. That is the circuit breaker.

The circuit breaker state machine. After failure_threshold consecutive failures, the breaker goes from closed to open and the backend stops receiving traffic. Once cooldown has passed, exactly one trial request is let through: the half-open state. A success closes the breaker, and a failure opens it again. Two methods keep this correct under concurrency: Ready() has no side effects and is used to filter candidates, and Acquire() reserves the single half-open slot. When the health checker sees a backend recover, its breaker is reset too.

Reloading without dropping traffic. Apply validates the new config first, so an invalid file is rejected and the old config stays. It then reuses the *Backend values whose URL is unchanged, keeping their in-flight count, health and breaker state, and restarts the health checker. Both SIGHUP and file changes trigger it, and file changes are debounced. One detail I did not expect: the watcher looks at the directory, not the file, because editors replace files by renaming.

How to use it

Install the binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadbalancer/cmd/loadbalancer@latest

Or run it from a clone of the repository:

cp lb.example.json lb.json      # edit the backend URLs
go run ./cmd/loadbalancer -config lb.json
curl localhost:8080/            # proxied
curl localhost:9090/metrics     # Prometheus metrics
curl localhost:9090/status      # JSON view of the pool
kill -HUP <pid>                 # reload (saving the file also reloads)

The config is one JSON file:

{
  "listen": ":8080",
  "admin": ":9090",
  "strategy": "weighted",              // round_robin | weighted | least_conn
  "retries": 2,                        // extra attempts for idempotent requests
  "backends": [{"url": "http://127.0.0.1:9001", "weight": 3}],
  "health_check": {"path": "/healthz", "interval": "5s", "timeout": "1s",
                   "healthy_threshold": 2, "unhealthy_threshold": 2},
  "circuit_breaker": {"failure_threshold": 5, "cooldown": "10s"}
}

Leave health_check.path empty to turn off active checks, and set failure_threshold to 0 to turn off the breaker.

The tests need nothing external:

go test -race ./...

They all run against httptest backends. They cover strategy order and distribution, least connections with a blocked backend, breaker state transitions on a fake clock, a retry around a dead backend, health checks taking a backend out and putting it back, a reload that keeps state, the fsnotify watcher and the metrics output.

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README lists what a production load balancer has and this one does not:

  • It serves HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 to the client through net/http only. There is no TLS termination config: put it behind something, or add ListenAndServeTLS. There is no WebSocket-specific handling beyond what ReverseProxy already does, and no TCP (L4) mode.
  • No sticky sessions, no consistent hashing, no slow start for recovered backends, and no outlier detection beyond consecutive failures.
  • Changing listen or admin needs a restart. The reload logs a warning.
  • Metrics are written by hand in the Prometheus text format, and there are no latency histograms.
  • The breaker counts any 5xx from the backend as a failure. That includes a 500 caused by one bad request.

What I learned

The first lesson is that a retry is a promise about the request, not about the proxy. You can only retry when you know nothing reached the client and the request is safe to send twice. That is why the list of methods is short and why bodies are excluded. Being generous here is how a load balancer ends up creating two orders.

The second is that active and passive health detection are not alternatives. A probe every five seconds is too slow to protect the requests arriving in between, and a breaker alone never notices a backend that receives no traffic. Each covers the other's blind spot.

The third is about state. The simple way to reload is to throw away the pool and build a new one. That resets every breaker, every health result and every in-flight counter, at the exact moment someone is changing things. Reusing the unchanged backends is more code, and it is the difference between a reload and a small outage.

And the smooth weighted round robin is a nice example of an algorithm where the obvious version is correct on average and wrong in practice.

Get the code

The source, the example config and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadbalancer. It is MIT licensed. The breaker and the strategies are small files, and they are a good place to start reading.

title: redis-clone: a small Redis-compatible server in Go, built to learn
description:
Redis is one of those tools most backend developers use and few have looked inside. You type SET greeting hello EX 60, the key is there, and a minute later it is gone. Between those two moments sit a wire protocol, a keyspace, an expiry algorithm and a durability story. Each is a topic you can read about for hours without really understanding it.

I wanted to understand them by writing them. redis-clone is a small Redis-compatible server in Go. It speaks the RESP2 protocol, keeps a keyspace with strings, lists and hashes, expires keys, and persists data in two ways: an append-only file (AOF) with rewrite, and snapshots. Real Redis clients work with it, and the tests talk to it through go-redis.

It is a learning project, not a Redis replacement. This article is about what is in it and what each part teaches.

What it does

The server supports a practical set of commands:

group commands
connection PING, ECHO, QUIT, SELECT 0, CLIENT (no-op), HELLO (refused, so clients fall back to RESP2), COMMAND, INFO
keys GET, SET (EX, PX, EXAT, PXAT, NX, XX, KEEPTTL, GET), DEL, EXISTS, TYPE, KEYS (glob), DBSIZE, FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB
counters INCR, DECR, INCRBY, DECRBY (with overflow checks)
expiry EXPIRE, PEXPIRE, EXPIREAT, PEXPIREAT, TTL, PTTL, PERSIST
lists LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP/RPOP (with count), LLEN, LRANGE, LINDEX
hashes HSET, HGET, HDEL, HGETALL, HLEN, HEXISTS, HKEYS, HVALS, HINCRBY
persistence SAVE, BGSAVE, BGREWRITEAOF

The code is split into four folders. resp/ has the RESP2 reader and writer; the reader also accepts inline commands such as a plain SET a b line. store/ is the keyspace: a map of entries, a map of expiry times in milliseconds, and a glob matcher for KEYS. server/ has the TCP accept loop, one goroutine per connection, the command table, the cron (active expiry, the every-second fsync, auto-rewrite, periodic save) and the AOF and snapshot code. cmd/ is the binary.

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Wire protocols. RESP2 is a streaming, length-prefixed protocol. The lesson is in the word "streaming": a TCP read can end in the middle of a command, so the parser must not lose data across reads. Clients also pipeline, which means they send several commands before reading any reply. In this server, replies are buffered and only flushed once the client's pipeline is drained.

Single-threaded execution. Redis runs commands on one thread, which is why its data structures need no locks. I reproduced that with one mutex: each connection reads commands and calls Server.Exec, which holds the server mutex for the duration of one command. Many connections, one command at a time.

Expiry. There are two mechanisms working together. Lazy expiry checks a key's TTL every time it is accessed. That alone would leave dead keys in memory forever if nobody reads them, so there is also Redis's probabilistic active expiry cycle: sample 20 keys that have a TTL, delete the expired ones, and repeat while more than 25% of the sample was expired.

Durability. This is the largest part. Write commands append their RESP encoding to appendonly.aof. Relative expiries are rewritten as absolute ones (SET k v PXAT …, PEXPIREAT), so replaying the log days later still gives the right answer, and keys that expire are logged as DEL. On startup the log is replayed through the normal command table. If the server crashed in the middle of a write, the partial final command is truncated away.

A log that only grows needs compaction. For an AOF rewrite, the keyspace is deep-copied under the lock, then a goroutine writes the minimal commands (SET, RPUSH, HSET, PEXPIREAT) to a temp file. Writes that arrive in the meantime are kept in a rewrite buffer and appended when the goroutine finishes, and the temp file is atomically renamed over the log.

Snapshots use a custom binary format: an RCDB0001 magic header, typed records, uvarint lengths and a CRC-32 trailer. The file is written to a temp file, fsynced and renamed, so a reader never sees half a snapshot. On startup, the AOF is used if it is enabled and present; otherwise the snapshot is.

How to use it

Install the server binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/redis-clone/cmd/redis-clone@latest

Or clone the repository and run it from source, on a port that does not collide with a real Redis:

go run ./cmd/redis-clone -addr :6380 -dir ./data
redis-cli -p 6380 set greeting hello EX 60
redis-cli -p 6380 ttl greeting

The flags follow Redis's own names: -aof (on by default), -appendfsync always|everysec|no, -auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100, -auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 67108864 and -save-interval 5m.

The fsync policy is the classic trade-off. always syncs every write to disk and is the slowest. everysec syncs once a second, so a crash can lose about a second of writes. no leaves it to the operating system.

To run the tests:

go test -race ./...

They need no external services. The server tests start the server on a random port and talk to it through go-redis, and a fake clock drives TTLs and restarts.

Things to know

The README is direct about the limits, and they are worth reading because each one points at something real Redis does better:

  • Only RESP2, a single database (index 0), and three data types. There are no sets, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, transactions (MULTI/EXEC), Lua, replication, auth or cluster.
  • The snapshot format is its own format. It is not RDB-compatible, so you cannot load these files in Redis or the other way round.
  • Background saves and rewrites deep-copy the keyspace while holding the lock. Redis uses fork() and copy-on-write instead. With a large dataset, the copy pauses clients for its duration.
  • The everysec fsync runs while holding the command lock, so a slow disk stalls commands for that moment.
  • Lists are Go slices, so LPUSH is O(n) instead of O(1).
  • Some error messages and edge cases differ from real Redis.

What I learned

The first surprise was how much of Redis is about time. A relative TTL is easy in memory and wrong in a log: if you store "expire in 60 seconds" and replay it tomorrow, the key comes back to life. Rewriting every expiry as an absolute timestamp before logging it is a small rule with a big effect.

The second was that durability is mostly about the bad moments: a crash mid-write, a rewrite racing with new commands, a snapshot half on disk. The happy path is an append. The work is in truncating the torn tail, keeping a rewrite buffer, and using write-temp, fsync, rename so that a file is either the old version or the new one.

The third was that the limitations teach as much as the features. Writing the deep copy made it clear why Redis reaches for fork(): the operating system gives it a consistent view of memory almost for free, while my copy has to stop the world.

Get the code

The source and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/redis-clone. It is MIT licensed. If you have ever wondered what happens between SET and the disk, reading server/ next to the Redis documentation on persistence is a good afternoon.

title: unix-tools: rebuilding grep, wc, jq and tree in Go, byte for byte
description:
You use grep, wc, jq and tree every day without thinking about them. They look simple: search for a pattern, count lines, filter JSON, print a directory. Writing a rough version of each takes an afternoon.

Writing a version whose output is exactly the same as the real tool is a different exercise. The moment you compare bytes, you find rules you never noticed: how wide wc makes its columns, what + means in a basic regular expression, how jq prints 1e2, how a nested .gitignore overrides its parent.

unix-tools is my learning project built on that idea. It contains four small Go binaries, and a test suite that runs each one next to the real tool on the same input and requires byte-identical stdout and the same exit status.

What it does

The repository builds four separate binaries:

binary does flags
cmd/grep GNU-grep-compatible search -i -v -n -r -c, plus -E -F -q -H -e PAT
cmd/wc line, word, char and byte counts -l -w -m -c
cmd/jqlite a subset of jq -c -r -n
cmd/tree directory tree -a -d -L N --gitignore --noreport

The reference versions are GNU grep 3.12, GNU wc 9.x, jq 1.7.1 and tree 2.2.1.

jqlite understands a useful part of the jq language: paths such as .a.b, .[0], .[-1] and .[], the recursive .., the ? operator, pipes, ,, //, and, or, comparisons, arithmetic, array and object construction ({a, b: .x, (.k): .v}), and the builtins select map keys keys_unsorted length has type not add sort reverse tostring tonumber to_entries empty.

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Each tool hid its own lesson.

grep: basic regular expressions are not what you think. By default grep uses POSIX basic regular expressions. In that dialect + ? | ( ) { } are literal characters, and the operators are written \+ \| \( \). Go's regexp package uses RE2 syntax, where it is the other way round. So the tool has a translator from BRE to RE2. Matching grep also means getting the small output rules right: the filename prefix appears when there are several files or with -r, the leading ./ is dropped when -r has no operand, and the exit code is 0 for a match, 1 for no match and 2 for an error.

wc: the column width is computed. GNU wc does not use a fixed width. The width is the number of digits in the total size of the regular files. It is at least 7 when any input is a pipe, and 1 when a single number is printed for a single input. You only learn this when your output differs from the real one by a few spaces.

jqlite: a parser and a generator-style evaluator. jq's grammar has a precedence order: pipes bind looser than ,, which binds looser than //, then or, and, comparisons and arithmetic. I wrote a recursive-descent parser for it. The evaluator treats every filter as something that returns zero or more outputs, which is how .[] and select fit together naturally. Objects keep their key order. Numbers were the hardest part: jq 1.7.1 prints input literals in decNumber's canonical form (1e2 becomes 1E+2, 1.0 stays 1.0), while computed doubles use the shortest digits that round-trip (1e+17, 3.3333333333333335).

tree: Git's ignore rules. The --gitignore flag needs the real rules: **, negation with !, directory-only patterns, anchoring by a slash, and nested .gitignore files that override their parents. tree 2.x also has its own quirks: the root counts as a directory in the report, and the vertical bar is padded with two no-break spaces, not normal spaces.

How to use it

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64 and arm64) are on the releases page of the repository. Each archive contains the four binaries, the README and the license, and checksums.txt has the SHA-256 sums.

With Go installed, you can build from source:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/unix-tools/cmd/...@latest

One warning from the README: the binaries are named grep, wc and tree. If $(go env GOPATH)/bin comes first on your PATH, they may shadow the system tools.

Or clone the repository and try them from a local bin/ folder:

go build -o bin/ ./cmd/...
bin/grep -rn TODO .
printf 'a b\nc\n' | bin/wc
bin/jqlite -c '.items[] | select(.price > 10) | {name, price}' data.json
bin/tree --gitignore -L 2

How the tests work

The interesting part of this project is the test suite:

go test -race ./...

compare_test.go builds a fixture tree in a temporary directory: code, notes, logs, nested .gitignore files, UTF-8 text and a JSON document. Then it runs about 70 cases, with two checks:

  1. If the real tool is available (grep, wc, jq or tree on PATH, or $JQ_BIN / $TREE_BIN), its output is the expectation.
  2. In every case the output must also match a golden file in testdata/golden/, recorded from the real tools. So the suite still means something on a machine where jq or tree is not installed.

The tools run with LC_ALL=C (C.UTF-8 for wc -m and tree). The output of grep -r is sorted before comparing, because real grep walks directories in filesystem order. There are also unit tests for the BRE translator, the gitignore rules, the argument parser and jqlite's evaluator and number formatting. A small script, scripts/tree-docker.sh, runs tree 2.2.1 from a Debian container for machines that do not have it.

Things to know

These are learning-sized subsets, not replacements for the real tools. The README lists the gaps clearly:

  • grep: no context options (-A/-B/-C), no -o, -l, -w, -x, no colour, and no backreferences, because RE2 has none. Character classes follow Go, so locale-specific collation differs. -r visits files in sorted order, and binary detection is a simple NUL-byte check.
  • wc: no -L or --files0-from. It always decodes UTF-8 for -m, while GNU wc counts bytes in the C locale.
  • jqlite: no variables (as $x), reduce/foreach, function definitions, string interpolation, slices, assignment operators, --arg or -S. Results are fully materialised, with no lazy streams. Error messages are close to jq's but not identical.
  • tree: no -I, -P, sorting options, sizes, permissions or JSON output. Symlinked directories are listed but not followed. Only .gitignore files are read, not .git/info/exclude or the global excludes file.

What I learned

The main lesson is about testing. "It works on my examples" and "it prints the same bytes as the reference on 70 cases" are far apart, and the distance between them is where the learning is. A differential test against a real implementation finds the rules you did not know existed, and it tells you exactly which byte is wrong.

The second lesson is that small tools carry a lot of accumulated decisions. A column width, a no-break space, an exit code: each has a reason, and scripts depend on them. Rebuilding a tool is a good way to read its specification closely.

Get the code

The source, the test fixtures and the golden files are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/unix-tools. It is MIT licensed. If you want a good exercise, pick one of the missing flags from the limitations list and make the comparison test pass.

title: regex-engine: a regex engine from scratch in Rust, with no backtracking
description:
Regular expressions are one of those tools we use without asking how they work. Then one day a pattern like (a+)+$ meets a long input, and a service hangs. That failure has a name, catastrophic backtracking, and it is not a law of nature. It comes from one way of implementing regexes. There is another way, older and based on automata, that runs in time linear in the input no matter what the pattern is.

Russ Cox described that approach in a well-known series of articles. regex-engine is my implementation of it in Rust, written from scratch: a parser, a Thompson NFA, a Pike VM and a lazy DFA. It does not backtrack, and its results are checked against the regex crate by differential testing. This post is about what I built and what it teaches.

What I built

The engine is a pipeline of four stages.

1. The parser (parser.rs) is a recursive descent parser that produces an AST. Every literal, class and escape becomes a sorted list of char ranges, so the later stages only ever see one kind of leaf.

2. The Thompson NFA (nfa.rs) compiles the AST into a small instruction set: Class (match one char in some ranges), Split (try two branches), Save (record a capture position), Look (the ^ and $ assertions) and Match. Split is ordered: the first branch has priority, and that is the whole difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers. Counted repetition like {2,5} is expanded into copies.

3. The Pike VM (pikevm.rs) simulates all the NFA threads in lockstep, one input character at a time, in priority order. Each thread carries its own copy of the capture slots. When a thread matches, the lower-priority threads are cut, which gives leftmost-first semantics, the same rule Perl-style engines follow. It is used for find, captures and find_iter.

4. The lazy DFA (dfa.rs) builds DFA states, each one a set of NFA states, on demand while scanning, and caches the transitions: 128-entry tables for ASCII plus a map for other characters. The search is unanchored (the NFA start state is re-added after each character), and $ assertions stay pending until the end of the input. The cache is flushed when it passes 4096 states, so memory stays bounded. It is used for is_match, and as a quick reject before running the Pike VM.

The syntax it supports: literals, . (any char but \n), classes [a-z], [^...], []a], [a-], the escapes \d \w \s \D \W \S with ASCII definitions, \n \t \r \f \v, escaped punctuation, the anchors ^ and $ (start and end of text), groups ( ) and (?: ), alternation |, the quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} and their lazy forms *? +? ?? {n,m}?.

How to use it

Add it to a Rust project as a git dependency:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine

The API will look familiar if you have used the regex crate:

use regex_engine::Regex;

let re = Regex::new(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.(com|org)")?;
assert!(re.is_match("mail bob@example.org"));          // lazy DFA
let caps = re.captures("mail bob@example.org").unwrap(); // Pike VM
let m = re.find("x 12 345").map(|m| (m.start, m.end));
let all = re.find_iter("a@b.com c@d.org");

Note which engine answers which question. is_match only needs yes or no, so it goes to the DFA. captures needs group positions, which a DFA does not track, so it goes to the Pike VM.

The repository also has a tiny grep. Clone it and run:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine
cd regex-engine
cargo run --release --bin rgrep -- [-o] '<pattern>' file...

What I learned

Linear time comes from never going back. A backtracking engine tries one path through the pattern, and on failure rewinds the input and tries another. The Pike VM instead advances every possible path together and reads each input character once. The number of live threads is bounded by the size of the NFA, so the work per character is bounded too. Patterns that hang a backtracker are ordinary here.

Priority is the hard part, not matching. Deciding whether a string matches is easy with an NFA. Deciding which match to report, and which captures, is where the care goes. The order of the two branches of every Split, and the order in which threads are stepped, encode all of it.

A small compilation choice changes the captures. e* is compiled as a single loop, or as (e+)? when e can match the empty string. This is the same choice the regex crate makes, and the shape changes which captures a Pike VM reports. I did not find that by reading. The differential tests found it.

A DFA is a cache of the NFA simulation. Each DFA state is just "the set of NFA states I could be in". Building all of them ahead of time can blow up, so the lazy DFA builds only the ones the input actually reaches, and throws the cache away when it grows too large. That one idea explains why a DFA is fast and why it is still safe.

Differential testing is worth more than hand-written cases. tests/differential.rs generates random patterns (nested groups, alternations, every quantifier form, classes, escapes, anchors) and random haystacks. For each pair it checks is_match on both the DFA and the Pike VM, plus find, captures and find_iter, against the regex crate. When a case fails, examples/minimize.rs shrinks it to a minimal reproduction. That is how the (e+)? capture-priority issue was found.

cargo test                                  # unit tests + differential (200 patterns in debug)
cargo test --release --test differential    # 4000 random patterns x 25 haystacks
DIFF_PATTERNS=20000 cargo test --release --test differential

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README lists the limits:

  • Missing syntax. No flags ((?i), (?m), (?s)), no \b, no Unicode classes (\p{..}), no named groups, no nested classes or class set operations.
  • ASCII classes. \d \w \s are ASCII-only, while regex defaults to Unicode. The differential tests use ASCII haystacks, where the two agree.
  • The DFA only answers is_match. Match positions come from the Pike VM, which is much slower than a real DFA-based search.
  • Regex is not Sync, because the DFA cache sits in a RefCell.

For real work, use the regex crate. It is the reference this project is tested against.

Why I built it

I wanted to understand why some regex engines can promise linear time and others cannot. Russ Cox's articles explain the theory clearly, and they are the right place to start. But the theory fits on a page, and the difficulty is in the details the page skips: capture groups, greedy versus lazy, empty matches, anchors inside an unanchored search. Writing the engine is how those details become concrete.

Having a mature engine to compare against made the project much more honest. Without the differential tests I would have a regex engine that passes the cases I thought of. With them, I have one that agrees with regex on thousands of random patterns, within the syntax both support.

Get the code

The source, the differential tests and the minimizer are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine. It's MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Russ Cox's articles are at swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/.

title: bitcask-kv: a log-structured key/value store in Rust, from the paper
description:
A key/value store looks like the simplest database there is: put, get, delete. The hard part is not the API. It is what happens when the power goes out in the middle of a write, when the data files grow forever because old values are never reclaimed, and when the process restarts and must find every key again.

The Bitcask paper, written for the Riak database, answers all three with one idea: never modify data in place. Append every write to a log, keep an index in memory, and clean up in the background. The paper is a few pages long, which makes it a good first storage engine to build. bitcask-kv is my implementation in Rust: append-only data files, an in-memory hash index (the "keydir"), merge/compaction, hint files for fast startup, and crash recovery of torn writes. Here is what I built and what it teaches.

What I built

Append-only data files. Files named 0000000000.data and so on hold records in this layout, little endian:

crc32 | key_len | val_len | key | value

Only the newest file is written to. When it reaches max_file_size (64 MiB by default) it is closed and a new one starts. A delete does not remove anything: it appends a tombstone, a record whose val_len is u32::MAX.

The keydir. A HashMap<key, (file_id, offset, len)> with one entry for every live key. A get looks the key up in memory, then does one pread at the right offset and checks the CRC of the record. So a read costs one system call, whatever the size of the store.

Startup. Opening a store replays the files from oldest to newest and rebuilds the keydir. A file that has a hint file is indexed from the hint instead. Hint entries are key_len | rec_len | rec_pos | key, protected by a CRC, so the store learns where each value is without reading the values.

Crash recovery. Replay stops at the first record that is truncated or fails its CRC, and the file is truncated at that point. A torn write at the tail is discarded, and new writes continue after the last good record. The stats command reports how many bytes were dropped.

Merge. Over time the files fill up with overwritten values and tombstones. merge copies the live records into new files, which get the highest ids, writes their hint files, then deletes the old files, oldest first. The order matters: a crash at any point during the merge leaves a set of files whose replay gives the correct state.

A lock. A LOCK file with an OS advisory lock keeps two processes from opening the same directory.

How to use it

Clone the repository and build it. The command-line tool is called bitcask.

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv
cd bitcask-kv
cargo build --release
B=target/release/bitcask

$B ./db put greeting "hello"
echo -n "from stdin" | $B ./db put note
$B ./db get greeting
$B ./db keys
$B ./db del greeting
$B ./db stats
$B ./db merge

The first argument is the directory of the store. put takes the value as an argument or from stdin.

It is also a library:

let mut db = bitcask_kv::Bitcask::open("./db")?;
db.put(b"k", b"v")?;
assert_eq!(db.get(b"k")?, Some(b"v".to_vec()));
db.delete(b"k")?;
db.merge()?;

To use the library in another project, add it as a git dependency:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv

A good first experiment: put the same key a few thousand times, look at stats and the size of the directory, run merge, and look again. Then open one of the .data files in a hex viewer and find your keys.

What it teaches

Appending is the cheapest write, and the safest. A write never touches existing data, so a crash can only damage the last record. Recovery becomes a simple rule: read until something does not check out, cut there.

The CRC is what makes that rule work. A half-written record at the tail is not always shorter than expected. It can be the right length with garbage inside. The checksum at the front of every record is how replay tells a good record from a torn one. The tests cover both a truncated tail and a garbage tail.

Deletes are writes. In a log you cannot erase, you can only say "this key is gone" in a newer record. The tombstone has to survive until merge can prove that no older file still holds a value for that key.

The order of operations is the crash safety. Merge gives new files the highest ids and deletes old files oldest first. Because replay goes from oldest to newest, every intermediate state replays to the right answer. Nothing here needs a transaction log. It needs the right order.

Startup time is a design problem. Rebuilding the index by reading every value is slow for a large store. Hint files are the fix: a small side file with keys and positions only.

A model check finds what examples miss. The store tests compare the store against a plain in-memory map across reopens, merges and file rotation. If the two ever disagree, there is a bug.

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README states these limits:

  • Single writer, not thread-safe. Writes take &mut self. There is no concurrent merge.
  • The whole keydir lives in memory, as in Bitcask. Every key must fit in RAM. A scan also reads each data file fully into memory.
  • Corruption in the middle of an older file is treated like a torn tail: everything after it in that file is dropped.
  • Durability is opt-in. sync_on_write is off by default. The CLI fsyncs after each command; the library does it only on sync(), rotation and merge.
  • No key expiry and no range scans. A hash index has no order.
  • Unix only. It uses FileExt::read_exact_at.

What was tested. cargo test covers the record codec and the store: the model check across reopens, merges and rotation, truncated-tail and garbage-tail recovery, CRC corruption, and the CLI. cargo bench runs criterion benchmarks. The README gives example numbers from a laptop with 100-byte values and no fsync: about 7 µs for a put, about 7 µs for a get, about 10 ms to open by scanning 10k records, and about 12 ms to merge 10k writes over 1k keys. Without fsync, those numbers measure the code path and the page cache, not a disk.

Why I built it

I wanted to understand how a storage engine survives a crash, and I wanted to learn it on a design small enough to hold in my head. Bitcask is that design. There is no B-tree to balance and no write-ahead log separate from the data: the log is the database.

The limits are part of the lesson too. Keeping every key in memory and giving up range scans are the price of one-seek reads, and seeing that trade in your own code explains why other engines, like LSM trees, made different choices.

Get the code

The source, tests and benchmarks are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv. It's MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome. The Bitcask paper it follows is linked from the README.

title: Oracle publica 655 patches e corrige falha Java4Shell
description:
Escopo da atualização de novembro

A Oracle publicou 655 patches de segurança na Atualização Crítica de Segurança (CSPU) de novembro de 2026. Desse total, 640 aparecem nas matrizes de risco dos produtos. Os demais incluem vulnerabilidades adicionais corrigidas pelos patches e CVEs de terceiros que a empresa considera não exploráveis em seus produtos.

Pouco mais de 300 patches corrigem falhas que podem ser exploradas remotamente sem autenticação. O pacote também resolve 62 vulnerabilidades críticas, incluindo seis classificadas com severidade máxima, o que torna a atualização relevante para organizações que utilizam os produtos afetados.

Produtos com mais correções

O Hyperion recebeu o maior conjunto, com 267 patches, dos quais 107 corrigem falhas remotas exploráveis sem autenticação. A atualização de Supply Chain inclui 74 correções, sendo 36 para vulnerabilidades com essa mesma condição de exploração.

Fusion Middleware e E-Business Suite receberam 71 patches cada. No Fusion Middleware, 53 tratam de falhas remotas sem autenticação; no E-Business Suite, são 19. Communications recebeu 31 correções, incluindo 21 desse tipo, enquanto Analytics teve 29, com nove vulnerabilidades remotas sem autenticação.

Java4Shell e outros produtos afetados

A atualização do Java SE corrige 11 falhas, todas exploráveis remotamente, entre elas Java4Shell, identificada como CVE-2026-114938. O problema envolve corrupção de memória e pode levar a vazamentos de memória e à execução remota de código.

Siebel CRM recebeu 19 patches, nove para falhas remotas sem autenticação; PeopleSoft teve 13, incluindo seis desse grupo. Financial Services Applications e Virtualization receberam 11 correções cada, com uma e três falhas remotas sem autenticação, respectivamente. Para MySQL, foram publicados dez patches, três voltados a falhas desse tipo.

As correções de severidade máxima incluem cinco falhas no Fusion Middleware e uma em Analytics. Também receberam patches Database Server, APEX, Autonomous Health Framework, REST Data Services, Application Testing Suite, Commerce, Construction and Engineering, Enterprise Manager e JD Edwards.

Aplicação das correções

A Oracle não mencionou exploração de nenhuma dessas vulnerabilidades em ambientes reais, mas recomenda-se que as organizações apliquem os patches o quanto antes. Falhas em produtos da empresa são alvos atrativos para atacantes.

As equipes de TI podem consultar as matrizes de risco da atualização para identificar as correções correspondentes aos produtos usados em seus ambientes. A lista abrange aplicações empresariais, middleware, bancos de dados e Java SE, por isso a revisão deve considerar os sistemas efetivamente utilizados por cada organização.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/oracle-libera-655-patches-de-seguranca-e-corrige-falha-java4shell/

title: Structured concurrency is finally leaving preview in JDK 28. Here's the API you'll actually use
description:
If you've been eyeing StructuredTaskScope but didn't want --enable-preview anywhere near production, the wait is almost over: JEP 543, Structured Concurrency, has been Targeted for JDK 28 since October 21. In the JDK 28 early-access docs the API no longer carries the preview mark.

It took a while. StructuredTaskScope has been in preview since JDK 21 and the API was reworked along the way: open() and open(Joiner) date from JDK 25, open(Joiner, UnaryOperator) from JDK 26 and open(UnaryOperator) from JDK 27. If you tried it in 21 and gave up, what you'll find now looks very different.

The idea, in one example

You start several subtasks inside a block, wait for them, and if one fails the others are cancelled. Nothing keeps running outside the try.

record CustomerView(Customer customer, List<Order> orders) {}

CustomerView loadView(long id) throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> customerRepo.find(id));
        Subtask<List<Order>> orders = scope.fork(() -> orderRepo.byCustomer(id));

        scope.join(); // if one fails, the other is cancelled and ExecutionException is thrown

        return new CustomerView(customer.get(), orders.get());
    }
}

open() with no arguments applies the most common policy: all succeed, or the first failure wins. If everything finishes, join() returns null and you read each result with get(). If one fails, join() throws ExecutionException with the original exception as the cause, and the subtasks still running are cancelled via interruption.

By default each subtask runs in an unnamed virtual thread. If you need something else, withThreadFactory lets you plug in your own.

Joiners decide when it's over

You change the policy by passing a Joiner to open. The factories in JDK 28:

  • awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(): the one from the example above; join() returns null.
  • allSuccessfulOrThrow(): join() returns a List<T> with every result.
  • anySuccessfulOrThrow(): the first successful result wins; it only fails if all of them fail.
  • allUntil(Predicate): returns every subtask and cancels when the predicate says so; failures don't make join() throw.

The first three have a variant that takes a Function<Throwable, R_X> so you choose which exception join() throws. That's what the third type parameter of StructuredTaskScope<T, R, R_X extends Throwable> is for.

A classic case: ask two replicas for the same thing, keep the fastest, and don't wait more than two seconds.

String fetchFastest(String key) throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(
            Joiner.<String>anySuccessfulOrThrow(),
            cfg -> cfg.withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)))) {
        scope.fork(() -> mirrorA.fetch(key));
        scope.fork(() -> mirrorB.fetch(key));
        return scope.join(); // the first one to answer wins; the other is cancelled
    }
}

If the timeout fires, join() throws ExecutionException whose cause is a StructuredTaskScope.CancelledByTimeoutException. The config also has withName to name the scope.

If you already used the preview

The interface declaration, the join() signature and the Joiner names used here are the same in the JDK 27 preview and in the JDK 28 early access. So if your code compiles today with --enable-preview on JDK 27, chances are that moving to JDK 28 just means removing --enable-preview from javac and java.

One caveat: Targeted means the JEP is planned for JDK 28, and the early-access docs warn that the spec isn't final yet. Try your code on a JDK 28 build before taking anything for granted.

Check yourself in 2 minutes

Structured concurrency sits on top of virtual threads, and that's where most interview questions go. Three short challenges, no sign-up needed (they're in Spanish, the code isn't):

  • Virtual threads: scale, not speed
  • Pinning: when a virtual thread gets stuck
  • From ThreadLocal to ScopedValue

They come from NextPatch, a small daily habit I'm building for Java developers: a 45-second summary of one change between versions, then a 2-minute challenge.

Are you planning to use StructuredTaskScope once 28 ships, or are you sticking with CompletableFuture? I'm curious what's holding people back.

Originally published in Spanish on the NextPatch blog, with links to the JEP and the JDK 28 early-access javadoc.
